entries.headline: GitLab's critical patch fixes an unauthenticated CVSS 10.0 RCE in Org-mode rendering; no exploitation reported
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-110264updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-110264, GitLab CE/EE: an unauthenticated code-execution flaw in the Org-mode renderer's regular-expression handling, fixed in 19.5.1, 19.4.3 and 19.3.6 and backported to four older lines (CVSS 10.0)

GitLab's ad-hoc critical patch release of 2026-10-21 fixes CVE-2026-110264 (CVSS 3.1 10.0), an integer overflow while compiling a specially crafted regular expression that could let an unauthenticated user execute code on the GitLab server (GitLab, 2026-10-21). GitLab's detection write-ups place the flaw in the rendering of Org-mode files: the org-ruby gem builds a regular expression from a custom TODO keyword in a .org file, a keyword with more than 32,767 repeats makes the Onigmo engine write out of bounds when it matches, and with heap grooming that becomes command execution as the git user (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). The attack needs no authentication, only one public project that can hold the .org payload (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). Affected are all versions from 7.0 before 18.11.13, 19.0 before 19.0.10, 19.1 before 19.1.9, 19.2 before 19.2.9, 19.3 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3 and 19.5 before 19.5.1; GitLab.com is already patched, and GitLab Dedicated tenants on 19.3.5-internal0, 19.4.2-internal0 or later need no action (GitLab, 2026-10-21). The builds 19.4.2, 19.3.5 and 19.2.8 from GitLab's earlier regular-expression fixes do not contain this fix (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). GitLab does not state that the flaw is exploited, and its patch notes and detection pages mention no public proof of concept (GitLab, 2026-10-21). The bug is in Ruby's Onigmo regular-expression engine: the Ruby project released 4.0.9, 3.4.12 and 3.3.13 on 2026-10-23 with the fix, the release of 4.0.8 lacks the fix for this flaw, and GitLab fixed its own servers by patching the Ruby it ships (Ruby, 2026-10-23).

Exposure
Self-managed GitLab CE and EE on the versions above; the vulnerable path is reached when GitLab renders a .org file, so an instance with public projects, or one where untrusted users can create them, is the exposed shape, and until patching GitLab advises reducing public visibility (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). A Ruby application outside GitLab is exposed to the same bug when it compiles a regular expression from a string an attacker controls, through Regexp.new, Regexp.union, Regexp.compile or interpolation into a regexp literal; applications that only use patterns written by their own developers are not affected (Ruby, 2026-10-23).
Detection
GitLab's two detections key on, first, five or more render timeouts from the Org-mode renderer on .org files from one client within 30 minutes in the Rails exceptions log, with the request that actually crashes a worker visible only as a 502 on the .org blob route in the Workhorse log, and second, a native Ruby crash report in the Puma error log whose backtrace runs through org-ruby or Onigmo frames (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). In repository content, scan each suspect checkout for .org files with an oversized TODO-keyword line, and in the Rails request log look for editor preview requests whose file_path ends in .org while the URL names another file type, which forces the Org renderer (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). A successful exploit is quiet and does not reliably crash, so the absence of a hit never clears an instance (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). On an exposed, unpatched instance, hunt for unexpected child processes of Puma, new files owned by git in the temporary directory, outbound connections and changed crontabs or SSH keys for the git user, and treat the secrets, CI/CD variables, runner tokens and access tokens the git user can read as at risk (GitLab security, 2026-10-21).

Triage: a reader of documentation .org files renders each file once and quickly, while an attack produces a burst of timeouts from one client over a few minutes (GitLab security, 2026-10-21); a worker crash with no accompanying render burst from one client is more likely a benign parser bug than an attack (GitLab security, 2026-10-21).

Defender takeaway
Upgrade to the fixed build of the instance's line now, internet-reachable instances and those with public projects first; an instance that moved to 19.4.2, 19.3.5 or 19.2.8 for the earlier flaws is not yet fixed for this one (GitLab, 2026-10-21). For other Ruby applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns, Ruby recommends upgrading to 4.0.9, 3.4.12 or 3.3.13 or later, or avoiding compiling such patterns, and says neither Regexp.timeout nor a pattern-length limit reliably protects; Ruby has not requested CVE identifiers of its own for now and tells operators to track the issues under GitLab's identifiers (Ruby, 2026-10-23).
Update24 Oct 2026 03:42 UTCrun 2026-10-24T0255Z-intelaffected_productsbodycvesevidencesourcessourcing_notesummaryentities

The Ruby project published an advisory on 2026-10-23 and released Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12 and 3.3.13 with fixes for the bugs in its Onigmo regular-expression engine behind four GitLab flaws: CVE-2026-89078 (a double free when parsing a pattern fails after an alternation), CVE-2026-93577 and CVE-2026-97229 (an integer overflow in the size of a compiled pattern) and CVE-2026-110264 (an overflow of internal IDs in a pattern with many repeats) (Ruby, 2026-10-23). Ruby's table gives the first release of each series that carries each fix: the fix for CVE-2026-110264 first appears in 4.0.9, so 4.0.8 is not enough, and 3.4.12 and 3.3.13 carry all of them; GitLab fixed its own servers by patching the Ruby it ships (Ruby, 2026-10-23).

The advisory widens the exposure beyond GitLab to any Ruby application that compiles a regular expression from a string an attacker controls, says Regexp.timeout does not protect against these bugs and that limiting pattern length does not reliably protect, and says Ruby has not requested CVE identifiers of its own and that operators should track the issues under GitLab's identifiers (Ruby, 2026-10-23).

entries.action_label: Stolen UpdraftCentral keys install backdoor plugins…
actions: On every WordPress site your organisation, its web agencies or its hosting suppliers run with UpdraftPlus, free or premium, including old municipal, campaign and project sites, check for an UpdraftCentral key (wp option get updraft_central_localkeys, or Settings > UpdraftPlus Backups > Advanced Tools > UpdraftCentral) and delete every key even if nobody remembers using UpdraftCentral, then update to 1.26.13 or 2.26.13 or later; deleting a key stops remote management only, and backups keep working.

On any site where a plugin, must-use plugin or Editor account holding manage_options appears that nobody created, delete the UpdraftCentral key first, then restore the site from a backup taken before 17 October, rotate every administrator and UpdraftCentral password, the teamupdraft.com account password (which UpdraftPlus Premium can leave stored in the site database and its backups) and end all sessions.

entries.classification_html: NATOB1
entries.headline: Stolen UpdraftCentral keys install backdoor plugins on WordPress sites; the plugin update alone does not evict them
entries.html:
HIGHupdatedNATOB1

TeamUpdraft breach: stolen UpdraftCentral connection keys are used to push backdoor plugins to connected WordPress sites, with no flaw in UpdraftPlus and no CVE; deleting the keys is the fix

TeamUpdraft says unauthorised access to teamupdraft.com on 17 and 18 October and that it believes its customer database was accessed, which holds connection keys for UpdraftCentral, UpdraftVault and UpdraftClone; it says UpdraftPlus plugin files and downloads were not affected, that the attacker used a compromised key to access its site, and that there is no evidence the attacker still has access, and it suspects, without giving evidence, that the attacker used AI to accelerate the attack (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19). Patchstack reports that an attacker holding valid UpdraftCentral dashboard keys has been installing backdoor plugins on connected WordPress sites since 2026-10-18 at 15:32 (the page gives no time zone), and that this is not a vulnerability in UpdraftPlus: the UpdraftCentral client ships inside every copy of the plugin and executes any command signed with the dashboard's private key once the site holds a key (Patchstack, 2026-10-19; BleepingComputer, 2026-10-20).

The attacker sends a signed plugin.upload_plugin command as an ordinary POST to the site root and WordPress installs and activates the plugin; each delivered plugin wakes on a secret URL parameter carrying a 32-character token, creates an account with a hardcoded password, gives it the Editor role and then the manage_options and install_plugins capabilities, and logs the visitor in with a cookie, which bypasses the login form, two-factor authentication and login-protection plugins (Patchstack, 2026-10-19). The account stays after the plugin is removed, and early samples crash the site with an HTTP 500 and must not be repaired, because fixing the error switches the backdoor on (Patchstack, 2026-10-19). Nethemba adds a variant that logs the attacker in as an existing administrator without a database trace (Nethemba, 2026-10-19).

A site holds a key if it was connected to UpdraftCentral or if a teamupdraft.com account was logged in from the plugin, where the option to add the site to UpdraftCentral is ticked by default, and keys do not expire (Patchstack, 2026-10-19); on UpdraftPlus 1.26.4 or 2.26.4 and earlier an attacker needs no key at all, through CVE-2026-10795, fixed in 1.26.5 and 2.26.5 (Patchstack, 2026-10-19). BleepingComputer reports an estimate of up to about 400,000 sites (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-20; Nethemba, 2026-10-19). TeamUpdraft says UpdraftPlus 1.26.13 and 2.26.13 disconnect every UpdraftCentral connection made before 13:07 BST (12:07 UTC) on 18 October; Nethemba says 1.26.12 and 2.26.12 deleted none and that 1.26.13 does not delete keys created on 18 October between 12:07 and 21:00 UTC, which have to be deleted by hand (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19; Nethemba, 2026-10-19). Nethemba saw the attacker send UpdraftCentral commands to two of its sites on the morning of 2026-10-21, after 1.26.13 had shipped, blocked by Nethemba's own blocking plugin, with the keys already deleted, and says sites that neither run 1.26.13 or 2.26.13 nor have deleted the key by hand remain at risk (Nethemba, 2026-10-19).

Exposure
A WordPress site running UpdraftPlus, free or premium, that holds an UpdraftCentral key; wp option get updraft_central_localkeys prints it, including on sites whose owners never used UpdraftCentral (Patchstack, 2026-10-19). Self-hosted UpdraftCentral is not affected (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19).
Detection
Web server access logs for POST requests to the site root carrying an UpdraftCentral command whose user agent lacks the library version and URL that genuine dashboard traffic carries, and for GET requests with a short underscore-prefixed parameter and a 32-character token, which mean a backdoor was used; the UpdraftCentral log on the site for plugin.upload_plugin and plugin.delete_plugin commands without a matching administrator action; the plugin and must-use plugin directories on disk; and the user table for an Editor that also holds manage_options (Patchstack, 2026-10-19; Nethemba, 2026-10-19). TeamUpdraft asks users to look at the sites listed under their UpdraftCentral account for any they did not knowingly connect since 2026-10-19 and says it is seeing a pattern of unexpected Editor roles (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19). The backdoor account stays after the plugin is removed (Patchstack, 2026-10-19).
Defender takeaway
Delete the UpdraftCentral key on every site first, then update; if a backdoor is found, delete the key before removing it or the attacker pushes a replacement, and treat the site as compromised (Patchstack, 2026-10-19). IP blocking is not a control, since Patchstack saw the source addresses rotate within a day (Patchstack, 2026-10-19). On UpdraftPlus Premium sites Nethemba reads the code as leaving the teamupdraft.com account password stored in the database, and so in backups, until add-ons are claimed with a token, although the vendor says it is removed after the first connection, a reader found it on all three of their premium sites and in backups going back to 2022, and Nethemba has not found the samples it analysed reading it; changing that account password is therefore part of the cleanup (Nethemba, 2026-10-19).
Update24 Oct 2026 03:42 UTCrun 2026-10-24T0255Z-intelactionsbodyevidencesourcessourcing_notesummary

TeamUpdraft's updates of 2026-10-21 and 2026-10-22 say the attacker used a compromised key to access its site, that there is no evidence the attacker still has access, and that the speed of the exploits and the initially faulty backdoor plugins suggest AI was used to accelerate the attack, which is the vendor's inference and comes with no evidence (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19). It asks users to look at the sites listed under their UpdraftCentral account for any they did not knowingly connect since 2026-10-19, says it is seeing a pattern of unexpected Editor roles, and stresses that UpdraftPlus Premium users should check for unexpected plugins and new administrators even if they never used UpdraftCentral (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19).

Nethemba reports that the attacker kept going after the fix: on 2026-10-20 it tried the secret triggers of already removed backdoors on at least six sites of four administrators, and on the morning of 2026-10-21 it sent UpdraftCentral commands to two of Nethemba's sites after 1.26.13 had been released, blocked by Nethemba's own blocking plugin, with the keys no longer existing (Nethemba, 2026-10-19). A site that has a stolen key and neither updated nor deleted it by hand therefore stays exposed, and a removed backdoor is still probed. Nethemba also reads the code of UpdraftPlus Premium as storing the teamupdraft.com account password in the site database as entered and deleting it only after add-ons are claimed with a token, so it can stay in the database and in backups; a reader found it on all three of their premium sites and in backups going back to 2022, and Nethemba on one of its three, while the vendor says it is removed after the first connection and Nethemba has not found the samples it analysed reading it (Nethemba, 2026-10-19).

entries.action_label: PK Softech apparently kept Publica data it had…
actions: Tell the helpdesk, HR and payroll teams of every body whose staff are insured with Publica (including the federal administration and the ETH domain) or with the Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich, which says data of its insured persons and pensioners was stolen, that AHV number, date of birth, address, salary and IBAN may now be known to criminals and must not count as proof of identity, and route requests that quote them, a request to change a payout account included, to a call-back on a known number; for staff insured with Pensionskasse Post, the Bernische Pensionskasse (which now says it must be assumed personal data left), the Ticino cantonal fund IPCT (which found data of about 1,800 of its insured persons on the attacked server and writes to all its insured because it cannot exclude more), a fund administered or advised by Libera AG or the Bernische Lehrerversicherungskasse apply the same rule until those funds report the scope; also tell insured staff that cantonal police warn of investment-fraud calls from people who know their salary and pension details, which prove nothing about the caller.

If your organisation's pension administration, HR or payroll runs on PK Softech software, is being migrated to it or tested on it, or your staff are insured with Pensionskasse Post, ask the supplier or the fund in writing whether your data, test data included, was in the affected environment, project, test and migration copies included, and what it holds outside the productive system.

entries.classification_html: NATOA2
entries.headline: PK Softech apparently kept Publica data it had promised in writing to delete; Tamedia says Akira holds about 100 GB
entries.html:
HIGHupdatedNATOA2

PK Softech, software supplier of Swiss pension funds: malware and a data outflow at Publica, with the City of Zurich fund PKZH saying its insured persons' test data was stolen, the Bernese funds BPK and BLVK and Pensionskasse Post also reporting the supplier incident, and the Federal Prosecutor's Office investigating

The Confederation, in a release headlined "data outflow confirmed" (translated from German), says an external software supplier of the federal pension fund Publica detected a cyberattack at the end of September, informed its other customers, and that the Federal Prosecutor's Office has opened an investigation; no other federal office has a business relationship with the supplier (Swiss Federal Administration, 2026-10-08); the supplier, PK Softech AG, says unknown persons used malware to reach part of its IT infrastructure and that it must be assumed data left its systems, with type and scope still under investigation (PK Softech, 2026-10-08). Publica insures, among others, staff of the federal administration and the ETH domain, about 70,000 active members and 41,600 pensioners at the end of 2025 (watson.ch, 2026-10-08), and its own page lists name, date of birth, AHV number, address, business and private contact details, pension data such as salary and insured earnings, civil status, partner details and IBAN as data that could be affected, adding that its investigation indicates personal data of insured persons has presumably left and that it cannot rule out that an individual member's data left (Publica, 2026-10-08). Netzwoche reported on 2026-10-08 that it was still unclear whether data of the pension fund actually left (Netzwoche, 2026-10-08); no access vector is public, and on 2026-10-08 no actor was public either and Publica declined to say whether a ransom was demanded (watson.ch, 2026-10-08); the supplier is a software supplier of a federal institution, and Publica data may be affected (Swiss Federal Administration, 2026-10-08). The Bernische Pensionskasse says its supplier is the same company (BPK, 2026-10-09), and the Bernische Lehrerversicherungskasse (BLVK, 2026-10-08) and Pensionskasse Post (Pensionskasse Post, 2026-10-09) report the supplier incident too. The Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich, which still runs another provider's system and plans to move to PK Softech's in early 2027, says its inquiries indicate that personal data of its insured persons and pensioners, handed over as test data, was stolen (PKZH, 2026-10-15), and Pensionskasse Post says personal data did leave but not yet whether its insured persons' data is among it (Pensionskasse Post, 2026-10-15). Tamedia's Tages-Anzeiger reports that the Akira ransomware group holds about 100 GB of compressed pension data on well over 100,000 current and former federal employees, including staff of the security authorities, and demands ransom, which Inside IT relays without the volume; as of 2026-10-20 neither the Confederation nor Publica had confirmed the perpetrator or the demand, and Publica said it still had no indication that data was published on the darkweb (Tages-Anzeiger, 2026-10-20; Inside IT, 2026-10-20; Publica, 2026-10-20). Netzwoche, relaying the same paper, adds that the Federal Council and the security authorities now assume data on practically all current and former federal and federally affiliated staff left, federal judges and former Federal Council members among them (Netzwoche, 2026-10-21).

PK Softech had confirmed in writing to Publica in January 2026 that it deleted the data of the 2019 migration and held no personal data in plaintext, and the Tages-Anzeiger reports that this apparently did not happen, because the data was still on its servers when the attackers got in (Tages-Anzeiger, 2026-10-21; Inside IT, 2026-10-22). Publica confirmed the sequence to the paper: after the Xplain case it asked PK Softech to delete all legacy data, including that of the 2019 migration, and received written confirmation, and it is now clarifying why personal data presumably lay on the servers, while PK Softech did not answer and says it does not comment on individual customer relationships (Inside IT, 2026-10-22). Inside IT, citing Tamedia, adds that the Federal Prosecutor's Office confirmed that data was extracted by the Akira ransomware group, which 20 Minuten words as according to findings so far; the statement is second-hand and Publica's own page of 2026-10-20 still says it is clarifying whether and whose Publica data left (Inside IT, 2026-10-22; 20 Minuten, 2026-10-22; Publica, 2026-10-20). The Ticino cantonal pension fund IPCT first said through Corriere del Ticino, relayed by Ticinonline, that potentially all of its insured could be involved (Ticinonline, 2026-10-20); its letter of 2026-10-23 to its roughly 17,000 active insured and 10,000 pensioners narrows that: PK Softech told it on 2026-10-14 that the authorities had established that personal data were taken from the supplier's servers, its own checks found data of about 1,800 persons among the documents on the attacked server, it has no certain evidence that these data were taken but finds it plausible, and it decided to write to all insured because it cannot exclude that more was affected (IPCT, 2026-10-23; Ticinonline, 2026-10-23).

Exposure
A body whose staff are insured with Publica, which insures federal administration and ETH domain staff (watson.ch, 2026-10-08), the Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich (PKZH, 2026-10-15), Pensionskasse Post (Pensionskasse Post, 2026-10-15), the Bernische Pensionskasse (BPK, 2026-10-09) or Lehrerversicherungskasse (BLVK, 2026-10-08), the Ticino fund IPCT (IPCT, 2026-10-23) or a fund that Libera AG manages (NZZ, 2026-10-17), or whose pension administration runs on PK Softech software, whose customers include several further funds (Inside IT, 2026-10-09); each fund's own notice or letter says whether and which of its insured persons' data is affected.
Detection
Publica warns that misuse of the data cannot be ruled out and asks members to watch for unusual e-mails, calls or messages (watson.ch, 2026-10-08), so the telemetry to watch is mail-gateway logs and the helpdesk, HR and payroll call and ticket records of affected bodies for contact that cites an AHV number, a salary, a partner's details or an IBAN.
Defender takeaway
Until Publica reports the scope, AHV number, date of birth, address, salary and IBAN should not serve as proof of identity, and a request that quotes them, a request to change a payout account included, deserves a call-back through a known number; an organisation that runs PK Softech software should ask the supplier in writing whether its data was in the environment, and bodies whose staff are insured with the Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich, which says data of its insured persons was stolen (PKZH, 2026-10-15), should treat the same data the same way, as should bodies whose staff are insured with Pensionskasse Post, which confirms that personal data left without saying whose (Pensionskasse Post, 2026-10-15), the Bernische Pensionskasse, which told the NZZ that, contrary to the supplier's earlier information, it must be assumed personal data left (NZZ, 2026-10-17), a fund that Libera AG manages, since Libera says it is also affected and cannot yet say whose data left (NZZ, 2026-10-17), or the Bernische Lehrerversicherungskasse, which is still checking (BLVK, 2026-10-08), until those funds report the scope; the exposed files at IPCT (checks and recalculations), the Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich (migration tests) and, apparently, Publica (the 2019 migration) were project, test or migration data held at the supplier (IPCT, 2026-10-23; PKZH, 2026-10-15; Inside IT, 2026-10-22), so the check to make at any supplier is which personal data it holds outside the productive system and whether its written deletion confirmation is true; staff should also hear that cantonal police warn of investment-fraud calls built on the leaked salary and pension data (Cybercrimepolice, 2026-10-13).
Update10 Oct 2026 03:48 UTCrun 2026-10-10T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummaryprioritysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

The supplier's customer base is now partly public and includes cantonal-level institutions. The Bernische Pensionskasse (BPK) states in a notice dated 2026-10-09 that an external software supplier of the BPK suffered a cyberattack at the end of September 2026 and that this is "the same company that also supplies the federal pension fund Publica" (translated from German); the supplier filed a criminal complaint, informed the relevant federal bodies and its affected customers, various federal bodies are clarifying with it which data is affected, and the Federal Prosecutor's Office has opened an investigation (BPK, 2026-10-09). The BPK says there are currently no indications that its data was stolen but that this cannot be entirely excluded, and that insured persons are being informed (BPK, 2026-10-09). Netzwoche reports that the Canton of Bern's own notice names the BPK and the Bernische Lehrerversicherungskasse (BLVK) as concretely affected, that the BPK insures canton staff and the personnel of the three cantonal universities (42,145 active insured and 18,321 pensioners on 31 December 2025) and that the BLVK insures 21,417 active Bernese teachers (Netzwoche, 2026-10-08). The BLVK's own notice does not name its supplier; it says the supplier took the affected environment off the network, brought in external specialists, informed the authorities and filed a criminal complaint, and that the supplier and the BLVK are still checking whether and to what extent BLVK data is affected (BLVK, 2026-10-08). Pensionskasse Post, the occupational pension fund of Swiss Post, names PK Softech and says whether and to what extent its insured persons' data is affected is under review; it states that its data at PK Softech is anonymised and holds no particularly sensitive personal data such as IV disability-insurance files, a claim that is the fund's own and not independently verified (Pensionskasse Post, 2026-10-09). Inside IT, working from the AWP agency, lists the BLVK, the BPK, Migros-Pensionskasse, Pensionskasse Post and Syngenta Pensionskasse as customers of the manufacturer "among others" and says some of the funds have already announced that they are checking with PK Softech for a possible data outflow (Inside IT, 2026-10-09). PK Softech says it has been fully available to its customers again since 2 October 2026 (PK Softech, 2026-10-08). The access vector, the actor, which data belongs to which fund and whether a ransom was demanded were not public in any source read as of that date.

Improvement13 Oct 2026 03:38 UTCrun 2026-10-13T0256Z-intelsummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Publica's own page, dated 2026-10-08, lists civil status, details of the spouse or partner and the IBAN among the data that could be affected, besides name, date of birth, AHV number, address, contact details and pension data, and Publica says its investigation indicates that personal data of insured persons has presumably left, while it cannot rule out that an individual member's data left (Publica, 2026-10-08). The AWP report, which relays the software firm's position, says the firm knows that data left but not yet whether personal data is among it, that it could also be business data unrelated to member files, and that the volume is rather small (cash.ch, 2026-10-09). Publica's wording is stronger than the supplier's, and which data left is still open; a request that quotes an IBAN deserves the same call-back as one that quotes an AHV number.

Update15 Oct 2026 03:48 UTCrun 2026-10-15T0256Z-intelsourcesevidencesourcing_noteactions

The City of Zurich's pension fund has commented, and its position differs from the other funds': the Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich (PKZH) says in a notice dated 2026-10-13 that PK Softech was hit at the end of September, that it currently works with another software provider and plans to move to PK Softech's administration system in early 2027, so the attack does not touch the system it uses today, and that it is still clarifying whether, because of tests carried out ahead of that switch, PKZH data is also affected (PKZH, 2026-10-13). It adds that the incident does not affect insured persons' pension assets (PKZH, 2026-10-13). PKZH's concern is that migration tests may have left PKZH data at the supplier; it has not said that they did. Publica's page now carries a status of 2026-10-14 saying that it currently has no indications that data from the attack on its software supplier has been published on the darkweb and that it keeps monitoring the situation; its list of data that could be affected is unchanged (Publica, 2026-10-20). Neither statement says which data left, how the attackers got in or who they are.

Update16 Oct 2026 04:11 UTCrun 2026-10-16T0256Z-intelsummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

On the Cybercrimepolice platform, dated 2026-10-13, the cantonal police warn that after a cyberattack on a software provider of a pension fund, criminals could use the leaked personal and financial data to phone those affected and lure them into fraudulent investments of their pension assets (translated from German); the page describes a ransomware attack at the end of September and names no company (Cybercrimepolice, 2026-10-13). SwissCybersecurity.net ties the warning to PK Softech, names the cantonal police of Zurich and Bern as its authors, and reads its conditional wording as meaning no case of actual misuse had been registered yet (SwissCybersecurity.net, 2026-10-15). The police ask pension funds to tell insured persons that knowing someone's personal details or the size of their pension assets is no proof that a caller is trustworthy, and to let them check enquiries through official channels (Cybercrimepolice, 2026-10-13).

The Zurich cantonal fund BVK, which insures the cantonal administration and has bought PK Softech software since 2011, says through its spokesperson that the application runs in the BVK's own data centre independently of the supplier, so it is from today's view not directly affected, and that PK Softech holds only working material from it such as documentation, troubleshooting reports and further-development concepts (translated from German; NZZ, 2026-10-13). PK Softech told the NZZ that it can neither confirm nor rule out that further customers are affected and left the question whether a ransom was demanded unanswered (NZZ, 2026-10-13). Inside IT adds that the Istituto di previdenza del Cantone Ticino is listed on the Simap procurement platform as a PK Softech customer since 2018 and has made no statement on whether its data is at risk (Inside IT, 2026-10-14).

Update17 Oct 2026 03:35 UTCrun 2026-10-17T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

The Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich (PKZH), the City of Zurich's pension fund, has moved from checking to confirming. Its notice of 2026-10-15 says its inquiries so far indicate that personal data of PKZH insured persons was also stolen in the attack, and that this data had been used in tests for the planned system switch (PKZH, 2026-10-15); its FAQ adds that data was taken from PK Softech's system, including personal data of insured persons and of pensioners (PKZH, 2026-10-15). Inside IT reports that PKZH currently uses another software provider and plans to move to PK Softech's system in 2027 (Inside IT, 2026-10-16); PKZH's own FAQ says the system it uses to manage assets and pay pensions is not affected and dates the move to the beginning of 2027 (PKZH, 2026-10-15). The page still carries its earlier line that PKZH is checking whether its data is affected next to the confirmation (PKZH, 2026-10-15). It says a switch of this kind has to be tested with data that reproduces the real pension relationships as completely as possible, that PK Softech is contractually bound to protect and keep the data confidential, and that whether it met that duty is being investigated (PKZH, 2026-10-15).

Which data was stolen is still being clarified; in the worst case the fields are first name, name, date of birth, AHV number, address, private and business e-mail and telephone, insured earnings and retirement assets, civil status, partner details and IBAN (PKZH, 2026-10-15). PKZH was told on 2026-10-13 that data of its insured persons might be affected, has filed a criminal complaint and has reported the incident to the data-protection office (PKZH, 2026-10-15). It says a payout needs a signed written request and an identity check and that a change of bank details is checked additionally, so the data alone cannot trigger one, but that criminals can use it to appear credible (PKZH, 2026-10-15).

Pensionskasse Post's notice of 2026-10-15 says the investigation has shown that personal data did leave, and that it remains unclear whether data of its insured persons is affected, though that is possible (Pensionskasse Post, 2026-10-15). It does not repeat its earlier statement that its data at PK Softech is anonymised, and lists name, address, date of birth, AHV number, contact details, e-mail address and pension data as data that could be affected (Pensionskasse Post, 2026-10-15). The access vector, the actor and any ransom demand were not public in any source read as of that date.

Update20 Oct 2026 03:39 UTCrun 2026-10-20T0256Z-intelheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

SonntagsBlick reports that Federal Councillor Karin Keller-Sutter brought information on the supplier incident to the Federal Council's meeting of Wednesday 2026-10-14, and that a confidential information note says the Confederation internally expects "considerable damage", calls the incident "serious" and tells current and retired federal staff to expect longer-term effects (translated from German; Blick, 2026-10-18). The note says the security organs of the Confederation are particularly affected, which Blick glosses as the Federal Intelligence Service (NDB), the Defence Group in the VBS department and the Federal Office of Police (fedpol) (Blick, 2026-10-18). Blick adds, from its own information, that the cantons were also informed because a combination of certain stolen data sets may allow conclusions about Swiss defence capability, and that the Confederation warns internally that some employees could be recognised and questioned by the authorities of another country (Blick, 2026-10-18). The Finance Department confirms only that the Federal Council was informed on Wednesday and says neither the Federal Council nor a department supervises Publica; Publica says it set up a crisis staff and is still establishing which data and how many people are affected (Blick, 2026-10-18). The scenario of matching stolen federal data against entry lists is Blick's reading and an unnamed insider's, not an authority finding.

The NZZ reports that the pension consultancy Libera AG confirmed on Friday 2026-10-16 that it also works with PK Softech and is therefore affected, and that PK Softech first told Libera on 2026-10-14 that personal data had also left, without knowing which; Libera can neither confirm nor rule out that the funds it manages or individual insured persons are affected (NZZ, 2026-10-17). The Bernische Pensionskasse told the NZZ that, contrary to the supplier's earlier information, it must be assumed that personal data left, which replaces its earlier statement that it had no indication of theft, and PK Softech cannot currently say which of its customers are affected (NZZ, 2026-10-17). Publica concedes that it did not carry out regular on-site security audits at PK Softech, although after the Xplain incident it had old data deleted there (NZZ, 2026-10-17). The access vector, the actor and any ransom demand were not public in any source read as of that date.

Update21 Oct 2026 03:47 UTCrun 2026-10-21T0256Z-intelheadlinesummarytagsentitiestechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_notebodypriority

Tamedia's Tages-Anzeiger reported on 2026-10-20 that the Akira ransomware group stole about one hundred gigabytes of compressed pension fund data, that data on well over a hundred thousand current and former federal employees is affected, that special agents and elite soldiers could be identified from it, and that Akira now demands ransom (translated from German; Tages-Anzeiger, 2026-10-20); the article is paywalled. Inside IT, summarising the investigation, adds that the data sets contain employer details of people who work under a cover identity for fedpol or the Federal Intelligence Service (NDB), that an internal assessment sees a danger to life and limb for individual persons, that the NDB is forgoing certain operations for now without recalling agents from abroad, that the State Secretariat for Security Policy has already seen first fraudulent contact attempts connected with Publica, and that State Secretary Markus Mäder set up a task force under the federal information security officer Anne Rivera (translated from German; Inside IT, 2026-10-20). It says the involved federal bodies assume Akira is responsible and that the group holds the data and threatens to publish or sell it if unpaid, and that at that date neither the Confederation nor Publica had confirmed the perpetrator or an alleged ransom demand (Inside IT, 2026-10-20).

Inside IT recalls that Akira was also behind the attack on a US subsidiary of the state-owned arms company Ruag a year ago, where Ruag paid the ransom, and that the Federal Prosecutor's Office, fedpol and the Federal Office for Cybersecurity warned in October 2025 of stepped-up Akira activity in Switzerland (Inside IT, 2026-10-20). Publica's page, updated on 2026-10-20, says it is still examining whether data left its holdings and whose, still has no indication that data was published on the darkweb, and has updated its list of questions and answers (Publica, 2026-10-20).

Update22 Oct 2026 03:47 UTCrun 2026-10-22T0256Z-intelbodyevidencesourcessourcing_notesummary

Netzwoche updated its running story on 2026-10-21, relaying the paywalled article that Tamedia's Tages-Anzeiger published on 2026-10-20: the Federal Council and the security authorities now assume that data on practically all current and former employees of the Confederation and of federally affiliated bodies left, among them federal judges, former Federal Council members (the sitting members are said to be spared), intelligence-service staff, elite soldiers and cleaning staff (translated from German; Tages-Anzeiger, 2026-10-20; Netzwoche, 2026-10-21). According to the paper, an on-site inspection at PK Softech on 2026-10-07 established the outflow of security-relevant federal data, and Publica's letter to its insured persons mentions neither Akira nor the ransom demand (Netzwoche, 2026-10-21). This is one chain of reporting, and the article quotes no confirmation of the actor, the ransom demand or the scope from the Confederation, Publica or PK Softech (Netzwoche, 2026-10-21).

Update23 Oct 2026 03:40 UTCrun 2026-10-23T0256Z-intelheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Tamedia's Tages-Anzeiger reported on 2026-10-21 that PK Softech AG had confirmed in writing to Publica that it deleted the data, and that this apparently did not happen: its summary says the company reported in January that it had deleted the information on former Federal Councillors and agents, "but this was false" (translated from German; Tages-Anzeiger, 2026-10-21); the article is paywalled. Inside IT, working from the Tamedia research, dates the written confirmation to January 2026 and says PK Softech confirmed it held no personal data in plaintext and had deleted the data of the 2019 migration, that Publica confirmed the sequence (after the Xplain case it asked the supplier to delete all legacy data, including that of the 2019 migration, and received written confirmation), that Publica is clarifying why personal data presumably lay on the servers regardless, and that PK Softech did not answer and does not comment on individual customer relationships (Inside IT, 2026-10-22). 20 Minuten reports the same sequence and notes that PK Softech received the data in 2019 in a migration for Publica (20 Minuten, 2026-10-22).

Inside IT also relays, from Tamedia, that the Federal Prosecutor's Office confirmed that data was extracted by the Akira ransomware group, which still threatens to publish or sell it; 20 Minuten writes that according to findings so far Akira stole the data (Inside IT, 2026-10-22; 20 Minuten, 2026-10-22). This is a reported confirmation of the actor by an authority, but it reaches the reader second-hand through the paywalled Tamedia article: the Federal Prosecutor's Office is not quoted directly, and Publica's own page, in its entry of 2026-10-20, still says it is clarifying whether data of Publica left and whose (Publica, 2026-10-20).

The Ticino cantonal pension fund IPCT says through Corriere del Ticino, relayed by Ticinonline on 2026-10-20, that potentially all of its insured could be involved but that there is no evidence yet that their data was actually taken; it has filed a complaint with the Federal Prosecutor's Office and is preparing a letter to the insured warning of telephone and e-mail fraud (Ticinonline, 2026-10-20). TicinoNews adds, from its own information, that a folder labelled IPCT with the data of a few hundred insured persons was on the supplier's server, while IPCT, which has about 27,000 affiliated persons, says it has no certainty yet that data of its insured is involved (TicinoNews, 2026-10-21).

Update24 Oct 2026 03:41 UTCrun 2026-10-24T0255Z-intelactionsbodyevidencesourcessourcing_notesummary

The Ticino cantonal pension fund IPCT has put numbers on its exposure in a letter of 2026-10-23 to its roughly 17,000 active insured and 10,000 pensioners (IPCT, 2026-10-23). PK Softech told it in the late afternoon of 2026-10-14 that the authorities had established that personal data were taken from the supplier's servers, without saying which funds the data belonged to, and the fund's checks to date found among the documents on the attacked server data of about 1,800 persons, held there for two ongoing projects of spot checks and recalculations (IPCT, 2026-10-23). About 1,700 are persons who left the fund through resignation or death in 2024 and 2025: surname, first name, postal address, date of birth, AHV number and insured number, the exit-benefit amount and the receiving fund with its bank account (IBAN), and the personal IBAN for about 50 who were paid out directly, with no e-mail address or telephone number (IPCT, 2026-10-23). About 80 are insured persons on a disability pension whose passive pension data was being updated: name, date of birth, AHV number, insured number, passive insured salary, passive retirement assets, degree and start of invalidity, with no contact data (IPCT, 2026-10-23).

The fund says it has no certain evidence that these data were taken but that it appears plausible, that savings capital and pensions of all insured are untouched, that the cantonal administration's IT centre hosting the fund's infrastructure was not breached, and that it filed a criminal complaint against unknown persons and was recognised as private plaintiff, while the Federal Prosecutor's Office and the federal police investigate (IPCT, 2026-10-23; Ticinonline, 2026-10-23). It decided to send the letter to all insured because its information is partial, the analyses are still evolving and it may never have certainty, and it asks them to watch for unexpected e-mails, calls and messages over the coming weeks and never to disclose passwords, access data or personal data unless sure of the requester (IPCT, 2026-10-23). The letter names PK Softech's other customers as Publica, large cantonal public funds such as Bern and Zurich and company funds such as Migros and Post, for hundreds of thousands of insured persons in total (IPCT, 2026-10-23).

entries.summary: PK Softech AG, the software supplier of Publica and other Swiss pension funds, says unknown attackers used malware to reach part of its IT and that data must be assumed to have left; the Confederation headlined its 2026-10-08 release "data outflow confirmed", and the Federal Prosecutor's Office is investigating. Tamedia reports that PK Softech had confirmed in writing in January 2026 that it deleted Publica's 2019 migration data, which apparently stayed on its servers, and that Akira holds about 100 GB and demands ransom; Inside IT relays this and adds that the Federal Prosecutor's Office confirmed Akira took data, and Netzwoche relays that the authorities assume data on practically all current and former federal and federally affiliated staff left. Publica says personal data of insured persons has presumably left; the Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich says its insured persons' test data was stolen, the Pensionskasse Post says personal data left, the Bernische Pensionskasse says it must be assumed so, the Ticino fund IPCT says data of about 1,800 of its insured persons sat on the attacked server and writes to all its insured because it cannot exclude more, and other funds are still checking. As of 2026-10-22 neither the Confederation nor Publica has itself named the actor or the demand.
entries.title: PK Softech, software supplier of Swiss pension funds: malware and a data outflow at Publica, with the City of Zurich fund PKZH saying its insured persons' test data was stolen, the Bernese funds BPK and BLVK and Pensionskasse Post also reporting the supplier incident, and the Federal Prosecutor's Office investigating

updates.summary: The supplier's customers are now named: the Bernische Pensionskasse (canton of Bern staff and three cantonal universities) says its supplier is the same company that serves Publica, the Bernische Lehrerversicherungskasse and Pensionskasse Post report the supplier incident, and Inside IT lists Migros-Pensionskasse and Syngenta Pensionskasse among the customers. None of the funds has confirmed which member data left.

Publica's own page of 2026-10-08 lists civil status and the IBAN among the data that could be affected and says its investigation indicates personal data of insured persons has presumably left. The AWP agency relays the software firm's position that it knows data left but not yet whether personal data is among it, that it may be business data, and that the volume is rather small.

The Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich, the City of Zurich's pension fund, says on 2026-10-13 that it currently uses another provider, plans to move to PK Softech's system in early 2027 and is checking whether data from migration tests was affected. Publica's page says as of 2026-10-14 that it has no indications that data from the attack was published on the darkweb.

Cantonal police warn that criminals could use the leaked salary and pension data to phone insured persons with investment-fraud offers, SwissCybersecurity.net ties the warning to PK Softech, and the Zurich cantonal fund BVK says its PK Softech software runs in its own data centre so it is not directly affected; PK Softech can neither confirm nor rule out further affected customers, and the Ticino fund listed as a customer has made no statement.

The Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich, the City of Zurich's pension fund, now says in its notice of 2026-10-15 that its inquiries indicate personal data of its insured persons and pensioners, handed to PK Softech as test data for a planned 2027 switch, was stolen, and that which fields were taken is still being clarified. Pensionskasse Post says in its notice of the same date that personal data did leave and no longer repeats its earlier anonymisation statement, though it is still unclear whether its insured persons' data is among it.

SonntagsBlick reports, from a confidential federal information note, that the Confederation rates the incident as serious and says the security organs of the Confederation are particularly affected, which it glosses as the Federal Intelligence Service, the Defence Group and fedpol, that the Federal Council was briefed on 2026-10-14 and that the cantons were informed; the Finance Department confirms only the briefing. NZZ adds that the pension consultancy Libera AG is also affected, that the Bernische Pensionskasse now says it must be assumed personal data left, and that Publica ran no regular on-site audits at the supplier.

Tamedia reports, and Inside IT relays, that the Akira ransomware group holds about 100 GB of the pension data of well over 100,000 current and former federal employees, with employer details of staff under cover identity among it, and demands ransom; neither the Confederation nor Publica confirms the actor or the demand.

Netzwoche, relaying Tages-Anzeiger, reports that the Federal Council and the security authorities now assume data on practically all current and former federal and federally affiliated staff left, federal judges and former Federal Council members among them, and that an on-site inspection at PK Softech on 2026-10-07 established the outflow of security-relevant data; neither the Confederation nor Publica has confirmed the actor, the demand or the scope.

The supplier's written pledge to delete Publica's 2019 migration data was apparently not kept, Inside IT relays that the Federal Prosecutor's Office confirmed Akira exfiltrated data, though that is second-hand and neither the Confederation nor Publica has itself named the actor, and the Ticino cantonal fund IPCT says all its insured could potentially be involved but has no evidence yet that data was taken.

The Ticino cantonal fund IPCT says in a letter of 2026-10-23 that data of about 1,800 of its insured persons (about 1,700 who left in 2024 and 2025, with exit-benefit amounts and IBANs, and about 80 on disability pensions) sat on the attacked supplier server for two ongoing projects; it has no certain evidence the data were taken but finds it plausible, and it writes to all insured because it cannot exclude more.

entries.action_label: LiteLLM 1.107.0 on PyPI and in the official images…
actions: Find every host, build agent and container that installed litellm 1.107.0 from PyPI between 11:39 and 13:23 UTC on 2026-10-21, or pulled the v1.107.0, latest, main-latest or main-stable tag of the official GHCR or Docker Hub LiteLLM images between 11:46 and 14:20 UTC; treat each as compromised, inspect it with tooling that does not start Python in the affected environment, rebuild it from a reviewed artifact pinned to 1.106.2 or an image digest, and rotate every cloud, Kubernetes, registry, SSH, database and AI-provider credential it could read, including the provider keys stored in a LiteLLM proxy database.

entries.headline: LiteLLM 1.107.0 on PyPI and in the official images stole cloud and AI credentials; removing the package does not stop it
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB1

LiteLLM 1.107.0: the PyPI wheels and the official Docker images carried a credential stealer and a dormant remote-code loader that Python starts at every launch, published through the maintainers' own release workflow with stolen developer tokens

Socket reports that LiteLLM 1.107.0, an open-source LLM gateway, carries malicious Python startup files in all seven wheels, and that Upwind found the same payload in the published images (Socket, 2026-10-21). A startup hook and a second startup module in the Python library directory run at every Python start without the application importing LiteLLM: the first collects cloud, Kubernetes, CI, registry and database credentials, SSH, GPG and TLS private keys, browser stores, AI-tool credential files, environment variables and, where configured, the credentials saved in a LiteLLM proxy database; the second forks a detached loader that polls a file in a GitHub repository for a domain and would execute Python downloaded from it with no signature or hash check, though at 13:01 UTC the pointer returned an empty body, which stops the loader before its download stage (Socket, 2026-10-21).

The payload is not in the git tag: a packaging setting in an untagged commit pulls it into the wheel, and the container build provenance records a source repository named Berri-AI/litellm, one hyphen away from BerriAI/litellm (Socket, 2026-10-21). The maintainers' root-cause post of 2026-10-23, which they call the canonical account and which corrects assumptions in their earlier status updates, traces the chain to a configuration file committed on 2026-05-27 to a public repository with the master key of an experimental internal agent service; the commit was force-pushed over but the key was never revoked (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). On 2026-10-10 the attacker used that key against the service's API, which returned the GitHub CLI OAuth token of an organization owner, not a service account and not scoped down, and from then on the attacker held owner-level access to every repository; such CLI tokens are post-2FA and exempt from GitHub's re-authentication for sensitive actions (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). With it the attacker pushed throwaway branches whose workflows posted CI secrets to an external capture endpoint, yielding the CLI tokens of two maintainers, and deleted the workflow runs minutes later (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). Socket found secret-exfiltration workflows running in the repository on 2026-10-10 from its Actions performance metrics, eleven days before the release attack, says it has not established how the attacker first obtained access and does not claim that the 2026-10-10 theft produced the access used on 2026-10-21, while LiteLLM says its audit logs tie the token stolen on 2026-10-10 to the approval of the release (Socket, 2026-10-23). On 2026-10-21 a push to the private release-orchestration repository with a maintainer's token was rejected by branch protection, and the owner's token then overrode it so that the build could be pointed at the look-alike repository; the owner's token dispatched the staging build, a second maintainer's token approved the production gate, a third maintainer's token deleted the run records, and the owner's token force-pushed the history clean, after the maintainers had relaxed the release rule earlier that week so that any two engineers could trigger and approve a release (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). LiteLLM distributes an embargoed release for a vulnerability whose disclosure is scheduled for 2026-10-27 to enterprise customers through a private registry (LiteLLM, 2026-10-21). PyPI quarantined 1.107.0 and the images were pulled the same day (Aikido, 2026-10-21; LiteLLM, 2026-10-21).

Exposure
An environment that installed litellm 1.107.0 from PyPI between 11:39 and 13:23 UTC on 2026-10-21, or pulled the v1.107.0, latest, main-latest or main-stable tag of the official images from GHCR (until about 13:51 UTC) or Docker Hub (until 14:20 UTC); lockfiles, caches, build logs and running image digests show which (Socket, 2026-10-21; LiteLLM, 2026-10-21).
Detection
In the cloud audit logs of every account the host could reach, a caller-identity check followed by a Bedrock model listing and IAM enumeration, made with an instance-role credential harvested from CI runners or Kubernetes nodes from an address outside your estate, which Wiz saw from 16:20 UTC on 2026-10-21 (Wiz, 2026-10-21); on hosts, startup hooks and sitecustomize modules in a Python library directory that your tooling did not install, a detached Python process holding a lock file, and an encrypted archive posted to a path labelled as a health check (Socket, 2026-10-21). In the GitHub organization audit log, short-lived throwaway branches that add a single workflow file, workflow runs deleted minutes after they ran, and branch-protection and force-push-block overrides made with an owner's token; the log records a hash of the token behind each action, which tied the stolen maintainer token to the release approval (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). Starting Python or pip in an affected environment can run the payload again, and removing the package directory does not remove the startup files or stop a running loader (Socket, 2026-10-21).
Defender takeaway
Rotate every credential the host could reach (LiteLLM, 2026-10-21), because removing the package does not remove the startup files (Socket, 2026-10-21) and stolen cloud credentials were in use within hours (Wiz, 2026-10-21); rebuild from a reviewed release and pin container digests (Socket, 2026-10-21), and move to 1.106.2 or an explicit earlier version as the maintainers advise (LiteLLM, 2026-10-21). For your own pipelines, the root cause was a key that was removed from a public repository's history but never revoked, and an organization owner's CLI token held by an automation service; the maintainers call it an illustration of the risk of failing to rotate a potentially exposed key (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23).
Update24 Oct 2026 03:40 UTCrun 2026-10-24T0255Z-intelbodyevidencesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniques

The maintainers published a root-cause post on 2026-10-23 that supersedes the earlier hypothesis that the tokens were read from the logs of an internet-exposed internal deployment: their request logs show the first token came from a different service, an experimental agent platform whose master key had been committed to a public repository on 2026-05-27 and never revoked (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). The attacker used the key on 2026-10-10 to obtain an organization owner's GitHub CLI token, so access began eleven days before the release, and the same day throwaway branches in two repositories ran workflows that posted CI secrets to an external capture endpoint and were deleted minutes later, yielding the tokens of two further maintainers (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23).

Socket found the same activity independently from the repository's Actions performance metrics, including a second run on 2026-10-12 that took 14 further secrets, and says it has not established how the attacker first obtained access (Socket, 2026-10-23). On 2026-10-21 three credentials did different jobs: the owner's token overrode branch protection and later force-pushed the history clean, a second maintainer's token approved the production gate and a third maintainer's token deleted the run records, after the maintainers had relaxed the release rule earlier that week so that any two engineers could trigger and approve a release (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). The maintainers say they are revoking every token tied to every internal system and vendor platform, and that the attacker's activity on other systems focused on upstream inference API tokens (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23).

entries.headline: Palo Alto: PHP2Shell affects PAN-OS and Panorama; PAN-OS hotfixes due 26 to 30 October
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-109618 +1updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS and Panorama: the PHP2Shell flaws affect every release, reaching PAN-OS through its management web interface; PAN-OS hotfixes are scheduled for 2026-10-26 to 2026-10-30

Palo Alto Networks' advisory of 2026-10-21 lists every release of PAN-OS 12.2, 12.1, 11.2, 11.1 and 10.2 and of Panorama as affected by CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, with no fixed build released (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-21); the revision of 2026-10-23 gave estimated dates from 2026-10-26 to 2026-10-30 for hotfix builds of every PAN-OS train and noted that Cortex XCORE (SaaS) and WildFire Cloud were remediated on 2026-10-21 and 2026-10-22 (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-23). The advisory's timeline dates a correction of the WildFire appliances WF-500 and WF-500-B to 2026-10-23, and the table now lists them as unaffected, although the revision that morning had listed them as affected; the table no longer distinguishes Panorama, a note says the issue applies to PAN-OS software on PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and on Panorama (virtual and M-Series), and the mitigation text covers PAN-OS and Panorama together (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-24). The revision of 2026-10-24 added updated threat-signature and content-version details (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-24). The two flaws are the unauthenticated remote-code-execution bugs in the PHP runtime that the PHP project fixed in its releases of the same day (PHP, 2026-10-21). Palo Alto says no special configuration is required to be affected, that the issue strictly affects the management web interface, which includes the HTTPS web UI and the XML API service, and that a dataplane interface is affected only where a management profile is attached to it (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-21). It states that the GlobalProtect portal and gateway and the captive portal are not impacted (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-21).

Palo Alto describes the flaws as remote code execution but scores their impact on its own product CVSS-B 8.7 (severity high, urgency moderate), with high availability impact and none on confidentiality or integrity, against a vendor-level 9.2 with high impact on all three, and says the risk is highest where management access is allowed from external addresses on the internet; restricting management to a single jump box lowers its rating to 7.1, and it is not aware of any malicious exploitation against its products (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-21). Unit 42 says it has seen proof of concept of the PHP flaws (Unit 42, 2026-10-21). Until fixes ship, Palo Alto recommends restricting management access to trusted internal addresses and offers Threat Prevention coverage (Threat IDs 543004 and 97622 to 97625 and twenty further IDs from 97643 to 97678, Applications and Threats content versions 9162, 9163, 9164 and later) that applies only when management traffic is routed through a dataplane interface, the certificate for inbound management traffic has been replaced, inbound management traffic is decrypted so the firewall can inspect it, and threat prevention is enabled on that traffic (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-24).

Exposure
Every PAN-OS firewall and Panorama appliance, whatever the configuration, through its management web interface; the service is reachable from the internet where the management port, or a dataplane interface carrying a management profile, answers HTTPS or XML API requests from outside the administrator range (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-21).
Detection
In management-plane access and system logs, any request from an address outside the administrator range, though Palo Alto does not say which logs record request bodies; in threat logs, hits on the Threat IDs above where the signatures are active and the four conditions hold. Palo Alto publishes no flaw-specific indicator and reports no exploitation of its products, so no post-compromise check is defined yet (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-21).
Defender takeaway
Move management access behind a jump box or trusted internal addresses now, and remove management profiles from dataplane interfaces that face untrusted networks; Palo Alto lists no workaround beyond that restriction and the Threat Prevention coverage; its revision of 2026-10-23 schedules the first PAN-OS hotfixes for 2026-10-26 (10.2.18-h13, 11.1.16-h4 and 11.2.10-h16) and the rest by 2026-10-30, so install the hotfix of each train when it is released, while the advisory's note and mitigation text cover PAN-OS and Panorama together and its table no longer distinguishes Panorama, so apply the same management-access restriction to Panorama (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-24).
Update23 Oct 2026 03:42 UTCrun 2026-10-23T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummaryentitiesaffected_productscvessourcesevidencebody

Palo Alto Networks revised its advisory on 2026-10-23: the WildFire appliances WF-500 and WF-500-B are now listed as affected in all versions, and the footnotes say Cortex XCORE (SaaS) was remediated on 2026-10-21 and WildFire Cloud on 2026-10-22 (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-23). The advisory now also gives estimated availability dates for hotfix builds of every supported PAN-OS train, from 2026-10-26 (for example 10.2.18-h13, 11.1.16-h4 and 11.2.10-h16) to 2026-10-30, while Panorama and the WildFire appliances remain with no date (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-23). Palo Alto still states that it is not aware of malicious exploitation against its products, and the Threat Prevention coverage and the jump-box restriction are unchanged (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-23). The advisory names the management web interface only for PAN-OS and does not say which interface of the WildFire appliances is reachable.

actions: Update the PHP runtime, not the CMS or its plugins, on every internet-facing server and container image to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 or to your distribution's patched package, restart PHP-FPM, Apache and every long-running worker, rebuild images, and confirm the running version, because a distribution backport can keep the old version string; isolate any application that cannot be updated from public networks until it is.

After updating, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 on every PHP host and keep it there until PHP's next regular bugfix release: CVE-2026-115560, which the October releases do not fix, needs session upload progress to be enabled.
