entries.headline: ConnectWise SkyKick app credential used in 162+ Microsoft 365 tenants; disabling it does not undo planted access
entries.html:
HIGHexploitedupdatedNATOA1

ConnectWise Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick): the vendor's Microsoft 365 application credential was used to sign in to customer tenants, with directory-role self-assignments in about 50 tenants and, Huntress reports, added credentials in two

ConnectWise says it identified unauthorized access to application identities within its Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick) environment; on 2026-10-17 it disabled seven application identities, suspended the service, says the shared Cloud Backup credentials are no longer valid, and warns that disabling does not reverse changes already made in a tenant (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). As of ConnectWise's update of 2026-10-19 01:15 UTC, Cloud Backup, SaaS Security and Cloud Management remained suspended with no confirmed restoration time, which also took ConnectWise's SaaS Security monitoring and alerting out of service (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19), and heise reports on 2026-10-21 that ConnectWise has since begun restoring the services step by step over several days (heise online, 2026-10-21); ConnectWise reports no successful threat activity in the environments it monitors since it implemented mitigations (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19) and says it cannot independently determine whether a given partner or customer tenant was affected (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). Huntress and Todyl report that on 2026-10-15 the app's identity signed in to customer Microsoft 365 tenants from one hosting-provider address and received app-only Microsoft Graph tokens; the credential sits in the vendor's own tenant, so no user, MFA prompt or user Conditional Access was involved, and the app's consent covers read and write access to mail, files and Teams chats (Huntress, 2026-10-16; Todyl, 2026-10-15). Huntress confirmed unauthorized sign-ins in 162 tenants by 2026-10-16 and later counted almost 1,000 tenants with sign-in activity from that address, over 300 successful, after password spraying against four law-firm tenants on 13 and 14 October, and a separate failed wave targeted 16 tenants in policy and national-security sectors (Huntress, 2026-10-16). In about 50 of its tenants, ConnectWise Cloud Management apps assigned themselves directory roles, mostly Exchange Administrator; in one the Teams app added itself to Global Administrator and client secrets were added to an MSP management application and to Huntress's own application within about five minutes, the credential additions from private Azure space (Huntress, 2026-10-16). Huntress later identified a second tenant with the same sequence, the application granting itself Global Administrator and then planting a new secret on a small number of other applications, within two minutes of the first around 03:45 UTC on 2026-10-15, with the choice of applications apparently random (Huntress, 2026-10-16). It says the unauthorized sign-ins with the credential were bunched across the morning of 2026-10-15 UTC, that the last successful one it observed was at 08:44 UTC that day with only failed attempts afterwards in the tenants where it can read sign-in logs, and that in the two tenants it reviewed it found no mailbox or file manipulation and no user or policy changes (Huntress, 2026-10-16). Microsoft Threat Intelligence, as BleepingComputer relays it, called it an active supply-chain attack and assessed likely abuse of existing permissions including Directory.ReadWrite.All (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-17). Microsoft Threat Intelligence later assessed that Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, was responsible, using the ARTEX agentic-AI framework to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). How the credential was obtained and what was read remain unknown (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19; BleepingComputer, 2026-10-17).

Exposure
Every Entra tenant, including each customer tenant an MSP manages, in which a ConnectWise or SkyKick Cloud Backup or Cloud Management app was ever consented, dormant connections included; ConnectWise lists seven application client IDs, among them Cloud Backup (506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae), and says to match on client ID (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). Todyl says to find every SkyKick and ConnectWise app in a tenant, inherited ones included, and that all SkyKick apps are published from one vendor tenant (named ConnectWise S-K LLC, ID 3f9cd7a0-127a-4ed4-bf06-2f830d5616b7); SpecterOps hunts for apps owned by that tenant and notes that older tenants may list them under SkyKick names (Todyl, 2026-10-15; SpecterOps, 2026-10-17).
Detection
Entra service-principal sign-in logs for these apps from any address outside Microsoft and Azure ranges, which misses the credential additions, made from private Azure space (Huntress, 2026-10-16); the sweep of sign-ins itself, which Sophos saw come from a single virtual private server in strictly ascending tenant-ID order with Python HTTP-library user agents (Sophos, 2026-10-19); directory audit events Add member to role, Update application and Add service principal credentials initiated by a ConnectWise or SkyKick app (Huntress, 2026-10-16); Graph activity logs (Entra ID P1 or P2, not retroactive) for per-request source addresses (Todyl, 2026-10-15); and mailbox forwarding, inbox and transport rule and delegation changes (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). Huntress notes that Microsoft Graph directory reads leave no audit record, so a clean audit log does not rule out reads of the directory (Huntress, 2026-10-16). Disabling the apps does not remove credentials, roles or consents already planted, and revoking user sessions does not end this access (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19; Todyl, 2026-10-15). Disabling an app stops new tokens only: a token issued before the disable stays valid for up to 90 minutes (Todyl, 2026-10-15; SpecterOps, 2026-10-17), and ConnectWise says that after its own certificate revocation previously issued tokens may remain usable until they expire (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). The service-principal sign-in log records an application's authentication (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19), while per-request use of a token appears in the Graph activity logs named above (Todyl, 2026-10-15), so the review of that period belongs there. Microsoft asks tenants to review service-principal sign-ins from at least 2026-10-15, and from 2026-10-01 where records exist, and to search by application ID rather than display name (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). Any alerting a tenant took from ConnectWise SaaS Security is out of service while that service is suspended (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19).

Triage: the vendor's apps sign in from Azure addresses with a .NET SDK user agent, while the credential additions used a Python user agent; Python and curl are common in administration, so Huntress says the combination of actor, operation and user agent is the signal (Huntress, 2026-10-16). Role self-assignments carrying the vendor's own user agent are not proven benign, since Huntress has not confirmed vendor automation (Huntress, 2026-10-16).

Defender takeaway
Where any ConnectWise or SkyKick app is consented, disable it by client ID without deleting it, keep it disabled until ConnectWise gives restoration instructions, and review credentials, roles, owners, consents and Conditional Access exclusions since 13 October (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19; Huntress, 2026-10-16). An MSP should review its own management and security tools first, since a foothold there can reach its customers, but the review covers every application, because Huntress saw secrets planted on apparently random ones (Huntress, 2026-10-16). ConnectWise cannot independently determine whether a given partner or customer tenant was affected, so the answer for a tenant has to come from its own sign-in and audit logs (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19).
Improvement19 Oct 2026 03:47 UTCrun 2026-10-19T0256Z-intelactionssourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

ConnectWise's update of 2026-10-18 01:00 UTC took SaaS Security and Cloud Management offline in addition to Cloud Backup, which had been suspended since 2026-10-17, so ConnectWise SaaS Security monitoring and alerting is out of service as well, and the update of 2026-10-19 01:15 UTC still gives no restoration time (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). Disabling an app stops new tokens only: Todyl and SpecterOps each state that tokens already issued stay valid for up to 90 minutes, and ConnectWise says that after it revoked the Cloud Backup certificates previously issued tokens may remain usable until they expire (Todyl, 2026-10-15; SpecterOps, 2026-10-17; ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). Todyl says to find every SkyKick and ConnectWise app in a tenant, inherited ones included, and that all SkyKick apps are published from one vendor tenant, and SpecterOps hunts for apps owned by that tenant, noting that older tenants may list them under SkyKick names (Todyl, 2026-10-15; SpecterOps, 2026-10-17).

Update20 Oct 2026 03:57 UTCrun 2026-10-20T0256Z-inteltitlesummaryactionssourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

Huntress's update of 2026-10-19 13:30 ET identified a second tenant with post-compromise activity, a tenant Huntress did not originally protect, where it got deployed to collect telemetry (Huntress, 2026-10-16). In both tenants the activity was fast and scripted, within two minutes of each other around 03:45 UTC on 2026-10-15: the application granted itself Global Administrator and then planted a new secret on a small number of other applications to keep a foothold (Huntress, 2026-10-16). The choice of applications appeared random: the same flow picked two different sets, one application present in both was backdoored in only one, and in one tenant the applications that received secrets were among the least privileged in the environment while far more powerful ones were untouched (Huntress, 2026-10-16).

Huntress says the unauthorized sign-ins with the credential were tightly bunched across the morning of 2026-10-15 UTC, the last confirmed successful sign-in it observed was at 08:44 UTC, and it saw only failed attempts afterwards in the tenants where it can read sign-in logs (Huntress, 2026-10-16). The access may have been used for Microsoft Graph directory reads, which leave no audit record, and in the two tenants Huntress reviewed it found no evidence of mailbox or file manipulation or of user or policy changes (Huntress, 2026-10-16). The check for planted credentials therefore has to cover every application registration and enterprise application in the tenant, and a clean audit log does not exclude directory reads. ConnectWise's latest readable update (2026-10-19 01:15 UTC) gives no restoration time (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19).

Improvement21 Oct 2026 03:47 UTCrun 2026-10-21T0256Z-intelsourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

Sophos X-Ops independently observed the token requests: on 2026-10-15 a single virtual private server authenticated as the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application and requested app-only Microsoft Graph tokens for about 96 minutes, from 07:11 UTC, in strictly ascending tenant-ID order, one to six minutes apart, using Python HTTP-library user agents, and the sweep included tenants with no active backup subscription (Sophos X-Ops, 2026-10-19). Sophos found no hands-on-keyboard activity and no evidence that the application created new secrets, applications, consents or role assignments in the tenants it reviewed, which differs from the role grants and added secrets Huntress reports in other tenants; Sophos says it is unclear how the credential was obtained and what was done with the tokens (Sophos X-Ops, 2026-10-19). The two vendors' sweep timings differ: Huntress puts the first app sign-ins at 06:13 to 08:34 UTC on 2026-10-15 with tenants taken in sorted GUID order a few seconds apart (Huntress, 2026-10-16), where Sophos gives about 96 minutes from 07:11 UTC, one to six minutes apart; the vantage points differ, so both are reported as stated.

Update22 Oct 2026 03:46 UTCrun 2026-10-22T0256Z-intelbodyentitiesevidencesourcessourcing_notesummary

Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor active since 2021, was responsible for the compromise. It says AI agents running the ARTEX framework kept signing in to customer tenants as the ConnectWise applications, without an interactive user sign-in, and in multiple tenants went on to Microsoft Graph reconnaissance, application credential changes and attempts to change privileges (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). It counts attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants at up to 2,900 attempts a minute and links the activity to an automated cross-tenant password spray between 2026-10-10 and 2026-10-14 against 327 accounts at eight organizations, from the same network range and including an address that ConnectWise's advisory later listed among its indicators; the spray produced no successful authentication (Microsoft, 2026-10-21).

Microsoft warns that the application credential changes can remain active as a backdoor after the vendor application is remediated, and asks tenants to review service-principal sign-ins from at least 2026-10-15, and from 2026-10-01 where records exist, together with the Entra audit trail for credential additions, role assignments, consents and owner changes (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). Expel, which analysed the activity separately, relays the attribution, notes that ConnectWise's fix leaves secrets planted on other applications in place and that Graph directory reads leave no Entra audit record, and says Huntress has not tied its Global Administrator observation to the same operator (Expel, 2026-10-21). ConnectWise itself says that, based on the evidence available to it, including threat intelligence shared by Microsoft, it appears a China state-aligned group was responsible and used an openly available agentic AI framework (ConnectWise, 2026-10-21). It began restoring services in controlled phases on 2026-10-21, expects it to take several days, says the start of restoration does not mean all capabilities are available, and tells partners to keep affected connections disabled until formal instructions apply to their service, while noting that its actions do not remove unauthorized access already established in individual customer tenants (ConnectWise, 2026-10-21; heise online, 2026-10-21). ConnectWise publishes updates twice daily from 2026-10-22 (ConnectWise, 2026-10-21).

entries.headline: Group-IB: k0t takes edge devices in bulk and decrypts FortiGate configurations offline; enable private-data-encryption
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2025-64446 +2exploitedNATOB2

k0t: Group-IB and NyxLab describe a probable access broker that mass-exploits FortiWeb and PAN-OS GlobalProtect, brute-forces FortiGate and decrypts stolen FortiGate configurations offline with the default key, with victims later listed by Qilin and The Gentlemen

Group-IB and NyxLab describe a campaign by an operator they track as k0t (Group-IB lists CryptoFeel as a potential alias, and Scrooge as a likely collaborator and possible alias) that enumerates internet-facing VPN and firewall appliances in bulk and attacks the product directly, chiefly Fortinet firewalls and Palo Alto GlobalProtect portals (Group-IB, 2026-10-21). A custom script exploits CVE-2025-64446 against FortiWeb, a relative path traversal that lets an unauthenticated attacker run administrative commands, or brute-forces exposed Fortinet devices as a fallback (Group-IB, 2026-10-21; CISA KEV, 2026-10-21). Against PAN-OS it exploits CVE-2026-0257, the GlobalProtect authentication bypass, with a forged authentication-override cookie (Group-IB, 2026-10-21). On a compromised FortiGate the tool downloads the configuration and decrypts its secrets locally with the default FortiOS key, the weakness tracked as CVE-2019-6693, recovering LDAP and Active Directory bind and, Group-IB says, administrator credentials, although Fortinet's advisory excludes the administrator's password and says FIPS-CC devices are not impacted; unless private-data-encryption is set, the device falls back to that known key (Group-IB, 2026-10-21; Fortinet, 2019-11-19).

After access the operators work by hand with NetExec, Impacket, Kerbrute, relayed PetitPotam and Mimikatz, keep access through OpenConnect, MeshCentral agents, AdaptixC2, Atera and AnyDesk, and exfiltrate with Rclone to Wasabi and MEGA (Group-IB, 2026-10-21). Group-IB sees victim overlap with the Qilin and The Gentlemen leak sites and assesses the operators are probably initial-access brokers, but says no relationship is confirmed, and it found indications of a possible connection with the FortiBleed cluster alongside negligible overlap in the compromised credentials (Group-IB, 2026-10-21). CISA lists all three CVEs in KEV, with ransomware use marked known for CVE-2026-0257 and CVE-2019-6693 (CISA KEV, 2026-10-21).

Exposure
Internet-reachable FortiGate administrator and VPN logins, FortiWeb up to 8.0.1, 7.6.4, 7.4.9, 7.2.11 or 7.0.11 on its branch (Fortinet, 2025-11-14), and PAN-OS GlobalProtect portals and gateways below the per-branch fixed builds (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-05-13); every FortiGate except FIPS-CC models is exposed to the offline decryption step once its configuration has been downloaded unless private-data-encryption, available from FortiOS 5.6.11, 6.0.7 and 6.2.1 and off by default, is enabled with an operator-defined key, which Fortinet warns can cause install errors and split-brain on FortiManager-managed or HA FortiGates until FortiManager 6.2.7 and FortiGate 6.2.6, 6.4.4 or 6.6.0 and later (Group-IB, 2026-10-21; Fortinet, 2019-11-19).
Detection
On edge appliances, unexpected local administrator creation, configuration exports, trusted-host changes, repeated authentication failures, lockout-and-retry patterns and administration from unusual source addresses; on directory infrastructure, the NetExec, Impacket and relay pattern against domain controllers; on endpoints, remote-management agents and dual-use tools without an approved owner. The decryption leaves no trace on the appliance, so a patched or cleaned device may already have yielded its secrets (Group-IB, 2026-10-21). After upgrading FortiWeb, Fortinet advises reviewing configuration and logs for unexpected changes and unauthorised administrator accounts, and until then disabling HTTP and HTTPS on internet-facing interfaces (Fortinet, 2025-11-14).

Triage: OpenConnect, MeshCentral, Atera, AnyDesk and Rclone are legitimate tools, so Group-IB advises judging execution context, installation source, operator account, destination and timing rather than tool names (Group-IB, 2026-10-21).

Defender takeaway
Enable private-data-encryption with an operator-defined key on every FortiGate and rotate the directory and administrator secrets stored in any configuration that may have left the device, because patching or rebuilding does not undo a copy already decrypted; Group-IB also advises investigating lockout events and raising the lockout time against brute force (Group-IB, 2026-10-21).

Builds on: Qilin and Inc ransomware exploit the GlobalProtect bypass; one intrusion pivoted to vCenter and… · FBI and Secret Service: FortiBleed is still active, locks admins out of FortiGates and feeds…

entries.headline: Microsoft: Storm-0940 runs the ARTEX agent framework at machine speed; Expel adds an Okta self-registration technique
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

ARTEX: Microsoft reports Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, running an open-source multi-agent LLM penetration-testing framework against hundreds of organizations, with privileged cloud access in under three hours in some cases, and Expel sees the same infrastructure abuse Okta self-service registration

Microsoft Threat Intelligence reports that as early as September 2026 Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor active since 2021, used the agentic penetration-testing framework ARTEX to automate attacks on hundreds of organizations across many industries, government and military among them (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). ARTEX is an open-source multi-agent LLM system that can use any AI model and runs a penetration test from reconnaissance to exfiltration with little human involvement (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). Microsoft says ARTEX accelerated the abuse of compromised applications already granted access to Microsoft 365 tenants (Microsoft, 2026-10-21), and Expel adds that it is not a vulnerability and only speeds up familiar techniques such as password spraying and OAuth-application abuse (Expel, 2026-10-21); most targeting failed, yet several cases went from first targeting to privileged cloud access in under three hours (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). Microsoft assesses the same actor was behind the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application-credential abuse (Microsoft, 2026-10-21).

Expel saw Storm-0940 infrastructure scan a customer and, from 2026-10-13, abuse its Okta self-service registration with no ConnectWise application involved: the attacker created five accounts of its own, enrolled Okta Verify on three of them about a minute after activation, made 50 single sign-on logins with more than 100 OAuth tokens issued and ran a password spray that Okta ThreatInsight blocked (Expel, 2026-10-21). Expel says the shared source address is its only link to Storm-0940, the activity alone does not prove ARTEX was used, and it had not seen the technique reported before (Expel, 2026-10-21). Other actors use it: CrowdStrike analysed an unnamed, probably Chinese-speaking and financially motivated actor that ran ARTEX against South Korean financial institutions from late September (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-07), and Recorded Future, which tracks that activity as TAG-217, says use of ARTEX and other AI penetration-testing tools is not limited to it (Recorded Future, 2026-10-16).

Wiz Research independently reports that throughout October 2026 it tracked an actor using ARTEX-associated tooling, overlapping with Storm-0940, against IT and software vendors, focused on identity providers (Okta, Entra, Cognito) and Microsoft 365 integrations, and says that most attempts failed and that none of the techniques is novel (Wiz, 2026-10-22). It describes a consistent sequence: downloading JavaScript bundles, exposed source maps, runtime configuration and OpenAPI documents, then calling internal API routes by name minutes later; fabricated authorization codes and malformed state values against Microsoft OAuth callbacks; unsigned JWTs tried against more than 60 SSO route variants in two minutes; and account-recovery, sign-up and Cognito calls such as InitiateAuth, ForgotPassword and ResendConfirmationCode (Wiz, 2026-10-22). Its password sprays against Entra and Okta hit hundreds of users, mainly software engineers, in bursts of 20 to 60 minutes with a unique user agent per burst, a median gap of one second between attempts and new source addresses within minutes of a block (Wiz, 2026-10-22).

Exposure
Any tenant that relies on password sign-in or grants OAuth consent to applications, and any Okta org with self-service registration enabled; not using ConnectWise does not exclude exposure (Expel, 2026-10-21).
Detection
In the authentication logs of every identity provider in use, bursts of failed logons and lockouts spread over many accounts; in the Okta system log, newly self-registered accounts that enrol Okta Verify and start single sign-on within minutes; and in the Entra audit log, credentials or certificates added to applications that nobody on your team created and any application that assigns itself a directory role (Microsoft, 2026-10-21; Expel, 2026-10-21). A clean audit log is not proof of no access, because Microsoft Graph directory reads leave no Entra audit record (Expel, 2026-10-21). In web access logs of an application exposed to the same actor, Wiz points to source-map and OpenAPI downloads followed minutes later by calls to internal routes that appear only in those files, and to sign-in telemetry showing a new user agent for each burst of attempts at a one-second cadence (Wiz, 2026-10-22).

Triage: Python and curl user agents match common legitimate automation, so Expel treats them as supporting evidence only, and a Python user agent on an application that normally calls Microsoft Graph with a .NET SDK is the anomaly (Expel, 2026-10-21).

Defender takeaway
Expel's reading is that the framework adds speed, not a new vulnerability, so the levers are the identity controls it runs into: least privilege on multi-tenant application permissions and consent grants, alerting on credential additions and privileged role assignments by applications, and a review of self-registered Okta accounts since 2026-10-13 (Microsoft, 2026-10-21; Expel, 2026-10-21).
Improvement24 Oct 2026 03:45 UTCrun 2026-10-24T0255Z-intelbodyevidencesourcessourcing_note

Wiz Research reports an actor using ARTEX-associated tooling, overlapping with Storm-0940, against IT and software vendors throughout October 2026, focused on Okta, Entra and Cognito and on Microsoft 365 integrations, with most attempts failing (Wiz, 2026-10-22). It describes the log signatures of the agent: source-map and OpenAPI downloads followed minutes later by calls to internal routes that appear only in those files, fabricated OAuth callback values, unsigned JWTs tried against more than 60 SSO route variants in two minutes, account-recovery and sign-up calls, and password-spray bursts of 20 to 60 minutes against Entra and Okta with a unique user agent per burst and a median gap of one second between attempts (Wiz, 2026-10-22). Wiz says chaining, automatic adaptation to rate limits and blocks, and tests against heavily scrutinised Microsoft OAuth flows separate the agent from a human operator (Wiz, 2026-10-22).

entries.headline: Cisco: unauthenticated root RCE on clustered Expressway, fixed only in X15.5.20; X14 and earlier must migrate
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-76466 +4NATOA2

CVE-2026-76466, Cisco Expressway-C and Expressway-E: unauthenticated root command execution on clustered devices, fixed in X15.5.20 with no workaround (CVSS 9.8), alongside same-day hardening releases for Unified CM, Unity Connection and Snort 3

Cisco's advisory of 2026-10-21 fixes CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS 3.1 9.8, network, no privileges, no user interaction) in the database service of Expressway-C and Expressway-E, virtual and appliance: an unauthenticated remote attacker with network access can run operating-system commands as root (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21). The cause is the use of persistent cookies together with insufficient validation of client certificates for clustering, even when TLS Verify Mode is enabled; an attacker who possesses the cookies connects to the database service and invokes remote procedure call commands, and Cisco does not say how an attacker obtains the cookies (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21). Only devices configured in a cluster are affected; X15.5.3 and earlier are fixed in X15.5.20, X14 and earlier must migrate to a fixed release, there is no workaround, and Cisco's PSIRT is not aware of any public announcement or malicious use (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21). The X15.5.20 release also carries Expressway's own hardening fixes, whose worst class scores 8.6 (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21).

The same day Cisco ships two further hardening releases whose worst classes are exploitable over the network without authentication. For Emergency Responder, Prime Collaboration Deployment, Unified CM, Unified CM IM&P, Unified CM SME and Unity Connection, regardless of device configuration, the worst classes score 9.8 (CVE-2026-76473, improper control of a resource through its lifetime, and CVE-2026-76474, improper authentication); release 15 is fixed in 15SU5 and release 14 must migrate (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21). For Snort 3 in Secure Firewall Threat Defense, Cyber Vision, Unified Threat Defense (UTD) on IOS XE and other Snort-based products, the worst classes score 9.0 with high attack complexity (CVE-2026-20043, an out-of-bounds write, and CVE-2026-20236, an incorrect calculation); FTD is fixed in 7.0.10, 7.2.12, 7.4.8, 7.6.6, 7.7.13, 10.0.2 and 10.1.0, Snort in 3.12.4.0, Cyber Vision in 5.6.0 and UTD on IOS XE in 17.12.8, 17.15.6, 17.18.5, 26.1.2 and 26.2.1, while Meraki MX devices that are online and connected to the Dashboard and Cisco's cloud firewall services were updated automatically on 2026-10-21 (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21). Cisco says the flaws were found during internal security testing using existing processes as well as frontier AI models, and are not known to be actively exploited (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21; Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21).

Exposure
Expressway-C and Expressway-E in a cluster on X15.5.3 or earlier, or on X14 or earlier; the affected component is the database service, and Cisco does not say on which network it listens, so an Expressway-E in a cluster is the case to check first (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21). A standalone Expressway is outside the vulnerable-product statement for CVE-2026-76466 (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21), but it still needs X15.5.20 for the hardening fixes, which Cisco lists for every Expressway-C and Expressway-E regardless of configuration (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21).
Detection
Connections to the database service from hosts that are not cluster peers, and new root-owned processes started by that service; Cisco publishes no flaw-specific indicator and states no exploitation, so no post-compromise check is defined (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade Expressways to X15.5.20, clustered ones first, and schedule the move of X14 and earlier, Unified CM family and Unity Connection to 15SU5 (release 14 migrates), and FTD to the fixed build of its train; Cisco reports no exploitation of any of them and lists no workaround for the Expressway flaw (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21; Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21; Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21).

entries.headline: Microsoft says its Digital Crimes Unit will keep bringing cases after six leaked Windows zero-days; three fixed in June
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-45585exploitedupdatedNATOA1

Microsoft calls Nightmare Eclipse's six uncoordinated Windows zero-day releases "never justifiable"; the three May drops were fixed in June 2026

In a blog post on 2026-05-27, the Microsoft Security Response Center said the vulnerabilities known as RedSun, UnDefend, BlueHammer, YellowKey, GreenPlasma and MiniPlasma "were not responsibly disclosed" and that uncoordinated disclosures putting proof-of-concept code for unpatched flaws "into the hands of bad actors are never justifiable"; it added that its Digital Crimes Unit "will continue bringing cases against these actors and those that enable their criminal activity" (Microsoft MSRC blog, 2026-05-27). The Record reported the post on 2026-05-29 as Microsoft's first response to the release campaign, noted that the researcher's GitHub account had since been removed, and reported that the researcher threatened a further release on 14 July 2026, the date of Microsoft's July Patch Tuesday (The Record, 2026-05-29).

Contradiction: the outlets read the statement differently. The Record says Microsoft "stopped short of directly threatening legal action" (The Record, 2026-05-29), while heise writes that the company "is threatening lawsuits and the police" (heise Security, 2026-05-29).

The first three drops, BlueHammer (CVE-2026-33825), UnDefend (CVE-2026-45498) and RedSun (CVE-2026-41091), all disclosed in April, have been exploited in live intrusions and appear on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue (The Record, 2026-05-29); UnDefend lets a standard user block Microsoft Defender definition updates (BleepingComputer, 2026-06-10). The three May drops had no patch and no confirmed exploitation when The Record reported (The Record, 2026-05-29). YellowKey, tracked as CVE-2026-45585, is a BitLocker security feature bypass that needs physical access (Microsoft MSRC). The researcher says MiniPlasma abuses the HsmOsBlockPlaceholderAccess routine of the Cloud Filter driver cldflt.sys, and that it is the flaw Google Project Zero reported in 2020 as CVE-2020-17103, "still present, unpatched"; BleepingComputer's test on a fully patched Windows 11 Pro system with the May 2026 updates opened a SYSTEM command prompt from a standard user account (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-17).

Microsoft fixed the three May drops on 2026-06-09: GreenPlasma as CVE-2026-45586, a CTFMON elevation of privilege that can give SYSTEM (MSRC CVE-2026-45586), MiniPlasma by re-releasing CVE-2020-17103 with the June 2026 updates (MSRC CVE-2020-17103), and YellowKey in the same Patch Tuesday (BleepingComputer, 2026-06-10).

Exposure
Windows systems without the June 2026 updates: GreenPlasma and MiniPlasma are local privilege escalations open to any logged-on user (MSRC CVE-2026-45586) (MSRC CVE-2020-17103), and YellowKey needs physical access to a BitLocker device not protected by TPM+PIN (Microsoft MSRC).
Detection
For MiniPlasma, ThreatLocker advised watching registry-modification telemetry from the EDR for changes under the user hive's Software\Policies\Microsoft\CloudFiles\BlockedApps key and the .DEFAULT\Volatile Environment key (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-17).
Defender takeaway
The decision is patch level, not the dispute: three of the researcher's six drops were exploited after release (The Record, 2026-05-29), and the other three are closed by the June 2026 Windows updates (BleepingComputer, 2026-06-10).
Update21 Oct 2026 15:40 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1149Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevent_dateevidenceheadlinereferencessourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitle

Microsoft fixed the three May drops in the June 2026 Patch Tuesday updates of 2026-06-09: YellowKey (CVE-2026-45585) and GreenPlasma, now tracked as CVE-2026-45586 (BleepingComputer, 2026-06-10), and MiniPlasma through CVE-2020-17103, which Microsoft re-released "to comprehensively address the vulnerability identified by CVE-2020-17103" (MSRC CVE-2020-17103). BleepingComputer also reports that Microsoft backtracked on its initial threats of legal action after blowback on social media, saying it would work with law enforcement when a security researcher "breaks the law and engages in malicious activity causing real harm to our customers" (BleepingComputer, 2026-06-10).

entries.headline: Leaked BitLocker bypass "YellowKey" and CTFMON privilege escalation "GreenPlasma" were fixed in the June 2026 updates
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-45585 +1updatedNATOA1

Windows BitLocker "YellowKey" (CVE-2026-45585) and CTFMON "GreenPlasma" (CVE-2026-45586) zero-days: public PoCs in May, fixed in the June 2026 Windows updates

On 2026-05-13 BleepingComputer and The Register reported that the researcher Nightmare Eclipse (also Chaotic Eclipse) had published exploit code for two Windows zero-days, YellowKey and GreenPlasma (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-13) (The Register, 2026-05-13). The researcher's earlier BlueHammer (CVE-2026-33825) and RedSun drops began to be exploited in the wild shortly after release (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-13).

YellowKey is a BitLocker bypass that needs physical access. The researcher says it affects Windows 11 and Windows Server 2022/2025 and works by placing crafted FsTx files on a USB drive or the EFI partition, rebooting into the Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) and holding CTRL to trigger a shell (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-13). Will Dormann reproduced it with the files on a USB drive but not on the EFI partition: to boot WinRE, Windows replays the NTFS logs in \System Volume Information\FsTx directories on attached drives, the replay deletes X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, and WinRE then opens CMD.EXE instead of the recovery environment, with the disk still unlocked (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-13). Because it abuses TPM-only automatic unlock, the public exploit works only on the original device, not on a removed drive, and does not work with TPM+PIN (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-13). Microsoft tracks it as CVE-2026-45585, a security feature bypass by physical attack (CWE-77, CVSS 6.8), publicly disclosed and not exploited; its fixed builds are Windows 11 24H2 build 10.0.26100.8655, 25H2 build 10.0.26200.8655, 26H1 build 10.0.28000.2269 and Windows Server 2025 build 10.0.26100.32995, and its product table does not list Windows Server 2022 (MSRC CVE-2026-45585).

Contradiction: the researcher says an unpublished variant also defeats TPM+PIN (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-13); Microsoft states that "if you are using TPM+PIN the vulnerability is not exploitable" (MSRC CVE-2026-45585).

GreenPlasma is a local privilege escalation in CTFMON: an unprivileged user can create arbitrary memory-section objects within directory objects writable by SYSTEM, and the leaked PoC lacks the component needed for a full SYSTEM shell (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-13); in its current state it triggers a UAC consent prompt in default Windows configurations (The Register, 2026-05-13). Microsoft tracks it as CVE-2026-45586, a link-following flaw (CWE-59, CVSS 7.8) in the Windows Collaborative Translation Framework that lets an authorized local attacker gain SYSTEM privileges, released on 2026-06-09 with fixes for Windows 10, Windows 11 and Windows Server 2012 to 2025, publicly disclosed and not exploited (MSRC CVE-2026-45586).

Exposure
For YellowKey, TPM-only BitLocker devices (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-13) on Windows 11 24H2, 25H2 or 26H1 or Windows Server 2025 below the fixed builds, given physical access (MSRC CVE-2026-45585). For GreenPlasma, any Windows 10, Windows 11 or Windows Server 2012 to 2025 system without the June 2026 update, for an attacker who already runs code as a local user (MSRC CVE-2026-45586).
Detection
No cited source describes an artifact YellowKey leaves inside Windows; the attacker's media carries \System Volume Information\FsTx directories that WinRE replays at boot (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-13). GreenPlasma's public partial PoC raises a UAC consent prompt in default configurations (The Register, 2026-05-13).
Defender takeaway
The June 2026 Windows update fixes YellowKey (MSRC CVE-2026-45585) and GreenPlasma (MSRC CVE-2026-45586), and Microsoft's interim WinRE script need not be reverted, since the update keeps its behavior (MSRC CVE-2026-45585). Microsoft says TPM+PIN makes YellowKey not exploitable (MSRC CVE-2026-45585), which the researcher disputes (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-13), and Kevin Beaumont advised TPM+PIN along with a BIOS password (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-13).
Update20 May 2026 05:00 UTCrun 2026-05-20-a0f7b07factionscvessourcesbody

Microsoft formally assigned CVE-2026-45585 to the BitLocker / WinRE bypass disclosed by "Nightmare Eclipse" on 2026-05-12 and confirmed there is still no security update. The MSRC update guide entry, published 2026-05-19, classifies it as CWE-77 (command injection in BitLocker / Windows Recovery Environment), CVSS 6.8 (AV:P/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), with exploit-code maturity rated E:P (proof-of-concept) and remediation level RL:W (workaround only).

Microsoft's interim mitigation, which it recommends that customers "consider implementing" if they are concerned their devices and data are at risk of being compromised or stolen, is per-device work: mount the WinRE image, remove the autofstx.exe entry from the BootExecute registry value inside the WinRE image, commit the image, then re-establish BitLocker trust for WinRE (MSRC CVE-2026-45585). The MSRC FAQ states: "A successful attacker could bypass the BitLocker Device Encryption feature on the system storage device. An attacker with physical access to the target could exploit this vulnerability to gain access to encrypted data."

A pre-boot PIN avoids depending on the WinRE edit: the public exploit relies on TPM-only automatic unlock and does not work with TPM+PIN (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-13), and NCSC-CH advises that BIOS passwords and a BitLocker PIN mitigate the current public PoC (NCSC-CH Security Hub #12574, 2026-05-14).

Update21 Oct 2026 15:38 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1149Z-auditactionsaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesentitiesevent_dateevidenceheadlineprioritysectorssourcessummarytagstechniquestitle

Microsoft fixed both flaws in the June 2026 Windows updates of 2026-06-09. Revision 2 of the CVE-2026-45585 record "Added links to June 2026 Windows security updates", with fixed builds Windows 11 24H2 build 10.0.26100.8655, 25H2 build 10.0.26200.8655, 26H1 build 10.0.28000.2269 and Windows Server 2025 build 10.0.26100.32995 (MSRC CVE-2026-45585). GreenPlasma received its own identifier, CVE-2026-45586, released the same day with fixes for Windows 10, Windows 11 and Windows Server 2012 to 2025 (MSRC CVE-2026-45586), and BleepingComputer reported that the June 2026 Patch Tuesday fixed GreenPlasma, MiniPlasma and YellowKey (BleepingComputer, 2026-06-10). Before the fix, on 2026-05-21, Microsoft had replaced its manual WinRE steps with a script that removes autofstx.exe from the WinRE BootExecute value and re-seals WinRE so BitLocker trust remains intact (MSRC CVE-2026-45585). Microsoft marks neither flaw as exploited (MSRC CVE-2026-45585) (MSRC CVE-2026-45586).

entries.headline: Metabase Cloud was breached through its own 0-day; self-hosted instances stay vulnerable until manually upgraded
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-72898exploitedupdatedNATOA1

Metabase CVE-2026-72898: an unauthenticated SQL-injection zero-day gave attackers administrator access to BI instances, exploited since at least 3 August, with VenariX counting fifteen downstream victims

Metabase, an open-source business-intelligence platform run both self-hosted and as a managed cloud service, disclosed on 2026-08-06 that its own Metabase Cloud environment had been attacked by someone using an unknown vulnerability affecting versions 1.58 and above, and that it blocked the endpoints used in the attack before identifying and patching the flaw (Metabase, 2026-08-06). The mechanism matters more than the platform: an unauthenticated caller injects arbitrary SQL against the Metabase application database, and that yields administrator access to the instance, from which the attacker can change the application configuration, steal the stored credentials Metabase holds for the databases it connects to, read anything reachable through those connections, and export it (Metabase, 2026-08-06; Metabase GitHub advisory, 2026-08-06). Neither the vendor nor the reporting locates the injection point precisely, but the vendor's stated interim workaround for anyone who cannot upgrade immediately is to block the /api/session/reset_password endpoint outright, and its published attack pattern runs through that same route (Metabase, 2026-08-06). BleepingComputer, quoting the associated security advisory, reports it is rated critical at CVSS 10.0 with active exploitation confirmed, and that no CVE identifier had been assigned (BleepingComputer, 2026-08-07). The advisory later assigned CVE-2026-72898, and CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-08-11 (CISA, 2026-08-11).

The exposure split is the part defenders need to act on. Metabase Cloud customers were upgraded and patched by the vendor, while self-hosted instances remain vulnerable until an administrator upgrades them by hand (Metabase, 2026-08-06). The minimum safe point releases are 0.58.24, 0.59.21, 0.60.17, 0.61.11, 0.62.9 and 0.63.5 for their respective branches, and anything on a lower point release of those branches is still vulnerable; installations below version 58 are not affected (Metabase, 2026-08-06).

Two organisations have confirmed data theft from their own instances. Framework, the laptop manufacturer, told customers that the attackers stole full names, email addresses, login IP addresses, billing and shipping address details, phone numbers and company names, with VAT, EIN and billing email address additionally in scope for its business customers, and said Metabase notified it on 6 August that its instance had been vulnerable and was accessed on 3 August (BleepingComputer, 2026-08-07). Tally, an online form builder, notified users that its Metabase analytics environment was compromised on the same date and that the attackers reached email addresses and password hashes, while its forms and the responses submitted to them are stored separately and were not reached (BleepingComputer, 2026-08-07). Those two were the first confirmed victims. VenariX's tracker has since counted fifteen downstream incidents, set out in the updates below.

Detection is unusually well specified for a flaw that went its first week without a CVE, because the vendor published the request sequence rather than indicators. The attack shows up as a call to POST /api/session/reset_password returning a 400 status code followed by a call to GET /api/user/current returning 200, and Metabase states that finding that pattern in application logs or in Metabase server ingress logs means the instance was likely compromised (Metabase, 2026-08-06). After upgrading, the vendor's own follow-up steps for any instance whose reset endpoint was publicly reachable are to revoke every active session by deleting all rows in the core_session table, review and delete unrecognised API keys, check administrator accounts for unexpected changes, rotate the credentials for every connected database, and review both data-warehouse logs and Metabase's own activity and query history for unauthorised access (Metabase, 2026-08-06).

Defender takeaway
The reason this deserves attention beyond the patch is what a BI platform holds. Metabase sits in front of production data warehouses with standing credentials for each one, so administrator access converts directly into read access across every system it was ever pointed at. Any self-hosted instance that was internet-reachable on an affected point release before the upgrade needs the credential rotation and the log review, not just the version bump. The week without a CVE is a process lesson worth naming internally: while exploitation was already under way, an asset patched on the strength of CVE feeds, KEV listings or scanner findings got no signal for this at all.

Triage: a 400 on the password-reset route is ordinary, users mistype addresses and reset flows reject malformed requests all day, and on its own the 400 means nothing. The discriminator is what follows it from the same source: an unauthenticated client that is genuinely failing a password reset has no session and cannot then get a 200 from /api/user/current, so it is the ordering and the success of the second call that separate exploitation from noise (Metabase, 2026-08-06).

Update12 Aug 2026 04:46 UTCrun 2026-08-12T0411Z-intelactionscvesevidenceregionssectorssourcestagstechniquesbody

The entry on Metabase's unauthenticated SQL-injection zero-day closed on the observation that no CVE identifier had been assigned, so a purely CVE-driven patch process would not surface the exposure at all. That gap is now closed in both directions. GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-vwf4-m7j8-wcjf assigns CVE-2026-72898 with a CVSS 3.1 base score of 10.0 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H), and Metabase's own advisory text states that "Metabase has confirmed active exploitation of this vulnerability" and that the flaw "allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to inject arbitrary SQL into the Metabase application database, which can give them administrator access to the instance" (Metabase, 2026-08-06). CISA added the CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-08-11 with a 14 August due date (CISA, 2026-08-11).

The second half of the delta is the affected-version matrix, which the vendor's original blog post did not carry in this form. The advisory lists the affected ranges per release line as >= x.58.0 < x.58.23, >= x.59.0 < x.59.20, >= x.60.0 < x.60.16, >= x.61.0 < x.61.10, >= x.62.0 < x.62.8 and >= x.63.0 < x.63.3, and names the patched versions separately as x.58.24, x.59.21, x.60.17, x.61.11, x.62.9 and x.63.5; note the two lists do not meet, so a build sitting between an affected upper bound and its patched release is not described either way and should be treated as needing the named patched version (Metabase, 2026-08-06). That turns "upgrade Metabase" into a query an asset inventory can answer, and it is what a scanner needed in order to report anything at all.

Nothing here changes the exposure of an instance that has not been upgraded; the exploitation window has been open since at least 3 August per the earlier coverage, and the interim control is unchanged: block the /api/session/reset_password endpoint if an upgrade cannot happen immediately. What changed is visibility, and that is the operationally useful part. An organisation whose vulnerability management runs off CVE identifiers, SBOM matching or KEV feeds got no signal on this flaw for over a week while it was being exploited; the same tooling will now produce a finding on the next scan cycle. The advisory's post-upgrade guidance also stands and is worth re-reading against what an attacker with administrator access would already have taken: revoke active sessions, audit API keys and administrator accounts, and rotate the stored credentials for every connected data source, because those credentials are what an instance-level compromise reaches.

Update19 Aug 2026 05:02 UTCrun 2026-08-19T0410Z-intelactionscvesevidencesectorssourcestagstechniquesbody

The count of downstream victims is now the story. A tracker maintained by VenariX, first published 2026-08-10 and updated 2026-08-17, states that "This brings the number of publicly confirmed downstream organizations tracked by VenariX to nine" (VenariX, 2026-08-17), n8n, Framework, Tally and Kilo Code from the first wave, with Stocksy United Co-op, ShipMonk, Checkly, Cypress.io and Bits of Gold added on 2026-08-17. The earlier entries covered the flaw itself: an unauthenticated SQL injection reachable at the password-reset endpoint, CVSS 10.0, exploited, catalogued as such on 2026-08-11.

The mechanism behind the growing list is a property of business-intelligence tooling rather than of this bug. Metabase stores the connection configuration, including credentials, for every external database and warehouse it queries; an attacker who reaches administrative context in the application can therefore read those stored credentials and query or export whatever they reach (VenariX, 2026-08-17). The blast radius of any given instance is set entirely by what it was wired to; VenariX's own framing is that a deployment connected only to a restricted reporting database is a materially different incident from one connected to a production warehouse, which is the assessment question a defender should be answering first.

The victim disclosures show the range. n8n's investigation found the attacker queried 136 records containing names and email addresses, five of which also carried bcrypt password hashes tied to n8n Cloud accounts, and reported that the queries returned a variable set of rows, which prevented it from determining exactly which individual records were returned. Framework confirmed customer data was stolen including names, email addresses, phone numbers, login IP addresses and billing and shipping addresses, with payment information not included. Tally's exposure covered email addresses and password hashes while form content was stored separately and unaffected, and Kilo Code's included names, email addresses, billing addresses, location data and, for a subset of users, partial or full prompts (VenariX, 2026-08-17). Of the newly added names, Bits of Gold separately disclosed on 2026-08-17 that an attacker gained unauthorized access to a third-party data analytics network and obtained names, national ID numbers and emails for roughly 200,000 customers (DataBreaches.net, 2026-08-17), the company describes the platform class, not the product, and it is VenariX that places the incident in this campaign.

The operational point is the one most likely to be got wrong in a remediation ticket. Metabase's own guidance, as VenariX relays it, is that "Credential rotation is especially important if exploitation is suspected, because patching the application does not invalidate credentials that may already have been exposed" (VenariX, 2026-08-17). An estate that upgraded Metabase and closed the ticket has fixed the injection and left the attacker holding working warehouse credentials. Metabase's fuller recommendation set for potentially exposed instances is to revoke active sessions, review administrator accounts and API keys, rotate credentials for connected databases, and review both Metabase and warehouse logs; where an immediate upgrade is impossible it recommends temporarily blocking access to the reset-password endpoint.

Detection has an unusually crisp anchor for a SQL-injection flaw, because the vendor published one. Metabase identified a recurring two-request pattern associated with exploitation (a POST to /api/session/reset_password returning HTTP 400, immediately followed by a GET to /api/user/current returning HTTP 200) and "Metabase states that this pattern in application or ingress logs indicates that the instance was likely compromised" (VenariX, 2026-08-17). Beyond that, the investigative surface is Metabase's own query history, database and warehouse audit logs, administrator accounts, API keys, and any unexpected use of the stored connection credentials; the last being where a compromise that started in the BI tier becomes visible in the warehouse tier.

Triage: a failed password reset followed by a session check is not by itself unusual in a web application's logs, which is exactly why the ordered pair matters rather than either request alone; a genuine failed reset does not produce an authenticated /api/user/current success on the same session immediately afterwards. Downstream, the discriminator for warehouse activity is whether queries arriving under the Metabase service credential match the dashboards and questions that credential is actually used for: bulk selects against tables no saved question references, or access at hours the reporting schedule does not run, are the signal, while high query volume under that identity is normal by design.

Update27 Sep 2026 04:38 UTCrun 2026-09-27T0404Z-intelsourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

The downstream count grows again, and through a further intermediary this entry had not yet named. Shipup, a French platform used by more than 700 e-commerce brands to send delivery-tracking notifications and post-purchase communications, ran a Metabase instance that was compromised through the same CVE-2026-72898 unauthenticated SQL injection, with unauthorized access to the Shipup instance confirmed between 31 July and 17 August 2026, a window that starts earlier than the "since at least 3 August" this entry's own earlier coverage had established for the campaign (Cyberattaque.org, 2026-09-26). At least six of Shipup's retail clients have since notified their own customers of exposure: Carrefour notified some customers in early September, and Cyberattaque.org had already separately documented Printemps, Citadium, Aroma-Zone, Micromania and Easypara as affected through the same Shipup compromise (Cyberattaque.org, 2026-09-26; French Breaches, 2026-09-27). The exposed categories match the pattern this campaign has shown throughout: names, email addresses and phone numbers; Carrefour states no banking data or passwords were affected, and neither its own site, customer accounts nor internal systems were compromised, consistent with the exposure being limited to data it had shared with Shipup for delivery notifications. Carrefour has not disclosed the exact number of customers affected or confirmed whether the exposure window matches Shipup's own 31 July-17 August dates.

Shipup is a new entry in this campaign's chain of intermediary vendors, distinct from the data warehouses and analytics platforms this entry's earlier coverage described (n8n, Kilo Code and the others connected directly to a compromised Metabase instance): here, the retail brands are themselves downstream of a vendor that was downstream of the Metabase flaw, a second hop the credential-rotation and log-review guidance in this entry's original analysis already covers, since it applies to any instance that was reachable and unpatched during the exploitation window regardless of how many contractual layers separate the ultimate data subject from the compromised application.

Correction27 Sep 2026 13:28 UTCrun 2026-09-27T1308Z-auditbody

The Shipup paragraph above stated that the 31 July to 17 August 2026 access window matched the exposure window this entry had already established for the campaign. It does not. This entry's earlier coverage places exploitation "since at least 3 August", so the Shipup window opens three days earlier and widens the campaign's known exposure period rather than corroborating it. For a defender scoping a log review against a Metabase instance or a downstream vendor relationship, the earlier start date is the operative one, and the sentence now says so.

Update29 Sep 2026 22:50 UTCrun 2026-09-29T2134Z-audittitlesummarytagsentitiessourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

VenariX's tracker has grown from nine confirmed downstream incidents to fifteen. The additions since the 2026-08-17 count are Privy, Paradigm Connect Asia, Statista, Dodo Payments, Marsello and LEGO Certified Stores South Africa (VenariX, 2026-08-10, revised since). The Shipup compromise and its retail clients, covered in the update of 2026-09-27, are not on that list, so the real total is higher still.

The larger change is who is using the flaw. VenariX says it has confirmed that Dire Wolf, a ransomware and data-extortion group, exploited CVE-2026-72898 in at least two incidents against self-hosted Metabase deployments, at Statista and Dodo Payments, and suspects the group targeted fourteen more companies the same way. It is explicit that it has no evidence Dire Wolf discovered the zero-day or is behind the other confirmed incidents (VenariX, 2026-08-10, revised since). Dodo Payments, a payments company, confirms the vector without naming an actor: an unauthorised party exploited CVE-2026-72898 in a self-hosted Metabase instance used for internal reporting, viewed and queried the reporting datasets that system could reach, and the company contained it within hours of learning of it on 16 August (Dodo Payments, 2026-08-17). A dark-web listing dated 16 August, reviewed but not verified by MediaNama, claims about 60.8 GB and 39.3 million rows from four ClickHouse analytics databases, including tables it labels API keys, one-time passcodes and identity-provider credentials, where Dodo says API keys and credentials were not in the affected system (MediaNama, 2026-09-01).

For a defender this moves the self-hosted exposure from opportunistic data theft to an extortion operator's target list. The dispute over what left Dodo's warehouses is the point this entry has made since August: the reach of a compromised Metabase instance is whatever its stored connections reach, and the vendor's statement of what the BI tool itself held does not bound it. An instance that was internet-reachable on a vulnerable build between late July and its upgrade should be scoped as a warehouse compromise, not an application one.

Update21 Oct 2026 03:48 UTCrun 2026-10-21T0256Z-intelregionssectorssourcesevidencesourcing_notebodytitle

Republik, a Swiss online magazine, reported that an unauthorised access that had been going on since August ended on Wednesday 2026-10-14, when one of its analysis tools stopped working and it took its own Metabase installation offline; its statement says the vulnerability had been known since 6 August and that the magazine failed to take countermeasures in good time (swissinfo.ch, 2026-10-16). Netzwoche quotes it saying it had not subscribed to the manufacturer's security warnings and had no automatic check that reports a known gap in the software it runs (translated from German; Netzwoche, 2026-10-19).

The attackers certainly retrieved the records of all registered users, at least names and email addresses and in part date of birth and gender, and demonstrably sampled postal addresses, comments and votes; Republik reported the incident to the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner on 2026-10-15 (Netzwoche, 2026-10-19; swissinfo.ch, 2026-10-16). Republik believes it was a broad automated wave in which the attackers first looked for what every Metabase installation holds, such as login details and keys for AI services that could be resold, and says nothing indicates anyone targeted the magazine specifically (swissinfo.ch, 2026-10-16). It will use Metabase again only when it is updated and no longer reachable from the open internet, and says the stolen data had not surfaced online (Netzwoche, 2026-10-19).

entries.summary: Metabase disclosed on 2026-08-06 that its Metabase Cloud platform was attacked through a previously unknown vulnerability in versions 1.58 and above: an unauthenticated attacker injects arbitrary SQL against the application database and obtains administrator access to the instance, from which they can rewrite configuration, steal the stored credentials for every connected database and export the data those connections reach. The only interim workaround the vendor offers is to block the /api/session/reset_password endpoint, which is also where its published attack pattern runs. Cloud instances were patched by the vendor; self-hosted deployments stay vulnerable until manually upgraded to 0.58.24, 0.59.21, 0.60.17, 0.61.11, 0.62.9 or 0.63.5. Laptop maker Framework and form builder Tally were the first to confirm customer data was taken, on 2026-08-03. The flaw went a week without a CVE identifier before it was assigned CVE-2026-72898 and added to CISA's KEV catalog on 2026-08-11. VenariX now tracks fifteen publicly confirmed downstream incidents and ties two of them, at Statista and Dodo Payments, to the Dire Wolf extortion group working against self-hosted instances.
entries.title: Metabase CVE-2026-72898: an unauthenticated SQL-injection zero-day gave attackers administrator access to BI instances, exploited since at least 3 August, with VenariX counting fifteen downstream victims

updates.summary: Metabase's unauthenticated SQL-injection zero-day, covered here on 2026-08-09 when no CVE existed, has been assigned CVE-2026-72898 in GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-vwf4-m7j8-wcjf at CVSS 3.1 10.0, and CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-08-11. The advisory publishes affected ranges per release line and confirms active exploitation in Metabase's own words. For self-hosted instances nothing about the exposure changed, but the flaw is now visible to every scanner, SBOM pipeline and CVE-keyed patch process that could not see it a week ago.

A tracker maintained by VenariX, updated 2026-08-17, now counts nine publicly confirmed organisations whose compromised Metabase environments were used to reach connected data warehouses, n8n, Framework, Tally and Kilo Code, joined on 2026-08-17 by Stocksy United Co-op, ShipMonk, Checkly, Cypress.io and Bits of Gold. This pipeline covered CVE-2026-72898 on 2026-08-09 and 2026-08-12 as an exploited CVSS 10.0 unauthenticated SQL injection in the password-reset endpoint; the delta is the downstream pattern. Because Metabase stores the credentials for every database it connects to, administrative access to the application yields those credentials, and Metabase's own guidance is that patching does not invalidate credentials already exposed. Metabase also published a two-request log pattern that indicates a given instance was compromised.

The downstream victim list grows again through a further intermediary: Shipup, a French package-tracking platform used by 700+ e-commerce brands, was compromised through the same vulnerability, and at least six of its retail clients, including Carrefour, Printemps, Citadium, Aroma-Zone, Micromania and Easypara, have since notified their own customers of exposed contact data.

The Shipup section claimed the 31 July to 17 August access window was the same one this entry's earlier coverage had already established for the campaign. It was not: the earlier coverage says "since at least 3 August", three days later, so the Shipup window widens the campaign's known exposure period rather than confirming it. The sentence now states that difference instead of asserting agreement. Recorded for the audit trail and not otherwise fixable: the changelog record of the same day declared a change to the evidence list that its commit did not make.

VenariX's tracker now counts fifteen publicly confirmed downstream incidents, up from nine, adding Privy, Paradigm Connect Asia, Statista, Dodo Payments, Marsello and LEGO Certified Stores South Africa. It attributes two of them, at Statista and Dodo Payments, to the Dire Wolf ransomware and extortion group exploiting self-hosted Metabase, and suspects fourteen more targets. Dodo Payments' own disclosure confirms a self-hosted Metabase instance breached through CVE-2026-72898. The title, the summary and the main analysis no longer describe the flaw as having no CVE or Framework and Tally as its only victims.

A Swiss victim: Republik, a Swiss online magazine, says attackers used the Metabase flaw against its own installation from August until the tool failed on 2026-10-14, retrieved the records of all registered users and reported the incident to the federal data protection commissioner; it had not subscribed to the vendor's security warnings.

actions: Patch every PAN-OS GlobalProtect portal and gateway to the fixed build in Palo Alto's advisory for its minor release (users then re-authenticate once, because the fixed firewall regenerates the override cookie), or until then disable Authentication Override or give the cookies a certificate that no other feature uses.

On every GlobalProtect gateway that was internet-reachable and unpatched at any time since 2026-05-17, treat the network behind it as a ransomware compromise-assessment target: review VPN sessions that authenticated by cookie from unexpected sources, check Windows hosts for the artifacts Arctic Wolf describes (a ransomware payload staged under C:\\PerfLogs, a PsExec service, an LSASS dump written through comsvcs.dll to an .odt file, an ntdsutil media copy of the Active Directory database, and cleared event logs), and extend the assessment to the virtualization and backup tier: vCenter and ESXi audit logs for a changed execInstalledOnly setting and for access to a domain controller's virtual disk, and the Veeam backup server, because Unit 42 describes one intrusion that pivoted from the gateway to vCenter and dumped domain credentials offline, which in-guest EDR does not see.
