entries.headline: Qilin and Inc ransomware exploit the GlobalProtect bypass; one intrusion pivoted to vCenter and ESXi past in-guest EDR
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-0257exploitedupdatedNATOA1

CVE-2026-0257, Palo Alto PAN-OS GlobalProtect: pre-auth authentication bypass via certificate reuse, marked by CISA as used in ransomware campaigns

Authentication override cookies in PAN-OS GlobalProtect let a portal or gateway issue a cookie that a user presents in place of re-authenticating, and the feature is not enabled by default (Rapid7, 2026-05-29). Palo Alto Networks says the flaw affects firewalls with a GlobalProtect portal or gateway where authentication override cookies are enabled and a specific certificate configuration exists, classes it as CWE-565 (reliance on cookies without validation and integrity checking), and scores it CVSS 4.0 7.8 with exploit maturity Attacked (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-05-13). Rapid7's analysis is that when the certificate used for the cookies is reused for another feature such as the HTTPS service of the portal or gateway, a remote unauthenticated attacker can discover that certificate's public key, forge an arbitrary cookie that the server decrypts and trusts, and bypass authentication; Rapid7 Labs published a proof-of-concept script that tests for it (Rapid7, 2026-05-29). Palo Alto Networks says it is aware of limited exploit attempts on unpatched devices without mitigations applied (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-05-13); Rapid7 MDR dates the earliest observed exploitation to 17 May 2026 and saw two waves, on 18 May from Vultr-hosted infrastructure and on 21 May from Dromatics Systems, which it believes are likely the same threat actor because of a consistent MAC address (Rapid7, 2026-05-29). CISA's KEV catalog lists the CVE with a date added of 29 May 2026 (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-10-04).

Affected are PAN-OS 12.1, 11.2, 11.1 and 10.2 releases below the fixed builds in Palo Alto's table and Prisma Access 11.2 and 10.2; Panorama and Cloud NGFW are not affected (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-05-13). The solution table names the first fixed build for each minor release, for example 12.1.4-h6 or 12.1.7 and later for 12.1.2 through 12.1.4, 11.2.12 or later for 11.2.11, 11.1.15 or later for 11.1.14, and 10.2.18-h6 or later on the 10.2 train, while Prisma Access 11.2 needs 11.2.7-h13 or later and 10.2 needs 10.2.10-h36 or later (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-05-13). After the upgrade users must re-authenticate once, because the firewall regenerates the cookie with a more secure method (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-05-13). Palo Alto's mitigations are a dedicated certificate used only for authentication override cookies, or disabling Authentication Override (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-05-13).

Exposure
Firewalls with a GlobalProtect portal or gateway where the option to generate or accept a cookie for authentication override is checked and the cookie certificate is reused for another feature such as the HTTPS service; Palo Alto's advisory gives the management-interface path under Network > GlobalProtect to check whether cookies are enabled (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-05-13; Rapid7, 2026-05-29).
Detection
GlobalProtect gateway authentication logs. Rapid7 saw cookie authentication to the local admin account from hosting-provider address space with a generic non-human client name, followed by VPN IP assignment and POST requests to the HIP report and getconfig endpoints once a tunnel was established (Rapid7, 2026-05-29). Behind a gateway that was exposed, the post-exploitation artifacts Arctic Wolf describes for Qilin intrusions are the compromise check (Arctic Wolf, 2026-07-20), and Unit 42's reported pivot in one case adds the vCenter and ESXi audit logs and the backup server, because the domain-controller credential theft it describes runs against the virtual disk and not inside the guest (Unit 42, 2026-10-20).

Triage: cookie logins are routine wherever Authentication Override is enabled, because users present the cookie in lieu of re-authenticating (Rapid7, 2026-05-29). In some intrusions Arctic Wolf saw a cookie-based authentication failure with the error Cannot decrypt cookie, followed quickly by a successful cookie-based authentication from the same source, although the error was not present in every intrusion (Arctic Wolf, 2026-06-11).

Defender takeaway
Upgrade to the fixed build for each minor release, or use a dedicated cookie certificate or disable Authentication Override until then, and expect users to re-authenticate once; treat any gateway that was exposed with the cookie feature on and unpatched since 17 May as a ransomware compromise-assessment target rather than a finished patch, one that includes vCenter, ESXi and the backup server because Unit 42 saw a pivot there in one case, because CISA marks the flaw as used in ransomware campaigns, Arctic Wolf traced Qilin deployments to it and Unit 42 names Qilin and Inc (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-10-04; Arctic Wolf, 2026-07-20; Unit 42, 2026-10-20).
Update10 Jun 2026 05:00 UTCrun 2026-06-10-c84347b2actionsevidencesectorssourcesbody

Unit 42's 9 June update on CVE-2026-0257 confirms that a limited number of probed PAN-OS GlobalProtect devices had attacker-established, gateway-connected VPN sessions, moving this from "exploit attempts observed" to confirmed successful exploitation (Unit 42, 2026-06-09). The bug (CWE-565, reliance on a cookie without integrity checking) lets an attacker extract the encryption certificate's public key from the TLS handshake and forge authentication-override cookies when that certificate is shared with another function; Rapid7 dates successful exploitation to 17 May from low-cost hosting IPs (Rapid7, 2026-05-29).

Affected: PAN-OS 10.2/11.1/11.2/12.1 and Prisma Access where authentication override is enabled with a shared certificate; patched in 12.1.7+, 11.2.12+, 11.1.15+, 10.2.18-h6+ and corresponding Prisma builds (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-05-13). After the upgrade users must re-authenticate once, because the fixed firewall regenerates the cookie with a more secure method; as a workaround disable authentication override or assign it a dedicated certificate (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-05-13). Hunt GlobalProtect gateway logs for cookie-based authentications from unexpected source addresses; Rapid7's log of the attack shows the authentication method recorded as a cookie (Rapid7, 2026-05-29).

Update17 Jun 2026 05:14 UTCrun 2026-06-17-e102009cevidenceregionssectorssourcesbody

Palo Alto's Unit 42 confirms an active exploitation campaign against the GlobalProtect cookie authentication-bypass (CVE-2026-0257) (Unit 42, 2026-06-09). The flaw (CWE-565, reliance on cookies without validation and integrity checking) lets an attacker forge a session and establish a VPN tunnel without credentials when the override feature is enabled (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT).

Arctic Wolf saw exploitation attempts across insurance, finance, manufacturing, education, engineering and healthcare targets in North America and Europe, and in a subset of intrusions automated internal SMB reconnaissance consistent with Impacket tooling (anonymous NTLM logon, share enumeration and domain-user discovery); it says the follow-on activity did not progress substantially beyond the initial SMB session setup and lightweight reconnaissance (Arctic Wolf, 2026-06-11). NCSC-CH refreshed its Security Hub advisory on 2026-06-16 to flag the Unit 42 confirmation (NCSC-CH Security Hub, 2026-06-16). Defenders: disable "Authentication Override" if not required, patch to fixed PAN-OS builds, and audit sessions since 17 May for anonymous NTLM logons and SMB share enumeration from VPN-assigned addresses.

Update06 Oct 2026 05:01 UTCrun 2026-10-06T0405Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarypriorityimmediate_actiontagsentitiestechniquesaffected_productssourcesevidencesourcing_noteclassificationactionsbody

CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (version 2026.10.04) now marks CVE-2026-0257 as used in known ransomware campaigns; the record names no group and its date of addition remains 2026-05-29 (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-10-04). Arctic Wolf Labs' report of 2026-07-20 says it investigated multiple distinct intrusions in June 2026 that ended in Qilin ransomware deployment, all originating from exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 against Palo Alto Networks firewalls, and that the post-exploitation tradecraft ranged from rapid encryption-only operations to double extortion, possibly suggesting several affiliates of the Qilin ransomware-as-a-service operation (Arctic Wolf, 2026-07-20).

The chain Arctic Wolf describes starts with a GlobalProtect VPN session obtained through the cookie bypass, in some cases from systems that identified themselves as kali, and continues with registry Run-key persistence that points at a ransomware payload staged under C:\PerfLogs, remote-access tools (AnyDesk, Ngrok, LogMeIn and, in one case, a scheduled task consistent with MeshAgent), LSASS credential theft through rundll32 and comsvcs.dll into a file with an .odt extension, a full copy of the Active Directory database with ntdsutil, lateral movement with PsExec over administrative shares and RDP, a PowerShell routine that clears every Windows event log with records, and Microsoft Defender real-time protection disabled in some cases (Arctic Wolf, 2026-07-20). In the double-extortion cases data went to the MEGA cloud storage service with Rclone before encryption, and the attackers targeted the Veeam backup infrastructure before deploying the ransomware; some intrusions involved no data theft before encryption (Arctic Wolf, 2026-07-20). A gateway that was reachable and unpatched therefore needs a compromise assessment of the Windows estate behind it, not only the patch.

Correction11 Oct 2026 13:51 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-auditbodyevent_date

Arctic Wolf's June telemetry shows automated SMB reconnaissance consistent with Impacket tooling (anonymous NTLM logon, share enumeration, domain-user discovery) in a subset of intrusions, and Arctic Wolf states the activity did not progress substantially beyond the initial SMB session setup and lightweight reconnaissance (Arctic Wolf, 2026-06-11); the 2026-06-17 note had called it lateral movement. Before the Qilin reporting, Rapid7 saw no indication of successful lateral movement from the compromised devices (Rapid7, 2026-05-29), and Unit 42 reported no post-access behavior or lateral movement as of 9 June (Unit 42, 2026-06-09). Rapid7 saw the same spoofed MAC address on the attacker's client in both May waves, a pivot for VPN session logs (Rapid7, 2026-05-29), although Arctic Wolf found MAC spoofing was not consistent across later intrusions (Arctic Wolf, 2026-06-11). Rapid7 Labs published a public proof of concept on 29 May, the same day CISA added the flaw to its catalog (Arctic Wolf, 2026-06-11).

Update21 Oct 2026 03:45 UTCrun 2026-10-21T0256Z-intelheadlinesummaryentitiessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Unit 42 updated its threat brief on 2026-10-19 and 2026-10-20: it continues to see attempted exploitation by ransomware operators, naming Spikey Scorpius (Qilin) and Tarnished Scorpius (Inc), and says it is aware of public reporting that attributes exploitation to actors using Settra ransomware (Unit 42, 2026-10-20). Its investigations have run since early June 2026 and span industries including government (Unit 42, 2026-10-20). The attackers use the flaw for an initial foothold, bypass multi-factor authentication to establish a VPN session, then run reconnaissance with dual-use remote monitoring and management tools, move over RDP and SMB and stage credential harvesting, exfiltration and ransomware (Unit 42, 2026-10-20).

The change Unit 42 stresses is a direct pivot to the virtualization layer: in one case the attackers went from the compromised VPN gateway to the vCenter management appliance, disabled the execInstalledOnly security control on ESXi hosts and used a custom tool for offline credential dumping from a domain controller's virtual disk, which bypasses in-guest EDR; it also saw this access chained with exploit tools aimed at Veeam backup infrastructure (Unit 42, 2026-10-20). The brief adds that GlobalProtect profiles mapped to HTTP or HTTPS services on management interfaces can expose the management interface on ports 4443 and 3879 without the administrators knowing, and that an out-of-band HTTPS connection to the management address on those ports shows whether it is exposed (Unit 42, 2026-10-20). The brief dates the flaw's addition to CISA's catalog to 13 May 2026, whereas the catalog's own record says 29 May 2026 (Unit 42, 2026-10-20; CISA KEV catalog, 2026-10-04).

Correction21 Oct 2026 08:21 UTCrun 2026-10-21T0800Z-auditactionscvesbody

The one-time re-authentication is a consequence of the upgrade, not a step to force: with the fix, a firewall that uses authentication override cookies regenerates the cookie with a more secure method, so GlobalProtect users re-authenticate once after the upgrade even when they hold a valid cookie (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-05-13). Cookie logins are routine where Authentication Override is enabled; in some intrusions Arctic Wolf saw a cookie-based authentication failure with the error Cannot decrypt cookie, followed quickly by a successful cookie-based authentication from the same source (Arctic Wolf, 2026-06-11).

entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Symantec: APT28's hidden-Edge backdoor hit law-enforcement and defence targets; at a shipbuilder it added an SSH tunnel
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

APT28 (Swallowtail) used the HOOKEDGE backdoor against a law-enforcement agency, a naval shipbuilder and an aircraft-engine maker in two NATO states; at the shipbuilder it then pushed an SSH key for a persistent tunnel, captured NTLM handshakes and ran a reflective loader

Symantec's Threat Hunter Team reports that Swallowtail, which it equates with APT28, Fancy Bear and Forest Blizzard, targeted organizations in two NATO member states: a law-enforcement agency, a naval shipbuilder and a manufacturer of military aircraft engines, none named (Symantec, 2026-10-20). Recorded Future had documented the HOOKEDGE backdoor in August, from campaigns between late September 2025 and early April 2026 against government and diplomatic organizations in Romania, Spain and Turkiye, and assesses with moderate confidence that BlueDelta, which overlaps APT28, is behind it (Recorded Future, 2026-08-27).

At the shipbuilder the vector was a macro-enabled Word document opened from the Outlook attachment cache on 2026-07-24, so it arrived by email; its macro dropped a VBScript launcher, an HTML pair that auto-submits a hidden form to a webhook endpoint and a batch script (Symantec, 2026-10-20). The batch script kills any running Microsoft Edge and restarts it as a one-pixel, off-screen window carrying an inline script instead of a URL, so the browser fetches the next task from the public webhook.site service, and the batch script then runs the task and uploads its output to the same endpoint (Symantec, 2026-10-20). A second stage then took its tasks from a dedicated address, and seven tasks arrived in about 30 seconds, a cadence Symantec reads as interactive (Symantec, 2026-10-20).

The operators then pushed an SSH private key onto the host and at once opened an outbound SSH session to their own server with host-key checking disabled, legacy RSA algorithms enabled and a background remote port forward, a persistent route into the internal network; separately a short PowerShell script ran an HTTP listener on loopback and net use against it, forcing the host to authenticate to itself so the NTLM handshake could be captured (Symantec, 2026-10-20). On 2026-07-31 they ran a previously undocumented reflective loader, which decrypts an encrypted file in memory; the payload was not recovered, and the launcher was last seen on 2026-09-24 (Symantec, 2026-10-20).

Exposure
Windows endpoints where users can open Office documents from mail and macros from internet-originated documents are allowed, and hosts with outbound access to webhook services. Symantec names no victim or country.
Detection
Process-creation telemetry with parent lineage for Word spawning script hosts or the command shell, then msedge.exe killed and restarted with a one-pixel window, an off-screen position and a data: URL argument; network and proxy telemetry for msedge.exe or curl reaching a webhook service; ssh.exe started with an identity file, a remote forward and host-key checking disabled; a PowerShell HTTP listener on loopback followed by net use to localhost; and scheduled-task creation by the launcher or installer, since Symantec says the second-stage installer has a scheduled task and Recorded Future advises detecting scheduled-task abuse (Recorded Future, 2026-08-27) (Symantec, 2026-10-20).

Triage: the distinctive sequence is an Office document's script host, then Edge killed and relaunched as a one-pixel off-screen window carrying an inline script instead of a URL; the Edge launch alone is not the signal.

Defender takeaway
Block macro execution from internet-originated documents and, on any host where a HOOKEDGE launcher is found, hunt for the credential theft and the SSH tunnel described above and reset the credentials the host used, because the shipbuilder intrusion continued long after the dropper ran (Symantec, 2026-10-20).

entries.classification_html: NATOA2
entries.headline: Joint advisory on SafePay: VPN credentials and five old edge and backup flaws in, backup NAS wiped before encryption
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2020-3259 +4exploitedNATOA2

AA26-293A: FBI, CISA and German and UK law enforcement describe SafePay ransomware, which enters through VPN credentials and five edge-device and backup-server flaws and factory-resets backup NAS devices before encrypting

CISA, the FBI, the US Secret Service, Germany's Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz and UK law enforcement published advisory AA26-293A on 2026-10-20, drawing on investigations as recently as August 2026; they say SafePay has affected businesses and critical infrastructure in North America, South America, Europe and Australia since August 2024, was among the most active ransomware groups in 2026 and has impacted at least 600 separate victims (CISA et al., 2026-10-20). Initial access is exposed credentials, brute force password attacks and VPN access, with the actors using Mullvad VPN addresses and phished account profiles to reach victim networks and exploit CVE-2020-3259 and CVE-2023-20269 on edge devices, and automated scripts exploiting CVE-2023-27532, CVE-2024-40711 and CVE-2024-40766 on internet-exposed systems (CISA et al., 2026-10-20). CISA's catalog names them as Cisco ASA and Firepower Threat Defense (the first two), Veeam Backup & Replication (the next two) and SonicWall SonicOS flaws (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-10-20).

Once inside, the actors take administrative rights on existing accounts or create new ones, run commands remotely with PsExec and WinRM, enumerate network shares with ShareFinder.ps1 and SharpShares.exe, disable security software, bypass User Account Control, then move over RDP and remote-management tools (CISA et al., 2026-10-20). They compress data with 7-Zip or WinRAR and exfiltrate it with WinSCP, RClone, FileZilla or OneDrive, and sometimes install AnyDesk or TeamViewer (CISA et al., 2026-10-20). Before encrypting they halt the Volume Shadow Copy Service and reset network-attached storage that holds backup data to factory settings; encryption then appends .SafePay (CISA et al., 2026-10-20).

Exposure
An internet-facing Cisco ASA or Firepower Threat Defense, Veeam Backup & Replication or SonicWall SonicOS system that one of the five flaws affects, and any VPN or remote-access account protected by a password alone; the advisory states neither affected versions nor fixes, so they come from each vendor's advisory for the CVE. Cisco calls CVE-2020-3259 reachable by an unauthenticated, remote attacker and SonicWall's CVSS vector for CVE-2024-40766 needs no privileges and no user interaction (Cisco, 2024-02-21; SonicWall, 2024-11-20). CISA's catalog says CVE-2020-3259 affects only specific AnyConnect and WebVPN configurations, and describes CVE-2023-27532 as a Cloud Connect flaw for an unauthenticated user within the backup infrastructure network perimeter (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-10-20).
Detection
VPN and firewall authentication logs for repeated failures then a success, Mullvad exit addresses and new accounts; directory audit logs for administrator-group changes; process-creation events for PsExec, WinRM and remote-management tools installed outside a change window; archive and file-transfer tools run by non-administrative workflows; and backup and NAS audit logs for a shadow-copy service stop or a factory reset.

Triage: 7-Zip, WinRAR, RClone, FileZilla, AnyDesk, TeamViewer, PsExec and WinRM are everyday administrative tools, and the advisory warns against calling them malicious without evidence of actor use (CISA et al., 2026-10-20); a shadow-copy service stop or a factory reset of backup storage that follows them is the discriminating step.

Defender takeaway
Confirm that every Cisco ASA or Firepower Threat Defense, Veeam Backup & Replication and SonicWall SonicOS system has the vendor's fix or mitigation for the five flaws, require multi-factor authentication on VPN and administrator accounts, and keep offline backups that are encrypted and immutable so that a factory reset of the NAS does not remove the restore path; the advisory recommends offline, encrypted and immutable backups (CISA et al., 2026-10-20).

Builds on: Manno restored from backup within an afternoon; SafePay was recorded listing the commune on 28… · SonicWall CVE-2024-40766: why patched firewalls keep falling to Akira and Fog

entries.headline: Oracle's October CPU carries six unauthenticated CVSS 10.0 rows and two WebLogic 9.8 flaws; none is reported exploited
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-87337 +10NATOA2

Oracle October 2026 Critical Patch Update: six unauthenticated network CVSS 10.0 rows in Access Manager, SOA Suite, E-Business Suite and JD Edwards, and WebLogic CVSS 9.8 flaws reachable over HTTP and T3/IIOP

Oracle's Critical Patch Update advisory of 2026-10-20 contains 1295 new security patches (Oracle, 2026-10-20). Its risk matrices score 112 rows at CVSS 3.1 9.0 or higher, and 90 of those, covering 73 distinct CVE ids, are marked as remotely exploitable without authentication with a network attack vector (Oracle, 2026-10-20). Six rows score 10.0: CVE-2026-87337 in the Access Manager Authentication Engine (HTTP), CVE-2026-91231 in the SOA Suite Adapters (HTTP), CVE-2026-91216 and CVE-2026-91221 in the SOA Suite Fabric Layer (T3 and IIOP), CVE-2026-101809 in the E-Business Suite Workflow Notification Mailer (HTTP, 12.2.3 to 12.2.15) and CVE-2026-91299 in the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne Orchestrator security component (HTTP, 9.2.0.0 to 9.2.26.5) (Oracle, 2026-10-20). WebLogic Server 12.2.1.4.0, 14.1.1.0.0, 14.1.2.0.0 and 15.1.1.0.0 carry CVE-2026-91323 (HTTP) and CVE-2026-83399 (T3 and IIOP) at 9.8 and CVE-2026-87302 (HTTP) at 9.1; Identity Manager's End User Self Service has CVE-2026-91408 (T3 and IIOP, 9.8) and Access Manager's SAML path CVE-2026-87251 (9.8) (Oracle, 2026-10-20). The advisory states no exploitation for any row and carries only Oracle's standing sentence that it receives reports of attempts to exploit already-patched flaws (Oracle, 2026-10-20). Oracle points to My Oracle Support documents for patch availability (Oracle, 2026-10-20).

Exposure
A WebLogic, SOA Suite, Access Manager or Identity Manager server whose HTTP, T3 or IIOP listener, or SAML endpoint, answers from a network that is not the management network; an E-Business Suite 12.2.3 to 12.2.15 web tier with the Workflow Notification Mailer; a JD Edwards EnterpriseOne 9.2 server with the Orchestrator. The product version comes from the product's own version command or the inventory.
Detection
Oracle names no indicator, so no flaw-specific signature exists. Watch web and application-server access logs and the WebLogic and SOA server logs for requests to the affected components from untrusted sources, T3 and IIOP connections from unexpected networks in flow or load-balancer logs, and Java process-creation events where the middleware process spawns a shell, an interpreter or a download tool.
Defender takeaway
Apply the October 2026 update to the six 10.0 components first wherever they are reachable beyond the management network, then to the WebLogic and Identity Manager rows; where a patch cannot go in at once, take T3, IIOP and the administration console off untrusted networks. Oracle's next scheduled update is the Critical Security Patch Update of 17 November 2026 (Oracle, 2026-10-20).

entries.headline: The compromised actions-cool GitHub Actions were re-enabled in September with malicious tags and ran the payload again
entries.html:
HIGHupdatedNATOB2

actions-cool/issues-helper GitHub Action compromised in Mini Shai-Hulud: 53 tags moved to imposter commits that read Runner.Worker memory, re-enabled in September with the tags intact

StepSecurity disclosed on 2026-05-18 that every existing tag of the actions-cool/issues-helper GitHub Action, 53 in total, had been moved to its own imposter commit that is not reachable from the action's default branch, and that all 15 tags of the companion actions-cool/maintain-one-comment action were moved the same way (StepSecurity, 2026-05-18). The payload downloads the Bun JavaScript runtime to the runner, then a python3 child process reads the memory of the Runner.Worker process, which holds the workflow's decrypted secrets, filters the captured bytes for values flagged as secret and sends them over HTTPS to an attacker-controlled domain (StepSecurity, 2026-05-18). The 53 imposter commits carry fake "Build action for vX.Y.Z" messages in the maintainer's style and were all created within 3 minutes 16 seconds on 2026-05-18 (StepSecurity, 2026-05-18). Socket's head of threat intelligence told The Hacker News that the @antv npm compromise in the Mini Shai-Hulud campaign is likely linked to the actions-cool hack because the two share an exfiltration domain, and that "the overlap is strong enough that we're treating them as related" (The Hacker News, 2026-05-19). GitHub's security team disabled both repositories on 2026-05-19 but left the malicious tags in place; both became reachable again on 2026-09-16, so every workflow referencing either action by tag ran the payload again until GitHub disabled them a second time by 2026-09-25 (Socket, 2026-09-24). SafeDep found six more repositories infected through issues-helper between 2026-09-20 and 09-24, with the payload also committing Claude Code and VS Code hooks that run on a developer's machine when the project is opened (The Hacker News, 2026-09-25).

Exposure
Any workflow that referenced either action by a version tag pulled the malicious code on its next run after the tags moved; "Only workflows pinned to a known-good full commit SHA are unaffected" (StepSecurity, 2026-05-18). That happened on 2026-05-18 to 05-19 and again from 2026-09-16 until the second disable by 2026-09-25, and for issues-helper alone GitHub's dependency graph lists about 15,000 dependent repositories (Socket, 2026-09-24).
Detection
On the runner, the Bun runtime appearing under /home/runner/.bun/bin/bun, a python3 child process reading /proc/<Runner.Worker PID>/mem, gh auth token and sudo python3 executions, tr and grep pipelines filtering for secret-flagged values, and an outbound HTTPS connection to a domain outside the workflow's normal destinations (StepSecurity, 2026-05-18). In workflow definitions, an action reference that resolves to a commit matching no legitimate tag or branch head of the action's repository is the signature of this attack (StepSecurity, 2026-05-18). In workflow run history, runs of either action that start succeeding after a stretch of job-setup failures, or whose duration jumps from seconds to minutes, with runner logs showing Bun being set up for the action (Socket, 2026-09-24); in repository history, commits from 2026-09-16 onward that nobody can account for (Socket, 2026-09-24), in particular added Claude Code or VS Code hook configuration (The Hacker News, 2026-09-25).

Triage: an issue-housekeeping action has no reason to install a separate JavaScript runtime or run a multi-minute script; a scheduled workflow that switches from failing in seconds to running for minutes without any change to its own code means the tagged action became downloadable again (Socket, 2026-09-24).

Defender takeaway
Treat any workflow run that used either action by tag on 2026-05-18 to 05-19 or from 2026-09-16 to 09-25 as a secrets exposure: rotate every secret the workflow could read, review what its GitHub token was allowed to do, audit the repository for commits from 2026-09-16 onward, and remove the actions or pin them to a full commit SHA verified to predate 2026-05-18 (Socket, 2026-09-24). Disabling a repository leaves its tags untouched, so a later re-enable reactivates the compromise without any change to your own workflow file; SHA pinning removes that dependency (Socket, 2026-09-24). Runner egress control is the layer that still holds when a compromised action runs: StepSecurity added the exfiltration domain to Harden-Runner's global block list, which blocks outbound connections to it even in audit mode, so that "even if a compromised action somehow runs, the credentials cannot leave the runner" (StepSecurity, 2026-05-18).
Correction30 Sep 2026 06:54 UTCrun 2026-09-30T0639Z-auditbodyclassificationtechniquestitleheadlinesummaryevent_date

The Hacker News reports that GitHub disabled access to the companion maintain-one-comment repository, and Socket described the link to the Mini Shai-Hulud npm campaign as likely, based on the shared exfiltration domain, rather than confirmed; no cited source ties it to PyPI (The Hacker News, 2026-05-19). The Nx Console extension compromise named in the earlier summary is a separate incident, and no cited source says EU or Swiss organisations were affected.

Update20 Oct 2026 08:49 UTCrun 2026-10-20T0835Z-auditactionsbodyevidenceheadlinesourcessummarytechniquestitle

Socket reported on 2026-09-24 that GitHub's security team had disabled both actions-cool/issues-helper and actions-cool/maintain-one-comment on 2026-05-19, not only maintain-one-comment, and that both became reachable again on 2026-09-16, between 09:09 and 16:16 UTC, with every release tag still pointing at the content introduced on 2026-05-18, so any workflow referencing either action by tag ran the payload again on its next run; Socket could not determine why they were re-enabled (Socket, 2026-09-24). Socket places the compromise in the May 2026 Mini Shai-Hulud campaign and notes that GitHub's dependency graph lists about 15,000 dependent repositories for issues-helper alone (Socket, 2026-09-24). SafeDep found six more repositories infected through issues-helper between 2026-09-20 and 09-24, and says the payload steals the CI secrets and then commits Claude Code and VS Code hooks into the repository, which run the malware on the machine of a developer who pulls the change and opens the project (The Hacker News, 2026-09-25). GitHub disabled both repositories again by 2026-09-25, so referencing workflows now fail at job setup (Socket, 2026-09-24; The Hacker News, 2026-09-25).

entries.headline: GhostAction: fake security workflows now harvest whole git histories; rotating Actions secrets is not enough
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB1

GhostAction returns: stolen maintainer credentials push a fake security-audit workflow into the victims' own GitHub repositories, which now harvests credentials from the entire git history

StepSecurity reports that on 2026-10-08 the GhostAction GitHub Actions credential-theft campaign used the accounts of two open-source maintainers to push a workflow disguised as a security improvement to 345 repositories in two automated sweeps, among them an Uber-owned repository that one maintainer could still write to (StepSecurity, 2026-10-09); Socket's independent analysis counts 346 (Socket, 2026-10-09). The operator holds a maintainer's GitHub credential, which StepSecurity assesses as most plausibly a personal access token leaked through infostealer logs or credential dumps, then commits a workflow titled to look like a security audit straight to the default branch under the victim's own identity, unsigned and without a pull request; that push runs it, and nothing in an audit log looks anomalous unless the content is read (StepSecurity, 2026-10-09). GitGuardian says the technique was later reused in the Shai-Hulud campaigns and remains at the core of the Mini Shai-Hulud malware family (GitGuardian, 2026-10-07).

The newer payload sends the named Actions secrets and every cloud, AI-provider and SaaS credential pattern found in the working tree and the entire git history to a hardcoded address over plain HTTP, so no DNS lookup occurs (StepSecurity, 2026-10-09). StepSecurity saw the attacker's server acknowledge the request four seconds into the run at the Uber-owned repository (StepSecurity, 2026-10-09); neither it nor Socket has seen a malicious package release from the stolen credentials yet (Socket, 2026-10-09; StepSecurity, 2026-10-09). The wave was far larger than those first counts: Socket's update of 9 October reports more than 500 accounts committing the workflow to tens of thousands of repositories since 7 October (Socket, 2026-10-09), and GitGuardian's update of 13 October counts more than 30,000 repositories across 3,000 users and organisations between 8 and 12 October, reached by compromising about 1,900 GitHub accounts (GitGuardian, 2026-10-07).

Exposure
Any GitHub account whose token or session credential has leaked, and every repository it can write to; StepSecurity says a workflow posing as a security audit or an Actions security workflow that appeared in a repository you maintain since 2026-08-31 means treat it as a confirmed breach (StepSecurity, 2026-10-09).
Detection
Source-control audit logs: workflow files added straight to default branches without a pull request by a maintainer identity, unsigned commits landing in many repositories within minutes; an organisation-scoped code search with StepSecurity's published content-marker queries for security-themed workflow files (audit, check or Actions security); runner egress logs: an HTTP POST to a bare IP address with no preceding DNS lookup (StepSecurity, 2026-10-09). Removing the workflow does not undo the theft: StepSecurity says any secret ever committed to a repository must be treated as compromised, so treat each run as an exfiltration, scan the full history and rotate every credential found (StepSecurity, 2026-10-09); GitGuardian adds that the GitHub credential that allowed the injection must be revoked too, or someone else will reuse it (GitGuardian, 2026-10-07).

Triage: the audit-log pattern separates this from a team adding a scanning workflow: no pull request, unsigned commits across many repositories, and a manual dispatch right after creation (StepSecurity, 2026-10-09).

Defender takeaway
Search the GitHub organisations your teams and suppliers administer for security-themed workflow files (audit, check or Actions security); on a hit revoke the committing credential and rotate everything in the repository's full history. StepSecurity saw requiring approval for workflow runs stop the exfiltration and names branch protection on .github/workflows so workflow changes need pull-request review (StepSecurity, 2026-10-09).
Update20 Oct 2026 08:42 UTCrun 2026-10-20T0835Z-auditbodyevidencesourcing_notesummary

GitGuardian updated its analysis on 2026-10-13 from its own dataset: between 8 and 12 October the campaign targeted more than 30,000 repositories across 3,000 users and organisations by compromising the GitHub accounts of about 1,900 users, and tried to extract 3,174 secrets from public repositories' CI, with the largest spike on 8 and 9 October (GitGuardian, 2026-10-07). Socket's update of 9 October, with more than 500 accounts and tens of thousands of repositories since 7 October, is of the same order (Socket, 2026-10-09). GitGuardian says GitHub started preventing the malicious workflow from running on 9 October, so the further waves it saw on 10 and 12 October, with the same payload, could not extract any secrets (GitGuardian, 2026-10-07); a workflow from those later waves still means the account that committed it is compromised. Part of the October victims had already been hit in the September 2025 and August 2026 waves, and GitGuardian assesses that the operator likely relies in part on secrets left unrotated since earlier campaigns (GitGuardian, 2026-10-07).

entries.headline: Zammad 6.5.5 is an emergency fix for the exploited session-leak RCE on 6.5; 7.2.2 fixes the root escalation
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-102489 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-102489 / CVE-2026-102490, Zammad helpdesk: a session-hijack remote code execution and a zammad-to-root escalation, both reported exploited since 21 September; 7.2.2 fixes the root flaw on DEB and RPM installs

DIVD, the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure, says attackers first reached its systems on 2026-09-21 and that they got in through two zero-days in Zammad, the customer-service ticketing software (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-09), which together allowed session hijacking, remote code execution and privilege escalation from the Zammad user to root "in seconds" (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-09). From there the attackers could access other services and exfiltrate data; DIVD says network segmentation and its incident response stopped them going deeper, and that volunteer data such as email addresses and possibly contact details got out (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-09). DIVD assesses the attack as driven by AI agents, because the attacker's scripts carry notes in which the agent justifies its own actions, and says it sees no link to any known public threat actor (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-09).

CVE-2026-102489 is a session hijack that leads to remote code execution as the zammad user in versions 6.3.0 to 6.5.4; the defect is also present in 7.0.0 to 7.1.3 but DIVD says it is not exploitable there because of environment conditions (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-01). NCSC-NL describes it as exploitable by an attacker who has not logged in (NCSC-NL, 2026-09-30), while DIVD's CVE record scores it CVSS 4.0 8.7 with passive user interaction (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-09-29). CVE-2026-102490 lets the local zammad user escalate to root, in all versions including the latest alpha according to DIVD's case page (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-01) and in DEB and RPM (packager.io) installations only according to Zammad's advisory of 2026-10-08 (Zammad advisory GHSA-p97w-927q-8vxq, 2026-10-08), and DIVD scores the pair 9.4 when chained (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-09-29). NCSC-NL states both flaws have been actively exploited since 2026-09-21, rates likelihood and damage as high, said then that Zammad had released an update for the first flaw only and that the second "is not yet fixed" (translated from Dutch) (NCSC-NL, 2026-09-30). DIVD's case page instead lists patch status Available, recommends upgrading to Zammad 7 or taking Zammad offline, and says it is scanning for and notifying owners of vulnerable instances (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-01).

Exposure
Self-hosted Zammad. The code-execution flaw needs a version from 6.3.0 to 6.5.4 per DIVD and NCSC-NL (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-01; NCSC-NL, 2026-09-30), and Zammad says only 6.5 and older are exploitable and 7.0 and later are not affected (Zammad, 2026-10-01); the root escalation was reported by DIVD as present in every version from 1.5.0 (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-01), while Zammad's advisory of 2026-10-08 limits it to installations from the DEB and RPM packages (packager.io), says every released packaged version was affected and says installations from source or the official container images were not (Zammad advisory GHSA-p97w-927q-8vxq, 2026-10-08); Zammad assesses it as a local privilege escalation that needs prior access to the server (Zammad, 2026-10-05), so it matters as the second stage after the code-execution flaw or any other foothold as the zammad user. Zammad says SaaS customers need take no action for 7.2.1 because their instances are already patched (Zammad, 2026-10-06), and the 27 advisories of 2026-10-06 list affected versions up to 7.2.0 (Zammad advisory records, 2026-10-06); the two critical ones concern the public sign-up form and accounts with multi-factor authentication configured that never completed email verification (Zammad advisory GHSA-79wh-8g2f-xj2c, 2026-10-06; Zammad advisory GHSA-f3qr-94c2-7mx2, 2026-10-06).
Detection
Web and application logs on the Zammad host. DIVD links a log-check script for the code-execution flaw that searches the Zammad application and nginx logs for error lines carrying session material, a cookie value or a client list, and says to look for unfamiliar processes and files as well (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-01; DIVD log-check script, 2026-10-01). Horizon3's public exploit shows the flaw from the attacker's side: a single request to the /ws WebSocket endpoint makes the server return an error carrying every active user's session cookies, so those error log lines are the trace, and an administrator session obtained that way can install a package through the admin interface that writes a template over the password-reset email view, so unexpected packages and overridden view templates in the application directory are the follow-on artifact (Horizon3, 2026-10-07). DIVD lists no process or network indicators, so these follow from the mechanism and from DIVD's account that the attackers reached other services: shells or interpreters as children of the Zammad service account, a privilege change from that account to root, and connections from the ticket host to internal services it does not normally contact. Updating to 7.2.2 closes the escalation but does not show whether it was already used: Zammad's advisory says an attacker holding a foothold as the zammad account could have reached root within seconds (Zammad advisory GHSA-p97w-927q-8vxq, 2026-10-08), so on any host where code ran as that account, look for new root-owned files, services and processes as well. More generally, updating does not show whether an instance was already compromised: NCSC-NL asks operators to copy application and network logs before installing the update so the second flaw's use can be investigated later (NCSC-NL, 2026-09-30). For the two critical flaws of 2026-10-06 the advisories' mechanics point to application and authentication logs: sign-ups that carry account attributes the form should ignore, such as an organization membership or a pre-confirmed state, and a session established through an email-verification link with no second-factor step, followed by creation of a personal access token, which outlives the session (Zammad advisory GHSA-79wh-8g2f-xj2c, 2026-10-06; Zammad advisory GHSA-f3qr-94c2-7mx2, 2026-10-06).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade to Zammad 7.2.2 after saving the logs, as Zammad says to upgrade to the latest version immediately (Zammad, 2026-10-08): 7.2.2 fixes the root escalation on DEB and RPM installs (Zammad advisory GHSA-p97w-927q-8vxq, 2026-10-08), 6.5 and older receive no regular security fixes (Zammad, 2026-10-01), with 6.5.5 as an emergency fix for the code-execution flaw on 6.5 only where upgrading is not yet possible (Zammad, 2026-10-15), and 7.2.0 is affected by the advisories published on 2026-10-06 (Zammad advisory records, 2026-10-06); treat any internet-reachable instance on 6.3.0 to 6.5.4 since 2026-09-21 as possibly compromised, including the ticket data and anything the host can reach, since NCSC-NL says an attacker can take over the system, read, change or delete data and use it for further attacks (NCSC-NL, 2026-09-30), and treat a DEB or RPM host where code ran as the zammad account as possibly root-compromised, since the upgrade does not undo an escalation already made; keep restricting access to the underlying server to trusted administrators, as Zammad advises (Zammad, 2026-10-05), and keep Zammad behind authentication or off the internet and segmented, as DIVD credits segmentation for stopping its own intruders (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-09).
Update04 Oct 2026 04:43 UTCrun 2026-10-04T0405Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

CISA added both CVE-2026-102489 and CVE-2026-102490 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-02 and describes them as chainable (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-10-02). Zammad published its own statement on 2026-10-01: exploitation of CVE-2026-102489 is "only possible on Zammad 6.5 and older, because of the runtime environment those versions use", those versions no longer receive security fixes, Zammad 7.0 and later are not affected, and the code is hardened in 7.2.0, the current stable release (Zammad, 2026-10-01). For CVE-2026-102490 Zammad says "DIVD has not given us any technical details about this vulnerability", so it cannot confirm the flaw, its scope or the affected versions, names no fix, and disputes DIVD's handling of the disclosure, citing a report to Zammad on 2026-09-24 and public scanning and disclosure on 2026-09-26 (Zammad, 2026-10-01). Zammad also says it first received a report about CVE-2026-102489 in August 2026 and analysed it then, which is before the exploitation DIVD dates to 2026-09-21, so the vendor may have known of the flaw before it was exploited (Zammad, 2026-10-01).

Update06 Oct 2026 04:58 UTCrun 2026-10-06T0405Z-intelsummarycvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Zammad published its own security advisory for both CVEs on 2026-10-05 (Zammad, 2026-10-05). For CVE-2026-102490 it now says it has received DIVD's technical details and is analysing the issue as a high-priority item, assesses it as a local privilege escalation that cannot be exploited remotely on its own because an attacker would need access to the underlying server beforehand, and says the issue is related to a confirmed vulnerability in packager.io and that its team is working on a solution (Zammad, 2026-10-05). The advisory names no fixed release for it. Zammad recommends that administrators still on 6.5 or older update immediately, since those versions no longer receive security updates, and that access to the underlying server be restricted to trusted administrators (Zammad, 2026-10-05).

Update07 Oct 2026 04:52 UTCrun 2026-10-07T0404Z-intelheadlinesummarytagstechniquescvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Zammad released 7.2.1 on 2026-10-06 as an important security update that addresses critical vulnerabilities, with no action needed for SaaS customers and an immediate upgrade advised for self-hosted installations (Zammad, 2026-10-06). The release comes with 27 security advisories published the same day, rated by Zammad as two critical, twelve high, ten medium and three low (Zammad advisory records, 2026-10-06); every affected range ends at 7.2.0 and none carries a CVE id yet (Zammad advisory records, 2026-10-06). 7.2.0, the release Zammad recommended on 2026-10-01, is therefore affected itself.

The two critical advisories: the public sign-up form accepted account fields it should have ignored, so an attacker without any account could register on an email address they did not own, have that account treated as already confirmed and add it to any organization, then read and reply to other customers' tickets in those organizations, with a second flaw letting a customer change fields of another customer's ticket in the same organization (Zammad advisory GHSA-79wh-8g2f-xj2c, 2026-10-06); and the email-verification flow established a fully authenticated session for an account that had never completed email verification and had multi-factor authentication configured, without the second factor, which needs possession of the account's verification email but no password and carries the account's permissions up to administrator (Zammad advisory GHSA-f3qr-94c2-7mx2, 2026-10-06). Among the high-rated advisories are a remote code execution through a template sanitizer bypass in automation configuration, a session identifier disclosed in an authenticated configuration response that enabled off-host session takeover, and a second-order SQL injection in ticket overview sorting (Zammad advisory records, 2026-10-06).

No source reports exploitation of any of the 27 flaws. Zammad's advisory of 2026-10-05 still says its team is working on a solution for CVE-2026-102490 and none of the 27 titles names that flaw, so whether 7.2.1 closes the exploited root escalation is not stated (Zammad, 2026-10-05; Zammad advisory records, 2026-10-06).

Update08 Oct 2026 04:57 UTCrun 2026-10-08T0404Z-intelheadlinesummarytagstechniquescvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Horizon3 published a reverse-engineering of CVE-2026-102489 on 2026-10-07, with a proof-of-concept repository (Horizon3, 2026-10-07). Zammad keeps the state of every connected WebSocket client, including the session Cookie header, in a class-level registry that is passed to every event; a single request to the /ws WebSocket endpoint carrying the event name base makes the dispatcher instantiate an event class that has no implementation, and the resulting error message, which includes the object's full representation, is returned to the caller together with the cookies of all active users (Horizon3, 2026-10-07). With a leaked administrator session an attacker writes files into the application directory through the package installation endpoint, overrides the built-in password-reset email view with a malicious template and triggers a password reset for any user, which executes the template as the zammad user (Horizon3, 2026-10-07).

Horizon3 says it believes the privilege escalation is CVE-2026-102490, that it remains unpatched, and that it is withholding those details (Horizon3, 2026-10-07). Horizon3's write-up names no Zammad version; Zammad's advisory of 2026-10-05 says CVE-2026-102489 is exploitable only on 6.5 and earlier (Zammad, 2026-10-05).

Update10 Oct 2026 03:43 UTCrun 2026-10-10T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Zammad released 7.2.2 on 2026-10-08 as an important security update that addresses a vulnerability affecting only DEB and RPM packages built with packager.io; SaaS customers need take no action and self-hosted installations are told to upgrade immediately (Zammad, 2026-10-08). Its GitHub advisory GHSA-p97w-927q-8vxq describes a local privilege escalation to root: services started as root and executed files that the unprivileged zammad account owned and could write before dropping privileges, and that account could write to the installation directory, so an attacker already running code as zammad could have reached root within seconds because the services restarted automatically whenever they stopped; installations from source or the official container images were not affected and every released packaged version was (Zammad advisory GHSA-p97w-927q-8vxq, 2026-10-08). The advisory record lists CVE-2026-102490, names 7.2.2 as the patched version and versions up to 7.2.1 as vulnerable (Zammad advisory GHSA-p97w-927q-8vxq, 2026-10-08), and DIVD's case page says Zammad has fixed the first flaw in release 7.2 and the second in release 7.2.2 (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-09). Zammad's advisory page of 2026-10-05 still says its team is working on a solution (Zammad, 2026-10-05), so the vendor's own pages disagree on status. As of 2026-10-10 nothing had changed for the code-execution flaw: it stayed exploitable only on 6.5 and older, which received no security fixes.

Update20 Oct 2026 08:40 UTCrun 2026-10-20T0835Z-auditactionsbodycvesevidenceheadlinesourcessummary

Zammad released 6.5.5 on 2026-10-15 as an exceptional security release for the unsupported 6.5 series: it hardens the WebSocket server code to address CVE-2026-102489 and is meant for customers who cannot yet move to a supported version (Zammad, 2026-10-15). It is available only through a new package repository that administrators must switch to before updating, and Zammad says it is a temporary measure that does not extend the 6.5 support lifecycle; 6.5 users who cannot upgrade to 7.2.2 yet are told to install it immediately, and every self-hosted installation is still told to upgrade to 7.2.2 as soon as possible (Zammad, 2026-10-15). The release notes name only CVE-2026-102489 and do not say whether the 6.5.5 packages also carry the root-escalation fix that 7.2.2 brought to DEB and RPM installs (Zammad, 2026-10-15). The release is for the 6.5 series only, so 6.3 and 6.4 installations, which DIVD lists as vulnerable (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-09-29), still have to be upgraded.

entries.headline: Three configuration-dependent NGINX heap flaws (CVSS 9.2) are fixed in 1.30.6 and 1.31.7; Debian stable is not yet
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-15176 +4NATOA2

CVE-2026-15176 / CVE-2026-93479 / CVE-2026-97205, NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus: three unauthenticated heap-corruption flaws rated CVSS 4.0 9.2, reachable only in specific configurations and fixed in 1.30.6 and 1.31.7

nginx's change log for 1.30.6, dated 14 October 2026, lists five security fixes, which nginx.org's advisories page ties to 1.30.6 (stable) and 1.31.7 (mainline) (nginx.org change log, 2026-10-14; nginx.org, 2026-10-14); three of them are CVE-2026-15176, a heap buffer overflow in the core module that CCB describes as reachable where a location uses alias together with rewrite and a set or return directive referencing $request_filename, or where $request_filename appears in an access-log format; CVE-2026-93479, a heap buffer overflow in script evaluation that affects configurations whose regex map captures are referenced in root or an access-log format before the map's output variable, or that use a non-cacheable variable in a string expression; and CVE-2026-97205, a use-after-free when asynchronous file I/O is enabled, which Daily CyberSecurity relays from F5 as triggered by an SSI page with include virtual commands (Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium, 2026-10-19; Daily CyberSecurity, 2026-10-14). Each is scored CVSS 4.0 9.2 and reachable by an unauthenticated network attacker, the first two under conditions beyond the attacker's control, with CCB's warning and vector covering the first two and Daily CyberSecurity all three (Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium, 2026-10-19; Daily CyberSecurity, 2026-10-14). F5's CNA text says the overflow may restart the worker process and that attackers can execute code where ASLR is disabled or can be bypassed (Debian Security Tracker, 2026-10-20). Daily CyberSecurity reports that F5 has confirmed no public proof of concept for any of the three, and no exploitation is reported (Daily CyberSecurity, 2026-10-14). Help Net Security reports that VulnCheck flagged exploitation attempts against an earlier NGINX flaw, CVE-2026-42945, three days after the flaw and its proof of concept were public (Help Net Security, 2026-05-18). The other two are CVE-2026-95101 (with HTTP/3, part of an unknown frame might be treated as the request body, bypassing client_max_body_size or injecting data into the proxied request) and CVE-2026-97629 (with TLS session ticket key rotation, one key was left uninitialised, which might allow forging a session) (nginx.org change log, 2026-10-14); nginx.org rates all five medium (nginx.org, 2026-10-14).

Exposure
Nginx 0.1.29 to 1.31.6 depending on the flaw, with branches older than 1.30 outside the range of CVE-2026-93479, and NGINX Plus R33 to R36 and 37.0.0 to 37.1.0 for the first two (nginx.org, 2026-10-14; Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium, 2026-10-19). A build is affected only if its configuration matches one of the patterns above, which nginx -T prints with every include; the version string alone is not enough, because distribution packages carry their own fixes. The Debian tracker marks bookworm (1.22.1-9+deb12u10) and trixie (1.26.3-3+deb13u9) vulnerable and shows a fix only in forky and sid at 1.30.4-8 (Debian Security Tracker, 2026-10-20).
Detection
F5 says the overflow leads to a worker restart, so process-supervision and error-log telemetry for unexpected worker exits and respawn bursts, matched against the unauthenticated requests to the affected locations in the access log, is the signal (Debian Security Tracker, 2026-10-20). Patching does not remediate a compromise that already happened (Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium, 2026-10-19).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade to 1.30.6 or 1.31.7 (NGINX Plus 37.0.5.1 or 37.1.0.1), starting with internet-facing instances whose configuration matches a pattern above; until a package is fixed, F5's workarounds are aio off or ssi off for CVE-2026-97205, named captures confined to the matching block for CVE-2026-93479, and no alias in the affected locations or no $request_filename reference for CVE-2026-15176 (Daily CyberSecurity, 2026-10-14).

entries.headline: Citrix confirms attacks on a new NetScaler SAML flaw that the September fixed builds do not close
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-88779exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-88779, Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway: a SAML-triggered memory overflow still hits appliances on the September fixed builds, and Citrix confirms targeted attacks (CVSS 4.0 8.7)

Citrix's bulletin CTX697174 describes CVE-2026-88779, a memory overflow in customer-managed NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway reachable only when the appliance is configured as a SAML service provider or identity provider; the CVSS 4.0 vector is network, no privileges, no interaction, availability impact only (Citrix, 2026-10-03). Citrix says it "has observed targeted attacks on unmitigated NetScaler deployments which can lead to Denial of Service" and has not identified an integrity impact on customer data (Citrix, 2026-10-03). The flaw is independent of the vulnerabilities disclosed in the earlier bulletin CTX697096 (Citrix, 2026-10-02), so an appliance already on 14.1-73.37 or 13.1-64.23 is still affected, and Citrix tells operators who meet the SAML precondition to "upgrade your deployment again" (Citrix, 2026-10-03). The fixed builds are 14.1-73.41, 13.1-64.28, 14.1-73.41 FIPS and 13.1-37.282 (Citrix, 2026-10-03).

Until the upgrade, Citrix offers Global Deny List signatures through NetScaler Console with virtual patching enabled, for builds from 14.1-73.37 up to 14.1-73.41 and from 13.1-64.23 up to 13.1-64.28; they "can help to mitigate" the flaw, but the upgrade is the fix (Citrix, 2026-10-03).

Other reporting reads more into the flaw: administrators reported repeated crashes and reboots of appliances running patched releases, including 14.1-73.37, with the nsaaad authentication service failing after crafted SAML-related requests, one seeing a script-download command in the logs that did not succeed and another a payload in the username field (Cyber Press, 2026-10-03). heise relays researcher Kevin Beaumont's observation that one of two patched honeypots was running a downloaded binary, and a statement that watchTowr Labs reproduced the flaw (heise online, 2026-10-03); ASD's ACSC says an attacker "may induce system crashes, denial of service and potential exploitation" and that it is aware of impacts to Australian organisations (ASD's ACSC, 2026-10-03). None of these sources gives evidence of code execution beyond that observation and reproduction claim, and CISA added the flaw to its KEV catalog on 2026-10-04 (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-10-04).

Exposure
A customer-managed NetScaler ADC or Gateway (Secure Private Access Hybrid deployments using NetScaler instances too) whose configuration holds a SAML service-provider or identity-provider action (Citrix, 2026-10-03); Citrix ties the issue to deployments that use SAML authentication with Gateway or AAA virtual servers, and its check is a configuration search for add authentication samlAction or add authentication samlIdPProfile, then compare the running build with the fixed list above (Citrix, 2026-10-03).
Detection
Appliance system, authentication-daemon and HA logs: repeated nsaaad crashes, failovers and reboots on a SAML-configured appliance, correlated with inbound SAML request volume in gateway access and firewall logs, since heise says the exploit likely works by sending a massive number of SAML requests (heise online, 2026-10-03). The Citrix pages for this flaw list no signs of compromise to look for (Citrix, 2026-10-03), and the crash signs are administrator reports (Cyber Press, 2026-10-03; heise online, 2026-10-03). For the compromise check, watchTowr's Jake Knott says Citrix provides an indicator-of-compromise script that teams can run against exposed appliances, though a clean result is not definitive proof (The Register, 2026-10-05).

Triage: reboots alone are not proof of compromise; crashes together with malformed authentication traffic and scanning warrant incident-response handling until forensics rules out intrusion (Cyber Press, 2026-10-03).

Defender takeaway
Treat every SAML-configured NetScaler as exposed even if it is already on the September fixed builds: upgrade to the .41 and .28 builds or the FIPS builds, move identity-provider appliances on to 14.1-73.46, 13.1-64.29 or the FIPS builds that close CVE-2026-107406, and use the Global Deny List signatures only as a bridge for this flaw. Do not read the denial-of-service scoring as a reason to wait: crashes are reported on appliances already on the September builds, code execution through this flaw alone is unconfirmed, and Rapid7 saw the crash used as the reboot trigger of a root-execution chain together with CVE-2026-88771, so repeated crashes on an appliance not yet patched for that flaw warrant its compromise checks (Rapid7, 2026-10-19).
Improvement05 Oct 2026 04:32 UTCrun 2026-10-05T0404Z-intelsummarytagscvessourcesevidencebody

CISA added CVE-2026-88779 to its KEV catalog on 2026-10-04, after Citrix's bulletin (CISA, 2026-10-04); the catalog describes a memory-buffer flaw that "could allow for a denial of service" (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-10-04). That is the scope Citrix states, so the listing confirms exploitation without adding evidence of code execution, and the upgrade guidance above is unchanged.

Update09 Oct 2026 03:52 UTCrun 2026-10-09T0255Z-intelsummaryactionsreferencessourcesevidencebody

Citrix published bulletin CTX697191 on 2026-10-08 for CVE-2026-107406, a memory overflow in customer-managed NetScaler ADC and Gateway that leads to remote code execution or denial of service (CVSS 4.0 9.5) and applies to the same SAML configurations (Citrix, 2026-10-08). For an appliance configured as a SAML identity provider the affected builds run through 14.1-73.41, 13.1-64.28 and the FIPS and NDcPP equivalents (Citrix, 2026-10-08), and those are the builds named above as the fix for CVE-2026-88779 (Citrix, 2026-10-03); the fixed builds for the new flaw are 14.1-73.46, 13.1-64.29, 14.1-73.46 FIPS and 13.1.37.283 and later (Citrix, 2026-10-08). An appliance that is only a SAML service provider is listed as affected only before 14.1-73.37 and 13.1-64.23, so the 14.1-73.41 and 13.1-64.28 builds remain enough for it (Citrix, 2026-10-08). Citrix's blog of the same day says that as of the bulletin's publication it is not aware of any unmitigated exploits of the new flaw (Citrix, 2026-10-08).

Update20 Oct 2026 03:40 UTCrun 2026-10-20T0256Z-intelsummaryactionssourcesevidencebody

Rapid7's incident analysis of an early-October compromise of a NetScaler ADC on an affected 14.1 build shows CVE-2026-88779 used as the crash and reboot condition in a two-flaw sequence with CVE-2026-88771, the pre-authentication log-poisoning flaw that supplies attacker-controlled command text: repeated nsaaad crashes and a Pitboss reboot followed text inserted into an authentication username, and after the reboot the call-home crash handler processed the retained text and executed a payload as root (Rapid7, 2026-10-19). The root execution therefore came through the log-poisoning flaw and the crash handler, with this flaw supplying the reboot, and Rapid7 reports persistence, internal reconnaissance and exfiltration of the appliance configuration after it; the full account is in the CVE-2026-88771 analysis (Rapid7, 2026-10-19).

Improvement21 Oct 2026 08:16 UTCrun 2026-10-21T0800Z-auditbodyevidencesources

watchTowr's Jake Knott told The Register that "Citrix provides an indicator-of-compromise script that teams can run to check exposed appliances for signs of compromise, though a clean result is not definitive proof" (The Register, 2026-10-05). Citrix's own guidance for this flaw names no such script and tells customers to follow their standard incident response processes if they identify signs of compromise (Citrix, 2026-10-03).

actions: Upgrade every internet-facing NetScaler ADC/Gateway to 14.1-73.37+ (14.1-FIPS 14.1-73.37 FIPS+) or 13.1-64.23+ (13.1-FIPS/NDcPP 13.1-37.279+) now (a SAML-configured appliance needs the later builds named for CVE-2026-88779, and an identity provider 14.1-73.46 or 13.1-64.29); on a 13.1-branch appliance run `show ns variable` first; if it returns any variables, install 13.1-64.24 instead to avoid a known reboot loop.
