entries.headline: Two exploited NetScaler zero-days: one in default configuration, one on by default on VPN servers; no workaround
entries.html:
CRITICALCVE-2026-88771 +7exploitedupdatedNATOA1

CVE-2026-88771 / CVE-2026-88772, Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway: unauthenticated pre-auth RCE zero-days exploited before a patch existed (CVSS 4.0 9.5)

Citrix's security bulletin CTX697096, published 2026-09-27, fixes eight NetScaler ADC / NetScaler Gateway vulnerabilities, two of which Citrix says have been exploited (Citrix, 2026-09-27); watchTowr notes they were exploited as zero-days, "before any fix existed" (watchTowr, 2026-09-27). CVE-2026-88771 (CWE-20, improper input validation, CVSS 4.0 9.5) lets an unauthenticated remote attacker execute arbitrary commands on every NetScaler ADC/Gateway deployment in its default configuration; no feature needs to be enabled first. CVE-2026-88772 (CWE-119, memory overflow to RCE or DoS, CVSS 4.0 9.5) is reachable wherever DTLS is enabled, which Citrix states is the default on any VPN virtual server, so most VPN-fronting Gateway deployments meet the precondition unless DTLS was explicitly disabled. Citrix's own bulletin states plainly: "Exploits of CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 on unmitigated NetScaler deployments have been observed" (Citrix, 2026-09-27). CISA added both to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-09-27 and flags them for forensic triage (CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog, 2026-09-27), and CERT-EU's advisory the same day states "Citrix has confirmed active exploitation of these 2 critical vulnerabilities in the wild" and recommends a compromise assessment on every internet-facing appliance (CERT-EU, 2026-09-27).

The disclosure path itself is a defender-relevant data point. NetScaler administrators reported being told by IT suppliers and security teams to shut appliances down over the weekend of 26-27 September, before any CVE identifier or vendor advisory existed; BleepingComputer reports that NCSC-NL reportedly sent a pre-notification to its constituency and that NCSC-NL declined to confirm the leaked notice's contents (BleepingComputer, 2026-09-27) but published its own public advisory NCSC-2026-0394 the same day once Citrix's bulletin shipped (NCSC-NL, 2026-09-27). watchTowr independently and publicly flagged credible rumors of unpatched, in-the-wild NetScaler RCEs on 2026-09-26, a day ahead of Citrix's own bulletin. No public attribution of the exploiting activity exists; watchTowr's FAQ states "No attribution has been made public," while noting NetScaler perimeter appliances have historically been targeted by both state-sponsored and ransomware-affiliated actors, consistent with the CitrixBleed (CVE-2023-4966) and CitrixBleed 2 (CVE-2025-5777) history on the same product line (watchTowr, 2026-09-27).

The same bulletin fixes six configuration-dependent companion flaws not reported exploited: an HTTP request-smuggling flaw (CVE-2026-88773, CVSS 9.3), a policy-bypass flaw via HTTP URL-based expressions (CVE-2026-88774, CVSS 7.0), three further memory-overflow conditions gated respectively on a Gateway/AAA virtual server, an Oracle-type load-balancing virtual server, or a non-HTTP Layer-7 protocol on an LB/CS/CGNAT-LSN/NAT64 device (CVE-2026-88775/88776/88777, each CVSS 8.8), and a predictable-TCP-ISN weakness (CVE-2026-88778, CVSS 8.8) whose remediation is not covered by the version upgrade alone: it additionally requires enabling Enhanced ISN Generation. This is a distinct CVE family from CVE-2026-19490 and from the CitrixBleed/CitrixBleed 2 lineage named above; watchTowr states directly that appliances already patched for CVE-2026-19490 remain vulnerable to CVE-2026-88771/88772 unless running one of the new fixed builds (watchTowr, 2026-09-27). Fixed builds are 14.1-73.37, 13.1-64.23, 14.1-73.37 FIPS and 13.1-37.279 (FIPS/NDcPP); watchTowr flags an upgrade caveat on the 13.1 branch: run show ns variable first, and if it returns any variables, install 13.1-64.24 instead to avoid a known reboot loop during the upgrade. A separate bulletin of 2026-10-03 adds CVE-2026-88779 for SAML-configured appliances, which these builds do not fix (see the 2026-10-04 update below).

Detection and hunting. Citrix has published no workaround for either exploited flaw (watchTowr, 2026-09-27); Mandiant's interim network controls are described in the update below, and its DTLS and UDP/443 controls address CVE-2026-88772 alone, so the priority is upgrading, not mitigating in place. Before patching, capture logs, an instance snapshot where the appliance is virtual, a support bundle and a core dump from every appliance that has been internet-facing, since the upgrade can overwrite forensic evidence of prior compromise (watchTowr, 2026-09-27; Unit 42, 2026-09-30). A limited IOC scan is available from 14.1-73.36+ with telemetry enabled via the NetScaler Console Security Advisory page or through Citrix Support, but Citrix itself cautions the indicators do not cover every exploitation technique (watchTowr, 2026-09-27), so a clean scan is not proof an appliance was not already compromised before patching, and CERT-EU recommends a compromise assessment on every internet-facing appliance (CERT-EU, 2026-09-27). Zscaler's telemetry adds appliance-initiated downloads to unfamiliar addresses, an unexpected executable under /var and a Perl CGI handler in the web server configuration to the post-exploitation checks (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-10-16). Rapid7 adds, from one investigated intrusion, a setuid bit set on /bin/sh, web shells behind CSS-looking Apache aliases, nsaaad crashes followed by Pitboss reboots, an outbound agent that polls an external endpoint every 15 seconds and implant files synchronised to the HA peer, and says to inspect both nodes of every HA pair and to rotate the LDAP and RADIUS credentials, SSL private keys and key-encryption material held in the configuration, which that intrusion staged and exfiltrated (Rapid7, 2026-10-19).

Triage: for CVE-2026-88771 the precursor sits in the appliance's own logs: header, username or other request values carrying shell metacharacters (semicolons, backticks) together with Pitboss crash-message text such as "PPE unexpectedly died", which the crash-log monitor script later parses as root (watchTowr Labs, 2026-09-28). Legitimate clients have no reason to send crash-message text in a request field, so such a log line is the signal rather than a benign lookalike. For CVE-2026-88772, GTIG names a DTLS handshake-failure "Internal Error" line in the syslog, which successful exploitation produced, and packet-engine termination or watchdog "NOT restarting" lines in the FreeBSD system log, which NetScaler does not forward to a SIEM by default. A handshake failure followed within minutes by a packet-engine termination on the same appliance is a strong exploitation signal, but GTIG advises alerting on the watchdog messages and terminations independently rather than requiring both (GTIG/Mandiant, 2026-09-29).

Defender takeaway
Every internet-facing NetScaler ADC/Gateway deployment needs the patch now regardless of whether DTLS is knowingly enabled: Citrix states it is the VPN vServer default, so an administrator who never explicitly configured DTLS may still be exposed to CVE-2026-88772. NetScaler Gateway is a perimeter VPN and remote-access layer (watchTowr, 2026-09-27), and CERT-EU, NCSC-NL and CERT.at each issued same-day advisories (CERT-EU, 2026-09-27; NCSC-NL, 2026-09-27; CERT.at, 2026-09-27), with NCSC-CH's Cyber Security Hub following on 2026-09-28 (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-09-28). GTIG lists government among the sectors likely impacted in North America and Europe (GTIG/Mandiant, 2026-09-29).
Update29 Sep 2026 04:35 UTCrun 2026-09-29T0405Z-inteltechniquessourcesevidenceactionsbody

watchTowr Labs' root-cause analysis, published 2026-09-28, names the actual vulnerable component behind CVE-2026-88771: not the nsppe packet engine that has carried most historical NetScaler CVEs, but ns_monuploadd_err.pl, a Perl script that searches NetScaler system logs for Pitboss packet-engine crash messages, "missed too many heartbeats" or "unexpectedly died", to recover a core-dump filename (watchTowr Labs, 2026-09-28). The pre-patch script extracted that filename with an unsanitized shell pipeline and re-interpolated the attacker-influenced string into a second backtick command: "The Command Injection happens in the next line, when Perl interpolates that string into another backtick command" (watchTowr Labs, 2026-09-28), executing as root because nearly every NetScaler process runs with root privileges. Critically, the trigger is not confined to the SSLVPN/AAA login form watchTowr used to demonstrate it: "it is worth mentioning that this is not limited to a single endpoint. Any endpoint or port that logs data controlled in an HTTP header can trigger this vulnerability" (watchTowr Labs, 2026-09-28): failed logins, rate-limited requests and arbitrary request parameters or User-Agent headers can all poison the log the monitor script later parses. Citrix's fix replaces the unsafe pipeline with a strict regex capture that only accepts a well-formed PPE name and numeric PID and executes find via Perl's list form rather than shell interpolation. watchTowr also clarifies exploitation-status granularity across the eight-CVE bulletin: only CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 are confirmed exploited, matching Citrix's bulletin, and has published a public detection-artefact tool. NCSC Switzerland's Cyber Security Hub, NCSC UK and CERT-FR each published same-day advisories on 2026-09-28 relaying Citrix's confirmation of active exploitation (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-09-28; NCSC UK, 2026-09-28; CERT-FR, 2026-09-28).

Update30 Sep 2026 04:50 UTCrun 2026-09-30T0404Z-intelsummaryimmediate_actiontagscvesentitiestechniquessourcesevidenceactionsbody

Exploitation predates the bulletin. Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group identified in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-88772 and report that the campaign has run since at least early September, with organizations in North America and Europe in government, financial services, technology, education, and legal and professional services likely impacted (GTIG/Mandiant, 2026-09-29). eSentire independently reports CVE-2026-88771 exploited against internet-facing NetScaler Gateway appliances as early as 5 September (eSentire, 2026-09-29), and GreyNoise recorded a failed pre-disclosure attempt on 24 September that already used the setuid-and-handler playbook described below (GreyNoise, 2026-09-28). GTIG and GreyNoise name no actor. CERT-EU traced the activity through NetScaler logs from the European Court of Auditors and the European Central Bank, which showed requests carrying Base64-encoded shell commands in the HTTP User-Agent header (CERT-EU, 2026-09-28). An appliance upgraded after the 27 September bulletin may therefore already have been compromised: "Patching does not remove persistence an attacker already installed" (Censys, 2026-09-30).

What the actor leaves behind. After the DTLS exploit runs shellcode as root, a first-stage web shell rewrites the appliance web-server configuration so that files with non-script extensions run as PHP; in one variant an alias maps requests for image files under the VPN media path onto a staged shell, so the traffic looks like image fetches, and the shells answer with HTTP 404 while taking Base64 commands from HTTP request headers, including NSC-prefixed ones (GTIG/Mandiant, 2026-09-29). The installer sets the setuid bit on /bin/sh so later web requests run as root, scrubs its staging path from /etc/crontab and reboots the appliance to apply the change (GTIG/Mandiant, 2026-09-29). The PHP shell WHIPSHOT relays requests over loopback to SLAPSHOT, a Python TCP tunneler that Mandiant saw used for internal reconnaissance and credential theft in at least one intrusion (GTIG/Mandiant, 2026-09-29).

Exploit availability for CVE-2026-88772. GTIG states it holds no exploit code (GTIG/Mandiant, 2026-09-29). watchTowr published a root-cause analysis and a detection-artifact generator on 29 September: DTLS handshake reassembly keeps almost the whole record for each one-byte fragment, so after 120 records the buffer chain holds about 174 KB, which a packet-engine function copies into a 35,840-byte scratch buffer without a size check (watchTowr Labs, 2026-09-29). NCSC Switzerland's advisory now lists a proof of concept for both CVEs (NCSC-CH, 2026-09-29), and Help Net Security reports the activity turned into opportunistic mass exploitation after a public root-cause analysis and proof of concept for CVE-2026-88771, while its text says there was no public proof of concept for CVE-2026-88772 (Help Net Security, 2026-09-29).

Interim controls and containment. For appliances that cannot be patched at once Mandiant lists three network restrictions: disabling DTLS on internet-facing Gateway virtual servers where it is not needed and blocking inbound UDP/443 at an upstream firewall or edge router (local ACLs let the traffic reach the packet engine first) are specific to CVE-2026-88772 and "should not be relied on to mitigate CVE-2026-88771", while upstream IP allow-listing, where source ranges are predictable, is not scoped to one CVE and may be impractical for large remote workforces (GTIG/Mandiant, 2026-09-29). For a suspected compromise it advises isolating the node, halting high-availability configuration sync until both nodes are validated because a compromised node can replicate a modified web-server configuration to the standby, restricting appliance egress, and, after patching, rotating appliance and integration credentials and terminating Gateway and ICA sessions (GTIG/Mandiant, 2026-09-29). NetScaler 12.1 and 13.0 are end of life and no longer receive security updates, and Citrix has not said whether they are affected (Tenable, 2026-09-27). Censys counts 42,735 exposed NetScaler ADC and Gateway hosts, with Switzerland among the countries at roughly 4% each; these are exposed instances, not confirmed-vulnerable ones (Censys, 2026-09-30).

Hunting. By telemetry class: appliance web-server configuration containing handler or alias directives that point public paths at script directories; script content in the client plug-in and media directories, which should hold compiled clients and static assets; 404 responses with multi-kilobyte bodies or long processing times on media paths; the setuid bit on /bin/sh; lock and port-pointer files in the temp directory; and, for CVE-2026-88772, a DTLS handshake-failure "Internal Error" line in the syslog, and packet-engine termination or watchdog "NOT restarting" lines in the FreeBSD system log, which NetScaler does not forward to a SIEM by default (GTIG/Mandiant, 2026-09-29). GTIG treats a handshake failure followed within minutes by a packet-engine termination as a strong exploitation signal, but advises alerting on each event on its own rather than requiring both, alongside configuration drift (GTIG/Mandiant, 2026-09-29).

A shared municipal operator shut down as a precaution. The two municipal data centres of the Rhineland-Palatinate association ZIDKOR shut down centrally hosted specialist applications on Sunday 27 September after a security vulnerability became known, taking resident-registration, ID-card, vehicle-registration and civil-registry services offline across all 194 full-time administered municipalities, cities and counties while they installed the vendor's patches; the operators say no successful cyberattack occurred, and each administration ran its own continuity plan with no central instruction (ZIDKOR release via AK-Kurier, 2026-09-28). Mainz and Kaiserslautern reported regular service again on the morning of 29 September (dpa via Rhein-Zeitung, 2026-09-29). The operators name no vendor; heise assesses that the trigger was probably the NetScaler updates released that weekend, a link it added to its article after publication (heise online, 2026-09-29). Cantonal and communal IT providers that host citizen services behind a shared NetScaler front end face the same trade-off between shutting down to patch and staying reachable.

Update02 Oct 2026 04:56 UTCrun 2026-10-02T0404Z-intelheadlinesummarytechniquessourcesevidenceactionsimmediate_actionbody

Unit 42's threat brief, updated 2026-09-30, adds first-party telemetry on the pre-disclosure activity (Unit 42, 2026-09-30). Its earliest observed activity is on 2026-08-21: requests for an admin-UI stylesheet and a Gateway language resource that those two hosts and a third address then repeated against more than 100 other systems on 21 and 22 August, which Unit 42 reads as version fingerprinting (Unit 42, 2026-09-30). Between 2026-09-04 and 2026-09-24 the DTLS exploitation delivered web shells as .deb packages that the actor repeatedly fetched from the appliance's /vpn/scripts/linux/ client-installer folder, rotating infrastructure over that period; the recovered PHP web shell offers command execution, file download and upload over an RC4-encrypted channel and uses the appliance's SUID helper for privilege escalation (Unit 42, 2026-09-30). From 2026-09-10 to 2026-09-27 a continuous stream of requests reached the Gateway's /logon/LogonPoint/Authentication/GetUserName page, which Unit 42 calls anomalous and worth investigating (Unit 42, 2026-09-30).

On 2026-09-21 Unit 42 saw a three-stage chain against a US-based target: a request with a Base64 dropper command in the User-Agent, answered with a 404 and written to the VPN HTTP access log; a login request whose extra text is logged in ns.log after the pitboss PPE missed too many heartbeatsNSPPE marker; and the vulnerable ns_monuploadd_err.pl script then running that text, which retrieves and decodes the staged payload and pipes it to sh or php (Unit 42, 2026-09-30). The payload sets the SUID and SGID bits on /bin/sh, creates a hidden PHP receiver under the Gateway's custom directory, adds Alias directives that present it as a versioned CSS file, switches php_flag engine to on in httpd.conf and reloads Apache with SIGHUP, leaving no restart entry (Unit 42, 2026-09-30). Unit 42 counted 50,277 exposed instances that could potentially be vulnerable as of 2026-09-27 and cautions that activity after that date may not match the original actors' indicators or TTPs (Unit 42, 2026-09-30).

Update04 Oct 2026 04:42 UTCrun 2026-10-04T0405Z-intelsummaryimmediate_actionactionsreferencessourcesevidencebody

Citrix published a second NetScaler bulletin on 2026-10-03, CTX697174, for CVE-2026-88779, a memory overflow reachable when the appliance is configured as a SAML service provider or identity provider; Citrix says it has observed targeted attacks and scopes the impact to denial of service (Citrix, 2026-10-03; Citrix, 2026-10-03). The flaw is independent of the vulnerabilities disclosed in the earlier bulletin CTX697096 (Citrix, 2026-10-02), and Citrix tells operators who upgraded to the September builds and meet the SAML precondition to upgrade again (Citrix, 2026-10-03). The fixed builds are 14.1-73.41, 13.1-64.28, 14.1-73.41 FIPS and 13.1-37.282 (Citrix, 2026-10-03). A SAML-configured appliance on 14.1-73.37 or 13.1-64.23 is therefore fixed against the exploited command-injection and DTLS flaws described above but not against this one.

Correction04 Oct 2026 10:36 UTCrun 2026-09-30T0639Z-auditheadlinebody

For CVE-2026-88771, the precursor in the appliance's own logs is header or username values carrying shell metacharacters together with crash-message text such as "PPE unexpectedly died" (watchTowr Labs, 2026-09-28). For CVE-2026-88772, GTIG names a DTLS handshake-failure line, packet-engine terminations and watchdog "NOT restarting" lines, and advises alerting on each on its own rather than requiring both (GTIG/Mandiant, 2026-09-29). Citrix has published no workaround (watchTowr, 2026-09-27), and Mandiant's DTLS and UDP/443 controls apply to CVE-2026-88772 only, while its upstream IP allow-listing is not scoped to one CVE (GTIG/Mandiant, 2026-09-29).

Improvement09 Oct 2026 03:53 UTCrun 2026-10-09T0255Z-intelsummaryimmediate_actionactionssourcesbody

The pointers above to the 14.1-73.41 and 13.1-64.28 builds for SAML-configured appliances are not the end of the upgrade path for identity providers: Citrix's bulletin CTX697191 of 2026-10-08 lists those builds as affected by CVE-2026-107406 when the appliance is a SAML identity provider, and names 14.1-73.46, 13.1-64.29, 14.1-73.46 FIPS and 13.1.37.283 and later as fixed (Citrix, 2026-10-08).

Improvement18 Oct 2026 03:35 UTCrun 2026-10-18T0256Z-intelentitiesreferencesactionssourcesevidencebody

Zscaler ThreatLabz published first-party telemetry of exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 on 2026-10-16 (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-10-16). The chain it captured matches the log-poisoning sequence in the sections above: a payload stored in the User-Agent of GET requests to four default logon and VPN paths, a forged packet-engine failure record in the authentication request that searches the access log for the marker, decodes the payload and runs it when the vendor's crash-log script selects that record (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-10-16). Two post-exploitation behaviours are not described above: the payload writes PHP and Perl CGI web shells into six web-served directories and adds a handler that runs .pl files as CGI, besides switching PHP on in the web server configuration, and a shorter variant makes the appliance download a Rust-built 64-bit FreeBSD binary and run it from /var (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-10-16). ThreatLabz saw at least 26 source addresses send the forged record together with that downloader within about six to seven minutes (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-10-16). It says the download server also appeared in its earlier exploitation data for CVE-2026-75650, the Adobe Commerce and Magento flaw it tracks as StyleSmuggler, and calls the overlap an investigative lead that does not establish attribution, because shared hosting, a malware-distribution service or payload reuse by unrelated operators could explain it (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-10-16).

Update19 Oct 2026 16:17 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-auditsummarycvessourcesbody

Belgium's Centre for Cybersecurity reported on 2026-10-06 that a proof of concept is publicly available for CVE-2026-88773, the HTTP request-smuggling flaw in the same bulletin, which an unauthenticated attacker can use on appliances with the HTTP configuration enabled to view and edit restricted data; it had seen no exploitation in the wild by that date (CCB, 2026-10-06). Citrix lists 14.1-73.37 and 13.1-64.23 and later as fixed, so an appliance on the September builds needs nothing further for this flaw (Citrix CTX697096).

Contradiction: CCB's advisory lists the affected software as 14.1 - 14.1-73.37 and 13.1 - 13.1-64.23 (CCB, 2026-10-06), while Citrix names those builds as the first fixed releases (Citrix CTX697096); Citrix, as the vendor, is the authority on its own fixed builds.

Correction19 Oct 2026 21:08 UTCrun 2026-10-18T1307Z-auditheadlinesourcesevidencebody

Only CVE-2026-88771 applies to every deployment in default configuration; CVE-2026-88772 needs DTLS, which is on by default only on VPN virtual servers, as described above, so the headline no longer calls both default-configuration. watchTowr shows the crash-log script searching the logs for two Pitboss packet-engine messages, "missed too many heartbeats" or "unexpectedly died", and says it can take up to 24 hours to run (watchTowr Labs, 2026-09-28). Citrix's instruction to customers who had already upgraded for CVE-2026-88771 through CVE-2026-88778 and meet the CVE-2026-88779 preconditions is to "upgrade your deployment again" (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-04); the quote now cites that report.

Update20 Oct 2026 03:40 UTCrun 2026-10-20T0256Z-intelsummarytechniquesactionssourcesevidencebody

Rapid7 published an incident analysis on 2026-10-19 of an early-October compromise of a NetScaler ADC on an affected 14.1 build, build number not given (Rapid7, 2026-10-19). Its logs show CVE-2026-88771 chained with CVE-2026-88779: text similar to a Pitboss crash message was inserted into an authentication username, repeated nsaaad crashes and a Pitboss reboot followed, and after the reboot the call-home crash handler processed the retained text and executed a payload as root, a chaining that avoided waiting 24 hours for the injected payload to run (Rapid7, 2026-10-19). The crash-and-reboot cycle recurred over several days and let the operator refresh persistence and deploy new components (Rapid7, 2026-10-19).

After the first root execution the operator installed cookie-authenticated PHP web shells behind Apache aliases that look like CSS files and answer with HTTP 404 bodies, set /bin/sh to mode 6555, and kept access through cron entries, boot scripts, watchdog loops, an outbound agent that polls every 15 seconds and an HTTP-fronted TCP proxy, with logic that synchronises implant files to the HA peer and forces a failover so the implanted node stays active (Rapid7, 2026-10-19). A Go tool recovered from the appliance mapped routes, DNS, LDAP and Active Directory, management services and VMware vCenter, and the configuration, historical configurations and system backups were staged and exfiltrated, one archive through the web root; Rapid7 says the archive can hold encrypted credentials, LDAP and RADIUS bind information, SSL private keys and key-encryption material (Rapid7, 2026-10-19). Rapid7 says the activity overlaps public WHIPSHOT and SLAPSHOT reporting and names no actor (Rapid7, 2026-10-19).

Rapid7 recommends patching to the fixed builds for both CVEs and verifying the September builds, collecting volatile evidence before rebooting or rebuilding, inspecting both nodes of every HA pair, and rotating all credentials and keys exposed through the configuration (Rapid7, 2026-10-19).

immediate_action.action: Citrix confirms CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 are being exploited against unmitigated NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances right now, and Google's Mandiant reports exploitation since at least early September. CVE-2026-88771 requires no configuration at all: every default deployment is reachable by an unauthenticated attacker; CVE-2026-88772 is reachable wherever DTLS is enabled, which Citrix states is the default on any VPN virtual server. Citrix lists no workaround, and Mandiant's interim network controls (disable DTLS where it is not needed, block inbound UDP/443 upstream) cover CVE-2026-88772 only. Capture forensic evidence (logs, an instance snapshot where the appliance is virtual, a support bundle, a core dump) from each exposed appliance before patching, since the upgrade itself can destroy evidence of prior compromise, then upgrade to 14.1-73.37+ or 13.1-64.23+ (run `show ns variable` first on 13.1; if it returns any variables, install 13.1-64.24 instead to avoid a known reboot loop), going straight to 14.1-73.41+ or 13.1-64.28+ where the appliance is configured as a SAML service provider or identity provider (CVE-2026-88779), and to 14.1-73.46+ or 13.1-64.29+ where it is an identity provider (CVE-2026-107406), and run a compromise assessment on every appliance that was internet-facing.
immediate_action.evidence_quote: Exploits of CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 on unmitigated NetScaler deployments have been observed.

entries.summary: Citrix's CTX697096 bulletin (2026-09-27) fixes eight NetScaler ADC/Gateway flaws, two of which, CVE-2026-88771 (unauthenticated command execution, every default deployment) and CVE-2026-88772 (memory overflow to RCE/DoS, reachable wherever DTLS is enabled, the VPN-vServer default), were exploited before any fix existed; CISA added both to KEV and Citrix lists no workaround. Mandiant, GTIG, Unit 42, Zscaler and Rapid7 describe the compromises: web-server-configuration persistence, web shells, and in one intrusion the SAML crash CVE-2026-88779 chained with CVE-2026-88771 so that the crash handler ran the payload as root, followed by exfiltration of the appliance configuration and key material. An appliance patched after the bulletin therefore still needs a compromise check and its configuration secrets rotated. SAML-configured appliances need the later builds named for CVE-2026-88779 (14.1-73.41 or 13.1-64.28) and identity providers 14.1-73.46 or 13.1-64.29 for CVE-2026-107406; CVE-2026-88773 has a public proof of concept with no exploitation seen.
entries.title: CVE-2026-88771 / CVE-2026-88772, Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway: unauthenticated pre-auth RCE zero-days exploited before a patch existed (CVSS 4.0 9.5)

updates.summary: watchTowr Labs published a full root-cause analysis on 2026-09-28: the vulnerable component for CVE-2026-88771 is ns_monuploadd_err.pl, a crash-log-monitoring script, not the nsppe packet engine historically named in NetScaler CVEs, and the trigger is not limited to the SSLVPN login form: any endpoint or port that logs attacker-controlled header data can poison the log the script later parses. watchTowr also confirms per-CVE exploitation status across the bulletin (only CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 exploited; the rest patched but not reported exploited, matching this entry's existing table) and published a public detection tool. NCSC-CH, NCSC-UK and CERT-FR each issued same-day advisories confirming active exploitation.

Google's Mandiant and GTIG report the exploitation campaign has run since at least early September, with government among the impacted sectors in North America and Europe, and describe post-exploitation web-server-configuration persistence, the WHIPSHOT web shell and the SLAPSHOT tunneler; eSentire places CVE-2026-88771 exploitation from 5 September. watchTowr published the CVE-2026-88772 root cause and NCSC Switzerland now lists a proof of concept for both flaws. Mandiant's interim controls (disable DTLS, block UDP/443 upstream) cover CVE-2026-88772 only, NetScaler 12.1 and 13.0 are end of life with no fix, and a shared municipal operator in Rhineland-Palatinate shut down citizen-service systems statewide as a precaution, a shutdown heise links to these NetScaler updates while the operators name no vendor.

Palo Alto Networks Unit 42's threat brief adds first-party telemetry: version fingerprinting of NetScaler Gateways from 2026-08-21, web shells delivered as .deb packages from the client-installer folder between 2026-09-04 and 2026-09-24, and a three-stage log-poisoning chain seen on 2026-09-21, with the log artifacts each leaves. Earlier text is corrected: the KEV remediation deadline is dropped; the evidence to capture before patching is an instance snapshot where the appliance is virtual (not a configuration snapshot), cited to watchTowr and Unit 42; the triage discriminator for CVE-2026-88771 now describes the logged crash-message imitation instead of a valid-session premise; the NCSC-CH, NCSC UK and CERT-FR advisories are described as relaying Citrix's confirmation, with links; the pre-notification reported by BleepingComputer is no longer presented as the source of the shutdown calls; a stale statement that NCSC-CH had not yet published an advisory is replaced; and a dead Censys link points to its canonical page.

Citrix's bulletin CTX697174 (2026-10-03) fixes CVE-2026-88779, a SAML-triggered memory overflow that the September fixed builds do not cover; Citrix confirms targeted attacks and tells SAML-configured appliances that already took the September builds to upgrade again, to 14.1-73.41, 13.1-64.28 or the FIPS builds.

The headline says Citrix has published no workaround. The Triage line follows watchTowr's root-cause analysis for CVE-2026-88771 and GTIG's log artifacts for CVE-2026-88772, which GTIG advises alerting on individually, and the zero-day timing is cited to watchTowr. Only Mandiant's DTLS and UDP/443 controls are limited to CVE-2026-88772 and its upstream IP allow-listing is not tied to one flaw, the KEV sentence drops the US directive, a reference to an exploitation table that does not exist is removed, and the takeaway adds GTIG's sector statement.

The pointers to the SAML builds now carry the 2026-10-08 bulletin CTX697191: identity-provider appliances need 14.1-73.46 or 13.1-64.29 (or the FIPS builds) after the 14.1-73.41 and 13.1-64.28 builds, which Citrix lists as affected by CVE-2026-107406.

Zscaler ThreatLabz's first-party exploitation telemetry (2026-10-16) adds post-exploitation behaviour to the compromise check: a Perl CGI handler enabled in the web server configuration besides PHP, and a variant that makes the appliance download and run a 64-bit FreeBSD binary, seen in a burst from at least 26 source addresses; the download server also appeared in its earlier Magento exploitation data, which ThreatLabz calls a lead and not attribution.

Belgium's CCB reports a public proof of concept for CVE-2026-88773 (unauthenticated HTTP request smuggling, CVSS 4.0 9.3) with no exploitation seen as of 2026-10-06; the flaw's status gains poc-public and the CCB warning joins the sources. The fixed builds are cited to Citrix's bulletin, with a contradiction line on CCB's affected-range wording.

The headline no longer calls both zero-days default-configuration: CVE-2026-88772 needs DTLS, on by default only on VPN virtual servers. The crash-log script is described by the two Pitboss messages watchTowr says it searches for. The Citrix "upgrade again" quote is cut to the words BleepingComputer reproduces and cited there.

Rapid7's incident analysis of an early-October NetScaler compromise shows CVE-2026-88771 chained with the SAML crash CVE-2026-88779, with the call-home crash handler running the payload as root after a reboot, followed by persistence that synchronises to the HA peer, internal reconnaissance and exfiltration of the appliance configuration and key material; an appliance that was reached needs the configuration secrets rotated as well as the patch.

entries.headline: BACS grades logins in five classes: static secrets should in principle go; session binding resists phishing
entries.html:
ROUTINENATOA2

BACS publishes five security classes for authentication methods: static secrets should in principle no longer be used, and only session-bound methods resist real-time phishing

BACS published on 2026-10-19 the technology assessment "Sicherheitsklassen für Authentifikationsverfahren, -mittel und -dienste", which sorts authentication methods, tokens and services into the three classes tief (low), mittel (medium) and hoch (high), with mittel and hoch each split further, five classes in all (BACS, 2026-10-19). The scheme follows the NIST authentication assurance levels 1 to 3 with slight adjustments and extends them for resistance to real-time phishing; BACS says the classification gives no basis for formal testing or certification and can serve organisations as a basis for security requirements and recommendations (BACS, 2026-10-19). In the assessment, class tief covers any method whose authentication information is static and identical at every login, such as a password or a cryptographic key, and the class does not rise when the secret travels over TLS; BACS concludes that methods in this class should in principle no longer be used (BACS, 2026-10-19). Class mittel needs authentication information generated anew for each login plus at least one further security feature, and the starred variant additionally needs session binding, which ties the session cryptographically to the authentication information or to the device, network or application; the assessment names TLS channel binding, Device Bound Session Credentials and OAuth DPoP as examples, against session hijacking, real-time phishing and adversary-in-the-middle attacks (BACS, 2026-10-19). BACS says the difference between mittel and hoch lies mainly in the use of additional hardware to store the cryptographic keys (BACS, 2026-10-19). Its annex of examples places a password, a static API key and a secret held in a cookie such as a session ID in tief; a password with an SMS code, a software authenticator app, Kerberos tickets, bearer tokens (SAML, OIDC, OAuth, JWT) and synced passkeys in mittel, the passkeys starred; and hardware OTP tokens, hardware certificates in TLS and FIDO2 without synchronisation or key export in hoch, with a footnote that SMS verification should be used only where no better alternative exists (BACS, 2026-10-19).

Defender takeaway
The classification binds no one and sets no deadline; it is a rough guideline (BACS's own term) that cantonal and communal bodies can use when writing authentication requirements. A login that rests on a static secret is class tief, which BACS says should in principle no longer be used, and a login resists real-time phishing and session hijacking only where it is session-bound (the starred classes) (BACS, 2026-10-19).

It says methods in class tief, those built on a secret that is the same at every login, should in principle no longer be used. The classification is non-binding and gives no basis for testing or certification; it is a rough guideline from the federal authority for writing authentication requirements.

entries.headline: Siemens confirms exploitation of a Software Center DLL side-loading flaw; attackers bring their own signed copy
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-110936exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-110936, Siemens Software Center: a ClickFix campaign runs a genuine signed copy of the application and side-loads its own DLLs, and Siemens confirms exploitation (CVSS 4.0 8.4)

Siemens ProductCERT says it has validated active exploitation of CVE-2026-110936, a DLL side-loading flaw in Siemens Software Center that Siemens fixed in version 4.0.9.8 and described in advisory SSA-580366 of 2026-10-15 (Siemens ProductCERT, 2026-10-19). The advisory scores it CVSS 4.0 8.4 (6.7 on CVSS 3.1, with a local vector and high privileges required) and lists every version before V4.0.9.8 as affected (Siemens ProductCERT, 2026-10-15). The attackers did not rely on a copy already on the victim's PC: they used a genuine, validly signed copy of Software Center and placed their own files next to it, chosen as a carrier because it is signed and trusted and because version 3.5.8.7, the latest at the time, loaded helper files from its own folder without checking them; the Siemens program itself was not modified, and Siemens says no Siemens system, product or update channel was breached to its knowledge (Siemens ProductCERT, 2026-10-19). Siemens labels the activity the Romulus multi-platform ClickFix campaign and names no actor (Siemens ProductCERT, 2026-10-19); one address that Siemens lists as the distribution channel of its malware bundle also appears among the ROMULUS hosts in Forescout's write-up of a ClickFix delivery platform, which does not mention Siemens software, and Forescout says it has no evidence that its panel is related to RomulusLoader, the malware Proofpoint reported (Forescout Vedere Labs, 2026-10-15). Huntress documented the same chain with other signed applications on 2026-09-28 and warned to expect more signed hosts (Huntress, 2026-09-28).

Exposure
Any Windows PC whose user pasted a command from a web page into the Run box or PowerShell, whether or not Siemens software is installed there, because the attackers bring their own copy; installed Software Center versions before V4.0.9.8 are affected as well until the application starts and updates itself (Siemens ProductCERT, 2026-10-19).
Detection
In process-creation telemetry, the signed Software Center executable running from a folder under the user profile's local Programs directory and started by msiexec, which Siemens names as the signal; in image-load and file telemetry, unexpected DLL and data files beside that executable outside the default installation folder; in persistence telemetry, a Software Center start-up entry or scheduled task on a PC that never had the product, and a service-named folder that the malware creates under the same Programs directory (Siemens ProductCERT, 2026-10-19). Siemens says to detect on folder and behaviour rather than on the file's fingerprint, because the file itself is genuine; where a PC matches, it says to isolate it, stop the process first, then remove the start-up entry and the task and reset passwords.

Triage: a real installation runs from the Siemens install location; the same executable running from the user profile's Programs folder, started by msiexec, with unexpected files beside it or start-up entries on a PC that never had the product, is the abuse (Siemens ProductCERT, 2026-10-19).

Defender takeaway
Update Software Center to V4.0.9.8 or later wherever it is installed, and hunt for the execution pattern above on every Windows endpoint, since the carrier is delivered with the lure and patching an installed copy does not stop it; the same hunt covers the other signed applications Huntress describes, and the lever at the front of the chain is the paste step into the Run box or PowerShell (Siemens ProductCERT, 2026-10-19; Huntress, 2026-09-28).

Builds on: Huntress: a ChatGPT Custom GPT lure feeds a ClickFix chain that ends in a signed-host DLL…

vulnerability20 Oct 03:36Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Siemens ProductCERT · Siemens ProductCERT (SSA-580366) · Huntress · Forescout Vedere Labs
entries.summary: Siemens ProductCERT says it validated active exploitation of CVE-2026-110936, a DLL side-loading flaw in Siemens Software Center versions before V4.0.9.8, which it fixed in advisory SSA-580366 of 2026-10-15; installed copies update themselves the next time the application starts. The attackers did not abuse an installed copy: they delivered a genuine, validly signed copy of version 3.5.8.7 with their own files beside it through what Siemens calls the Romulus multi-platform ClickFix campaign, so the check that finds it is behaviour on any Windows PC, not a Software Center inventory.

entries.action_label: Calendar-invite phishing spreads: Outlook and Gmail…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Calendar-invite phishing spreads: Outlook and Gmail add the lure on their own and keep it after the email is deleted
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

Phishing lures sent as ICS calendar invites land in Outlook and Gmail calendars without a click and stay after the email is deleted; EvilTokens used them for Microsoft 365 device-code phishing

Netcraft reports that attackers send phishing lures as ICS calendar files because the "text/calendar" type is treated as low risk by major email clients, and that the mail client's normal invite handling then places the lure in the victim's calendar with no user interaction, often keeping it there after the original email is deleted (Netcraft, 2026-10-16). In Netcraft's client table, Outlook desktop, Outlook on the web and Outlook Mobile with Exchange Online and Gmail with Google Calendar add the event automatically, mark it tentative and keep it after the email is deleted, Apple Calendar connected to Exchange Online often does the same, and Apple Mail with iCloud does not add it (Netcraft, 2026-10-16).

Campaigns using the EvilTokens toolkit, which steals Microsoft 365 tokens, used ICS invites disguised as meetings, alerts or voicemail notifications; the link leads to a page that gives the user a device code and tells them to enter it on Microsoft's device authorization page, which grants an attacker's device access to the account through OAuth (Netcraft, 2026-10-16). Netcraft now also sees smaller scams carrying ordinary phishing content inside ICS files (Netcraft, 2026-10-16). Sublime Security reports "exponential growth" in calendar phishing, with lures such as voicemail notices, payment receipts and renewal warnings that link to fake Microsoft, Google or PayPal logins or give a phone number, and Cofense says some senders use legitimate platforms such as Zoom to send the invitations, so filtering those platforms would also block real meetings (The Guardian, 2026-10-11).

Exposure
Users of Outlook with Exchange Online and of Gmail with Google Calendar, whose clients add external invites to the calendar on their own (Netcraft, 2026-10-16).
Detection
Netcraft names no telemetry; from the delivery path it describes, the traces are inbound external messages carrying a calendar part or ICS attachment in mail-flow logs, tentative events from external organizers the user never accepted in calendar audit logs, and, for the EvilTokens variant, a device-code sign-in to the account shortly after such an event (Netcraft, 2026-10-16). When responding to a reported phish of this kind, remove the calendar entry as well as the email, because the entry persists after the email is deleted (Netcraft, 2026-10-16).
Defender takeaway
Treat email-attached invites as part of the phishing attack surface: review whether the mail client settings add invites from outside the organization automatically for staff who do not expect them, and extend phishing guidance and purge procedures to calendar entries for those who do (Netcraft, 2026-10-16).

Builds on: Huntress: device-code phishing and ROPC token-spray defeat M365 tenants by routing around the…

threat19 Oct 21:15Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Netcraft · The Guardian
entries.summary: Netcraft reports that phishing lures delivered as ICS calendar files, adopted by widespread campaigns of the EvilTokens Microsoft 365 token-stealing kit, are now spreading to low-effort scams. Outlook with Exchange Online (desktop, web and mobile) and Gmail with Google Calendar add such an invite to the calendar automatically as tentative and keep it after the email is deleted, so purging the message leaves the lure in place. EvilTokens invites posed as meetings, alerts or voicemail and led to a device-code page that has the victim authorise an attacker's device through OAuth; Sublime Security, quoted by The Guardian, reports exponential growth in calendar phishing.

entries.headline: Bricksforge's Pro Forms upload flaw is exploited without login since 7 October; fixed in 3.1.8.10 and 4.0.0, related fix in 4.0.1
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-85097exploitedupdatedNATOB2

CVE-2026-85097, Bricksforge for WordPress: an unauthenticated upload in the Pro Forms module writes attacker PHP into the uploads directory, exploited since 7 October; fixed in 3.1.8.10 and 4.0.0, with a related upload fix in 4.0.1 (CVSS 9.8)

Bricksforge's Pro Forms module checks a file's type when it is first uploaded but trusts the file metadata the client sends when the form is submitted, in particular the url field of the temporaryFileUploads parameter (Patchstack, 2026-10-08). An attacker obtains a nonce from the unauthenticated bricksforge_regenerate_nonce AJAX endpoint, uploads a GIF/PHP polyglot that passes the type check, then submits a form whose file path names that image and whose url ends in a PHP extension; the plugin writes the image's content to the PHP path and one request to it executes the code (Patchstack, 2026-10-08). Versions up to and including 3.1.8.9 are affected (Patchstack, 2026-10-08). The vendor's changelog, revised after the disclosure, states that the flaw was fixed in 3.1.8.10 and in 4.0.0, and lists a related security fix in the same Pro Forms upload area in 4.0.1 of 2026-10-08 (Bricksforge, 2026-10-13); Patchstack also names 3.1.8.10 (Patchstack, 2026-10-08). Dr. Web credits Wordfence with a CVSS score of 9.8 and Patchstack with 10.0 (Dr. Web, 2026-10-09).

Patchstack's telemetry first recorded exploitation attempts on 2026-10-07 at 21:47 UTC, from 63 distinct source addresses, and it calls the activity automated without attributing it (Patchstack, 2026-10-08). Patchstack describes exploitation attempts and says an attacker with execution can deploy web shells, modify site content, read data and persist (Patchstack, 2026-10-08). It counts about 6,000 active installations (Dr. Web, 2026-10-09), Previdian lists it as exploited in the wild and links public proof-of-concept code (Previdian, 2026-10-08), and the flaw is not in CISA's KEV catalog (Dr. Web, 2026-10-09).

Exposure
WordPress sites running Bricksforge versions up to and including 3.1.8.9 (Patchstack, 2026-10-08) with the Pro Forms module active, including sites whose forms have no upload field (Bricksforge, 2026-10-13). Patchstack and Dr. Web bound the affected range at 3.1.8.9 (Dr. Web, 2026-10-09); the vendor states that 4.0.0 already carries the fix, while the related upload issue fixed in 4.0.1 affects every site with Pro Forms active, and the changelog names no 3.x build for that second fix (Bricksforge, 2026-10-13). Bricksforge is not in the wordpress.org plugin directory, so no public version statistics exist, and updates come with an annual licence, so a site with a lapsed licence may not receive the fix (Dr. Web, 2026-10-09).
Detection
In web server and WordPress access logs, POST requests to /wp-json/bricksforge/v1/form_submit or to admin-ajax with the bricksforge_form_submit action that carry a temporaryFileUploads value pairing an image path with a PHP-extension destination, preceded by a call to the nonce endpoint and repeated with changing extensions, case or encodings, from 2026-10-07 onward; in file-integrity and endpoint telemetry, new PHP files in the WordPress uploads tree, the plugin's temporary upload folder first, and web requests to them (Patchstack, 2026-10-08). Patchstack says a site that ran a vulnerable version without protection should have its historical logs and the host reviewed for unexpected PHP files, unusual application activity and unauthorized changes (Patchstack, 2026-10-08); Dr. Web adds a check of the user list for unknown administrator accounts (Dr. Web, 2026-10-09).
Defender takeaway
Update every Bricksforge site to 4.0.1 or later now, since the vendor lists the related Pro Forms upload fix only there; a 3.x site needs at least 3.1.8.10 (Bricksforge, 2026-10-13); where that is not possible, deactivate Pro Forms or the plugin and block PHP execution in the uploads directory (Dr. Web, 2026-10-09). On a site that was reachable and unpatched since 2026-10-07, run the log and file search above, and if code turns up restore from a backup older than 2026-10-07 and change all passwords (Dr. Web, 2026-10-09).
Update19 Oct 2026 21:03 UTCrun 2026-10-18T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummarycvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Bricksforge has revised its changelog: CVE-2026-85097 itself "was fixed earlier in 3.1.8.10 and in 4.0.0", and the 4.0.1 release of 2026-10-08 fixes a related issue in the same Pro Forms upload area that affects every site with Pro Forms active, including forms without upload fields (Bricksforge, 2026-10-13). The same changelog lists no 3.x build for that second fix, so a site on 3.1.8.10 is protected against the exploited flaw but not shown as covered for the related one; 4.0.1 or later carries both (Bricksforge, 2026-10-13). Version 4.0.2 of 2026-10-13 stops the upload check introduced in 4.0.1 from rejecting about one normal image in sixty and tightens access checks on the plugin's REST endpoints (Bricksforge, 2026-10-13). Previdian now lists the flaw as exploited in the wild, based on third-party reporting, and links public proof-of-concept code (Previdian, 2026-10-08).

vulnerability12 Oct 03:21Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Patchstack · Bricksforge (vendor changelog) · Dr. Web · Previdian
entries.summary: Patchstack reports that CVE-2026-85097, an unauthenticated arbitrary file upload in the Pro Forms module of Bricksforge, a paid WordPress add-on for the Bricks page builder, has been targeted in the wild since 2026-10-07: it lets an attacker with no account get a PHP file written to the uploads directory and executed, on versions up to and including 3.1.8.9 with Pro Forms active (about 6,000 active installations). Bricksforge's revised changelog states the flaw was fixed in 3.1.8.10 and 4.0.0 and lists a related Pro Forms upload fix in 4.0.1 of 2026-10-08; the exploitation report rests on Patchstack's telemetry.

actions: Find every Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb refrigeration controller in facilities you own or that a contractor manages for you and take its management interface off the internet now, restoring access only through a secure VPN or protected network (filtering to the contractor's source addresses is an emergency stop-gap, and CERT-FR asks you to check your insurance conditions before cutting the contractor's data uplink); an end-of-life unit that gets no fixes needs replacing, because a factory reset leaves it vulnerable and probably compromised again.

On every such controller that was reachable from the internet, check the whole configuration, defrost ranges included, against the intended one; for a Danfoss unit that may have been taken over, restart it or otherwise factory-reset it, restore access only through a secure VPN or protected network and reconfigure it for service, then update its firmware, set the security level to Strict and change the default passwords, and on every Copeland or Dixell XWEB unit confirm the factory Admin password was changed and give each contractor a named account with an expiry date.

entries.headline: CERT-FR adds Copeland and Dixell xweb to the hijacked refrigeration controllers; NCSC.ch rates the attacks exploited
entries.html:
HIGHexploitedupdatedNATOA2

Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb refrigeration controllers compromised, with forced defrost reported at hundreds of French supermarkets; CERT-FR and NCSC Switzerland say to remove internet exposure

Coopérative U, Intermarché and E. Leclerc confirmed to AFP a cyberattack on their refrigeration systems overnight on 11 to 12 October 2026; AFP reports from the retailers' statements at least 300 Intermarché or Netto shops and more than 100 Coopérative U outlets, and the Paris prosecutor opened an investigation (AFP, 2026-10-12). BFMTV puts the Intermarché and Netto count at 300, which it says is twice the first estimates of 150 points of sale, and Coopérative U below 100 stores, while Infosecurity quotes 150 Intermarché and 30 Netto stores (BFMTV, 2026-10-12; Infosecurity Magazine, 2026-10-12). BFMTV, writing in the conditional, reports that the attackers are said to have imposed a forced, continuous defrost with the setpoint at 50 degrees, on software older than version 4, heating the equipment for hours (translated from French) (BFMTV, 2026-10-12). CERT-FR's alert, in its revision of 2026-10-13, says it knows of numerous compromises of the remote refrigeration controllers Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series as well as Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb, and that exposing a management interface to the internet is contrary to good practice (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13). Danfoss told AFP that most affected units are legacy products that no longer receive software or security updates, naming the AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 regulators, and a person close to the Prime Minister said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software from a Danish company and that other countries may be affected (AFP, 2026-10-12). Intermarché told BleepingComputer that the attack reportedly affected a service provider that manages refrigeration systems in stores (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-12), and E. Leclerc told AFP that a cyberattack affected one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers (AFP, 2026-10-12). Infosecurity says the affected stores include those running vulnerable consoles with remote control and no adequately secured communication channel (Infosecurity Magazine, 2026-10-12). No source names an actor or the flaw or states how the attackers got in, and none confirms a tie to the 2025 AK-SM 8xxA vulnerabilities that Claroty found: BleepingComputer reports no tie (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-12) and NCSC Switzerland lists three of them only as alleged to be potentially related (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13); Censys names the same three as flaws that Danfoss patched more than a year earlier and says Danfoss has not confirmed the initial access vector (Censys, 2026-10-14).

Exposure
A Danfoss AK-SM or AK-SC refrigeration controller, or a Copeland or Dixell xweb unit, whose management interface is reachable from the internet, above all legacy units; Danfoss says the current AK-SM800A units that were affected ran outdated firmware (Cooling Post, 2026-10-12), and CERT-FR names no models, flaw or entry vector for the Copeland and Dixell units (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13). Copeland first declined to confirm CERT-FR's finding and has since acknowledged a vulnerability, which, Cybersecurity Dive reports, a Copeland spokesperson confirmed was found in discontinued end-of-life controllers, and says it is working with impacted customers to mitigate the risk; neither article names the flaw (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-15; Cybersecurity Dive, 2026-10-15). Infosecurity reports, without naming them, that supermarkets in Belgium and the Netherlands were also reportedly affected (Infosecurity Magazine, 2026-10-12); Blick reports that Migros confirms using, in a limited number of its Swiss stores, the same Danfoss refrigeration systems that were targeted and says nothing indicates an attack on them, while Aldi and Lidl say they are not concerned and Coop says it was not affected and declines to say whether it uses Danfoss (Blick, 2026-10-13); no source reports a Swiss victim, so ask whoever manages your refrigeration and building services whether a controller sits in your estate. For an AK-SM 800A, Censys maps the firmware to the published flaws: a build below 4.2 carries all three, 4.2.4 fixes only the date-based login and so still carries the two later ones, and 4.3.1 or later fixes all three, with 5.3.2 the current build it lists (Censys, 2026-10-14). For the Copeland and Dixell units, CERT-FR links a Dixell France guide (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16) that carries Copeland's own bulletin of 14 October, in which Copeland acknowledges the vulnerability on a generation of XWEB EVO controllers that is no longer marketed and has reached end of life, says to remove every XWEB EVO from the public internet immediately and says XWEB EVO no longer receives security patches, and that adds Dixell France's own recommendations, among them that XWEB PRO and EVO ship with the same factory Admin account (Dixell France, 2026-10-14). The bulletin names the affected generation but describes no flaw (Dixell France, 2026-10-14).
Detection
On the controller, defrost, setpoint and account changes outside a maintenance window; in firewall, provider VPN or ISP logs, inbound connections to the management interface from addresses other than the refrigeration contractor's; CERT-FR accepts filtering to the contractors' source addresses only as an emergency measure and wants access restored through a secure VPN or protected network (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13). For a controller that may have been taken over, CERT-FR's current text is to remove the internet exposure, restart the Danfoss unit or otherwise restore it with a factory reset, restore access only through a secure VPN or protected network, reconfigure it and apply the maker's practices, which for Danfoss means updating the firmware, setting the security level to Strict and confirming the default passwords were changed (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16); for a unit not known to be compromised it asks to check the whole configuration, notably the defrost ranges (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16). Le Monde reports that besides raising the defrost setpoint to 50 degrees the attackers lengthened the defrost operation from one hour to eight so that alarms trigger late (translated from French), which makes the defrost duration a tamper signal beside the setpoint (Le Monde, 2026-10-12; SecurityWeek, 2026-10-15).

Triage: a defrost cycle is normal; BFMTV reports, citing sector professionals, that installations can be programmed for two hours of defrost per 24 hours, whereas the reported attack is said to be a continuous forced defrost at a 50-degree setpoint held for hours (translated from French) (BFMTV, 2026-10-12).

Defender takeaway
Take any Danfoss AK-SM or AK-SC, Copeland xweb or Dixell xweb management interface off the internet now and restore access only through a secure VPN or protected network, as CERT-FR advises (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13), and ask the contractor whether its own remote access was affected; for the AK-SM800 and AK-SC355, replacement is the lever, since Danfoss says it had long advised supermarkets to move off those models (AFP, 2026-10-12), no fix exists for them according to NCSC Switzerland (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13), and CERT-FR says a factory reset on an unpatched end-of-life unit removes the compromised instance's persistence but leaves the device vulnerable and almost certainly compromised again (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13).
Update14 Oct 2026 03:44 UTCrun 2026-10-14T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummaryregionsentitiesaffected_productssourcesevidencesourcing_notereferencesactionsbody

CERT-FR revised its alert on 2026-10-13: the list of compromised remote controllers now includes Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb besides Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, campaigns against these devices are probably still ongoing, and an unpatched end-of-life unit kept on the internet is very likely to be compromised, so a factory reset alone is insufficient (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13). NCSC Switzerland published advisory 13054 on 2026-10-13 with the exploitation status Actively Exploited. It lists the Danfoss AK-SM 800 (end of life, no longer patched), the AK-SC 355 (phased out, no longer patched) and the current AK-SM 800A series when it runs outdated firmware, says no fixes exist for the two older models and that Danfoss urges replacing them, and says the attack could affect other sectors, such as healthcare for specialized cooling equipment, so organisations should check whether affected devices are in use (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13). Danfoss told Cooling Post that the AK-SM800 was declared end of life in 2021, that the AK-SC355 was phased out in 2016, and that the affected AK-SM800A systems ran outdated firmware (Cooling Post, 2026-10-12). Blick reports that Migros uses the same Danfoss refrigeration systems in a limited number of Swiss stores and sees no sign they were targeted, and that Aldi, Lidl and Coop say they are not affected (Blick, 2026-10-13); no source reports a Swiss victim. The advisory relays a six-step CERT-FR sequence (limit access to trusted addresses, factory reset, apply all fixes, rotate passwords and secrets, review accounts, reconfigure) and lists filtering to trusted addresses as a temporary measure (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13), whereas the revised CERT-FR page puts removal of internet exposure first, accepts source-address filtering only as an emergency stop-gap and lists no secret rotation or account review (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13).

Improvement15 Oct 2026 03:49 UTCrun 2026-10-15T0256Z-intelsourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

Censys, which scans for Danfoss StoreView control panels, says Danfoss has not confirmed the initial access vector and points to three AK-SM 800A flaws that Danfoss patched more than a year earlier: CVE-2025-41450 (March 2025), which Censys describes as letting an unauthenticated actor log in as an administrator with a code computed from the current calendar date, and CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452 (August 2025), which it says let authenticated users run commands and disrupt the management interface (Censys, 2026-10-14). Censys maps the firmware by build: below 4.2 carries all three, 4.2.4 fixes only the date-based login and still carries the two later ones, and 4.3.1 or later fixes all three (Censys, 2026-10-14). Its scan counted 1,825 exposed StoreView panels in France on 2026-10-11 and 537 on 2026-10-14, a fall of 71 percent, with builds below 4.2, build 4.2.4 and builds from 4.3.1 leaving at about the same rate, which it reads as operators taking controllers off the internet rather than patching them (Censys, 2026-10-14). Outside France the count fell from 1,166 to 966, and in ten of the twelve countries with the most exposed hosts more than 60 percent of the hosts run a build below 4.3.1, led by Poland at 81 percent and Romania at 80 percent (Censys, 2026-10-14).

Update18 Oct 2026 03:33 UTCrun 2026-10-18T0256Z-intelsummaryactionssourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

CERT-FR's alert now has a third version, dated 2026-10-16 and listed on the page as an update of the recommendations; the page does not show which sentences changed (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16). Its current text separates the two cases. For every unit it asks to remove the internet exposure of the affected units and of any unit on a public IP address, and to check the insurance contract conditions before cutting the data uplink to the refrigeration contractor (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16). For a unit not known to be compromised it then asks to check the whole configuration, notably the defrost ranges; for a compromised Danfoss unit it says to restart the equipment or otherwise restore it with a factory reset, and then to reconfigure it for service (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16). In both cases access returns only through a secure VPN or protected network, with source-address filtering for the contractors an emergency measure and not a lasting one, and the maker's practices apply (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16). The alert still says campaigns are probably ongoing, still names no flaw or entry vector, and gives the risk as not specified by the vendor (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16).

The alert's documentation section links an operator guide from Dixell France (Copeland) (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16). The file at that address was replaced on 2026-10-18; its current text, described in the correction of 2026-10-19T04:06:00Z, is Copeland's bulletin of 14 October 2026 followed by Dixell France's own complement (Dixell France, 2026-10-14). That complement says XWEB PRO and EVO ship with the same factory account, Admin with the password Admin, advises keeping the original Admin password sealed or in a password manager and not using it daily, gives each user a named account with an expiry date for an external contractor's account, and requires remote access through an encrypted VPN, with no port forward or DMZ and no remote-control software such as AnyDesk or TeamViewer on a site PC that stays on (Dixell France, 2026-10-14). CERT-FR does not say how the attackers got in, and SecurityWeek writes that neither Danfoss nor French authorities have tied the attack to the flaws Claroty disclosed (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16; SecurityWeek, 2026-10-15).

Correction19 Oct 2026 04:06 UTCrun 2026-10-19T0256Z-intelsummarysourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

The Dixell France guide that CERT-FR links was replaced on 2026-10-18, the file's date on the vendor's server, and now opens with Copeland's own security bulletin dated 14 October 2026 (Dixell France, 2026-10-14). The earlier update section's statements about XWEB PRO firmware 1.12.1, a CISA advisory and a March 2024 bulletin are no longer on that page and are removed from the summary and the body. The bulletin acknowledges the vulnerability on a generation of XWEB EVO controllers that is no longer marketed and has reached end of life, says to remove every XWEB EVO from the public internet immediately and then look for suspicious activity from the local network, and says XWEB EVO no longer receives security patches, while XWEB PRO is the supported platform and must not be exposed to the internet either (Dixell France, 2026-10-14). For an XWEB EVO that may have been accessed it gives a procedure: isolate the unit, restore the latest backup made before the access or otherwise check the users and profiles, set new passwords, check the alarm categories and recipients with a test alarm, and restore the device parameters from backup files or, without one, read each device's parameters and check setpoints, alarm thresholds and defrost parameters; it also says to check the product temperatures in the cabinets directly, since altered setpoints or alarm thresholds can compromise food safety (Dixell France, 2026-10-14).

Le Monde reports that besides raising the defrost temperature to 50 degrees the attackers lengthened the defrost operation from one hour to eight so that alarms trigger late, which delayed interventions and amplified the damage (translated from French) (Le Monde, 2026-10-12). SecurityWeek relays that detail and adds that the Paris prosecutor's office said the attack caused fires as well as food losses, that the Finance Minister put the number of affected supermarkets at about 700 of roughly 10,000, and that investigators are reportedly puzzled by the lack of a claim of responsibility or a ransom demand, citing Reuters (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-15). Cybersecurity Dive had already reported that a Copeland spokesperson confirmed the vulnerability was found in discontinued end-of-life controllers (Cybersecurity Dive, 2026-10-15).

entries.title: Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb refrigeration controllers compromised, with forced defrost reported at hundreds of French supermarkets; CERT-FR and NCSC Switzerland say to remove internet exposure

updates.summary: CERT-FR revised its alert on 2026-10-13 to add Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb to the compromised controllers, says campaigns are probably still running, and says a factory reset alone is insufficient on an unpatched end-of-life unit. NCSC Switzerland published an advisory rating the activity actively exploited and naming the current AK-SM 800A on outdated firmware, and Danfoss says that is the case for the affected current units. Blick reports that Migros uses the same Danfoss systems in a limited number of Swiss stores and sees no sign they were targeted.

Censys's exposure report of 2026-10-14 points to three published 2025 AK-SM 800A flaws that Danfoss patched more than a year earlier and gives their firmware boundaries (4.3.1 or later fixes all three; Danfoss has not confirmed the vector), and shows exposed French controllers falling about 71 percent in three days with patched and unpatched builds leaving at the same rate, which Censys reads as operators taking units offline rather than patching.

CERT-FR's alert has a third version dated 2026-10-16 whose guidance differs for compromised and uncompromised units: the whole configuration, defrost ranges included, is to be checked, and a compromised Danfoss unit is to be restarted or otherwise factory-reset and reconfigured, with a caution to check insurance conditions before cutting the contractor's data uplink. The Dixell France operator guide that the alert links says any XWEB PRO on firmware 1.12.1 or earlier must be updated without delay, that XWEB units ship with a factory Admin account, and that remote access must go through an encrypted VPN; neither document names an entry vector.

The Dixell France guide that CERT-FR links was replaced on 2026-10-18 and now carries Copeland's own bulletin of 14 October 2026, which acknowledges the vulnerability on a discontinued, end-of-life generation of XWEB EVO controllers, says to remove every XWEB EVO from the public internet at once, gives a restore procedure and says to check product temperatures in the cabinets directly; the earlier statements about XWEB PRO firmware 1.12.1, a CISA advisory and a March 2024 bulletin are no longer on that page and are removed. entries.headline: Some Rank Math PRO 3.0.123 downloads carried malware; updating to 3.0.124 does not remove what it left
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-111862updatedNATOA2

Rank Math SEO PRO 3.0.123: some packages served for about eleven hours carried malware that can leave hidden backdoors, rogue administrators and cron persistence that the update to 3.0.124 does not remove

Rank Math says that some copies of Rank Math PRO 3.0.123, downloaded between 2026-10-15 20:02 UTC and 2026-10-16 07:12 UTC, contained malware that could compromise a website if the plugin was activated, and that it removed the files and released 3.0.124 (Rank Math, 2026-10-16). It says the malware can recreate its hidden backdoor whenever someone visits the website, so removing suspicious files before disabling the mechanism that recreates them may not resolve the infection (Rank Math, 2026-10-16). Wordfence adds that the malware may establish persistent access, contact a remote host, and expose WordPress credentials, database credentials, API keys and other secrets that the web server can reach, and that Rank Math says it holds records of who downloaded an affected copy (Wordfence, 2026-10-17). The signs Rank Math lists are three malicious entries in the WordPress options table, hidden PHP backdoors in the must-use plugins directory and in other plugin and theme folders, unknown administrator accounts, a fake core file under wp-includes, .htaccess rules that let .cache files run as PHP, PHP files in the uploads directory and a web-user cron entry carrying a marker comment (Rank Math, 2026-10-16).

Exposure
A site that downloaded or updated Rank Math PRO 3.0.123 inside the stated window; Rank Math says the installed version shows under Plugins (Rank Math, 2026-10-16), and Wordfence stresses that 3.0.123 alone does not establish compromise (Wordfence, 2026-10-17). Rank Math says a copy installed and activated in the window means a compromised site, a copy installed but never activated means deleting the files, installing 3.0.124 and scanning, and a copy only downloaded shows no sign of compromise from this incident alone (Rank Math, 2026-10-16).
Detection
The web-server user's crontab and the WordPress scheduled events, the list of administrator accounts, WordPress core integrity (wp core verify-checksums), PHP files under the must-use plugins and uploads directories and in other plugins and themes, and web-server egress to the host Rank Math names (Rank Math, 2026-10-16). Rank Math also says the attacker may have changed things outside the WordPress directory, so review SSH authorized_keys files and other users' crontabs (Rank Math, 2026-10-16). Post-patch compromise check: updating replaces the affected package but does not remove files, accounts or scheduled tasks the malware already created elsewhere (Wordfence, 2026-10-17).
Defender takeaway
Treat a site that activated an affected copy as compromised: restore from a backup older than 2026-10-15 20:02 UTC, or, if cleaning by hand, delete the whole plugin folder (deactivating is not enough), remove the malicious options and block the malicious host Rank Math names before anything else, then clean the rest; either way rotate the WordPress, database, API, hosting and SSH credentials the site could reach, and install 3.0.124 only from the vendor's own account page, since Rank Math says it sends no login or download links by email (Rank Math, 2026-10-16).
Improvement19 Oct 2026 21:04 UTCrun 2026-10-18T1307Z-auditcvessourcesbody

Wordfence has assigned the malicious 3.0.123 packages the identifier CVE-2026-111862, recorded as embedded malicious code with a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8, affected version 3.0.123 and patched version 3.0.124 (Wordfence Intelligence, 2026-10-16), so vulnerability scanners and tickets keyed on the identifier match this incident. The record, like Rank Math, limits the affected packages to those obtained during the stated window and says version 3.0.123 alone does not establish compromise (Wordfence Intelligence, 2026-10-16).

actions: Upgrade every PaperCut NG/MF Application Server, Site Server and secondary/print server to the security maintenance release for its line (26.0.5, 25.0.13 or 24.1.11, the v24 build the September bulletin now names), starting with any still on Emergency Patch Release 1 or 2, because the emergency builds do not carry the fix for CVE-2026-82077, an administrator-only Scan-to-Fax code-execution flaw that the vendor's September bulletin lists as fixed in 26.0.5, 25.0.13 and 24.1.10; for v23 and earlier, immediately restrict the Application Server's web interface to trusted/internal IP addresses only; no patch exists for that line. On every server, patched or not, set the advanced config key auth.webservices.auth-token to a long random secret and limit auth.webservices.allowed-addresses to the hosts that call the XML-RPC API, because Hunt.io says an instance hardened against the Tapestry bypass is not necessarily protected against the XML-RPC route it recovered, which works when the allowlist is too permissive or no token is set.

Before patching or restarting an internet-facing server, preserve the server/logs directory and process tree; check server.log for the two vendor-documented error strings and for an unexplained gap or truncation, check server.log and derby.log for an in-memory Derby database booted under an attacker-chosen name, and hunt for a Windows service named "Remote Access Service" running SimpleService.exe (SimpleHelp) or an unexpected AnyDesk install, as PaperCut's own published incident data names both as an observed post-compromise access method.
