entries.headline: Exploited Ivanti Connect Secure chain: its root step had no fix at disclosure, and it evades the Integrity Checker
entries.html:
CRITICALCVE-2026-104935 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA1

CVE-2026-104935, Ivanti Connect Secure: an authentication bypass chained to code execution is exploited as a zero-day, and the root-escalation step of the chain was unpatched at disclosure (CVSS 8.6)

Ivanti disclosed a vulnerability in limited versions of Connect Secure on 2026-10-13 and says it is aware of limited exploitation in the wild (Ivanti, 2026-10-13). Rapid7 describes CVE-2026-104935 as an authentication bypass by spoofing that lets a remote unauthenticated attacker run commands, and scores it CVSS 8.6 (Rapid7, 2026-10-13). CISA added CVE-2026-104935 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day (CISA, 2026-10-13). Volexity found the activity on 2026-10-05, tracks the operator as UTA0576, a previously unknown cluster it assesses with low confidence as criminal, and dates exploitation of a fully patched 22.8R2.4 appliance to 2026-10-03 (Volexity, 2026-10-13).

The chain has three steps. A request to the public login script welcome.cgi names a protected script in an X-DSCGI-PATH header, so the URL passes the authentication check while the header picks the destination. The upload script wu.cgi writes a file to disk before checking that it is a ZIP, and parallel requests run a Perl script before it is deleted. A root escalation then abuses the dsinvoked service's trust in the shared DSCache configuration store (Volexity, 2026-10-13). Ivanti tracks the first two steps under CVE-2026-104935 and, according to Volexity on 2026-10-13, had not fixed the root escalation, which it said would ship in a future release in the coming weeks (Volexity, 2026-10-13); that step now has its own identifier, CVE-2026-111357 (GitHub Advisory Database, 2026-10-15). Every command re-runs the whole chain through HTTP requests with no web shell or backdoor, and the exploit patches library code in memory only, so Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool, which looks for file changes, does not detect it; Volexity also found entries removed from the debug and audit logs (Volexity, 2026-10-13). The operator then went after the Active Directory service account stored on the appliance: LDAP queries for LAPS passwords, BitLocker recovery keys and password attributes, a Kerberoast-capable tool, password spraying, and packet capture of plaintext LDAP, HTTP Basic and NTLM traffic (Volexity, 2026-10-13).

Exposure
Connect Secure 25.1.1.1 and prior (fixed 25.1.1.2), 25.1.2.2 and prior (fixed 25.1.3.1; Ivanti describes the flaw as affecting versions before 25.1.3.0 (ENISA EUVD, 2026-10-13) and Rapid7 lists release 25.1.3.0 as resolved, while CERT-FR counts it as affected (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14)) and 22.8R2.4 and prior (fixed 22.8R2.5) are affected, and 22.7.x and below are not (Rapid7, 2026-10-13); the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security labels the 25.x line 25.2.2 and prior (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, 2026-10-13). CISA says 22.8 reaches end of life on 2027-01-31 (CISA, 2026-10-13).
Detection
The appliance's own logs were tampered with, so start upstream: web proxy, load balancer or WAF logs for many requests to welcome.cgi, above all with an X-DSCGI-PATH header (the login page itself is ordinary) or one whose script differs from the URL path. On domain controllers, look for LDAP queries from the appliance's service account for LAPS, BitLocker recovery and password-bearing attributes, Kerberos activity and spraying from the appliance's address. Volexity names a hidden directory under the appliance's /data partition holding a renamed capture binary, and post-exploitation files in /tmp, says a clean Integrity Checker result does not show the appliance is safe, and advises network and memory forensics; patching does not evict an attacker who is already in.
Defender takeaway
Upgrade now, then treat every appliance that was exposed on an affected build as a compromise-assessment target and rotate what it could reach: the root-escalation step had no fix when Volexity reported and the Integrity Checker cannot clear it. Where compromise cannot be excluded, isolate the appliance and preserve its memory and logs before any reset, because CERT-FR knows of lateral movement using the LDAP and Active Directory secrets stored on it (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14). CISA's recovery sequence for a suspected compromise: back up the configuration, factory-reset and upgrade (rebuild cloud and virtual appliances), restore, then reset passwords, certificates, API keys and licence-server credentials (CISA, 2026-10-13).
Update16 Oct 2026 04:10 UTCrun 2026-10-16T0256Z-intelsummaryimmediate_actioncvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

CERT-FR's alert of 2026-10-14 says Ivanti reports the vulnerability as actively exploited and that CERT-FR itself is aware of lateral movement using the LDAP and Active Directory secrets stored on the appliance (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14). It puts the response in an order: fully isolate the appliance from both the internet and the internal network, snapshot the file system and memory of a virtual appliance, avoid powering it off so that traces survive, place the logs under seal and analyse the appliance with the Volexity indicators, and only then, on compromise, factory-reset it, upgrade and reset the secrets (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14). Its list of secrets to treat as compromised is wider than a password reset: the LDAP and Active Directory secrets, every certificate on the appliance (machine, user-authentication, code-signing and the TLS certificate of the exposed interface), the administration password, stored API keys, the passwords of local accounts including the service accounts used for authentication servers, the Kerberos tickets and other authentication material of those service accounts, and the licence-server authentication (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14). CERT-FR adds that running Ivanti's external Integrity Checker Tool needs physical access to the appliance and can interrupt service, and that some threats survive a factory reset (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14). Its affected-systems list names the 22.8Rx builds before 22.8R2.5, the 25.1.1.x builds before 25.1.1.2 and the 25.1.3.x builds before 25.1.3.1 and does not list a 25.1.2.x line; by counting 25.1.3.x builds before 25.1.3.1 as affected it includes 25.1.3.0, a build that Rapid7's table lists as resolved (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14).

Improvement17 Oct 2026 03:34 UTCrun 2026-10-17T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummaryimmediate_actioncvessourcesevidencebody

The root-escalation step of the chain now has its own identifier, CVE-2026-111357, published on 2026-10-15 and rated High on GitHub's advisory database as GHSA-fhw5-mpvj-x89m (GitHub Advisory Database, 2026-10-15). Its description reads "Ivanti Connect Secure 22.8R2.4 mishandles the manner in which the dsinvoked broker trusts DSCache configuration data, leading to privilege escalation to root, as exploited in the wild in October 2026." (GitHub Advisory Database, 2026-10-15), the same step Volexity describes as abusing the dsinvoked service's trust in the shared DSCache store (Volexity, 2026-10-13).

The record names only 22.8R2.4 as affected and states no fixed build; Volexity wrote that Ivanti was working on a fix for release in the coming weeks (Volexity, 2026-10-13), and no source read says whether any build now fixes it. The Canadian Cyber Centre's bulletin on the Ivanti advisory, updated 2026-10-16, adds that open-source reporting indicates CVE-2026-111357 is being exploited in the wild (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, 2026-10-13). A scanner, SIEM enrichment rule or ticket can now follow the unfixed step by this ID, and an appliance that was exposed still needs the compromise check above.

Improvement21 Oct 2026 08:20 UTCrun 2026-10-21T0800Z-auditbodyevidencesourcessourcing_notesummary

Ivanti's own description of CVE-2026-104935, as the numbering authority, reads "Authentication bypass by spoofing in ICS before version 25.1.3.0 allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands" (ENISA EUVD, 2026-10-13). Rapid7 relays that, according to Ivanti, a portion of the flaw was found through its product security program and patched in the July 2026 release of 25.1.3.0, and that exploitation occurred while Ivanti was backporting the fix to the other supported versions (Rapid7, 2026-10-13). CERT-FR still lists 25.1.3.x builds before 25.1.3.1 as affected (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14), so 25.1.3.1 remains the build to reach on that line.

entries.headline: Ahsay admits its earlier AhsayCBS patches were incomplete; the hotfixes are partner-only and CISA lists both flaws as exploited
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-105133 +1exploitedupdatedNATOB1

CVE-2026-105133 / CVE-2026-105134, AhsayCBS backup management console: an unauthenticated authentication-bypass and code-execution chain exploited since 7 October to drop webshells and a cryptominer; Ahsay says its earlier patches were incomplete and ships hotfixes 10.3.4.45 and 9.15.2.70 through its partner portal

Huntress reports that from 2026-10-07 23:20 UTC attackers exploited two flaws in AhsayCBS, the management console of Ahsay's backup software that managed service providers and system integrators mainly use, to gain unauthenticated remote code execution and deploy webshells on exposed servers (Huntress, 2026-10-08). CVE-2026-105133, an improper-authentication flaw in the checkSysPwd function of the API, is used first to bypass authentication; CVE-2026-105134, in the /rps/api/json/UpdateReceivers.do endpoint of the Replication Receiver component, then gives code execution as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, after which the attacker configured a malicious receiver and dropped a JSP webshell into the directory the application serves (Huntress, 2026-10-08). Horizon3's later source-level analysis traces the file write itself to the receiver's upload path, which a receiver created through that endpoint exposes (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-14). BleepingComputer reports that the activity targeted at least five organizations on 7 October and that CVE-2026-105133 has a public exploit (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-09).

Follow-on activity, per Huntress: commands spawned by the AhsayCBS service process fetch payloads over HTTP from cloud object storage into a Temp folder with curl and certutil; an XMRig Monero miner renamed to look like a Microsoft Edge binary runs as SYSTEM through a service that mimics the Edge updater and a renamed copy of the NSSM service manager, and reaches its mining pool on a non-standard port; and a PowerShell script that Huntress assesses as AI-assisted checks whether Task Manager is running, uses the host's local time to decide when to close it, and stops the miner while it is open (Huntress, 2026-10-08). The earlier patches did not close the flaws: public records had listed AhsayCBS up to 10.3.2 as affected (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-09), Huntress found on 2026-10-08 that 10.3.4 is also affected (Huntress, 2026-10-08), and Ahsay's release notes for 10.3.4 list no security fix (Ahsay, 2026-08-05).

Exposure
AhsayCBS servers (on Windows a service run from cbssvcX64.exe or cbssvcX86.exe; Horizon3 shows the same chain on the Linux build, where the service runs as root (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-14)), whose management web interface is reachable from untrusted networks and that run a v7 to v10 build below the hotfixes v10.3.4.45 or v9.15.2.70, which includes v10.3.4.0 and v9.15.2.59 (Ahsay, 2026-10-12; Huntress, 2026-10-08).
Detection
Process-creation telemetry with parent lineage: children of the AhsayCBS service process outside its normal startup and maintenance commands, because commands from an uploaded JSP webshell appear as direct children of the service, and curl or certutil from that lineage writing into a Temp folder; service inventory: a service named like the Edge update service running an Edge-named binary from a Temp folder as SYSTEM; PowerShell script-block logs: a script that checks for Task Manager and stops or starts a service to match; command lines that name WinRing0 next to a URL; and new .jsp files in the application directory. Huntress published four Sigma rules (Huntress, 2026-10-08). Horizon3's source-level analysis adds checks on the server itself, where the service process is the CBS JVM on Linux: new .jsp files under webapps/rps, webapps/cbs or any served application directory, especially ones that answer 404 unless a specific parameter is supplied; replication receivers whose home directory sits under the install directory and that were created outside a change window (a "Created new receiver" entry in the system log); unexpected system administrator accounts and API logon entries for accounts nobody provisioned; and requests to the JSON .do endpoints or the receiver upload path that carry a FromServlet field or X-RSW-Request headers from untrusted sources (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-14).

Triage: AhsayCBS legitimately spawns its own startup and maintenance commands, so a child process alone is weak; the discriminators Huntress gives are a child of the service that downloads files into a Temp folder, and an Edge-named binary run as SYSTEM from a Temp folder under a service that mimics the Edge updater (Huntress, 2026-10-08).

Defender takeaway
Apply the hotfix v10.3.4.45 or v9.15.2.70 to every AhsayCBS server, including those on the earlier patches, and reboot it (Ahsay, 2026-10-12); ask your backup suppliers whether they run it, because the hotfixes sit behind a partner login, and until it is applied keep the management interface on trusted addresses or a VPN, since the exploit targets the externally reachable web application (Huntress, 2026-10-08); where an indicator of compromise turns up, re-image the host from a trusted backup, since Huntress says attackers hid secondary backdoors for extended persistence (Huntress, 2026-10-08).
Update16 Oct 2026 04:09 UTCrun 2026-10-16T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummaryprioritytagstechniquescvessourcesevidenceverificationsourcing_noteconfidenceclassificationactionsbody

Ahsay now says its previous patches v9.15.2.59 and v10.3.4.0 "did not fully address" the two flaws, and tells partners to apply the AhsayCBS v10.3.4.45 hotfix on v10 and the v9.15.2.70 hotfix on v7, v8 and v9, both from the partner portal (a valid partner login is required), then to reboot the server (Ahsay, 2026-10-12). The announcement is dated 2026-10-12; Huntress, in an update of the same day to its report, dates the hotfix release to that day and says it independently verified that the v10.3.4.45 hotfix mitigates the initial entry point of the chain, which was still open on earlier v10 versions (Huntress, 2026-10-08).

CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-14 "based on evidence of active exploitation" (CISA, 2026-10-14). Bitdefender MDR reports three intrusions through the chain, the first two beginning around 7 to 8 October and a third identified on 14 October; in the first, attackers validated access through JSP webshells, staged PowerShell payloads, tried to stage payloads as command files in C:\Users\Public and tried to establish persistence; in the second they deployed JSP files, tried the same command-file staging, searched for stored credentials, elevated an account to SYSTEM and used obfuscated PowerShell to install and configure OpenSSH, which gives a way back that does not depend on the vulnerable web service, so patching alone does not end the incident; across its incidents the follow-on PowerShell scripts were staged on a subdomain of a public static-site hosting service; it attributes the activity to no named actor, and notes that the file names, tools and binaries differed from one incident to the next, so the dependable signal is how the server behaves after the exploit fires (Bitdefender, 2026-10-15).

Improvement18 Oct 2026 03:34 UTCrun 2026-10-18T0256Z-intelsourcesevidenceactionsbody

Horizon3.ai published a source-level analysis of both flaws on 2026-10-14, working from the Linux installer, and says its proof of concept for the chain, from authentication bypass to a webshell, is on its GitHub (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-14). For CVE-2026-105133, every action of the JSON API extends a base class whose administrator password check is skipped when the request body carries a FromServlet flag that the caller sets, so the JSON API is reachable without credentials, and the AddSysUser action, which creates a system administrator, never consults the caller (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-14). For CVE-2026-105134, an authentication-bypassed call creates a replication receiver whose home directory the attacker chooses; the system-folder denylist that screens that directory at creation is not applied to the upload path later built from two attacker-supplied headers, in which only the percent and colon characters are escaped, so a traversal sequence walks the write location into a served web application, and one upload of a .jsp file then runs as LocalSystem on Windows and as root on Linux (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-14). Horizon3 says Ahsay released its hotfixes on 12 October 2026 (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-14).

entries.headline: Palo Alto confirms limited exploitation of a PAN-OS management-interface root flaw; no workaround, 11.2.16 now published
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-0322exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-0322, Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS: code injection in the management interface gives an authenticated attacker root, exploited in very limited attacks and listed in CISA KEV (CVSS-B 8.6)

Palo Alto Networks' advisory of 2026-10-14 describes CVE-2026-0322, a code injection (CWE-94) in the management interface of PAN-OS that lets an authenticated attacker with network access run arbitrary code as root on PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and on Panorama (virtual and M-Series); Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access are not affected and no special configuration is needed to be affected (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-10-14). The advisory is tagged as attacked and says very limited exploitation has been observed targeting the management interface (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-10-14), and CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day (CISA, 2026-10-14). Palo Alto scores it CVSS-B 8.6 with a suggested urgency of highest, says the risk is highest when the management interface is reachable from the internet, and scores it 8.5 when access is restricted to a single jump box (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-10-14). It lists no workaround; Threat Prevention IDs 510046 and 510047 give limited coverage and only when management traffic is routed through a data-plane interface and decrypted, and Palo Alto warns that variations of the attack may not be detected (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-10-14). Fixes ship per train; a unit on 11.2.14 or 11.2.15 had no fixed build when the advisory appeared, and 11.2.16, the fix for those two releases, was published on 2026-10-15 (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-10-14). The advisory does not say how the attackers obtained the credentials the flaw requires, when exploitation began or who is behind it, and BleepingComputer says it asked Palo Alto when exploitation began, who is behind the attacks and whether attackers compromised firewalls or used them to reach internal networks (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-14).

Exposure
Any PA-Series or VM-Series firewall or Panorama (virtual or M-Series) on PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1 or 12.2 below the fixed build of its train, with no configuration needed; the exposure is greatest where the management interface accepts connections from outside trusted internal addresses (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-10-14). BleepingComputer reads the advisory as requiring existing credentials and network access to the management interface (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-14).
Detection
Look at authentication and administrator-change records on the management interface, and at inbound connections to the management address in upstream firewall or provider logs, for logins from unfamiliar sources; Palo Alto's advisory FAQ lists three source addresses associated with the limited exploit attempts to compare against (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-10-14). Root code execution means an upgrade does not evict an attacker who is already in, and the advisory gives no file or process artifact, so a device that was reachable from untrusted networks before the fix needs a compromise assessment as well as the patch.
Defender takeaway
Take the management interface off every network but trusted internal addresses, with a jump box as the tightest setting Palo Alto describes, and upgrade to the fixed build of each train; units on 11.2.14 and 11.2.15 upgrade to 11.2.16, which Palo Alto published on 2026-10-15 (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-10-14).
Update16 Oct 2026 04:08 UTCrun 2026-10-16T0256Z-intelheadlinesummarycvesevidenceactionsbody

Palo Alto Networks published 11.2.16 on 2026-10-15, the fixed build for units on 11.2.14 and 11.2.15, which had none when the advisory appeared; its solution table now reads "Upgrade to 11.2.16 or later" for those two releases and every other train keeps the fixed builds already listed (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-10-14). The advisory's exploitation status is unchanged at very limited exploitation, and it still lists no workaround (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-10-14).

entries.headline: Huntress: a lookalike VPN-client site harvests credentials, then hands over the real signed installer
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

A fake WatchGuard VPN download site captures the SSL VPN server, login and password in the browser and then serves the genuine signed installer, leaving no malicious file for endpoint tools to flag

Huntress's SOC investigated an incident on 2026-10-07 in which an administrator at a managed service provider searched Bing for a WatchGuard VPN download with a typo in the query and clicked through the standard Bing result redirect to a lookalike site titled "WatchGuard Firebox VPN Client", which Huntress classes as search-engine poisoning rather than malvertising (Huntress, 2026-10-13). Choosing any download option opens a pop-up asking for Server, Login and Password; one unobfuscated JavaScript file of about 150 lines posts the typed values as JSON to a separate collector domain, tagged as the first or second attempt, and always rejects the first submission with an "incorrect data" message so that the victim types again or tries a second set of credentials (Huntress, 2026-10-13). Only after the second submission does the page fetch the real WatchGuard Mobile VPN with SSL installer from WatchGuard's own CDN, an Authenticode-signed file whose digest Huntress recomputed and found unmodified, so there is no trojanized installer or malicious DLL for endpoint defenses to flag (Huntress, 2026-10-13). The victim's browser history showed no download in the observed window, so Huntress judges the user probably did not finish both rounds but may have typed credentials in the first, and Managed Defender flagged the incident 21 seconds after the lookalike domain loaded (Huntress, 2026-10-13). Both domains were registered within the previous two months, few reputation engines flagged either as of 2026-10-08, and the lure domain was offline by 2026-10-13 (Huntress, 2026-10-13). Huntress places the iteration in a campaign that WatchGuard's Secplicity team described in January 2026 as lookalike download sites for WatchGuard, F5, Fortinet, SonicWall and Sophos clients, and that Microsoft tied in March 2026 to a financially motivated actor it tracks as Storm-2561; the new element is that the fake client is gone from the middle (Huntress, 2026-10-13).

Exposure
Administrators and users who find an SSL VPN client through a web search, as an administrator at a managed service provider did here; the lure here impersonates WatchGuard, and Huntress describes the same campaign against clients of five vendors (Huntress, 2026-10-13). The credentials of any VPN account typed into such a page, and the gateway address with them, are in the attacker's hands.
Detection
No malicious file or process reaches the endpoint, so the signal is in web proxy and DNS telemetry (a visit that arrives from a search-result redirect to a domain that is not the vendor's, followed by a JSON POST to a second, recently registered domain; Huntress's Managed Defender did flag the browsing activity) and in VPN gateway authentication logs; Huntress advises watching for SSL VPN logins from hosting providers, unfamiliar ASNs and countries where the account has never connected (Huntress, 2026-10-13).

Triage: a genuine VPN client also asks for server, login and password, but only inside the installed client at connect time; a browser form that collects the three values before any installer has run, on a domain that is not the vendor's, is the signal.

Defender takeaway
If a user typed VPN credentials into a page found through search, reset every affected account and treat the VPN endpoint those credentials belong to as known to the attacker; enforce multi-factor authentication on the VPN, and publish and bookmark the official client download links in internal documentation so staff do not search for them (Huntress, 2026-10-13).

entries.headline: Exploited Nextcloud Collabora CODE app flaw: disabling the app does not help; update to 26.4.303 or remove it
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-110447exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-110447, Collabora Online Built-in CODE Server (Nextcloud richdocumentscode app): an unauthenticated command injection in proxy.php, exploited in the wild to plant PHP web shells, fixed in 26.4.303 (CVSS 4.0 9.2)

Collabora's own advisory, published 2026-10-14, says users of Nextcloud with the Collabora Online Built-in CODE Server app (richdocumentscode) can be vulnerable through proxy.php: a request can run an operating system command as the web server user, the attack works only while the built-in CODE server is not running (after a restart, an upgrade or a crash), and disabling the app is not sufficient, it must be upgraded to 26.4.303 or later or removed (Collabora Online security advisory, 2026-10-14). Users of end-of-life Nextcloud 29 or older should upgrade Nextcloud or remove the app, standalone Collabora Online servers are not affected, and the fix for CVE-2025-66208 does not prevent this flaw (Collabora Online security advisory, 2026-10-14). The GitHub Advisory Database record for CVE-2026-110447 says it was exploited in the wild in September and October 2026 (GitHub Advisory Database, 2026-10-14). Field reports came first: on 2026-09-11 a hoster reported on the app's issue tracker that several Nextcloud servers running richdocumentscode 26.4.302 had been compromised since the previous day through requests to proxy.php that carried shell command substitution and an encoded path traversal, with base64 payloads decoded and run through a shell to create PHP web shells in the app directory; on one server the attacker then searched for password-manager databases and cryptocurrency-wallet files, and the reviewed requests showed no archiving or upload commands (issue 354, 2026-09-11). Other administrators report the same compromise, one noticing it because Nextcloud's integrity check failed on an unexpected PHP file (issue 354, 2026-09-11). A reply on the issue says the flaw affects only the Development Edition in the Built-in CODE Server mode that downloads a local AppImage, and a later one that leftover web-shell files must be removed after upgrading (issue 354, 2026-09-11). A Nextcloud forum post of 2026-10-03 told users to update, saying that as far as the poster knew no CVE existed (Nextcloud community forum, 2026-10-03).

Exposure
A Nextcloud server with the "Collabora Online - Built-in CODE Server" app at 26.4.302 or older, including one patched for CVE-2025-66208; a restart, an upgrade or a crash that stops the built-in CODE server opens the window, and deactivating the app does not close it (Collabora Online security advisory, 2026-10-14).
Detection
In web access logs, requests to the app's proxy.php whose path carries $( command substitution and an encoded ..; in file telemetry, unexpected PHP files in the app directory, which Nextcloud's integrity check flagged on a compromised server; in process telemetry, the web server account starting a shell that decodes base64 and calls out with curl or wget to an external service (issue 354, 2026-09-11). The web shell survives the update, so the post-patch check is the same file and process search, and the reporter says secrets available to the web server account must be treated as potentially affected (issue 354, 2026-09-11).
Defender takeaway
Update the app to 26.4.303 or remove it on every Nextcloud server that has it, because disabling it does not stop the request, and on Nextcloud 29 or older upgrade Nextcloud or remove the app (Collabora Online security advisory, 2026-10-14); then search for dropped PHP files and the request pattern back to at least early September 2026, and on a hit rotate whatever the web server account can read (issue 354, 2026-09-11).

entries.headline: Cisco's mail gateway has a second exploited root flaw in four weeks; the fix ships as a Content Scanner Tools update
entries.html:
CRITICALCVE-2026-76519exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-76519, Cisco Secure Email Gateway: one crafted email attachment writes files and runs commands as root, exploited in the wild and listed in CISA KEV (CVSS 9.8)

Cisco's advisory of 2026-10-14 describes CVE-2026-76519, a relative path traversal in the Advanced Malware Protection feature of Cisco Secure Email Gateway: improper handling of email attachments when the file reputation service is enabled lets an unauthenticated remote attacker who sends a crafted attachment through the device write arbitrary files on the underlying operating system and run commands as root, and Cisco rates it CVSS 3.1 9.8 (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-14). Cisco states that in October 2026 its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation, and that it has directly contacted Cisco Secure Email Cloud customers on whose devices indicators of possible compromise were identified (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-14); CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day (CISA, 2026-10-14). Cisco gives no workaround; the fix is distributed through the Content Scanner Tools package for every supported AsyncOS release and needs no software upgrade or restart, and it is also in AsyncOS 15.5.5-014 and 16.5.0-780, while release 16.0 must migrate to a fixed release (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-14). It is the second exploited root-level flaw in this product in about four weeks: BleepingComputer notes that last month Cisco warned of CVE-2026-76461, which also lets unauthenticated remote attackers run commands as root (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-14).

Exposure
A physical or virtual Cisco Secure Email Gateway is exposed when both conditions hold: the File Reputation service is enabled and assigned to a mail policy (web interface, Mail Policies, Incoming or Outgoing Mail Policies, Advanced Malware Protection, "Enable File Reputation" ticked), and the Content Scanner Tools version, shown by the contentscannerstatus command, is earlier than 25.3.0.5525; Secure Email and Web Manager and Secure Web Appliance are not affected, and Cisco Secure Email Cloud Gateway customers need take no action (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-14). The attack arrives as an email attachment passing through the appliance, so exposure does not depend on its management interface being reachable (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-14).
Detection
Start with the appliance's own logs: Cisco's self-check is grep "System Security" system_logs on each cluster member, which returns "Suspected compromise indicator was found", "Security scan did not complete" or "No compromise indicator was found" (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-14). Cisco warns that an attacker with root may remove or hide evidence, so it also recommends cross-checking network and firewall logs outside the device for unexpected uploads from the appliance to external addresses or downloads from malicious addresses (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-14); that is egress telemetry from the gateway's own addresses.
Defender takeaway
Confirm Content Scanner Tools 25.3.0.5525 or later on every gateway today, since automatic updates deliver it and only gateways with updates disabled need the manual update, and run the log check on every one; for a virtual appliance with a compromise indicator, Cisco says to keep forensic data before upgrading, because upgrading a compromised instance destroys it, then deploy a new virtual machine on a fixed release, rebuild the configuration without importing an old file and renew credentials and cryptographic material (a physical appliance goes to Cisco TAC), and strongly recommends restoring every member of a cluster that contains a compromised appliance, since the cluster's SSH private keys could be accessed (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-14).

entries.headline: An attacker can reconstruct admin credentials for an exposed refrigeration controller offline, then silently disable cooling while the display reports normal
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-25085 +22updatedNATOB2

Claroty Team82: 23 vulnerabilities in Copeland XWEB Pro supervisory refrigeration controllers chain to unauthenticated root RCE; a deterministic admin password derived from the device's own MAC address is one of THREE independent pre-auth paths

Claroty Team82 disclosed 23 vulnerabilities (21 rated high) in Copeland XWEB300D/500D/500B PRO supervisory refrigeration controllers (firmware ≤1.12.1), which manage field devices such as the XR60CX controller over Modbus on an RS-485 serial network in commercial refrigeration and cold-chain deployments. Two named flaws chain to unauthenticated root RCE. CVE-2026-25085 is a logic flaw in the Lua user_authenticate handler: when an attacker supplies an unrecognized auth_mode value in the HTTP Authorization: Basic header, the function does not return nil/false but an unpopulated yet "truthy" table, "if an attacker supplied an unrecognized auth_mode, the user_authenticate function did not explicitly reject the request by returning nil or false. Instead, it returned an unpopulated table: { user = nil, role = nil, recovery = nil }" (Claroty Team82, 2026-08-09), and the router downstream checks only that something was returned, not its contents, so the malformed request slips through unauthenticated.

One of the three pre-auth paths is a deterministic admin-password generator: the credential is derived via a key-derivation function from a hardcoded firmware seed identical across the product line, plus the device's MAC address and the current date, both obtainable via unauthenticated public endpoints, so once an attacker has those two values, valid admin credentials can be computed offline: "because the seed values are identical across the product line and the variables (MAC address and date) can be obtained via unauthenticated public endpoints, an adversary can reconstruct the entire derivation chain offline" (Claroty Team82, 2026-08-09). A third pre-auth path, CVE-2026-24663 (CVSS 9.0), is an unauthenticated OS command injection reachable by sending a crafted request to the libraries installation route, with no authentication step to bypass at all.

Eighteen further CVEs (all listed above) are OS command-injection flaws across API/CGI endpoints (contacts import, firmware update, device templates, network/Wi-Fi configuration, the Modbus debug tool, the SMS service settings and others), each requiring prior authentication and each scored CVSS 8.0; Claroty documents seventeen of them (Claroty Team82, 2026-08-09), and CISA's advisory adds CVE-2026-3037, injected through the MBird SMS service URL or code on the utility route (CISA, 2026-02-26). CISA also lists two low-severity flaws reachable without authentication: an arbitrary file read (CVE-2026-22877, CVSS 3.7) and a stack-based buffer overflow in an API route that terminates the program (CVE-2026-20797, CVSS 4.3) (CISA, 2026-02-26). All are served by an embedded lighttpd instance where unsanitized user input reaches Lua system-execution calls running with elevated privileges, any of the three pre-auth primitives above chains directly to root: "since these services run with elevated privileges, successful exploitation results in immediate root-level code execution on the controller" (Claroty Team82, 2026-08-09). Claroty built a live physical demonstration: from an internet-exposed XWEB controller, an attacker works out the connected field controller's Modbus register addresses, many of which are not publicly documented, from the XR60CX datasheet and protocol analysis, and can set the temperature shown on the XR60CX display to any value while silently disabling cooling, spoiled food, or compromised temperature-sensitive medical supplies for pharmaceutical cold-chain. Copeland shipped firmware v1.13 through coordinated disclosure, fixing all 23 issues: "Copeland worked closely and collaboratively with us to develop a comprehensive remediation strategy. The vendor successfully patched these vulnerabilities and has uploaded firmware update version 1.13" (Claroty Team82, 2026-08-09); no source read reports exploitation of these flaws in the wild, but CERT-FR's alert of 2026-10-13 reports numerous compromises of Copeland xweb controllers without naming models, flaws or the entry vector (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13).

An anonymous, single-request path to full administrative control of internet-exposed cold-chain infrastructure demands action beyond a routine patch cycle, independent of confirmed exploitation: absence of exploitation is not evidence of safety when the exploit is a MAC address. Internet-exposed commercial refrigeration and cold-storage deployments are directly relevant to healthcare and food-safety cold-chain operations. Triage: the falsified display is itself the detection challenge: Claroty shows the temperature on the XR60CX field controller's display can be set to any value, so a normal reading on the display does not show that cooling is running; any authentication attempt using an auth_mode value the deployment does not use is a probe worth alerting on.

Correction30 Aug 2026 13:12 UTCrun 2026-08-30T1312Z-auditcvessourcing_noteactionsbody

Which CVE identifier covers the deterministic admin-password path is not something Claroty states, and this entry previously asserted it. Claroty's per-CVE table describes CVE-2026-21718 only as "an authentication bypass vulnerability... enabling any attackers to bypass the authentication requirement and achieve pre-authenticated code execution" with a CVSS v3 of 10.0, while the section walking through the MAC-address-and-date key derivation attaches no identifier to it (Claroty Team82, 2026-08-09). The three pre-auth paths and the mechanism of each are unchanged, and so is the remediation: firmware v1.13 fixes the disclosed set. What changes is that an operator matching a specific identifier against a vendor patch note or an asset-management ticket should not expect CVE-2026-21718 to be documented anywhere as the password-derivation bug.

Update14 Oct 2026 03:45 UTCrun 2026-10-14T0255Z-intelsummaryentitiessourcesevidencesourcing_notereferencesbody

CERT-FR revised its alert on refrigeration-controller compromises on 2026-10-13: it now says it knows of numerous compromises of the remote controllers Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC as well as Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb, that attack campaigns are probably still ongoing, and that access should come back only through a secure VPN or protected network, with filtering to the refrigeration contractors' source addresses accepted only as an emergency measure (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13). The alert names no Copeland models, no vulnerability and no entry vector, and does not tie the compromises to Claroty's findings, so it is not established that CVE-2026-25085 or any other flaw above was used.

Correction19 Oct 2026 21:06 UTCrun 2026-10-18T1307Z-auditsummarysectorscvessourcesverificationsourcing_notebody

CISA published an ICS advisory for these flaws on 2026-02-26, ICSA-26-057-10, contrary to the earlier statement that it could not be located; it lists all 23 identifiers with a summary and score each (CISA, 2026-02-26). The three not recorded before are CVE-2026-3037, an authenticated OS command injection through the MBird SMS service URL or code on the utility route (CVSS 8.0), so the authenticated command-injection flaws number eighteen, not seventeen; CVE-2026-22877, an arbitrary file read without authentication (CVSS 3.7); and CVE-2026-20797, a stack-based buffer overflow in an API route, reachable without authentication, that terminates the program (CVSS 4.3) (CISA, 2026-02-26). CVE-2026-21718 is an authentication bypass, as both Claroty and CISA call it, not a logic flaw (CISA, 2026-02-26).

Three descriptions above are corrected. The admin password is computed offline once the attacker has the MAC address and the date, which Claroty says can be obtained via unauthenticated public endpoints; the earlier "zero interaction with the target" overstated that (Claroty Team82, 2026-08-09). The supervisory controller reaches its field controllers over an RS485 serial network using Modbus, and Ethernet is its own network connection, not a field-device link (Claroty Team82, 2026-08-09). Claroty says the register addresses for many functions are not publicly documented and that it built the map from the XR60CX datasheet and protocol analysis (Claroty Team82, 2026-08-09). The sectors now read retail and healthcare, which Claroty names through supermarkets, food distribution and healthcare facilities, in place of energy, which no source supports (Claroty Team82, 2026-08-09); with CISA's advisory the flaws rest on two sources. The remediation is unchanged.

updates.summary: This entry stated that CVE-2026-21718 is the deterministic admin-password flaw. Claroty does not say that. Its per-CVE table text for that identifier is generic ("an authentication bypass vulnerability... enabling any attackers to bypass the authentication requirement and achieve pre-authenticated code execution", CVSS v3 10.0), and the narrative section that describes the MAC-address-and-date key derivation names no CVE id at all. The binding was an inference by elimination rather than a stated attribution, and a defender tracing the identifier to a patch note would have been misled. The mechanism description stands as reported; the id binding is removed from the title-adjacent claim, the CVE record's affected text, the body and the action, and the sourcing note now states what Claroty does and does not attribute.

entries.headline: GitLab's CVSS 10.0 CI regex flaw now has a public PoC; the demonstrated path needs push access to a public project
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-97229updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-97229, GitLab CE/EE: an integer overflow in the CI/CD regular-expression compiler allows code execution on self-managed servers and now has a public proof of concept; fixed in 19.4.2, 19.3.5 and 19.2.8, and 19.4.1 does not close it (CVSS 10.0)

GitLab's critical patch release of 2026-10-12 (19.4.2, 19.3.5 and 19.2.8) fixes CVE-2026-97229, an integer overflow in the CI/CD regular-expression compiler that, "under certain conditions", could allow an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server through a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration; GitLab scores it CVSS 3.1 10.0 with no privileges required (GitLab, 2026-10-12). Affected are self-managed CE and EE from 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5 and 19.4 before 19.4.2; GitLab.com already runs the patched version and Dedicated customers need no action (GitLab, 2026-10-12). CERT-EU and BleepingComputer give 19.3.4 as the 19.3 fix, but GitLab's page names 19.3.5 and says 19.3.4 had a merge-request page bug, so the GitLab figure governs (CERT-EU, 2026-10-12; BleepingComputer, 2026-10-12). The 19.4.1 release of 2026-09-23 fixed two flaws from the same reporter in the same component, a double free in the regular-expression parser and an integer overflow in the compiler, both rated for an authenticated user (GitLab, 2026-09-23); CVE-2026-97229 is rated without that requirement, and 19.4.1 is still affected. NCSC Switzerland and CERT-EU both published advisories on 2026-10-12 (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-12; CERT-EU, 2026-10-12); NCSC lists the exploitation status as unknown (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-12); Rapid7 reproduced the code execution on 19.4.1, published a proof of concept, and reports no confirmed exploitation in the wild (Rapid7, 2026-10-13). GitLab publishes the issue detail for a security fix 90 days after the release that carries it (GitLab, 2026-10-12).

Exposure
Self-managed GitLab CE or EE on 19.2.x below 19.2.8, 19.3.x below 19.3.5 or 19.4.x below 19.4.2; GitLab's table starts at 19.2 and lists no earlier branch (GitLab, 2026-10-12). NCSC Switzerland states the prerequisites as network access to the instance and delivery of a crafted regular expression through CI/CD configuration (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-12); Rapid7 found the conditions: an attacker must first commit a malicious CI/CD configuration file and a repository path containing UTF-8 characters to a branch in a public project, which an ordinary account can do by creating a public project where the instance allows it (Rapid7, 2026-10-13), and on instances where new users can self-register and create projects that constraint is removed (Rapid7, 2026-10-13). An instance with open sign-up, or with public projects that untrusted users can write to, is the case to prioritise.
Detection
GitLab and NCSC publish no indicators, so this is a hunt for the mechanism: in process-creation telemetry, shells, interpreters or network tools started as children of the GitLab application server processes, and in GitLab's audit and application logs, recently created or changed CI/CD configurations that carry unusual regular expressions, from accounts or addresses that have not used the instance before. Rapid7's proof of concept delivers the code through the public CI lint API without credentials, after pushing to a public project (Rapid7 proof-of-concept README, 2026-10-13): look for unauthenticated GET requests to /api/v4/projects/:id/ci/lint against a project that an account has just pushed to, and for application worker crashes that follow them, which the README says end the request with HTTP 502 while the worker is replaced (Rapid7 proof-of-concept README, 2026-10-13). A server where that turns up needs its CI/CD variables, runner registration tokens and deploy keys treated as exposed.

Triage: ordinary CI jobs run shells under the runners; only a shell spawned by the GitLab application server processes themselves matches this flaw, not one started inside a runner job; an anonymous CI lint request is ordinary on its own, and the signal is one aimed at a project that a newly created or little-used account has just pushed a CI configuration to.

Defender takeaway
Upgrade to 19.4.2, 19.3.5 or 19.2.8 now, starting with internet-facing instances as CERT-EU advises (CERT-EU, 2026-10-12); GitLab's release page lists no workaround as of 2026-10-13 (GitLab, 2026-10-12), Rapid7's interim controls (restrict anonymous access to public projects and stop untrusted users creating or writing to public projects) reduce exposure only to the path it demonstrated and do not fix the compiler flaw (Rapid7, 2026-10-13), and the proof of concept is tuned to one build while its author says analysis of additional reachable paths is ongoing (Rapid7 proof-of-concept README, 2026-10-13), so an instance that cannot be upgraded this week should be kept off untrusted networks; on a single-node instance the upgrade causes downtime, because migrations must finish before GitLab can start, so schedule the window now (GitLab, 2026-10-12).
Update14 Oct 2026 03:43 UTCrun 2026-10-14T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Rapid7 reports that it independently reproduced arbitrary code execution on the official GitLab CE 19.4.1 image with address space layout randomization enabled, that the same input did not execute on the patched 19.4.2 image, and that it found no confirmed exploitation in the wild (Rapid7, 2026-10-13). Its testing shows the unauthenticated label needs a qualifier: the attacker must first push a malicious CI/CD configuration and a UTF-8 repository path to a branch in a public project, which an ordinary account can do where users may create public projects (Rapid7, 2026-10-13); the proof of concept then triggers it with a request without credentials (Rapid7 proof-of-concept README, 2026-10-13). A proof of concept went public the same day; its README says the included offsets were tested only against the 19.4.1 CE Linux amd64 image, that other builds need adjusted offsets, and that the generated payload is slightly larger than 2 GiB, needing about 9 GiB of memory on the test host (Rapid7 proof-of-concept README, 2026-10-13). The affected and fixed versions are unchanged.

The demonstrated path needs push access to a public project (an ordinary account where users may create public projects), followed by a request to the CI lint API that carries no credentials. Self-managed CE and EE from 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5 and 19.4 before 19.4.2 are affected, and NCSC Switzerland and CERT-EU both published advisories on 2026-10-12.

entries.headline: German portal vendor reports an exploited zero-day and calls it AI-driven; police neither confirm nor deny that
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB3

Tangerhütte (Saxony-Anhalt): the vendor of the municipal citizen-portal software says attackers exploited a zero-day in it, classifies the intrusion as AI-driven, and four other communes took their portals offline

MDR AKTUELL reports on 2026-10-13 that the vendor of Tangerhütte's "digitales Rathaus" citizen portal says attackers found and exploited a vulnerability in its software that the vendor did not know of and for which no security update existed (MDR AKTUELL, 2026-10-13). The portal, an app-based service that went online in 2020, was taken offline in September, and MDR Sachsen-Anhalt reported on 2026-09-16 that the municipality said it had repelled an attack and gave no technical detail (MDR Sachsen-Anhalt, 2026-09-16). The software runs on systems that the state municipal IT provider KID operates for Tangerhütte; an IT employee noticed irregularities in the morning after the attack began at night, the server was isolated and cut from the internet, and the vendor analysed the secured logs on an offline notebook (MDR AKTUELL, 2026-10-13). Innocon told other affected communes, four of which also took their portals offline as a precaution although there was no sign of an attack on them, and says the attackers reached only test accounts and took no real data (MDR AKTUELL, 2026-10-13). Citizens could use the services only on paper for weeks (MDR AKTUELL, 2026-10-13).

The vendor classifies the intrusion as AI-driven for two reasons: commands were executed faster than copy-and-paste would allow, and the follow-on steps were not prepared in advance but developed on the city's server during the attack, whereas human attackers normally upload their own code and do not change it (MDR AKTUELL, 2026-10-13). That is the vendor's reading of its own logs. The state criminal police are investigating data espionage and can neither confirm nor deny an AI attack, and two professors told MDR the reading is plausible without having seen the logs (MDR AKTUELL, 2026-10-13). No CVE, product version, fixed release or entry vector is named.

Exposure
Municipalities running Innocon's digitales Rathaus, which is used for Tangerhütte and at least four further communes that Innocon informed; whether any Swiss body runs it is not reported. The case matters to communal administrations as a supplier-built citizen portal hosted by a shared municipal IT provider, where the customer cannot patch an unknown flaw itself.
Detection
The vendor's two observations are the pattern to look for in a portal host's logs: commands issued faster than a person could type them, and follow-on scripts written and run on the host within the same session rather than uploaded once.
Defender takeaway
For a citizen portal built on a supplier's software, an exploited unknown flaw leaves isolation as the only lever, and this case shows what worked: isolate the server, copy the logs and analyse them offline, and have the supplier warn its other customers, four of which pulled their portals as a precaution.

entries.headline: Microsoft patches an exploited Windows Shell zero-day that evades Mark of the Web protections on files and links
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-96951exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-96951, Windows Shell: a Mark of the Web bypass exploited as a zero-day, fixed in the 2026-10-13 cumulative updates and listed in CISA KEV (CVSS 8.8)

Microsoft's 2026-10-13 release fixes CVE-2026-96951, a Windows Shell security feature bypass that Microsoft marks as exploited and not publicly disclosed (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2026-10-13); CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day, citing evidence of active exploitation (CISA, 2026-10-13). Microsoft says an attacker who exploits it could evade Mark of the Web defenses, by sending a crafted file by email or instant message or enticing the user to click a link or open an attachment (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2026-10-13). Microsoft's record gives the root cause as improper neutralization of special elements in a command (command injection, CWE-77) (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2026-10-13). Rapid7 describes the effect as Windows not showing the dialog that says it protected the PC, because the tag that triggers it is bypassed, calls this the second exploited Windows Shell zero-day this year, and says the flaw also affected Outlook.com, patched in a build several weeks ago (Rapid7, 2026-10-13). Rapid7 says Windows Server 2012 receives no patch while Server 2012 R2 does (Rapid7, 2026-10-13), and Microsoft's record lists no Windows Server 2012 product for this flaw (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2026-10-13).

Exposure
Windows 10, Windows 11 and Windows Server 2012 R2 through 2025 where users open files or links from mail, chat or the web; the fixed build per release is in the CVE record, and Rapid7 reports no patch for Windows Server 2012.
Detection
Microsoft, CISA and Rapid7 name no actor, payload or victims and no source describes the exploit's behavior, so this is a hunt hypothesis that follows from the mechanism: the failed control is the Mark of the Web tag, so there is no warning dialog for a user to report. Look at mail gateway, chat and endpoint file-origin telemetry for internet-origin files, archives and shortcuts that execute without the usual download warning, and at process lineage from explorer.exe into scripting interpreters and living-off-the-land binaries shortly after a mail or browser download.

Triage: a file a user created or received from a trusted local source also carries no tag; the discriminator is an internet origin (mail, chat or web download) together with the absence of the tag on the opened item.

Defender takeaway
Install the October cumulative update now, ahead of the monthly cycle, on endpoints that open mail and web downloads first; because the tag is the control that failed, attachment blocking and mail-gateway detonation remain the compensating layer until the update is deployed, and Rapid7 reports no patch for Windows Server 2012.

entries.headline: NCSC.ch now rates the SonicWall SMA1000 pre-auth SSRF actively exploited; SonicWall still reports no evidence
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-102255 +3updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-102255, SonicWall SMA1000: a third unauthenticated CVSS 10.0 Work Place SSRF this year, affecting the hotfix builds that closed the September zero-days, with exploitation attempts reported that SonicWall has not confirmed

SonicWall's advisory SNWLID-2026-0017 of 2026-10-06 fixes four flaws in the SMA1000 secure remote-access appliances (models 6210, 7210 and 8200v). CVE-2026-102255 (CVSS 3.0 10.0) is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Work Place interface, attributed to an unintended alternate access path, through which a remote unauthenticated attacker can direct the appliance to issue requests on their behalf, reach internal functionality and perform unauthorized operations (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-10-06). The other three flaws need a login: an OS command injection that lets an administrator execute commands (CVE-2026-102256, 7.8), a Zip Slip in the Appliance Management Console that leads to code execution (CVE-2026-102257, 7.2) and a stored cross-site scripting flaw in that console (CVE-2026-102258, 5.5) (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-10-06). SonicWall's advisory says there is currently no evidence that any of them is exploited (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-10-06).

The pre-authentication flaw is not routine because of what came before it. The Hacker News counts it as the third time this year that SonicWall has fixed a 10.0-rated Work Place SSRF that needs no login; in July and September SonicWall said it had investigated attacks on the earlier pairs ("multiple cases" and "a case"), each pair combining an SSRF that needs no login with a second flaw that lets a logged-in administrator run commands (The Hacker News, 2026-10-07). CERT-FR notes that such pairs have been actively exploited several times this year on this product (CERT-FR, 2026-10-07). The affected builds include 12.4.3-03526 and 12.5.0-02952, the hotfixes SonicWall named on 1 September for the two exploited flaws, so an appliance patched against that chain is still affected (The Hacker News, 2026-10-07). Fixed builds are 12.4.3-03670 and 12.5.0-03082 and higher (The Hacker News, 2026-10-07; CERT-FR, 2026-10-07), whereas the Canadian Cyber Centre's bulletin lists the same two builds as affected "and prior" (Canadian Cyber Centre, 2026-10-07). Shadowserver tracks over 400 internet-exposed SMA1000 appliances, some of which may already be patched, and BleepingComputer says government agencies and managed service providers use the product to give VPN access to internal applications (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-07). NCSC Switzerland published an advisory on 2026-10-07 and on 2026-10-12 changed its exploitation status from unknown to actively exploited, citing honeypot attempts reported by Defused from 2026-10-08 and by Previdian from 2026-10-09 (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-12).

Exposure
SMA1000 6210, 7210 and 8200v whose Work Place interface is reachable from untrusted networks, on 12.4.3-03526 or older or 12.5.0-02952 or older, which includes appliances that already took the September hotfix; the SMA 100 series and SSL-VPN on SonicWall firewalls are not affected (The Hacker News, 2026-10-07).
Detection
SonicWall's advisory title calls the access path an unintended forward proxy, so the telemetry is the Work Place web access log, looking for requests that name internal hosts or services as the destination, and connections that the appliance itself opens to internal management endpoints without a user session behind them (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-10-06). On an appliance that was exposed before the September hotfix, SonicWall's earlier guidance still applies: check for indicators of compromise and, if any are found, re-image or redeploy the appliance, change user and administrator passwords and reset the TOTP tokens; SonicWall has given no such instruction for the new flaws (The Hacker News, 2026-10-07). Previdian's reported attempts are OPTIONS requests to the Work Place Extraweb interface that try to reach the appliance's internal CouchDB service on the loopback address, port 5984, traverse into a design document and invoke its _rewrite function, with an HTTP Basic Authorization header carrying a default-style administrator credential, so the same web access log is the place to look for OPTIONS requests that carry an Authorization header and name a loopback address (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-09).
Defender takeaway
Install 12.4.3-03670 or 12.5.0-03082 (or higher) on every SMA1000 this week, including appliances already on the September hotfix; the hotfix restarts the appliance and SonicWall lists no workaround (The Hacker News, 2026-10-07), so plan the maintenance window now, because two honeypot operators report attempts against the flaw and NCSC Switzerland rates it actively exploited (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-12).
Update10 Oct 2026 03:44 UTCrun 2026-10-10T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Previdian, which runs a honeypot network, told BleepingComputer on 2026-10-09 that its sensors had detected exploitation attempts consistent with CVE-2026-102255, three days after the patch (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-09). The requests targeted the Work Place Extraweb interface with a crafted OPTIONS request meant to reach the appliance's internal CouchDB service on the loopback address, port 5984, traverse into a design document and invoke its _rewrite function while carrying an HTTP Basic Authorization header with a default-style administrator credential (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-09). Previdian's page gives 9 October as its first observation (Previdian, 2026-10-12). Previdian has not established whether any of the attempts would have compromised a system (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-09), and SonicWall's advisory, as of 2026-10-10, still says there is currently no evidence that any of the flaws in the release is exploited (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-10-06); the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security's bulletin AV26-1017, updated on 2026-10-09, now says open source reporting indicates the flaw is being exploited in the wild without naming it (Canadian Cyber Centre, 2026-10-07). BleepingComputer adds that the product is often targeted because managed service providers, large corporations and government agencies use it for VPN access to internal applications, and that Shadowserver tracks more than 400 exposed SMA1000 appliances, a count that includes some that may be honeypots or already patched (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-09).

Update13 Oct 2026 03:37 UTCrun 2026-10-13T0256Z-intelheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

NCSC Switzerland edited its advisory on 2026-10-12 and now records the exploitation status as actively exploited, citing two honeypot operators: Defused, which observed exploitation attempts against its honeypots from 2026-10-08, and Previdian, from 2026-10-09 (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-12). SecurityWeek relays Defused's statement that the first attempts reached its SMA decoys on October 8, two days after disclosure (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-12), and The Hacker News relays Previdian's count of 135 attempts from two unique US addresses (The Hacker News, 2026-10-12). These are attempts against decoys: Previdian has not established whether any would have compromised a system (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-09), no source reports a compromised appliance, and SonicWall's advisory, read again on 2026-10-13, still says there is currently no evidence of exploitation (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-10-06). The Hacker News dates both operators' first detection to 8 October, while Previdian's own page gives 9 October as its first observation (The Hacker News, 2026-10-12; Previdian, 2026-10-12). The fixed builds remain 12.4.3-03670 and 12.5.0-03082.

Correction18 Oct 2026 13:59 UTCrun 2026-10-18T1307Z-auditbody

The update of 2026-10-10 said Previdian's page counted 135 attempts from two source addresses between 9 and 10 October. Previdian's page gives no such window. The figure of 135 attempts from two unique US addresses is the count The Hacker News relayed "to date" on 2026-10-12 (The Hacker News, 2026-10-12). Read on 2026-10-18, Previdian's page records 1,887 attempts from five addresses in Singapore and the United States, first observed on 9 October and last on 16 October (Previdian, 2026-10-12).

entries.headline: GitLab's maximum-severity file-read flaw drew in-the-wild probes by the day after its patch
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-85706 +2exploitedupdatedNATOA1

CVE-2026-85706, GitLab CE/EE: unauthenticated path traversal in the repository commits API reads arbitrary server files, and honeypots recorded probes by the day after the patch (CVSS 10.0)

GitLab's own patch-release notes name the root cause plainly: "improper path confinement and missing authentication enforcement in the repository commits API" let an unauthenticated caller read arbitrary files from the server (GitLab, 2026-09-10). The vulnerability, CVE-2026-85706 (CVSS 10.0, scope-changed, no privileges or user interaction required), affects every self-managed CE/EE release from 18.7 up to 19.1.8, 19.2.6 and 19.3.2, the versions GitLab shipped on 2026-09-10, with backports to 19.0.9 and 18.11.12 following on 2026-09-23; GitLab.com was already running the patched version, and GitLab Dedicated customers need no action. watchTowr warns that the readable files can include configuration files, secrets or other sensitive server-side data, and that GitLab instances often hold source code, credentials and CI/CD configuration data (watchTowr, 2026-09-11); in analyst judgement, that is what turns a file-read primitive into a foothold on the CI/CD and source-control plane GitLab manages. The flaw was reported through GitLab's HackerOne bug-bounty program by researcher s3ntago (GitLab, 2026-09-10).

watchTowr reproduced the vulnerability and validated exposure across client environments, and by 2026-09-11 its Attacker Eye honeypot network was already recording behavioral probes for the vulnerability, which watchTowr reads as attackers having already built an exploit (watchTowr, 2026-09-11). CISA added the CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-09-11 (CISA KEV, catalogue version 2026.09.11), and NCSC Switzerland's own advisory, published earlier that same day, still recorded exploitation status as "unknown", which shows how fast the status moved within a single day (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-09-11). The same release also fixed CVE-2026-87719 (CVSS 9.9), an insecure GraphQL-subscription deserialization issue that lets an authenticated user with Duo Chat access obtain Advanced Search configurations and credentials (GitLab, 2026-09-10); it is not KEV-listed, and NCSC Switzerland's advisory has since recorded it as exploited too (see the 2026-09-16 update below), though on materially thinner evidence than CVE-2026-85706's own KEV listing and honeypot corroboration.

Defender takeaway
Patch every self-managed GitLab instance now: the pre-auth, no-interaction nature of this flaw and its confirmed rapid weaponization make it a same-day action, not a routine maintenance-window item, for any organization running GitLab as source-control or CI/CD infrastructure. Triage: watchTowr names the marker to hunt for: HTTP POST requests to /api/v4/projects/{id}/repository/commits/ whose URI carries a file.path parameter identify potential exploitation attempts (watchTowr, 2026-09-11). GitLab has also published three detections for exploitation attempts: reads of gitlab.yml, inclusion through the metadata.path parameter, and file-path enumeration (GitLab, 2026-09-10).
Update13 Sep 2026 04:37 UTCrun 2026-09-13T0409Z-intelcvestagsbody

NCSC Switzerland's own advisory, published 2026-09-11, independently confirms CVE-2026-87719 (CVSS 9.9, GitLab EE only) alongside CVE-2026-85706 in the same posting. GitLab's own release notes describe the flaw: "GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could allow an authenticated user with Duo Chat access to obtain Advanced Search instance configurations and sensitive credentials using a specially crafted GraphQL subscription argument to bypass serialization and perform server object lookup" (GitLab, 2026-09-10). Affected versions are EE only, 18.3 up to the same 19.1.8/19.2.6/19.3.2 fixed releases named above; no exploitation is confirmed for this CVE. The same release also fixed CVE-2026-88765 (CVSS 8.5, GitLab EE only, sourced from GitLab's own release notes alone with no independent confirmation found): "GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could allow an authenticated user to achieve remote code execution by importing a specially crafted Git project export to overflow the Unicode conversion buffer used in Advanced Search indexing" (GitLab, 2026-09-10). This flaw's affected-version floor, EE 12.3, is substantially older than the other two flaws in this release, so any EE instance that has deferred upgrades for a long period carries the largest exposure window for this specific remote-code-execution path.

entries.action_label: Microsoft: a China-aligned implant hides in…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Microsoft: a China-aligned implant hides in legitimate software via DLL sideloading and takes modules over WebSockets
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

NeedyMantis: Microsoft details a modular post-compromise framework, found through the DAEMON Tools compromise, used against telecoms, universities, intergovernmental bodies and government contractors

Microsoft Threat Intelligence published its analysis of NeedyMantis on 2026-09-28: a modular post-compromise malware family seen since at least October 2025 in a limited number of targeted operations against telecommunications organizations, universities, medical nonprofits, intergovernmental organizations and government contractors (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-09-28). Microsoft found it by pivoting from indicators in Kaspersky's investigation of the DAEMON Tools supply-chain compromise and names Storm-3069, its designator for that activity, as at least one operator; it has seen further NeedyMantis activity beyond Storm-3069 that aligns with activity it associates with China-based actors, has not determined whether one actor is behind all of it, and assesses that Storm-3069's activity originates from China without attributing it to a Chinese nation-state actor (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-09-28). Microsoft has not seen NeedyMantis itself delivered through a supply chain; it is deployed after the operator already has access, and in one intrusion the operator used Impacket to copy the legitimate application, the malicious DLL and an encrypted archive from a network share and run them (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-09-28).

The first-stage loader is a DLL sideloaded by the legitimate program it ships with, in the analysed case a fake WinSparkle update component of the Poedit translation tool, with other pairings built on curl, Vim and TightVNC and DLLs masquerading as Microsoft Office, Broadcom, Intel and NVIDIA components under ProgramData and Program Files (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-09-28). It hides its strings and constants, checks for debuggers, and extracts a second-stage shellcode loader from a custom encrypted archive that in turn unpacks the main component (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-09-28). The main component reads its configuration from a file named after a Windows networking library, beacons with an HTTPS GET request whose cookie carries the computer name, user name, process list and Program Files listing, then switches to WebSockets with a binary protocol encrypted with RC4 after a key exchange; its handful of commands chiefly load, unload and pass data to further modules, whose capabilities Microsoft has not confirmed (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-09-28).

Detection
In image-load telemetry, a legitimate application such as Poedit, curl, Vim or TightVNC loading a same-named DLL from an unusual ProgramData or Program Files folder, next to an extension-less archive with the DLL's name; in network telemetry, an HTTPS request whose cookie carries Base64-encoded compressed system information followed by a WebSocket upgrade from that process; and in process telemetry, Impacket-style remote execution that stages such a bundle from a network share (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-09-28).

Triage: these tools legitimately load their own DLLs, and in the analysed case the malicious DLL replaced Poedit's own WinSparkle update component in its normal install folder, so the location alone does not decide it; the discriminator is the companion extension-less archive named like the DLL, which a genuine installation does not carry, together with a DLL that differs from the vendor's original component, and for the ProgramData pairings an application folder the organization never deployed (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-09-28).

Defender takeaway
NeedyMantis is a second-stage foothold, so a hit means an intrusion is already under way; organizations that ran an affected DAEMON Tools Lite build or that support intergovernmental bodies as contractors should hunt for the sideloading pattern rather than wait for an initial-access alert.
