entries.headline: Exchange OWA flaw used in Russia-aligned espionage is fixed since June 2026, but its mailbox foothold needs removing
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-42897exploitedupdatedNATOA1

CVE-2026-42897: Exchange OWA cross-site scripting exploited by TA488 with the OWAReaper implant; fixed since the June 2026 Security Update, which does not remove the mitigation

CVE-2026-42897 is a cross-site scripting flaw in Outlook Web Access on Exchange Server 2016, 2019 and Subscription Edition; Microsoft scores it 8.1, marks it exploited (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2026-07-14), and CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-05-15 (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-05-15). Exchange Online is not affected (Microsoft Exchange Team Blog, 2026-05-14). Microsoft first protected on-premises servers with mitigation M2, a URL Rewrite configuration delivered by the Exchange Emergency Mitigation Service (Microsoft Learn). The EM service runs on Mailbox servers (installed with the September 2021 CU or later) and needs outbound HTTPS to officeclient.microsoft.com, which must also be excluded from SSL inspection; servers that cannot reach it never receive the mitigation, and Get-ExchangeServer | Format-List Name,MitigationsApplied shows what each server has applied (Microsoft Learn). A server running an Exchange Server build older than March 2023 cannot check for new mitigations at all (Microsoft Exchange Team Blog, 2026-05-14).

The fix shipped in the June 2026 Security Update (Microsoft Exchange Team Blog, 2026-06-09), and Microsoft recommends the July 2026 Security Update, which also addresses the related CVE-2026-55008; installing either does not remove the earlier mitigation, which stays in place until administrators remove it by hand (Microsoft Exchange Team Blog, 2026-06-09) (Microsoft Exchange Team Blog, 2026-07-14) (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2026-07-14). From 2026-07-22 Proofpoint observed TA488 (Void Blizzard, LAUNDRY BEAR) exploiting the flaw against government, telecommunications, finance, hospitality and aerospace targets in the US and Europe with the OWAReaper implant, whose server-side persistence survives password resets and re-imaging (Proofpoint, 2026-07-29); the update below carries the detail.

Exposure
On-premises Exchange Server 2016, 2019 or Subscription Edition below the June 2026 Security Update; Exchange 2016 and 2019 receive fixes only through the Period 2 Extended Security Update programme (Microsoft Exchange Team Blog, 2026-07-14).
Update31 Jul 2026 04:09 UTCrun 2026-07-31T0409Z-intelactionsaffected_productscvesentitiesevidencereferencesregionssectorssourcestagstechniquesbody

CVE-2026-42897 was first an Exchange OWA flaw whose interim protection depended on the EM Service auto-mitigation. Two things changed. Proofpoint has now attributed in-the-wild exploitation to a named Russia-aligned actor and published the implant's full mechanics (Proofpoint, 2026-07-29), and the mitigation is no longer the remediation: the security updates are, with the mitigation now something Microsoft says administrators should remove (Microsoft Exchange Team Blog, 2026-07-14). NCSC-CH appended the Proofpoint reporting to its own advisory on 2026-07-30 (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-07-30).

The actor is TA488 (also tracked as Void Blizzard and LAUNDRY BEAR), the Russia-aligned email-espionage actor behind the Zimbra campaign that Proofpoint documented in a joint release with the NSA (Proofpoint, 2026-07-29). Proofpoint assesses OWAReaper as an evolution of that campaign's ZimReaper payload, citing shared code including the same sized, invisible pop-up and highly similar error handling (Proofpoint, 2026-07-29). Campaign activity began 2026-07-22 against government, telecommunications, finance, hospitality and aerospace targets across the US and Europe, using deliberately banal lure subjects with no call to action; Proofpoint says the unusual breadth may have been intentional blending with bulk mail. Its stated infrastructure-creation date of March 2026 precedes Microsoft's May disclosure by two months, which is the basis for its assessment that zero-day use is feasible; that is an inference from infrastructure dating, not a confirmed finding.

Execution. The flaw is a failure to sanitise HTML in the message body, so a loader script in an onload= handler reassembles a Base64 fragment from the rest of the message and evaluates it: no link click and no attachment open, only viewing the message in OWA. The exploit and payload fragments are hidden inside the message's social-media icon elements, with next-stage data placed after # fragment markers where the browser's Base64 image parser stops reading, so the payload is not visible to casual inspection of the HTML. On execution OWAReaper first rewrites the delivered message server-side to strip the exploit content and suppresses OWA pop-ups and right-click, then enumerates the victim's address, username and settings (Proofpoint, 2026-07-29).

Credential and token theft. It creates two invisible input elements and waits for the browser's own autofill to populate them with the saved OWA username and password. Separately it enumerates installed Outlook add-ins holding ReadWriteMailbox permission and, where one exists, abuses it to call GetClientAccessToken and obtain OAuth tokens (Proofpoint, 2026-07-29).

Persistence, in three independent layers. Client-side, the implant writes an encrypted copy of itself and a decryption wrapper into browser localStorage under a settings field of the legitimate PageDataPayload.OwaUserDefaultSettings key, which OWA itself evaluates during its own sync-restore flow, so every ordinary OWA tab-open re-launches it with no separate loader. A second client-side layer adds a hidden iframe to messages cached in OWA's offline IndexedDB store, so opening the cached message re-infects an endpoint even after a full re-image. The third is server-side and is the one that matters most: the implant calls UpdateFolder to grant Owner-level permission on every mail folder to the low-privilege "Default" preset alias that exists in every Exchange organisation. Proofpoint is explicit that this "requires deliberate removal from the Exchange server" and that credential rotation and re-imaging will not evict it (Proofpoint, 2026-07-29).

Command and control. Two channels, both over infrastructure defenders generally trust. The implant polls GitHub's public Commit Search API every 24 hours for crafted commit messages containing the target's own email address, decrypting matches to a four-character command header that selects toolkit replacement, C2-domain rotation, or one-off code execution; in parallel it re-parses cached inbound messages every five minutes for the same command structure. Exfiltration runs primarily over HTTPS with encrypted URI paths, either relayed through a set of legitimate image-CDN domains or sent directly to the actor-controlled server when those proxies fail; if the HTTPS method fails altogether, the implant switches to DNS label tunnelling, packing the data into the subdomain labels of ordinary DNS queries for an actor-controlled domain. Notably, Proofpoint states there is no mass mailbox exfiltration here, unlike the Zimbra campaign, so the mapped behaviour is browser-session and credential access rather than bulk email collection (Proofpoint, 2026-07-29).

Patching. The fix first shipped in the June 2026 Security Update (Microsoft Exchange Team Blog, 2026-06-09), and Microsoft now recommends the July 2026 Security Update, available as Exchange SE RTM publicly and for Exchange 2019 CU14/CU15 and Exchange 2016 CU23 only through the Period 2 Extended Security Update programme; organisations that were enrolled only in Period 1, which ended in April 2026 (Microsoft Exchange Team Blog, 2026-05-14), do not receive it (Microsoft Exchange Team Blog, 2026-07-14). Microsoft's own vulnerability record scores the flaw 8.1 and marks it exploited (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2026-07-14). Installing the update does not remove a previously applied mitigation: administrators who used the EM Service should remove the M2.1.0 IIS rules through the documented rollback, and those who ran the downloadable mitigation script should run its rollback (Microsoft Exchange Team Blog, 2026-07-14). The known operational side effects of the mitigation era (broken OWA calendar printing, inline-image rendering problems, OWA-light failing, and false-unhealthy calendar-proxy health alerts) are listed in the May post (Microsoft Exchange Team Blog, 2026-05-14), and the July post ties their clearing to installing the update and removing the mitigation (Microsoft Exchange Team Blog, 2026-07-14).

Detection
The highest-value signal is in mailbox audit and Exchange Web Services telemetry: a folder-permission change granting Owner rights to the "Default" alias, applied across many folders of one mailbox in quick succession. Client-side, monitor for writes to the OWA user-default-settings localStorage key outside the browser's own sync flow, and for OWA sessions in which invisible form inputs are created and immediately populated. On the network side, two egress patterns stand out from a mail client's normal behaviour: repeated polling of a public source-code hosting search API on a roughly daily cadence, and DNS queries with the label-length and entropy profile of tunnelled data.

Triage: OWA legitimately reads and writes its own settings keys constantly, so the presence of localStorage activity is not the signal; the discriminator is the specific settings-field path carrying an encrypted blob, and its correlation with a message open. For the server-side artifact the discrimination is cleaner: administrators do grant folder permissions, but they grant them to named users or groups for a specific folder, not Owner rights to the built-in "Default" alias across an entire mailbox. Treat any such grant as compromise until proven otherwise.

Defender takeaway
For any on-premises Exchange estate, "we patched in May" is the wrong answer to this one: May shipped a mitigation, June shipped the fix, July is the recommended update, and neither update removes the mitigation, which comes off by hand afterwards. Because the actor's durable foothold is a mailbox permission rather than anything on the endpoint, an organisation that resets passwords and re-images the affected workstation can still be read, since Proofpoint says the grant needs deliberate removal from the Exchange server (Proofpoint, 2026-07-29); the folder-permission audit is the part that actually evicts them.

entries.headline: Amazon Threat Intelligence traces three major npm compromises to one DPRK-linked actor, and describes a payload that only detonates on a specific input
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Amazon attributes the axios, debug and chalk npm compromises to a DPRK-linked cluster with medium confidence, and names a small 2025 package compromise as the rehearsal

Amazon's threat-intelligence team published an attribution assessment on 2026-07-29 linking three separate npm package compromises to one actor. The load-bearing sentence carries its own hedge, and it should be read with the hedge intact: "based on analysis of command-and-control (C2) indicators and TTPs, Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with medium confidence that these campaigns are attributable to the DPRK-linked threat actor tracked as SAPPHIRE SLEET, STARDUST CHOLLIMA, BlueNoroff, CageyChameleon, and Alluring Pisces" (AWS Security Blog, 2026-07-29). CyberScoop notes that researchers also track this cluster as UNC1069 (CyberScoop, 2026-07-29). Medium confidence is not attribution-by-consensus. Amazon is also precise about which part is new: it states that "while the axios compromise has been publicly attributed to this DPRK-linked threat actor, the typo-crypto, debug, and chalk incidents haven't previously been connected to it" (AWS Security Blog, 2026-07-29). For a defender the actor label changes little, but the tradecraft description below changes something real.

The compromises run from March 2025 to March 2026 and escalate in blast radius: debug and chalk in September 2025, then axios in March 2026, which Amazon describes as one of the most widely used JavaScript libraries at more than 100 million weekly downloads (AWS Security Blog, 2026-07-29). None of the three involved breaking the registry. In Amazon's words, "in each case with debug, chalk, and axios, the threat actor gained access by socially engineering a trusted maintainer of the package, then published a software update containing malicious code" (AWS Security Blog, 2026-07-29, corrected 2026-08-11), the trust chain held exactly as designed and delivered the malicious version, which is why provenance and signing controls do not help here.

The genuinely new element is the rehearsal. Amazon points at a March 2025 compromise of a package named typo-crypto, into which the actor committed a trojanised file that masqueraded as the unrelated legitimate core-js package, and assesses that "based on the limited number of observed downloads... this campaign was small scale and likely served as a testing ground for the more visible supply chain operations that followed in late 2025 and 2026" (AWS Security Blog, 2026-07-29). That is a patience pattern worth internalising: a package with negligible download counts is not necessarily a failed attack, it may be where the maintainer-social-engineering approach and the payload were refined before being pointed at something with a hundred million weekly installs.

Two mechanics from that rehearsal payload matter for anyone who triages suspicious dependencies. First, detonation was conditional on input rather than on time or environment: the trojanised file executed only when it received a hash input beginning with one specific literal value, and only then downloaded an operating-system-appropriate second stage, with behaviour tailored separately for Windows, macOS and Linux (AWS Security Blog, 2026-07-29). A package like that installs and runs cleanly in any sandbox that does not happen to feed it the trigger value, so "we installed it and nothing happened" is not a clean result. Second, the payload combined file-based persistence with payload rotation and layered obfuscation, base64-encoded text over an XOR cipher under a fixed key (AWS Security Blog, 2026-07-29), so a static scan of the shipped file yields little without unwrapping those layers.

Amazon separately describes a shift in how these operations are structured, observing that attackers increasingly split one malicious workflow across several individually unremarkable packages, and that "this approach is designed to defeat scanners that evaluate packages one by one instead of reasoning about how they interact in a real dependency graph" (AWS Security Blog, 2026-07-29). Amazon frames that as an observation rather than advice, but the implication for a review process is direct: a per-package verdict is the wrong unit of analysis when the malicious behaviour only exists once the pieces are resolved together.

Defender takeaway
The actor label is the least useful part of this report. What carries over is that a dependency compromise can arrive through a legitimate maintainer and a legitimate release, sit dormant unless given a specific input, and distribute its logic across packages that each look fine alone, so dynamic analysis that observes an install without exercising the code, and review that scores packages individually, are both weaker than their output suggests.

Triage: a benign minified or bundled dependency also carries base64 blobs and unreadable code, so obfuscation alone does not separate the two. The discriminators are behavioural and structural: a code path that stays inert unless a caller supplies a particular argument value, a second-stage fetch whose destination differs by host operating system, and persistence written outside the package's own installation tree. A dependency that reaches the network at all during a build or test run, when its documented function does not require it, is the anomaly worth pulling.

Amazon corrected its post on 2026-08-11 to say that the social engineering of a trusted maintainer applied to the debug, chalk and axios compromises specifically (AWS Security Blog, corrected 2026-08-11). This entry had stated it for every compromise, including the March 2025 typo-crypto package that Amazon calls a testing ground, for which Amazon names no access method. Amazon says the attribution and its other findings are unchanged.

entries.headline: VulnCheck's canaries show attackers exploiting a Langflow pre-auth RCE with no documented fix and no KEV entry, while the next CVE number is KEV-listed
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-0769exploitedupdatedNATOB2

CVE-2026-0769 in Langflow: a pre-auth eval-injection RCE with no documented fix that VulnCheck observes being exploited, and that CISA KEV does not list

Two facts about the same identifier, published six months apart, combine into something a vulnerability-management process organised around CISA KEV will not see. The first: CVE-2026-0769 is an eval injection in Langflow's eval_custom_component_code function, where a user-supplied string reaches Python execution without proper validation, and Zero Day Initiative states plainly that authentication is not required to exploit it (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-01-09). ZDI published it as a 0-day advisory. Its disclosure timeline records the report going to the vendor in July 2025, two follow-up requests over the following months and then notice of intent to publish, and its mitigation guidance is correspondingly blunt: restrict interaction with the product, given the nature of the vulnerability (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-01-09). ZDI scores it CVSS 9.8 and its advisory names no affected or fixed version (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-01-09); ZDI's CVE record lists Langflow 1.3.2 as the only affected version, a single listed version rather than a range (ENISA EUVD, EUVD-2026-4475).

The second fact is that this is no longer theoretical. VulnCheck reports observing attackers gain initial access to Langflow with exploits targeting both CVE-2026-0769 and a second Langflow flaw, CVE-2026-5027, then harvest credentials, which it assesses as likely for services such as OpenAI and Claude, deploy cryptominers, and attempt lateral movement; it does not say which flaw each intrusion used, and states explicitly that neither has been added to CISA KEV (VulnCheck, 2026-07-28). Neither ZDI's advisory nor VulnCheck's report includes exploit code (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-01-09) (VulnCheck, 2026-07-28). That detail is worth carrying: if the harvested credentials are model-provider keys, a compromised Langflow instance also exposes the AI-service accounts it is wired to, not only the host.

The KEV gap is the part with immediate procedural consequence, and it comes with a trap. As of the catalog of 2026-09-29, KEV lists six Langflow CVEs: CVE-2026-9198, CVE-2026-0770, CVE-2026-55255, CVE-2025-34291, CVE-2026-33017 and CVE-2025-3248 (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-09-29). CVE-2026-0769 is not one of them, while CVE-2026-0770, the next CVE number, is a different vulnerability. A pair of consecutive identifiers, one KEV-listed and one neither KEV-listed nor documented as fixed, is exactly the shape that produces a false all-clear when a ticket is closed against the wrong record. Any process that answers "are we exposed to Langflow?" by checking KEV membership will return a clean result for the flaw with no documented fix.

Exposure
Every self-hosted Langflow instance reachable from untrusted networks, because exploitation needs no authentication and the affected range is undefined: ZDI's advisory names no version or fix (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-01-09), and its CVE record lists only 1.3.2 (ENISA EUVD, EUVD-2026-4475).
Detection
With no documented fix, the operative telemetry is on the host and at its egress. Langflow runs Python, so the process-creation observable is the Langflow service process spawning children it has no business spawning: shells, package managers, download utilities, or a second Python interpreter outside the application's own worker pattern. In egress telemetry, look for outbound connections from the Langflow host to mining pools or to destinations unrelated to the model providers the application legitimately calls, and for authentication events at your model providers originating from addresses that are not the Langflow host. Triage: Langflow's whole purpose is executing user-authored component code, so "Python executing dynamic code" is the application working as designed and is not by itself a signal; the discriminators are the process's children stepping outside the interpreter, and egress to destinations the application has no configured relationship with.
Defender takeaway
A KEV check returns a clean result for this flaw, so the decision cannot wait for a listing. The only preventive control ZDI offers is restricting who can reach the product (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-01-09), which for most estates means removing internet exposure and putting authenticated proxy access in front of the rest. On any host that was exposed, rotate the model-provider keys and other credentials it held, since VulnCheck observed credential harvesting after exploitation (VulnCheck, 2026-07-28).

entries.headline: ServiceNow AI Platform sandbox escape gives unauthenticated code execution; self-hosted instances need the fixed release
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-6875exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-6875: ServiceNow AI Platform sandbox escape lets an unauthenticated request execute code on the platform (CVSS 9.5)

ServiceNow disclosed CVE-2026-6875, a "Sandbox Escape in ServiceNow AI Platform" rated CVSS 4.0 9.5, in security bulletin KB3137947 published 2026-07-13 (ServiceNow, 2026-07-13; ENISA EUVD, 2026-07-13). Per ServiceNow, the flaw "could enable an unauthenticated user, in certain circumstances, to execute code within the ServiceNow platform", an isolation failure in the AI Platform's code-execution environment. ServiceNow states it "addressed this vulnerability by deploying a security update to hosted instances," and provided updates to self-hosted customers and partners (ServiceNow, 2026-07-13). Fixed releases are Zurich Patch 7b/9, Yokohama Patch 12 Hot Fix 1b/13, Australia Patch 2 and Brazil EA/GA (ServiceNow, 2026-07-13).

Contradiction: ServiceNow's advisory states that it is "not currently aware of exploitation against ServiceNow instances" (ServiceNow, 2026-07-13). BleepingComputer reported on 2026-07-20 that the advisory still said so and that ServiceNow had yet to flag the flaw as actively abused, and a ServiceNow spokesperson told it that, based on its investigation to date, it had not observed evidence that the activity is related to instances ServiceNow hosts (BleepingComputer, 2026-07-20). Defused reports in-the-wild exploitation attempts since 2026-07-17 (BleepingComputer, 2026-07-20), and NCSC-CH gives the exploitation status as actively exploited, citing that reporting (NCSC-CH, 2026-07-20).

Defender takeaway
For self-hosted instances, apply the fixed release for your family (Zurich, Yokohama, Australia or Brazil) listed in KB3137947 rather than waiting for the next maintenance window (ServiceNow, 2026-07-13). The patches also include Guarded Script: complex server-side scripts (those using variables, if/else logic, loops or multiple statements) must be moved into a script include, and guest (unauthenticated) traffic is fully enforced immediately on upgraded instances. Enforcement for authenticated traffic phases in automatically over about four weeks on cloud instances, while on-premises administrators must advance each enforcement phase manually (ServiceNow, 2026-07-13). ServiceNow addressed hosted instances starting in April, and its spokesperson still encourages both self-hosted and ServiceNow-hosted customers to apply the relevant patches if they have not already done so (BleepingComputer, 2026-07-20). The in-the-wild payloads Defused observed hit the same pre-authentication sink Searchlight Cyber documented, /assessment_thanks.do, but reach the code-execution primitive by a different route than Searchlight's published proof of concept (BleepingComputer, 2026-07-20). Searchlight's route passes a javascript: expression in the sysparm_assessable_type parameter of that page, where it is evaluated inside a GlideRecord query, and then abuses gs.include() script-include evaluation to escape the sandbox (Searchlight Cyber, 2026-07-14). On self-hosted instances, hunt web access logs first for unauthenticated requests to /assessment_thanks.do carrying javascript: values in query parameters. gs.include() evaluation outside routine administrative workflows matches the published proof of concept, not necessarily the observed attacks.
Update21 Jul 2026 04:38 UTCrun 2026-07-21T0409Z-intelactionscvesevidenceprioritysectorssourcestagsbody

The unauthenticated ServiceNow AI Platform sandbox escape has moved from "no known exploitation" to reported active exploitation. NCSC-CH's advisory of 2026-07-20 gives the exploitation status as "Actively exploited" and cites news coverage of claims of active exploitation (NCSC-CH, 2026-07-20), and BleepingComputer reports attackers "begun exploiting a critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-6875) in the ServiceNow AI Platform," attributing the in-the-wild observation to threat-intelligence firm Defused, which saw first attempts on 2026-07-17 (BleepingComputer, 2026-07-20). Searchlight Cyber's analysis shows the mechanism: an unauthenticated caller gets server-side JavaScript evaluated through a GlideRecord query on a pre-authentication page, then escapes the script sandbox by obtaining the Function constructor through Class.create.constructor and running it during a gs.include() script-include evaluation, which ServiceNow runs without the sandbox's constraints (Searchlight Cyber, 2026-07-14).

The operational change is entirely one of urgency: exploitation attempts are reported, so any self-hosted AI Platform instance still missing the fixed release has crossed from "patch on the normal cycle" to "patch out of band." ServiceNow says it deployed a security update to hosted instances and provided updates to self-hosted customers and partners (ServiceNow, 2026-07-13), and its spokesperson still encourages self-hosted and ServiceNow-hosted customers to apply the relevant patches if they have not already done so (BleepingComputer, 2026-07-20). The hunt telemetry is in the takeaway above.

The summary above said no exploitation was known. BleepingComputer reports Defused observing first exploitation attempts on 2026-07-17, and NCSC-CH's advisory of 2026-07-20 flags the CVE as actively exploited, citing that news coverage (NCSC-CH, 2026-07-20; BleepingComputer, 2026-07-20). ServiceNow's advisory states that it is not currently aware of exploitation against ServiceNow instances (ServiceNow, 2026-07-13), and its spokesperson told BleepingComputer that it had not observed evidence that the activity relates to instances ServiceNow hosts (BleepingComputer, 2026-07-20).

The takeaway above also said no exploitation discriminator existed. The observed payloads hit the pre-authentication sink /assessment_thanks.do that Searchlight Cyber documented, by a different route than its published proof of concept (BleepingComputer, 2026-07-20). Searchlight's own route abuses javascript: values in GlideRecord query parameters and gs.include() evaluation (Searchlight Cyber, 2026-07-14). The sandboxed script cannot call eval or new Function, which the sandbox forbids. It reaches the Function constructor indirectly, through Class.create.constructor, and a gs.include() evaluation outside the sandbox then runs it (Searchlight Cyber, 2026-07-14). Its example request is a GET, not a POST.

entries.headline: Oracle E-Business Suite Payments pre-auth takeover CVE-2026-46817 is exploited and KEV-listed: patch or pull it offline
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-46817exploitedupdatedNATOA1

CVE-2026-46817: Oracle E-Business Suite Payments unauthenticated takeover, exploited in the wild and CISA KEV-listed (CVSS 9.8)

CISA added CVE-2026-46817 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 15 July 2026 on evidence of active exploitation (CISA, 2026-07-15); Oracle had fixed the flaw in its May 2026 Critical Security Patch Update (Oracle CSPU, 2026-05-28). The bug sits in the File Transmission component of Oracle Payments (CVSS 9.8) (Oracle CSPU, 2026-05-28), the payment-processing engine built into Oracle E-Business Suite (Help Net Security, 2026-06-30), and an unauthenticated attacker with HTTP network access can use it to compromise and take over Oracle Payments (Oracle CSPU risk matrix text); CISA's catalog classifies it as improper privilege management, improper authentication and missing authentication for a critical function (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-07-15). Affected releases are EBS 12.2.3 through 12.2.15.

Threat-intelligence firm Defused recorded the first in-the-wild exploitation against its EBS honeypot decoys on 27 June 2026, before any public proof-of-concept existed, as a single source running an unauthenticated file read against the Payments component rather than broad scanning (Help Net Security, 2026-06-30). Defused puts that at roughly six weeks after the patch (Help Net Security, 2026-06-30), but Oracle's advisory records its initial release on 28 May 2026, 30 days earlier (Oracle CSPU, 2026-05-28). The observed technique calls the ibytransmit endpoint in the File Transmission component, invoking an internal Oracle Java function directly and redirecting it to read /etc/passwd; the same primitive can be pointed at configuration files holding database credentials, encryption keys or payment-processor API keys (Help Net Security, 2026-06-30).

Exposure
Oracle E-Business Suite 12.2.3 through 12.2.15 without the May 2026 Critical Security Patch Update, with the Oracle Payments web tier reachable over HTTP by an unauthenticated attacker (Oracle CSPU, 2026-05-28); Shadowserver tracks more than 450 Oracle EBS instances online (BleepingComputer, 2026-06-29).
Detection
In web access logs, POST requests to /OA_HTML/ibytransmit, the File Transmission endpoint the observed exploit calls (Help Net Security, 2026-06-30).
Defender takeaway
Treat any internet-facing instance left unpatched past 28 May, the day Oracle released the fix (Oracle CSPU, 2026-05-28), as potentially compromised, as Help Net Security advises, and investigate before rotating the credentials and keys stored on the host (Help Net Security, 2026-06-30); CISA flags the flaw for forensic triage (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-07-15).
Correction11 Oct 2026 14:54 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitlesummarytagssectorscvessourcesactionsbodysourcing_note

Oracle and CISA describe CVE-2026-46817 as an unauthenticated takeover of Oracle Payments (Oracle CSPU, 2026-05-28) (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-07-15), and the exploitation Defused observed was a file read, so the earlier wording of remote code execution went beyond the sources. No cited source links ShinyHunters or UNC6240 to Oracle E-Business Suite. Shadowserver tracks more than 450 EBS instances online (BleepingComputer, 2026-06-29).

Correction21 Oct 2026 12:07 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1149Z-auditheadlinesourcesbody

Help Net Security's advice to treat internet-facing instances left unpatched past 28 May as potentially compromised (Help Net Security, 2026-06-30) therefore runs from Oracle's release date.

entries.headline: Progress told every on-prem ShareFile Storage Zone Controller customer to power off, then named a path-traversal flaw and shipped fixed builds
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-2699 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

Progress orders ShareFile Storage Zone Controller shutdown over a 'credible external threat'; the cause is a path-traversal flaw, fixed in 5.12.5 and 6.0.2

Progress Software has told every customer running an on-premises ShareFile Storage Zone Controller (SZC), the self-hosted IIS component that lets ShareFile's SaaS front end store files on customer-controlled storage (local filesystem, SMB, SharePoint, S3/Azure) rather than in Progress's cloud, to manually power off the Windows server hosting it, citing "a credible external security threat" first notified to customers on 2026-07-10 (BleepingComputer, 2026-07-10). Three days on, on 2026-07-13, the vendor status page still listed the Storage Zone Controller service as not operational and under investigation (Progress ShareFile status, 2026-07-13), and Progress had disclosed neither a CVE, a root cause, nor a patch or safe-restart timeline; the mitigation on offer was a full shutdown rather than an update, with no fix published as of 2026-07-13 (heise online, 2026-07-13; SecurityWeek, 2026-07-13). heise characterises the shutdown as a precautionary measure during an ongoing investigation. Progress stated it had no indication of unauthorized access to any ShareFile account or data at that point. Only on-premises SZC deployments are affected; cloud-only ShareFile tenants are not.

This sits on top of a chainable pre-auth RCE that watchTowr Labs disclosed in the same component in April 2026: CVE-2026-2699 (CVSS 9.8) is a CWE-698 execution-after-redirect authentication bypass in /ConfigService/Admin.aspx, where Response.Redirect() is called with the terminate flag set to false, so the admin page body still renders and executes after the browser is told to redirect to login; CVE-2026-2701 (CVSS 9.1) chains from that access, because the storage-location validation only checks writability, letting an attacker repoint the storage repository at the IIS web root and land an ASPX web shell (watchTowr Labs, 2026-04-02). Both were fixed in Storage Zone Controller 5.12.4 (the 6.x .NET-Core branch was unaffected); watchTowr counted roughly 30,000 internet-facing SZC instances at disclosure. Progress has not said whether the current threat relates to this chain or to a separate issue.

Defender takeaway. This is the same on-prem, internet-facing, managed-file-transfer-adjacent architecture class (ShareFile, MOVEit, GoAnywhere, Cleo) that has repeatedly produced mass pre-auth exploitation, and a vendor ordering customers to pull the plug rather than patch was, on 2026-07-13, a strong signal to treat any exposed SZC as untrusted until Progress published scope, which it did on 2026-07-14. Regardless of whether the July threat proves related to CVE-2026-2699/2701, any instance still on SZC 5.x below 5.12.4 carries a known, PoC-backed pre-auth RCE and should be upgraded or taken offline now. On 2026-07-13, with no mechanism confirmed by Progress, the CWE-698 chain was the working hunt hypothesis. Progress has since named a separate path-traversal flaw, as the updates record, so the chain remains a compounding risk on older builds rather than the explanation for the shutdown.

Triage: an authenticated administrator legitimately hits /ConfigService/Admin.aspx and receives a normal authenticated session; the anomaly for the known chain is a request to that path that returns a 302 whose response body nonetheless carries the full admin-panel HTML (the execution-after-redirect behaviour) rather than the redirect being honoured, followed by configuration changes to Zone/Primary-Zone-Controller/storage-repository fields outside a change window, and, downstream, an .aspx file appearing under a StorageCenter webroot subdirectory that is not part of the vendor's shipped file set.

Update14 Jul 2026 12:50 UTCrun 2026-07-14T1210Z-intelcvesevidencesectorssourcestagsbody

Two developments harden the picture around Progress's emergency ShareFile Storage Zone Controller (SZC) shutdown order. First, the shutdown was not precautionary in the abstract: the alert "arrived the same day that independent honeypots began detecting active, in-the-wild attempts to exploit" the pre-auth authentication-bypass flaw CVE-2026-2699, with Shadowserver Foundation honeypots first recording those attempts on Friday 2026-07-10 (BankInfoSecurity, 2026-07-13). This moves the flaw's status from PoC-public to actively exploited. Second, defenders responded at scale, the number of internet-exposed Storage Zone Controllers fell from watchTowr's April count of about 30,000 to roughly 1,000 by 2026-07-13, evidence of widespread emergency power-downs (BankInfoSecurity, 2026-07-13). Progress restored ShareFile cloud-service access for SZC customers but continues to require the on-prem controllers themselves stay powered off pending its investigation, and still reports no evidence of unauthorized access to customer data (The Register, 2026-07-13).

Recorded Future analyst Allan Liska publicly assessed that the pattern "smells like CL0P ransomware group activity," pointing to Clop's long record of mass-exploiting secure file-transfer software (Accellion FTA, GoAnywhere, MOVEit, Cleo Harmony, and Oracle E-Business Suite) (BankInfoSecurity, 2026-07-13). This is a named researcher's hypothesis, not an attribution: Progress has identified no actor and disclosed no root cause.

Defender takeaway. The one-day earlier guidance (treat any exposed SZC as untrusted and keep it powered off rather than patched) is now backed by confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, so it should carry more weight, not less, for any organisation that has not yet acted. The recommended state remains a full power-off of on-prem Storage Zone Controllers until Progress publishes scope; the original entry's shutdown and bounded-compromise-check actions still stand unchanged.

Update14 Jul 2026 20:21 UTCrun 2026-07-14T2009Z-intelactionsevidencesourcestagsbody

Progress Software has confirmed the root cause behind its emergency ShareFile Storage Zone Controller (SZC) shutdown order: a high-severity path-traversal vulnerability affecting SZC versions 5.x and 6.x that lets an authenticated administrative user read arbitrary files accessible to the application's service account, write malicious content to server directories, and enumerate the filesystem layout (BleepingComputer, 2026-07-14), a CWE-22-class flaw reachable through the SZC's internet-facing IIS component. Progress has shipped patched versions 5.12.5 and 6.0.2, and a CVE identifier is reserved but will not be published for two weeks. The vendor states it has "no indication of unauthorized access to any ShareFile customer account or data," a claim that sits alongside the earlier finding that Shadowserver honeypots recorded in-the-wild exploitation attempts against the same component from 2026-07-10. Progress's status page confirms Storage Zone Controller customer access "is currently being restored," with recovery instructions issued directly to account owners (Progress, ShareFile Status Page, 2026-07-14), closing out the multi-day outage that began with the 2026-07-10 shutdown order.

Defender takeaway
The new detail is the fix, patched versions (5.12.5, 6.0.2) and a named vulnerability class (path traversal, authenticated-admin scope) that the two prior entries in this thread lacked. Any organization that took SZC offline under the shutdown order should patch to the fixed build and complete Progress's recovery procedure before re-exposing the component; do not re-enable an unpatched controller. Triage: path-traversal exploitation of this component surfaces in the SZC's IIS/web request telemetry as requests carrying directory-traversal sequences to the storage-controller endpoints and in file-access telemetry as the service account reading or writing paths outside its normal content directories, legitimate SZC operation confines the service account to its configured storage paths, so out-of-tree file access under that account is the discriminator.
Correction29 Sep 2026 23:37 UTCrun 2026-09-29T2134Z-auditsourcesevidencetitleheadlinesummaryactionssourcing_notebody

The shutdown has a known cause and a fix. Progress has named the cause, a path-traversal flaw in Storage Zone Controller 5.x and 6.x reachable by an authenticated administrative user, and shipped fixed builds 5.12.5 and 6.0.2 (BleepingComputer, 2026-07-14), as the update of 2026-07-14 records. Its status page now reports that customer access "is currently being restored" (Progress ShareFile, 2026-07-14). Once the fixed builds are installed, Storage Zone Controllers can be brought back online (BleepingComputer, 2026-07-14).

entries.headline: Gitea Docker instances with reverse-proxy login enabled accepted a spoofed login header from anyone, and NCSC-CH rates it exploited
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-20896exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-20896: Gitea's official Docker image trusted the reverse-proxy login header from any source, so where reverse-proxy authentication is enabled anyone can impersonate any user

Gitea 1.26.3 (2026-06-20) fixes a large set of security flaws and 1.26.4 (2026-06-21) adds one more, and Gitea recommends upgrading directly to 1.26.4 (Gitea, 2026-06-21). The critical flaw, CVE-2026-20896 (CVSS 9.8) (NCSC-CH Cyber Security Hub, 2026-07-10), is in the official Docker images, whose app.ini template hard-codes REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES = * instead of the documented loopback-only default (GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4, 2026-06-21). When an administrator enables ENABLE_REVERSE_PROXY_AUTHENTICATION = true to put Gitea behind an authenticating reverse proxy, the image trusts the X-WEBAUTH-USER header from any source IP, so anyone who can reach the container's HTTP port directly can impersonate any user whose login name is known or guessable, with admin accounts the obvious targets (GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4, 2026-06-21). Binary and self-built deployments that follow app.example.ini keep the loopback-only default and are not affected (GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4, 2026-06-21). Version 1.26.3 removes the wildcard (The Hacker News, 2026-07-06) and makes reverse-proxy authentication opt-in and admin-configured (Gitea, 2026-06-21).

The same release fixes, among others, CVE-2026-27775, where the pre-receive hook cached the first ref's permission result and let a per-branch maintainer-edit grant escalate to full repository write (Gitea, 2026-06-21), CVE-2026-20779, a TOTP race and replay window across web login, password reset and the X-Gitea-OTP Basic-Auth surface (Gitea, 2026-06-21), and CVE-2026-22874, an incomplete SSRF protection in webhooks and migrations (Gitea, 2026-06-21). Germany's BSI issued WID-SEC-2026-2027 on 2026-06-22 rating the set "hoch" (BSI WID, 2026-06-22 · BSI WID CSAF, 2026-06-22). NCSC-CH set the exploitation status of CVE-2026-20896 to "Actively Exploited, Proof of Concept Available" on 2026-07-10 (NCSC-CH Cyber Security Hub, 2026-07-10), while the Sysdig telemetry behind the public reporting shows a first attempt that had not progressed beyond initial investigation (The Hacker News, 2026-07-06).

Exposure
Instances running the official Gitea Docker image 1.26.2 or earlier with ENABLE_REVERSE_PROXY_AUTHENTICATION = true whose HTTP port is reachable other than through the authenticating proxy (GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4, 2026-06-21) (The Hacker News, 2026-07-06). The flaw needs REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES left at the image default, so an instance whose administrator set it to the proxy's address is not exposed (GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4, 2026-06-21) (The Hacker News, 2026-07-06). Where ENABLE_REVERSE_PROXY_AUTO_REGISTRATION is also on, the same header lets an attacker create new accounts with any chosen username (GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4, 2026-06-21).
Detection
Network flow or container-host telemetry showing HTTP connections to the Gitea container port from hosts other than the authenticating proxy, since the attack has to bypass the proxy to set the header itself (GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4, 2026-06-21). After patching, look for accounts nobody requested on instances that had auto-registration enabled.

Triage: with reverse-proxy authentication on, a legitimate login also arrives as an X-WEBAUTH-USER header, set by the authenticating proxy, so the header alone is not the signal; the exploit is the same header on a direct connection from any other source, which signs the sender in with no password and no cookie (GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4, 2026-06-21).

Defender takeaway
Instances without reverse-proxy authentication enabled are not exposed to CVE-2026-20896 (GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4, 2026-06-21). Where it is enabled, upgrade to 1.26.4 (Gitea, 2026-06-21), or until then restrict REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES to the proxy's exact address.
Update10 Jul 2026 12:53 UTCrun 2026-07-10T1228Z-intelactionsaffected_productscvesevidenceregionssourcestagstechniquesbody

NCSC-CH added CVE-2026-20896 to its Cyber Security Hub on 2026-07-10 with the exploitation status "Actively Exploited, Proof of Concept Available", and names as the prerequisite a deployment on the official Docker image with reverse-proxy authentication enabled (NCSC-CH Cyber Security Hub, 2026-07-10).

The public exploitation reporting traces to Sysdig, which detected a first exploitation attempt 13 days after disclosure. Sysdig's Michael Clark told The Hacker News that the activity had "not so far progressed to any exploitation or attack progress" (The Hacker News, 2026-07-06). The Hacker News puts the number of internet-facing Gitea instances at about 6,200 (The Hacker News, 2026-07-06).

Contradiction: SecurityWeek, reporting the same Sysdig telemetry, says threat actors are exploiting the flaw to access internet-accessible instances (SecurityWeek, 2026-07-07), while Sysdig's statement to The Hacker News is that the activity had not progressed to exploitation (The Hacker News, 2026-07-06).

Correction30 Sep 2026 06:47 UTCrun 2026-09-30T0639Z-auditheadlinesummaryactionsbodyclassificationtitletagssectorscvesevidencesources

The earlier main text said no exploitation was reported. NCSC-CH set the flaw to "Actively Exploited, Proof of Concept Available" on 2026-07-10 (NCSC-CH Cyber Security Hub, 2026-07-10), while Sysdig, whose telemetry the public reporting rests on, told The Hacker News that the activity had not progressed to exploitation (The Hacker News, 2026-07-06). SecurityWeek reports the same telemetry as exploitation (SecurityWeek, 2026-07-07). The earlier summary and main text also presented the takeover as open to anyone who reaches the port. It works only where an administrator has enabled reverse-proxy authentication on the official Docker image and left the trusted-proxies setting at the image default, and the attacker needs a known or guessable username (GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4, 2026-06-21). The 1.26.3 release fixes more than four flaws, and CVE-2026-27775 is a cached permission check in the pre-receive hook, not a branch-protection race (Gitea, 2026-06-21). No cited source supports an earlier claim that Gitea dominates DACH and EU public-sector DevOps.

Improvement21 Oct 2026 08:22 UTCrun 2026-10-21T0800Z-auditbody

With reverse-proxy authentication on, legitimate logins also arrive as an X-WEBAUTH-USER header, which the authenticating proxy sets; the advisory's exploit is that header sent on a direct connection from any other source, which signs the sender in as the named user with no password and no cookie (GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4, 2026-06-21).

entries.summary: Gitea's official Docker image hard-coded REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES to the trust-all wildcard, so on instances where an administrator enabled reverse-proxy authentication, anyone who can reach the container's HTTP port can send an X-WEBAUTH-USER header and be signed in as any user whose login name is known or guessable, admins included (CVE-2026-20896, CVSS 9.8). NCSC-CH set it to actively exploited on 2026-07-10. Sysdig, whose telemetry the public reporting rests on, says the attempt it saw had not progressed to exploitation, though SecurityWeek reports the same telemetry as exploitation. Fixed in 1.26.3, and Gitea recommends 1.26.4.
entries.title: CVE-2026-20896: Gitea's official Docker image trusted the reverse-proxy login header from any source, so where reverse-proxy authentication is enabled anyone can impersonate any user

updates.summary: Switzerland's NCSC published an advisory on 2026-07-10 raising the exploitation status of the Gitea Docker-image reverse-proxy auth bypass (CVE-2026-20896, CVSS 9.8) to "Actively Exploited, Proof of Concept Available". The underlying flaw (the official Docker image trusting a spoofable X-WEBAUTH-USER header from any source IP for unauthenticated admin impersonation) was covered on 2026-06-23; the in-window delta is the national-CERT exploitation-status escalation. Public telemetry to date (Sysdig, via SecurityWeek/The Hacker News) still shows only reconnaissance-stage probing, so treat NCSC-CH's "actively exploited" label as a national-authority assessment and prioritise patching internet-reachable Docker instances now.

The main text still said no in-the-wild exploitation was reported after the 2026-07-10 update recorded NCSC-CH's actively-exploited status, and the summary and main text presented the takeover as open to anyone reaching the port. It requires reverse-proxy authentication to be enabled on the official Docker image with the trusted-proxies setting left at the image default, and a known or guessable username. The count of fixed flaws and the description of CVE-2026-27775 are corrected, an unsourced claim that Gitea dominates DACH and EU public-sector DevOps is removed, and hunting advice that relied on a log field no source documents is dropped.

The analysis gains a Triage line from the GitHub advisory: legitimate reverse-proxy logins also carry the X-WEBAUTH-USER header, set by the authenticating proxy, while the exploit sends it on a direct connection from any other source and signs in with no password and no cookie.

entries.headline: Microsoft ships the engine fix for RoguePlanet (CVE-2026-50656), the Defender SYSTEM-level LPE NCSC-CH has tracked with a public PoC since June
entries.html:
ROUTINECVE-2026-50656updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-50656: Microsoft Defender engine 'RoguePlanet' local privilege escalation now patched; NCSC-CH tracks the ongoing 'Nightmare Eclipse' zero-day series

NCSC-CH's running tracker on the "Nightmare Eclipse" (aka Chaotic Eclipse) researcher's 2026 zero-day PoC series was updated on 2026-07-09 to record that a CVE has been assigned to RoguePlanet: CVE-2026-50656, a local privilege-escalation vulnerability (CWE-59, improper link resolution before file access / "link following") in the Microsoft Malware Protection Engine that underpins Microsoft Defender, System Center Endpoint Protection and Microsoft Security Essentials (NCSC-CH, 2026-07-09) (Microsoft MSRC, 2026-07-08). The researcher first disclosed RoguePlanet as an unpatched zero-day on 2026-06-09, Patch Tuesday, describing a race condition in Defender that lets a local attacker "execute arbitrary code or spawn a command shell with SYSTEM-level privileges", at which point NCSC-CH logged its status as "Proof of Concept Available, no patch available" (NCSC-CH, 2026-07-09). Microsoft's own record shows the CVE was published 2026-06-16 (CVSS 3.1 7.8, AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N, rated "Exploitation More Likely", exploitation status "No") and remained without a fix for over three weeks; a revision dated 2026-07-08 confirms Microsoft has now shipped an engine update that closes it: last vulnerable Malware Protection Engine build 1.1.26050.11, first fixed build 1.1.26060.3008 (Microsoft MSRC, 2026-07-08).

NCSC-CH later recorded that a proof of concept dubbed ShieldBreak allegedly bypasses this fix; Microsoft tracks it as CVE-2026-69414 (NCSC-CH, 2026-07-09) and lists engine 1.1.26080.3 as the first build that addresses it (Microsoft Security Response Center, CVE-2026-69414).

Exposure
The Malware Protection Engine (mpengine.dll) at build 1.1.26050.11 or earlier, in Microsoft Defender, which runs on all supported versions of Windows, and in System Center Endpoint Protection and Microsoft Security Essentials; hosts with Defender disabled are not in an exploitable state even though vulnerability scanners flag the binaries still on disk (Microsoft MSRC, 2026-07-08).
Defender takeaway
Engine updates install automatically by default, so most estates already carry the fixed build and Microsoft's guidance is that no manual action is normally required, but it advises verifying that automatic deployment of engine updates works as expected (Microsoft MSRC, 2026-07-08); in analyst judgement that check matters most where engine updates are pinned, WSUS-gated, air-gapped or centrally deferred, such as System Center Endpoint Protection deployments and offline or OT-adjacent Windows hosts, and the build to confirm there is 1.1.26080.3 or later, which also carries the ShieldBreak fix (Microsoft Security Response Center, CVE-2026-69414).
Correction11 Oct 2026 14:55 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-auditreferencesclassificationbodysummarypriorityevidenceactionssources

Neither Microsoft's advisory nor NCSC-CH's tracker describes the exploitation mechanism beyond link following and a race condition, so the earlier triage guidance on symlink races against scanned files and on the engine's child processes is withdrawn. NCSC-CH has since recorded that a proof of concept dubbed ShieldBreak allegedly bypasses this fix, tracked by Microsoft as CVE-2026-69414 (NCSC-CH, 2026-07-09); Microsoft lists engine 1.1.26080.3 as the first build that addresses it (Microsoft Security Response Center, CVE-2026-69414). The priority moves from notable to routine: the flaw is local and the engine fix installs automatically. A pinned estate should therefore verify that build rather than the RoguePlanet fix alone.

Improvement21 Oct 2026 08:15 UTCrun 2026-10-21T0800Z-audittitlebody

Microsoft identifies the vulnerable engine as mpengine.dll and says Defender runs on all supported versions of Windows, so every Windows host with Defender enabled was in scope until its engine reached 1.1.26060.3008; hosts with Defender disabled are not in an exploitable state (Microsoft MSRC, 2026-07-08).

Builds on: Nightmare/Chaotic Eclipse zero-day wave; the Defender LPE now carries a CVE, a public PoC, and… · Microsoft has now shipped an engine fix (1.1.26080.3), and the same researcher claims a partial…

entries.headline: Akira ransomware hits Swiss imaging network Groupe 3R; administrative data stolen and published, medical data encrypted
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOA2

Groupe 3R (Réseau Radiologique Romand): Akira ransomware attack on 20 Swiss imaging centres, administrative data stolen and published, medical data encrypted

Groupe 3R (Réseau Radiologique Romand), which runs 20 medical-imaging centres in seven Swiss cantons (ICTjournal.ch, 2026-05-06), lists its centres in Vaud, Valais, Fribourg, Geneva, Neuchâtel, Berne and Zurich (Groupe 3R). It was hit on Thursday 2026-04-30 by a ransomware attack with data encryption; patient care was affected above all on 1 and 2 May, all centres stayed open, the attack was reported to the Federal Office for Cybersecurity, a criminal complaint was filed and no ransom will be paid (Groupe 3R). Akira listed the operator on its leak site, where ransomware.live recorded it on 2026-05-08 with an estimated attack date of 2026-04-30 (ransomware.live, 2026-05-08), announcing it would upload 48 GB of corporate data including employee identity documents, patient information, payment details and NDAs (DeXpose, 2026-05-09).

Groupe 3R now states that administrative data, including personal information of current and former employees, was encrypted and stolen, that medical data (exam results) was encrypted and made unusable, and that it is not possible to say with certainty whether patient medical data was also stolen (Groupe 3R). It acknowledged that internal documents stolen in the attack were published on the darknet, and attributes the attack to Akira because the gang's methods match what its specialist cybersecurity partners observed (ICTjournal.ch, 2026-07-06). This is its second attack in about a year: in April 2025 attackers stole medical and administrative data without disrupting operations (SwissCybersecurity.net, 2026-05-07), and Groupe 3R says the two attacks have different perpetrators and methods (Groupe 3R). Since 2026-06-26 all centres run on a rebuilt IT infrastructure with RIS, PACS, telephony and teleradiology restored, although some past examination data was still inaccessible in the operator's update of 2026-09-22 (Groupe 3R). No source states how the attackers got in; CISA's Akira advisory describes initial access mostly through VPN services using known CVEs, and encryption that is full or partial depending on file type and size (CISA AA24-109A).

Exposure
Current and former Groupe 3R employees, whose personal information was stolen, and patients of its centres, whose medical data was encrypted and may or may not have been taken (Groupe 3R).
Defender takeaway
Groupe 3R expects stolen data to be used for fraud such as fake supplementary invoices by email or post, and asks patients to check any invoice with it; patients insured under the LAMal system normally receive only a copy of the invoice sent to their insurer (Groupe 3R). With no access vector public, the case changes no patching or detection decision for other healthcare operators.
Update09 Jul 2026 12:25 UTCrun 2026-07-09T1211Z-intelactionssourcesbody

Groupe 3R (Réseau Radiologique Romand), the network of 20 medical-imaging centres in seven Swiss cantons, attributes the 30 April 2026 ransomware attack to Akira, saying the gang's methods match what its specialist cybersecurity partners observed, and has acknowledged that internal documents stolen in the attack were published on the darknet (SwissCybersecurity.net, 2026-07-07; ICTjournal.ch, 2026-07-06). The operator confirms that company administrative data was stolen and that medical data was encrypted and temporarily unusable; no publication of medical data has been observed so far, but whether it was also exfiltrated may never be established with certainty (ICTjournal.ch, 2026-07-06).

Groupe 3R refused to pay the ransom, filed a criminal complaint with the Valais cantonal police on 30 April, forwarded to the Office of the Attorney General of Switzerland on 12 May, and reported the attack to the Federal Office for Cybersecurity (ICTjournal.ch, 2026-07-06). As of 2026-07-06 all 20 centres run on a fully rebuilt infrastructure secured with ISO 27001-certified cybersecurity partners, with RIS, PACS, telephony and teleradiology restored, while the portal for referring physicians was still in security testing (ICTjournal.ch, 2026-07-06).

Correction21 Oct 2026 20:31 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditactionsbodyclassificationevent_dateevidenceheadlineprioritysourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

Exfiltration is confirmed by the operator, not only claimed by Akira: administrative data including personal information of current and former employees was encrypted and stolen, while whether patient medical data was also stolen cannot be said with certainty (Groupe 3R), and internal documents were published on the darknet (ICTjournal.ch, 2026-07-06). The attribution to Akira rests on methods matching what Groupe 3R's specialist partners observed (ICTjournal.ch, 2026-07-06), and Akira's leak-site listing was recorded on 2026-05-08 (ransomware.live, 2026-05-08). The seventh canton is Zurich (Groupe 3R). The April 2025 attack stole medical and administrative data without disrupting operations, so 2026 is the first outage rather than the second (SwissCybersecurity.net, 2026-05-07). No source states how the attackers got in; CISA describes Akira's usual access as VPN services exploited mostly through known CVEs (CISA AA24-109A), and the operator's concrete advice is to verify any invoice that appears to come from it (Groupe 3R).

Groupe 3R, which attributes the attack to Akira and refused to pay, confirmed that administrative data including employee personal information was stolen and internal documents published, and says it cannot establish whether patient medical data was also taken.
entries.title: Groupe 3R (Réseau Radiologique Romand): Akira ransomware attack on 20 Swiss imaging centres, administrative data stolen and published, medical data encrypted

updates.summary: Groupe 3R (Réseau Radiologique Romand), a 20-site medical-imaging network across seven Romandie cantons, has now confirmed through its own forensic investigation that the 2026-04-30 ransomware attack was carried out by Akira and that stolen corporate/administrative documents have since been published on the darknet, closing the attribution gap left when Akira first listed the victim on 2026-05-08. The operator refused to pay, rebuilt all 20 sites, and acknowledged it may never establish with certainty whether medical data was exfiltrated.

Groupe 3R confirmed that administrative data including employee personal information was stolen and internal documents published, so exfiltration is no longer only Akira's claim; whether patient medical data was taken cannot be established. Its 20 centres span seven cantons including Zurich, the 2025 attack stole data without disrupting operations, and Groupe 3R attributes the 2026 attack to Akira on the basis of methods its partners observed rather than a forensic finding. No source states the access vector.

entries.classification_html: NATOB1
entries.headline: Attackers log in to SimpleHelp RMM servers as new technicians through an OIDC flaw and push a stealer to managed endpoints
entries.html:
CRITICALCVE-2026-48558exploitedupdatedNATOB1

CVE-2026-48558: SimpleHelp RMM OIDC authentication bypass (CVSS 3.1 10.0) exploited to plant technician sessions that deliver the TaskWeaver loader and Djinn Stealer

CVE-2026-48558, scored CVSS 3.1 10.0 (CCB Belgium, 2026-06-19), is an authentication bypass in the OpenID Connect login flow of SimpleHelp 5.5.15 and earlier and of some 6.0 beta and release-candidate builds (SimpleHelp guide); SimpleHelp fixed it in 5.5.16 and 6.0 RC2 (SimpleHelp). CCB Belgium describes the flaw: with OIDC authentication configured, identity tokens submitted at login are accepted without verifying their cryptographic signature, so an unauthenticated attacker can submit a forged token with arbitrary identity claims and obtain a fully authenticated technician session (CCB Belgium, 2026-06-19). Horizon3, which found it, describes the conditions: an OIDC provider associated with at least one Technician group that has "Allow group authenticated logins" enabled; an attacker can then log in as a new technician, and MFA does not stop it because technicians register their own MFA method at first login (Horizon3.ai, 2026-06-12). Horizon3 found about 7.2% of a sample of exposed servers configured this way (Horizon3.ai, 2026-06-12).

Blackpoint investigated an intrusion in which an attacker used the bypass to open a technician session on an internet-facing SimpleHelp server and then used the RMM's trusted channel to run commands on managed systems: the TaskWeaver loader, an obfuscated script named to resemble a jQuery library and fetched from a temporary Cloudflare domain, installed Djinn Stealer, a cross-platform information stealer (BleepingComputer, 2026-06-29). CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-06-29 (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-06-29), and CCB Belgium reports it actively exploited (CCB Belgium, 2026-06-19).

Exposure
SimpleHelp servers on 5.5.15 or earlier, or on an affected 6.0 beta or release-candidate build, with OIDC group-authenticated technician logins enabled (SimpleHelp guide) (Horizon3.ai, 2026-06-12): an enabled OIDC authentication service and a Technician Group that has both that service and "Allow group authenticated logins" enabled, a setting in the Group's General Properties tab that is off by default for new Groups; servers without such a Group cannot be exploited this way (SimpleHelp guide).
Detection
In SimpleHelp, unfamiliar technicians under Administration > Technicians with "Show Group Authenticated Users" checked, and server-log lines registering a technician login or a configuration save by an unknown group-authenticated user (Horizon3.ai, 2026-06-12); on managed endpoints, the RMM software launching Node.js, PowerShell, Python, Deno or Bun, particularly from temporary, download, remote-support or user-writable directories (Blackpoint Cyber, 2026-06-29).
Defender takeaway
A compromised RMM server is a ready-made deployment channel to every managed endpoint, so patching must be followed by removing unrecognised technicians, invalidating their sessions and checking managed hosts for the loader (Horizon3.ai, 2026-06-12) (BleepingComputer, 2026-06-29). Where patching must wait, restrict where technicians can log in from under Administration > Login Security (Horizon3.ai, 2026-06-12); SimpleHelp says these technician login IP restrictions block the login from excluded ranges (SimpleHelp guide).
Correction11 Oct 2026 14:50 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryimmediate_actiontechniquesaffected_productscvessourcesevidenceclassificationbody

Horizon3's disclosure describes the conditions and indicators but not the token-validation mechanism, and the MFA bypass comes from technicians registering their own MFA at first login (Horizon3.ai, 2026-06-12). The sources describe TaskWeaver as a loader fetched from a temporary Cloudflare domain and give no persistence through scheduled tasks or launchd (BleepingComputer, 2026-06-29).

Improvement21 Oct 2026 12:07 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1149Z-audittitlecvessourcesbody

CCB Belgium gives the 10.0 score as CVSS 3.1 (CCB Belgium, 2026-06-19). SimpleHelp's guide limits the affected 6.0 versions to some beta and release-candidate builds, notes that "Allow group authenticated logins" is disabled by default for new Groups, and says technician login IP restrictions block a login from excluded ranges (SimpleHelp guide); Horizon3 recommends those restrictions where patching cannot happen in time (Horizon3.ai, 2026-06-12).

vulnerability30 Jun 05:10Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Horizon3.ai · BleepingComputer · CCB Belgium · SimpleHelp · CISA KEV catalog · Blackpoint Cyber

immediate_action.action: Upgrade SimpleHelp to 5.5.16 (or 6.0 RC2 on the 6.0 branch), then review group-authenticated technicians and server logs for unknown technician logins, because an attacker technician can run commands on every managed endpoint.
immediate_action.evidence_quote: Even when the SimpleHelp server is configured to enforce MFA for technicians, this issue allows the attacker to bypass this mechanism because on first login, technicians can self-register their own MFA method.
immediate_action.title: Patch internet-exposed SimpleHelp RMM servers and audit technicians now

entries.summary: CVE-2026-48558 lets an attacker log in to SimpleHelp 5.5.15 and earlier as a technician when OIDC group-authenticated logins are enabled, bypassing technician MFA. Blackpoint saw it used to push the TaskWeaver loader and Djinn Stealer to managed endpoints; CISA added it to its KEV catalog on 2026-06-29. Fixed in 5.5.16 and 6.0 RC2.
entries.title: CVE-2026-48558: SimpleHelp RMM OIDC authentication bypass (CVSS 3.1 10.0) exploited to plant technician sessions that deliver the TaskWeaver loader and Djinn Stealer

updates.summary: Horizon3 gives no signature-verification mechanism, and neither BleepingComputer nor Blackpoint says TaskWeaver persists through scheduled tasks or launchd. The hunts on SimpleHelp processes spawning shells and on MFA and VPN correlation had no source, and the evidence quotes were not verbatim. The entry is rewritten with the disclosure-day facts from the 2026-06-13 entry (affected versions, Horizon3's configuration conditions and log checks), the fixed releases, the KEV listing, Blackpoint's intrusion chain, verbatim evidence, a rating and an ATT&CK mapping; the 2026-06-13 entry's ShinyHunters and PeopleSoft material belongs to another finding and is not carried over. The main analysis now states the mechanism CCB Belgium gives, unsigned identity tokens accepted at OIDC login, and the endpoint detection line is cited to Blackpoint's own post, which is added as a source.

The 10.0 score is the CVSS 3.1 score CCB Belgium gives. SimpleHelp's guide, now a source, limits the affected 6.0 builds to some beta and release-candidate builds and says the group-authenticated login setting is off by default for new Groups; the takeaway adds technician login IP restrictions as the step to take where patching must wait.

entries.headline: A netadmin user on Cisco SD-WAN can become root through a crafted upload file; Mandiant saw zero-day use in April
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-20245 +2exploitedupdatedNATOA1

CVE-2026-20245: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN netadmin-to-root command injection exploited as a zero-day; fixed releases and a Live Protect shield available

CVE-2026-20245 (CVSS 7.8) is a privilege escalation in the CLI of Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, Manager and Validator: an authenticated, local attacker with netadmin privileges can inject commands through a crafted file and execute them as root (Cisco PSIRT). Netadmin access requires valid credentials or exploitation of the earlier authentication bypasses CVE-2026-20182 or CVE-2026-20127 (Cisco PSIRT). Cisco became aware of exploitation in June 2026 and has seen limited cases where it resulted in a configuration change pushed to edge devices (Cisco PSIRT), NCSC Switzerland relayed the advisory (NCSC-CH, 2026-06-05), and CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-06-09 (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-06-09). First fixed releases are 20.9.9.2, 20.12.7.2, 20.15.4.5, 20.15.5.3, 20.18.3.1 and 26.1.1.2; Cisco's Live Protect shield gives only temporary partial protection while upgrades are planned (Cisco PSIRT).

Exposure
Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, Manager or Validator below the first fixed release for its train, in particular Manager systems with ports exposed to the internet (Cisco PSIRT).
Detection
In /var/log/scripts.log, runs of the CLI upload scripts Cisco lists, vconfd_script_upload_tenant_list.sh, vconfd_script_upload_vsmart_serial_numbers.sh and vconfd_script_upload_chassis_number_file.sh (in Cisco's examples with a -cli path file under /home/admin), whose entries look the same for legitimate and malicious runs (Cisco PSIRT). In /var/log/auth.log, vmanage-admin logins from unexpected sources, admin password changes set and then reverted, and a successful su from admin to an unauthorized account; also password delta commits under /var/confd/rollback/ and the upload command in the CLI's show history (Mandiant, 2026-06-24).
Defender takeaway
Collect request admin-tech from each control component and retain logs before upgrading, then check for the indicators and verify the configuration of the edge devices; on a system confirmed compromised, the update alone does not resolve the vulnerability and Cisco TAC provides the remediation steps (Cisco PSIRT). Mandiant's actor restored the system configurations it modified and checked that its root account was gone, so an absent account does not clear a system (Mandiant, 2026-06-24); netadmin access on these systems should be treated as root.
Update26 Jun 2026 04:54 UTCrun 2026-06-26-6bbe4619cvesevidencesourcestagsbody

Mandiant published a forensic reconstruction of an intrusion at a service provider in which CVE-2026-20245 was exploited as a zero-day (Mandiant, 2026-06-24). From late 2025 to January 2026 Mandiant observed unauthorized peering connections to the victim's SD-WAN Manager devices and considers it possible that they exploited CVE-2026-20127 or CVE-2026-20182, then undisclosed; further rogue peerings from March 2026 ran on a version unaffected by CVE-2026-20127, and Cisco confirmed they did not use CVE-2026-20182 either and could rely on stolen certificate material (Mandiant, 2026-06-24). In March the actor logged in over SSH as vmanage-admin and manipulated default account passwords; in April 2026, from an SSH session as admin, it passed a crafted CSV file to the request tenant-upload tenant-list command, whose payload appended a new UID-0 account to /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow (Mandiant, 2026-06-24). It then deleted the files it had created, reverted its configuration changes and ran a validation script (Mandiant, 2026-06-24).

Update27 Jun 2026 05:17 UTCrun 2026-06-27-40e791d4cvesevidenceregionstagsbody

Mandiant's reconstruction dates the CVE-2026-20245 exploitation to April 2026, after rogue peering access that began in late 2025, and supports hunting for new UID-0 accounts and tenant-upload commands on Manager devices (Mandiant, 2026-06-24).

Correction11 Oct 2026 14:39 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryevent_datetagssectorstechniquesaffected_productscvessourcesevidencesourcing_notereferencesclassificationactionsbody

Fixed releases exist for every supported train, and Cisco offers a Live Protect shield as temporary partial protection (Cisco PSIRT). The flaw needs an authenticated attacker with netadmin privileges and scores 7.8 (Cisco PSIRT). Mandiant dates its zero-day exploitation to April 2026 at a service provider; the late-2025 to March activity was rogue peering, which may or may not have used the earlier bypasses, and the actor cleaned up by deleting its files and reverting configuration rather than wiping history or syslog (Mandiant, 2026-06-24).

Improvement21 Oct 2026 12:10 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1149Z-auditheadlinetechniquesactionsbody

Cisco's indicators cover three CLI upload scripts in /var/log/scripts.log, vconfd_script_upload_tenant_list.sh, vconfd_script_upload_vsmart_serial_numbers.sh and vconfd_script_upload_chassis_number_file.sh, not only the tenant-list one; Cisco has also seen limited cases where exploitation pushed a configuration change to edge devices, asks customers to verify the configuration of the edge devices, and describes its Live Protect shield as only temporary partial protection (Cisco PSIRT). entries.headline: NCSC-CH: Microsoft 365 "voicemail" phishing wave delivers malware such as infostealers and harvests M365 credentials
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOA2

NCSC-CH: Microsoft 365 "voicemail" phishing wave delivers malware such as infostealers and harvests M365 credentials

Switzerland's National Cyber Security Centre received a higher-than-usual number of reports about a dual-path Microsoft 365 / OneDrive-for-Business phishing campaign, its Week 25 review says (NCSC-CH, 2026-06-23). In the malware-delivery variant the email carries a ZIP "audio" attachment, and running its contents installs malware, such as an infostealer, that can harvest login details, cookies or wallet information. In the credential-harvest variant a fake Microsoft login page with a simulated audio player ("Play voicemail as guest") captures the M365 username and password. The link in the notification, or an HTML file attached to it, leads to that page. NCSC-CH notes that a compromised mailbox is then often used to send phishing to all of the victim's contacts ("chain phishing"), that the attackers read business communications to prepare CEO fraud and business email compromise from a real employee's address, and that data an infostealer harvests may also be resold and in some cases resurfaces weeks or months later.

Exposure
Organisations on Microsoft 365 or OneDrive for Business, whose users receive the fake voicemail notifications by email; stolen Microsoft 365 login details open the victim's email, OneDrive, SharePoint and Teams (NCSC-CH, 2026-06-23).
Detection
In mail-flow telemetry, inbound messages styled as Microsoft 365 or OneDrive voicemail notifications that carry a ZIP archive, an HTML attachment or a link, and later a burst of outbound mail from one mailbox to many of its contacts, the chain phishing NCSC describes (NCSC-CH, 2026-06-23). By inference from the mailbox monitoring NCSC-CH describes, hunt M365 audit logs for mailbox access from a new country or ASN shortly after a sign-in, and for inbox or forwarding rules created in that session.

Triage: genuine voicemails from telephone systems usually arrive as audio files such as .wav or .mp3, not as ZIP archives, and NCSC advises checking voice messages in the official app rather than through an email notification (NCSC-CH, 2026-06-23); a notification whose message plays only through an attachment or a "Play voicemail as guest" sign-in page is the lure.

Defender takeaway
In analyst judgement, phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 / certificate-based Conditional Access) blocks the fake-login path even when the lure succeeds, though not a session cookie an infostealer has already taken. Where the ZIP's contents ran, treat the host's login details, cookies and wallet information as harvested, since NCSC says such data may be resold and resurface weeks or months later in targeted follow-up attacks (NCSC-CH, 2026-06-23): reset those credentials and revoke the sessions rather than only cleaning the host.
Correction30 Sep 2026 06:43 UTCrun 2026-09-30T0634Z-auditsourcesevidencetechniquesclassificationtitleheadlinesummaryprioritysectorsentitiesbody

NCSC Switzerland's Week 25 review describes what attackers do with a compromised mailbox: they send phishing to the victim's contacts ("chain phishing") and read business communications to prepare CEO fraud and business email compromise (NCSC-CH, 2026-06-23). It does not describe forwarding rules or account manipulation, which the analysis had mapped. It also says genuine voicemails are usually sent as audio files rather than ZIP archives, and that data an infostealer harvests may be resold, where the analysis had said never and frequently. The analysis now follows the page, and the hunt for inbox and forwarding rules is marked as an inference from the mailbox monitoring NCSC describes. NCSC gives the infostealer only as an example of the malware the ZIP installs, and it names no sector and no Swiss public-sector recipients, so the title and analysis now say so and the entry's priority is notable rather than high. The citation now points at the page's new address on bacs.admin.ch, after the old ncsc.admin.ch page went dead.

Improvement21 Oct 2026 08:22 UTCrun 2026-10-21T0800Z-auditbodytechniques

NCSC advises checking voice messages in the official app rather than through an email notification, and it warns that login details, cookies and wallet information an infostealer harvests may be resold and resurface weeks or months later in targeted follow-up attacks (NCSC-CH, 2026-06-23). A host where the ZIP's contents ran therefore needs its credentials reset and its sessions revoked, not only cleaning.
