entries.action_label: Storm-2949 hijacked privileged Entra ID accounts…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Storm-2949 hijacked privileged Entra ID accounts through SSPR abuse, then mined Azure management features for data
entries.html:
HIGHupdatedNATOB2

Storm-2949: SSPR abuse of four privileged users turned into a data-theft sweep across Microsoft 365, Key Vault, SQL, Storage and Azure VMs

Microsoft Threat Intelligence published its account of an intrusion by Storm-2949 on 2026-05-18: a campaign whose singular focus was to exfiltrate as much sensitive data as possible from one target organization's high-value assets, across Microsoft 365, file hosting and the Azure production environment (Microsoft, 2026-05-18). The actor did not rely on traditional malware but on legitimate cloud and Azure management features that blend into administrative behavior (Microsoft, 2026-05-18). Storm is Microsoft's temporary designation for activity not yet classified, and Microsoft saw no follow-on extortion and no link to ShinyHunters (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-19).

Identity takeover. Microsoft assesses with high confidence that Storm-2949 abused Self-Service Password Reset (SSPR): the actor starts a reset on a targeted user's behalf and persuades the user to approve the resulting MFA prompts, likely through an organized and convincing phishing scheme, for example by posing as IT support (Microsoft, 2026-05-18). It then reset the password, removed the user's phone, e-mail and Authenticator methods and enrolled Microsoft Authenticator on its own device, locking the user out; the victims included IT personnel and senior leadership, and the actor repeated the process until it held four accounts (Microsoft, 2026-05-18).

Directory discovery and Microsoft 365 theft. A custom Python script enumerated users and applications through Microsoft Graph to find privileged identities, and an attempt to add credentials to a service principal failed for lack of permissions (Microsoft, 2026-05-18). The actor searched OneDrive and SharePoint for VPN configuration and remote-access documents and in one instance downloaded thousands of files from the OneDrive web interface in a single action (Microsoft, 2026-05-18).

Azure control plane. With privileged custom RBAC roles on several subscriptions, the actor called microsoft.Web/sites/publishxml/action to retrieve the publishing profiles of secondary App Service apps, which often hold FTP, Web Deploy and Kudu credentials; with an Owner role over one Key Vault it changed the vault's access configuration and read dozens of secrets within four minutes; Microsoft believes they held the credentials the actor then used to take over the primary production web app and change its password (Microsoft, 2026-05-18). It opened SQL server firewall rules with microsoft.sql/servers/firewallrules/write and deleted them after taking data, opened storage account network access to its own addresses with microsoft.storage/storageaccounts/write, and retrieved account keys and SAS tokens with microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listkeys/action to download blobs over several days with an Azure SDK script (Microsoft, 2026-05-18).

Virtual machines and endpoints. Through the VMAccess extension the actor created a local administrator on a VM, and through Run Command it tried to use the VM's managed-identity token from the Instance Metadata Service against Key Vault, which failed on permissions (Microsoft, 2026-05-18). A Run Command PowerShell script then attempted to weaken Defender Antivirus by disabling several protections, installed ScreenConnect from actor infrastructure under names resembling Windows components, and attempted to clear event logs, command history and temporary files; over ScreenConnect the actor ran host and domain discovery, exfiltrated .pfx certificate files and scanned file shares for password strings (Microsoft, 2026-05-18).

Exposure
Entra ID tenants where users with privileged Azure RBAC roles over Key Vault, App Service, SQL, Storage or VMs can reset their password through SSPR; Microsoft names no sector, country or victim (Microsoft, 2026-05-18).
Detection
Identity audit logs first: Entra ID records reset and registration activity in the Self-Service Password Management audit category, and combined security-information registration events, such as a new Authenticator registration, under Security > Authentication Methods (Microsoft Learn); the pattern here is a reset followed by removal of every existing method and a new Authenticator registration (Microsoft, 2026-05-18). Then the Azure activity log for the operations above from one principal (publishing-profile retrieval, Key Vault access changes, SQL firewall and storage network rule writes, key listing, VMAccess and Run Command), and on VMs the disabling of Defender protections, a new remote-access service and cleared event logs (Microsoft, 2026-05-18). Evicting the accounts is not enough: the actor's Authenticator registrations, the web app password it changed, the Key Vault secrets it read and the storage keys it listed all stay usable until they are removed or rotated.
Defender takeaway
Require phishing-resistant MFA for administrators and privileged users and make sure every privileged user already has a registered MFA method, which blocks the malicious registration step; limit publishing-profile access, Run Command and VMAccess through RBAC, and prefer Azure RBAC over Key Vault access policies (Microsoft, 2026-05-18).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:22 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditbodyclassificationevent_dateevidenceheadlineregionssectorssourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitleverification

Storm-2949 is not described as financially motivated: Microsoft's stated objective for the campaign is mass data exfiltration (Microsoft, 2026-05-18), Storm is its temporary designation for unclassified activity, and it observed no extortion and sees no link to ShinyHunters (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-19). The intrusion did not stay free of binaries: on VMs the actor installed ScreenConnect, tried to weaken Defender Antivirus and cleared event logs (Microsoft, 2026-05-18). SSPR abuse took over four privileged accounts, not one, and Microsoft hedges the social engineering as consistent with SSPR abuse and likely a phishing scheme, giving an IT-support call only as an example (Microsoft, 2026-05-18).

At Key Vault the actor changed the vault's access configuration and read dozens of secrets, connection strings and identity credentials among them (Microsoft, 2026-05-18); the Key Vault operation names given earlier for hunting are not in Microsoft's write-up, and Entra ID records SSPR activity in the Self-Service Password Management audit category (Microsoft Learn). Microsoft names no victim sector or country.

Sources: Microsoft Threat Intelligence · BleepingComputer · Microsoft Learn
entries.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence reported on 2026-05-18 that Storm-2949 abused Microsoft's Self-Service Password Reset to take over four privileged Entra ID accounts at one organization, re-enrolled MFA on its own devices, and used their Azure RBAC roles to pull App Service publishing profiles, Key Vault secrets, SQL and Storage data and VM access through Run Command and VMAccess. The actor relied mostly on legitimate cloud management features, installed ScreenConnect on VMs, aimed at mass data exfiltration and, per Microsoft, did not extort and shows no link to ShinyHunters.
entries.title: Storm-2949: SSPR abuse of four privileged users turned into a data-theft sweep across Microsoft 365, Key Vault, SQL, Storage and Azure VMs

updates.summary: Microsoft does not call Storm-2949 financially motivated: its objective was mass data exfiltration, Storm is a temporary designation, no extortion was seen and there is no ShinyHunters link, and the intrusion was not binary-free, since ScreenConnect was installed on VMs, where a script tried to weaken Defender and to clear event logs. Self-service password reset abuse took over four privileged accounts on a hedged phishing assessment.

entries.headline: The Gentlemen claims a Czech private university and a Swiss engineering firm on its leak site on 2026-05-18
entries.html:
ROUTINEupdatedNATOC3

The Gentlemen ransomware group lists Czech university VSFS and Swiss engineering firm DEVO-Tech AG on its leak site

The Gentlemen ransomware group claimed the Czech private University of Finance and Administration (VSFS) and the Swiss engineering firm DEVO-Tech AG on its leak site on 2026-05-18, threatening to publish stolen data unless the victims made contact or negotiated (DeXpose, 2026-05-19) (DeXpose, 2026-05-19); DEVO-Tech is a family-owned engineering company from Ziefen (ransomware.live, 2026-05-18). The listings carry no technical detail. Check Point Research's analysis of the group's leaked internal chats describes a locker written in Go and initial access mostly through exposed VPN appliances, firewalls and other edge devices, chiefly Fortinet FortiGate and Cisco, by brute-forcing credentials, exploiting known vulnerabilities or buying access (Check Point Research, 2026-05-13).

Detection
Authentication logs on internet-facing VPN and firewall panels, where the group brute-forces credentials (Check Point Research, 2026-05-13).
Defender takeaway
The listings alone change no decision outside the two victims and their partners; the transferable point is the group's edge-device entry, which puts exposed FortiGate and Cisco VPN and firewall management interfaces at the top of the review (Check Point Research, 2026-05-13).

The listings carry no technical detail, so nothing in them shows the group's methods unchanged; the group profile is Check Point Research's analysis of 2026-05-13, which names exposed VPN appliances and firewalls, chiefly FortiGate and Cisco, as the usual entry (Check Point Research, 2026-05-13), not SD-WAN gateways.

entries.headline: An unauthenticated Perl eval() flaw and five more in SEPPmail's gateway, with fixes shipped from 15.0.2.1 to 15.0.4
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-44128 +6updatedNATOA2

SEPPmail Secure E-Mail Gateway: unauthenticated code execution and five more flaws in NCSC-CH's advisory (CVE-2026-44128 et al., CVSS up to 9.3), fixed by 15.0.4

NCSC-CH's Security Hub post 12551 of 2026-05-08 lists six CVEs in the SEPPmail Secure E-Mail Gateway, scored from 6.9 to 9.3, with exploitation status unknown and vendor patches available since 2026-04-24 (NCSC-CH, 2026-05-08). SEPPmail's 15.0.4 release notes say test endpoints intended only for development had been left active in the beta GINA v2 web interface and are now removed (SEPPmail release notes). CVE-2026-44128 (9.3) is unauthenticated remote code execution through a parameter passed to Perl eval() and was already fixed in 15.0.2.1 (NCSC-CH, 2026-05-08) (InfoGuard Labs, 2026-05-18); CVE-2026-44126 (9.2), an insecure deserialization, was fixed in 15.0.3 (InfoGuard Labs, 2026-05-18), while NCSC-CH's advisory says the vulnerabilities were fixed in 15.0.4 (NCSC-CH, 2026-05-08); CVE-2026-44125 (9.3, missing authorization on GINA v2 endpoints), CVE-2026-44127 (8.8, file inclusion and arbitrary file deletion), CVE-2026-44129 (8.3, server-side template injection) and CVE-2026-7864 (6.9, exposure of sensitive information) were fixed in 15.0.4 (InfoGuard Labs, 2026-05-18); the scores are NCSC-CH's (NCSC-CH, 2026-05-08). The appliance is OpenBSD-based with Perl web applications, and self-registration, enabled by default, gives an attacker an authenticated session (InfoGuard Labs, 2026-05-18).

Exposure
SEPPmail appliances on a release older than 15.0.4 with the GINA v2 interface exposed; GINA v2 has to be explicitly activated in the system settings, which is how to tell whether its flaws apply (InfoGuard Labs, 2026-05-18). InfoGuard describes SEPPmail as widely used in the DACH region and counts several thousand public instances on Censys (InfoGuard Labs, 2026-05-18).
Detection
Internet requests to /v1/file.app, whose JSON body carries the path traversal in its file field (visible where a WAF or reverse proxy logs request bodies), and on the appliance a changed /etc/syslog.conf or an unexpected process started by syslogd after the 15-minute log-rotation reload, the chain InfoGuard uses for CVE-2026-2743 (InfoGuard Labs, 2026-05-18); an appliance that ran an affected build exposed to the internet needs that check after patching.
Defender takeaway
The GINA interface is internet-facing by design, so every appliance should run the current 15.0.x release, and an appliance that ran an affected build with GINA v2 exposed warrants a compromise check rather than a patch alone.
Update20 May 2026 05:00 UTCrun 2026-05-20-a0f7b07factionscvesregionssectorssourcestagsbody

InfoGuard Labs, which found CVE-2026-2743 and the GINA v2 flaws, published its technical write-up on 2026-05-18 (InfoGuard Labs, 2026-05-18). CVE-2026-2743 (CVSS 10.0 (The Hacker News, 2026-05-19)) is a pre-authentication path traversal in the Large File Transfer (LFT) component's /v1/file.app endpoint that writes files as the nobody user; because nobody can write /etc/syslog.conf, and newsyslog runs every 15 minutes and makes syslogd reload its configuration, the write becomes command execution (InfoGuard Labs, 2026-05-18). Only instances with LFT, which InfoGuard says most customers enable, are affected; /v1/file.app returning HTTP 404 means not affected (InfoGuard Labs, 2026-05-18). CVE-2026-2743 is not new: SEPPmail's 15.0.3 release notes already close it (SEPPmail release notes). The Hacker News reported the write-up (The Hacker News, 2026-05-19).

Contradiction: SEPPmail's release notes place the CVE-2026-2743 fix in 15.0.3 (SEPPmail release notes), while InfoGuard's table lists 15.0.4 (InfoGuard Labs, 2026-05-18); 15.0.4 or later covers both readings. InfoGuard also places the CVE-2026-44126 fix in 15.0.3 (InfoGuard Labs, 2026-05-18), while NCSC-CH's advisory says the vulnerabilities were fixed in 15.0.4 (NCSC-CH, 2026-05-08), so 15.0.4 is the safe floor for that flaw too.

Correction11 Oct 2026 14:28 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummarysectorstagscvesaffected_productstechniquessourcesverificationclassificationactionsbody

The fixes arrived across three releases: CVE-2026-44128 in 15.0.2.1, CVE-2026-44126 in 15.0.3 and the remaining four GINA v2 flaws in 15.0.4; 15.0.4.1 is an unrelated hotfix (InfoGuard Labs, 2026-05-18) (SEPPmail release notes). CVE-2026-2743 was closed in SEPPmail's 15.0.3 release, so it was not new in May; InfoGuard's May write-up gives 15.0.4 as its fix version (SEPPmail release notes) (InfoGuard Labs, 2026-05-18). CVE-2026-7864 exposes sensitive information and CVE-2026-44127 allows file inclusion and deletion; neither is code execution (InfoGuard Labs, 2026-05-18). SEPPmail AG is based in Neuenhof, not Steinach (SEPPmail).

InfoGuard's write-up traces that flaw to Perl eval(), places the insecure deserialization fix (CVE-2026-44126) in 15.0.3, and adds the LFT path traversal CVE-2026-2743 (10.0 per The Hacker News). No exploitation is reported.
entries.title: SEPPmail Secure E-Mail Gateway: unauthenticated code execution and five more flaws in NCSC-CH's advisory (CVE-2026-44128 et al., CVSS up to 9.3), fixed by 15.0.4

updates.summary: UPDATE (originally covered 2026-05-09 deep dive on CVE-2026-44128 cluster): InfoGuard Labs (the Baar-based Swiss security firm that performed the original SEPPmail review) published its full technical write-up on 2026-05-18.

The six GINA v2 flaws were not all fixed in '15.0.4 (patch 15.0.4.1)': CVE-2026-44128 was fixed in 15.0.2.1 and CVE-2026-44126 in 15.0.3, the rest in 15.0.4, and 15.0.4.1 is an unrelated hotfix. SEPPmail is based in Neuenhof, not Steinach, and the customer claims had no source. Four CVEs were mistyped as code execution. CVE-2026-2743 was already fixed in March, not new in May; the vendor and InfoGuard disagree on its fix version; and InfoGuard found it rather than performing an earlier review. The entry is rewritten with per-CVE types and fix versions, a contradiction line, a current-release action, a rating and an ATT&CK mapping. A Detection line follows InfoGuard's CVE-2026-2743 chain, the contradiction line adds the 15.0.3 or 15.0.4 split for CVE-2026-44126, and the 10.0 score for CVE-2026-2743 is cited to The Hacker News. The Detection line places the traversal in the request body InfoGuard shows, and the CVE-2026-44126 record states both fixed-version readings.

entries.headline: Cisco Talos: commodity "demo.pdb" BadIIS module for SEO fraud survives IIS restarts through a hidden backup copy
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Cisco Talos: the "demo.pdb" BadIIS variant is commodity IIS-module malware for SEO fraud, likely sold among Chinese-speaking crime groups and built by the author "lwxat"

Since 2024 Talos has investigated attacks, mainly in the Asia-Pacific region and a few in South Africa, Europe and North America, that use a BadIIS variant marked by "demo.pdb" strings, which it assesses with moderate confidence is commodity malware sold privately or shared among several Chinese-speaking cybercrime groups under a malware-as-a-service model (Cisco Talos, 2026-05-19). The BadIIS variants of the DragonRank and UAT-8099 groups Talos documented before relied on hardcoded C2 and statically compiled payloads, whereas this variant is configured with a recovered builder that injects parameters for JavaScript redirection of visitors to illicit sites, reverse proxying of illicit content to search-engine crawlers, site-wide content hijacking and backlink injection, and that encodes the C2 address with single-byte XOR (Cisco Talos, 2026-05-19). Service-based installers from the same author impersonate Windows services such as Winlogin, FaxService or AudiosService, authenticate to a C2 server, download further payloads, hide their command lines with custom Base64 and register the BadIIS DLL in the globalModules and modules sections of the IIS configuration, and the latest copies the DLL to a hidden backup location so it is restored every time IIS restarts (Cisco Talos, 2026-05-19). Talos ties development from at least September 2021 to January 2026, including a build to bypass Norton, to the alias "lwxat" with moderate-to-high confidence, from the builder's authentication string, a configuration parameter and a custom user agent seen in samples (Cisco Talos, 2026-05-19). Talos does not describe how the attackers first gain access to the IIS servers.

Exposure
Internet-facing Microsoft IIS servers that have already been compromised by means Talos does not describe; the victims it observed are mostly in the Asia-Pacific region (Cisco Talos, 2026-05-19).
Detection
In the IIS server configuration, unknown native modules in the globalModules and modules sections; in the file system, a second copy of the module DLL in a hidden backup location; in service telemetry, new services named like Windows components that run command lines altering the IIS module list (Cisco Talos, 2026-05-19). Deleting the DLL alone does not clean the server, because the backup copy returns it at the next IIS restart (Cisco Talos, 2026-05-19).
Defender takeaway
Operators of internet-facing IIS servers should check the server-level module list for modules they did not install; on a finding, remove the backup copy and the impersonating service along with the module, or BadIIS comes back at the next restart (Cisco Talos, 2026-05-19).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:44 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationentitiesevent_dateevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

The variant is not an ISAPI filter or extension: its installers register the malicious DLL in the globalModules and modules sections of the IIS configuration at server level, and the latest one keeps a hidden backup copy that restores it every time IIS restarts, so the place to look is the server module list and the backup location (Cisco Talos, 2026-05-19). Talos does not place it in DragonRank or UAT-8099 activity; it contrasts it with those groups' BadIIS variants, which used hardcoded C2 and static payloads, assesses it as commodity malware likely sold or shared among several Chinese-speaking cybercrime groups, and says the attacks are difficult to attribute to a single actor (Cisco Talos, 2026-05-19). The "lwxat" alias rests on the builder's authentication string, a configuration parameter and a custom user agent, and Talos does not say how attackers first reach the IIS servers (Cisco Talos, 2026-05-19).

entries.headline: vm2 sandbox escapes let untrusted JavaScript run code on the host; the May 2026 flaws are all fixed only in 3.11.4
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-24118 +20updatedNATOA2

vm2 Node.js sandbox: two waves of critical sandbox escapes in May 2026, fixed in 3.11.2 and then 3.11.4

The Hacker News reported on 2026-05-07 a dozen critical vulnerabilities in vm2, the Node.js library that runs untrusted JavaScript in a sandbox by intercepting and proxying objects, which let an attacker break out and execute arbitrary code on the host; fixes landed across versions 3.10.5 to 3.11.2, and users were told to update to 3.11.2 (The Hacker News, 2026-05-07). Among them, CVE-2026-43997 (CVSS 10.0) obtains the host Object despite earlier protections (vm2 GHSA-47x8-96vw-5wg6), CVE-2026-44006 (10.0) reaches BaseHandler.getPrototypeOf to get arbitrary prototypes (vm2 GHSA-qcp4-v2jj-fjx8), and CVE-2026-43999 (9.9) bypasses NodeVM's builtin allowlist whenever the module builtin is allowed, including through the '*' wildcard, so sandboxed code can load excluded builtins such as child_process (vm2 GHSA-947f-4v7f-x2v8); CVE-2026-44008 escapes through neutralizeArraySpeciesBatch() and CVE-2026-44009 through a null-proto exception, both 9.8 and fixed in 3.11.2 (The Hacker News, 2026-05-07). On 2026-05-18 the maintainer published a second set of advisories affecting 3.11.3 and earlier and fixed in 3.11.4 (vm2 GHSA-v6mx-mf47-r5wg), covered by BSI's WID-SEC-2026-1583 with CVE-2026-47131, CVE-2026-47135, CVE-2026-47137, CVE-2026-47139, CVE-2026-47140, CVE-2026-47141, CVE-2026-47208, CVE-2026-47209 and CVE-2026-47210; BSI says a remote, anonymous attacker can use them to execute arbitrary code, bypass security measures and disclose confidential information (BSI WID-SEC-2026-1583). Kodem Security describes the wave as vulnerability research rather than campaign reporting (Kodem Security, 2026-05-14).

Exposure
Any service that runs untrusted JavaScript through vm2 before 3.11.4, as a direct or transitive dependency: user-submitted code in plugin or SaaS environments, and LLM output produced in response to a manipulated prompt in AI-agent frameworks, CI/CD runners and online IDEs (Kodem Security, 2026-05-14).
Detection
Process lineage and runtime telemetry: shells (sh, bash, cmd.exe) parented to a Node.js runtime that should not start them, child_process calls originating in sandboxed contexts, reads of cloud, npm and Docker credential files or the process environment from inside an agent runtime, and egress from agent or CI runtimes to destinations outside the allowlist (Kodem Security, 2026-05-14). An escape before the upgrade ran with the host process's access, so after patching rotate the credentials the runtime could reach and audit its logs for those signs (Kodem Security, 2026-05-14).

Triage: the discriminator is whether the Node.js runtime is expected to start shells at all: Kodem's indicator is a shell parented to a runtime that should not invoke one, or a child_process call traced to a sandboxed context (Kodem Security, 2026-05-14).

Defender takeaway
Upgrade vm2 to 3.11.4 or later, which covers both sets (BSI WID-SEC-2026-1583); in Kodem's framing the decisive question is whether untrusted prompts or submitted code can reach a dynamic execution path that uses vm2, not merely whether the package is installed (Kodem Security, 2026-05-14).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:26 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevent_dateevidenceheadlinesectorssourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitleverification

The twelve critical vm2 CVEs were reported on 2026-05-07, with 3.11.2 as the version to update to (The Hacker News, 2026-05-07); BSI's WID-SEC-2026-1583 of 2026-05-18 covers a later, different set, CVE-2026-47131 and eight others, fixed in 3.11.4 (BSI WID-SEC-2026-1583). CVE-2026-43999 bypasses NodeVM's builtin allowlist when the module builtin is allowed, not when child_process is (vm2 GHSA-947f-4v7f-x2v8); CVE-2026-43997 obtains the host Object (vm2 GHSA-47x8-96vw-5wg6) while BaseHandler.getPrototypeOf is CVE-2026-44006 (vm2 GHSA-qcp4-v2jj-fjx8); and CVE-2026-44008 and CVE-2026-44009 are separate escapes, through neutralizeArraySpeciesBatch() and through a null-proto exception (The Hacker News, 2026-05-07). Kodem Security attributes the prompt-to-host-execution framing to Microsoft Security Research and gives no quoted chain (Kodem Security, 2026-05-14).

entries.headline: DirtyDecrypt: public Linux root exploit for an RxGK page-cache write on Fedora, Arch and openSUSE Tumbleweed kernels
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-31635updatedNATOB2

DirtyDecrypt (DirtyCBC): public root exploit for a Linux kernel RxGK page-cache write, mapped to CVE-2026-31635, on kernels built with CONFIG_RXGK

V12 found and reported DirtyDecrypt on 2026-05-09 and was told by the kernel maintainers that it duplicated a flaw already patched in mainline; Delphos Labs found it independently and calls it DirtyCBC (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-18). V12 describes it as an rxgk page-cache write due to a missing copy-on-write guard in rxgk_decrypt_skb (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-18), and Moselwal, quoted by The Hacker News, explains that the function decrypts incoming socket buffers on memory pages partly shared with other processes' page cache, so without the guard data is written into the memory of privileged processes or the page cache of privileged files such as /etc/shadow, /etc/sudoers or a SUID binary, giving root (The Hacker News, 2026-05-19). A working proof of concept from V12 was public by 2026-05-18, tested only against Fedora and the mainline kernel (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-18), and in containerized environments a vulnerable worker node could give a pod a way out (The Hacker News, 2026-05-19). Neither discoverer published a CVE id: Will Dormann says the details align with CVE-2026-31635, patched on 2026-04-25, and The Hacker News notes that the NVD record links the DirtyDecrypt proof of concept (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-18; The Hacker News, 2026-05-19). The kernel's own description of CVE-2026-31635 differs, an inverted length check that lets oversized RESPONSE authenticators reach rxgk_decrypt_skb() and hit a BUG_ON, scored CVSS 3.1 7.5 as a network denial of service, affecting kernels from 6.16 and fixed in 6.18.23, 6.19.13 and 7.0 (ENISA EUVD-2026-25528).

Exposure
Linux systems whose kernel is built with CONFIG_RXGK, which enables RxGK security for the AFS client and network transport; that limits the flaw to distributions that follow the latest upstream kernels, such as Fedora, Arch Linux and openSUSE Tumbleweed (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-18), on kernels from 6.16 before 6.18.23 or 6.19.13 (ENISA EUVD-2026-25528). Container worker nodes on such kernels add the risk of pod escape (The Hacker News, 2026-05-19).
Detection
In process and authentication telemetry on CONFIG_RXGK hosts, root shells or root-owned processes descending from an unprivileged user's session without a matching sudo or su event; the exploit gains root by writing into the page cache of files such as /etc/shadow, /etc/sudoers or SUID binaries (The Hacker News, 2026-05-19).
Defender takeaway
Install kernel updates that carry the fix (6.18.23, 6.19.13, 7.0 or later) on CONFIG_RXGK systems (ENISA EUVD-2026-25528; BleepingComputer, 2026-05-18); where patching must wait, BleepingComputer gives the Dirty Frag mitigation of blocking the esp4, esp6 and rxrpc modules through modprobe configuration, which breaks IPsec VPNs and AFS (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-18). Systems whose kernels lack CONFIG_RXGK have no decision to make.
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:45 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditactionsaffected_productsbodyclassificationconfidencecvesevent_dateevidenceheadlinesectorssourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

DirtyDecrypt's tie to CVE-2026-31635 is an attribution by Will Dormann and the NVD record's link to the proof of concept, not the discoverers' own: the kernel's description of CVE-2026-31635 is an inverted length check that lets oversized RESPONSE authenticators reach rxgk_decrypt_skb() and hit a BUG_ON, scored CVSS 3.1 7.5 as a network denial of service (ENISA EUVD-2026-25528; BleepingComputer, 2026-05-18; The Hacker News, 2026-05-19). The affected range is kernels from 6.16 before 6.18.23 or 6.19.13, with 7.0 also fixed, and older kernels fall outside it; no source says Debian Stable, RHEL or Ubuntu LTS are unaffected (ENISA EUVD-2026-25528). V12's proof of concept was already public when BleepingComputer reported it on 2026-05-18 (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-18). The interim mitigation BleepingComputer gives blocks the esp4, esp6 and rxrpc modules and breaks IPsec VPNs and AFS (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-18).

entries.headline: Microsoft Defender CVE-2026-45584 (CVSS 8.1): a heap overflow reached when Defender scans a malicious quarantined file
entries.html:
ROUTINECVE-2026-45584updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-45584: Microsoft Defender heap buffer overflow gives code execution when Defender scans a malicious quarantined file

Microsoft disclosed CVE-2026-45584 on 2026-05-19: a heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122) in Microsoft Defender allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network, scored CVSS 8.1 with high attack complexity (MSRC, 2026-05-19). Microsoft says a remote, unauthenticated attacker would have to entice a local user to take multiple actions that result in Defender scanning a malicious file that has been quarantined (MSRC, 2026-05-19). MSRC listed the flaw as neither exploited nor publicly disclosed at release (MSRC, 2026-05-19), and The Hacker News found no evidence of in-the-wild exploitation (The Hacker News, 2026-05-21). The last affected build is Malware Protection Engine version 1.1.26030.3008 and the first fixed build is Engine version 1.1.26040.8 (MSRC, 2026-05-19), the same engine release that fixes the exploited CVE-2026-41091 (The Hacker News, 2026-05-21).

Exposure
Defender runs on all supported versions of Windows, and System Center Endpoint Protection and Microsoft Security Essentials use the same engine; systems that have disabled Defender are not in an exploitable state, although scanners still flag their files on disk (MSRC, 2026-05-19).
Defender takeaway
No out-of-band step where Defender updates itself, because the default configuration keeps the engine up to date automatically (MSRC, 2026-05-19); confirm, as Microsoft recommends, that engine updates actually reach every host, offline and update-controlled machines first.
Correction21 Oct 2026 16:03 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitlepriority

Exploitation is not zero-click: Microsoft says a remote, unauthenticated attacker would have to entice a local user to take multiple actions that result in Defender scanning a malicious file that has been quarantined, and rates the attack complexity high (MSRC, 2026-05-19). The advisory does not say the attacker's code runs in the Defender process context. Malware Protection Engine version 1.1.26030.3008 and earlier are affected and Engine version 1.1.26040.8 fixes the flaw (MSRC, 2026-05-19).

It was neither exploited nor publicly disclosed at release, and Malware Protection Engine version 1.1.26040.8, which the default configuration installs automatically, fixes it.

entries.headline: Crafted traffic exploiting an undisclosed Huawei router flaw took down POST Luxembourg's network for three hours
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Previously unknown flaw in Huawei enterprise router software caused POST Luxembourg's nationwide telecom outage of July 2025; no CVE ten months later

An attack exploiting a previously unknown vulnerability in Huawei enterprise router software caused POST Luxembourg's nationwide outage on 23 July 2025, according to multiple sources briefed on the matter, disrupting mobile, landline and emergency communications for more than three hours (The Record, 2026-05-19). POST's head of communications Paul Rausch called it a denial-of-service attack on a network device that exploited "a non-public, non-documented behaviour, for which no patch was available at the time", and anonymous sources described it as a zero-day attack (The Record, 2026-05-19). Specially crafted network traffic sent the Huawei enterprise routers into a continuous restart loop: the public prosecutor said corrupted data relayed through POST in its role as internet service provider made its systems stop and reboot instead of relaying it, and a spokesperson for the High Commission for National Protection said investigators found "no evidence that an attack was specifically directed at POST Luxembourg as a chosen target" (The Record, 2026-05-19). POST said neither of the earlier, publicly disclosed denial-of-service flaws in Huawei's VRP operating system was involved, Huawei told POST it had never seen the attack among its customers, and no CVE or public warning has been issued (The Record, 2026-05-19).

Exposure
Operators running Huawei enterprise routers; it remains unclear whether the flaw was ever fully patched or whether similar Huawei systems remain vulnerable, and Huawei publishes enterprise advisories only through a restricted customer portal (The Record, 2026-05-19).
Detection
Network device health and availability telemetry: the failure was routers repeatedly stopping and rebooting on transit traffic they should have forwarded, and POST clarified that it was not a volumetric DDoS (The Record, 2026-05-19).
Defender takeaway
With no CVE or public advisory to patch against, an operator of Huawei enterprise routers has to ask Huawei, through the restricted customer portal or its account team, whether its router software carries a fix for the Luxembourg failure (The Record, 2026-05-19); without Huawei routers in the network there is no decision to make.
Correction21 Oct 2026 16:08 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditbodyclassificationentitiesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitle

The sources do not name Huawei's VRP operating system as the vulnerable software: The Record reports a previously unknown vulnerability in Huawei enterprise router software and mentions VRP only for earlier denial-of-service flaws that POST says were not involved (The Record, 2026-05-19). The finding that no attack was specifically directed at POST came from a spokesperson for Luxembourg's High Commission for National Protection, not from prosecutors, and the zero-day label rests on anonymous sources; no source attributes the attack to a state actor (The Record, 2026-05-19).

entries.action_label: Malicious Nx Console 18.95.0 stayed up to 36…
entries.classification_html: NATOA1
entries.headline: Malicious Nx Console 18.95.0 stayed up to 36 minutes on two extension marketplaces, stealing developer credentials
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOA1

Nx Console VS Code extension version 18.95.0 shipped a credential stealer, published with a contributor token stolen in the TanStack npm compromise

An attacker published Nx Console version 18.95.0 to the Visual Studio Marketplace at 12:30 UTC on 2026-05-18, where it stayed until 12:48 UTC, and to Open VSX from 12:33 to 13:09 UTC (Nx GHSA-c9j4-9m59-847w, 2026-05-18), times StepSecurity's account puts at 12:36 UTC for the Marketplace publication (StepSecurity, 2026-05-18); the Marketplace upload passed Microsoft's automated verification, and a maintainer caught it from the routine publisher-notification e-mail (Nx, 2026-05-21). The attacker published as a legitimate core contributor whose GitHub CLI OAuth token had been exfiltrated seven days earlier by a credential stealer that arrived through the 2026-05-11 TanStack npm supply-chain compromise, and no approval gate stopped a single contributor from releasing (Nx, 2026-05-21). The attacker had also planted an unsigned orphan commit in the nrwl/nx repository; the code injected into the extension runs when any workspace opens, fetches the 498 KB obfuscated payload from that commit (StepSecurity, 2026-05-18) and installs the Bun JavaScript runtime to run it (The Hacker News, 2026-05-19). The payload harvests Vault, npm, AWS (including the instance and ECS metadata services), GitHub, 1Password and filesystem secrets, exfiltrates them over HTTPS, the GitHub API and DNS, writes a Python backdoor with a macOS LaunchAgent for persistence and on Linux attempts a sudoers change (Nx, 2026-05-21); the macOS backdoor takes commands signed with a 4096-bit RSA key through the GitHub Search API as a dead drop (StepSecurity, 2026-05-18). Microsoft counts 28 Marketplace installs and Open VSX 41 downloads, while Nx's own analytics registered about 6,000 activations; the Nx CLI, the official plugins and Nx Cloud were not affected (Nx, 2026-05-21).

Exposure
Nx Console 18.95.0 exactly, in VS Code or a fork such as Cursor, on any machine that had the extension with auto-update enabled between 12:30 and 13:09 UTC on 2026-05-18; 18.100.0 and later are clean, and code --list-extensions --show-versions shows the installed version (Nx, 2026-05-21).
Detection
Process lineage and file telemetry on developer machines: the extension's code launching a background task that runs npx against a package taken from a GitHub commit, a Bun runtime installed under the user profile, and a Python process running a script from a hidden directory under the user's .local/share, with a new LaunchAgent on macOS (StepSecurity, 2026-05-18) (Nx, 2026-05-21). On the source-control side the stolen token showed as workflow runs and bulk run deletions nobody made, which Nx says audit-log monitoring would have caught during the attacker's week in its repositories (Nx, 2026-05-21). Updating the extension does not remove the backdoor or its persistence, which keep exfiltrating until they are killed and deleted (Nx GHSA-c9j4-9m59-847w, 2026-05-18).
Defender takeaway
A machine that ran 18.95.0 is compromised: remove the persistence and rotate every credential reachable from it, tokens, secrets and SSH keys, then audit access logs for those accounts (Nx GHSA-c9j4-9m59-847w, 2026-05-18). For teams that publish software, Nx's lesson is that any pipeline able to publish to a public registry must require approval gating (Nx, 2026-05-21).
Correction21 Oct 2026 16:09 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationentitiesevent_dateevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

The malicious version was live on the Visual Studio Marketplace from 12:30 to 12:48 UTC and on Open VSX from 12:33 to 13:09 UTC (Nx GHSA-c9j4-9m59-847w, 2026-05-18); 12:36 to 12:47 UTC is only the span from the maintainer's alert e-mail to the Marketplace unpublish, and Nx gives the exposure window as 12:30 to 13:09 UTC (Nx, 2026-05-21). The publishing credential was a core contributor's GitHub CLI OAuth token, stolen a week earlier through the TanStack npm compromise (Nx, 2026-05-21). The 2.2 million installs are the extension's total (StepSecurity, 2026-05-18); only 18.95.0 was malicious, with 28 Marketplace installs by Microsoft's count and about 6,000 activations by Nx's, and the upload was not too short-lived to scan: it passed Microsoft's automated checks, basic malware scans included (Nx, 2026-05-21).

entries.headline: Sparx Pro Cloud Server runs SQL for anyone who drops the model parameter; with WebEA it chains to code execution
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-42096 +4updatedNATOA2

Sparx Pro Cloud Server and Enterprise Architect: five CVEs including unauthenticated SQL execution and a WebEA race to code execution, public PoC, no vendor fix at disclosure

CERT Polska coordinated the disclosure of five vulnerabilities in Sparx Systems Pro Cloud Server (PCS) and Enterprise Architect (EA) on 2026-05-19, reported by Blazej Adamczyk (br0x) of Efigo (CERT Polska, 2026-05-19). CVE-2026-42097 lets an attacker omit the "model" query parameter and send the model name only in the POST request's binary blob, so PCS executes SQL queries without authentication, and CVE-2026-42096 lets any low-privileged user run arbitrary SQL queries in the database user context because permission checks are missing (CERT Polska, 2026-05-19). CVE-2026-42099 is a race condition in WebEA's /data_api/dl_internal_artifact.php: an attacker with repository access controls the name and contents of the file it writes, so a delayed response keeps a malicious PHP file reachable long enough for a second request to execute it; CVE-2026-42098 lets an authenticated EA user modify the client, for example with a debugger, to log in as any other user or administrator; and CVE-2026-42100 makes the PCS service terminate on a crafted SQL query (CERT Polska, 2026-05-19). The researcher scores the chain CVSS 4.0 10.0 because, with WebEA installed, the flaws give remote unauthenticated code execution in the web server context (sploit.tech, 2026-05-19); CCB lists CVSS 4.0 scores of 9.3 for CVE-2026-42097, 8.7 for CVE-2026-42096 and -42098, 7.7 for CVE-2026-42099 and 7.1 for CVE-2026-42100 (CCB, 2026-05-21). Proof-of-concept code exists for all five and no exploitation was known as of 2026-05-20: CCB's advisory title calls the flaws actively exploited, but its text reports no proof of exploitation as of that date (CCB, 2026-05-21); the published exploit script ships without the working key (GitHub br0xpl/sparx_hack), which sits in the freely downloadable EA client binary (sploit.tech, 2026-05-19). The vendor gave CERT Polska no details or vulnerable version range (CERT Polska, 2026-05-19) and had resolved none of the CVEs at disclosure (sploit.tech, 2026-05-19); Sparx's later Pro Cloud Server 6.5 release notes list WebEA security fixes, among them a corrected vulnerability when downloading internal artifacts and added validation of the model number parameter, without naming these CVEs (Sparx Systems).

Exposure
Pro Cloud Server through 6.1 and Enterprise Architect through 17.1, with other versions untested (CERT Polska, 2026-05-19); the unauthenticated SQL path works on both the TLS and the non-TLS port of the /SparxCloudLink.sseap endpoint, and code execution needs WebEA installed alongside PCS (sploit.tech, 2026-05-19).
Detection
Web and proxy access logs on the PCS host: POST requests to /SparxCloudLink.sseap that carry no model query parameter are the authentication bypass, and a request to WebEA's /data_api/dl_internal_artifact.php followed by repeated requests for a new PHP file under /data_api/ is the race being run (sploit.tech, 2026-05-19). Unexpected terminations of the PCS service point to CVE-2026-42100 (CERT Polska, 2026-05-19).

Triage: a legitimate EA client names its model in the model query parameter of the request URL; a POST to the endpoint with no or a wrong model parameter is the bypass, which is why the researcher suggests a proxy that drops such requests (sploit.tech, 2026-05-19).

Defender takeaway
With no vendor fix mapped to these CVEs, the researcher's workaround is the decision: isolate PCS instances from the internet and untrusted networks, keep frequent backups and review access logs (sploit.tech, 2026-05-19); a PCS without WebEA does not expose the code-execution path.
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:20 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditactionsaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevidenceheadlinepriorityregionssectorssourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitleverification

CVE-2026-42100 is improper handling of a syntactically invalid structure (CWE-228), not CWE-835 (CERT Polska, 2026-05-19), and CCB lists a CVSS 4.0 score for every one of the five, 8.7 for CVE-2026-42096 and 7.1 for CVE-2026-42100 included (CCB, 2026-05-21). Only CVE-2026-42097 needs no account: CVE-2026-42096, -42098, -42099 and -42100 need a low-privileged login or repository access (CCB, 2026-05-21), and the two SQL flaws are unauthorized SQL execution rather than SQL injection (CERT Polska, 2026-05-19).

The authentication bypass shows as a POST to /SparxCloudLink.sseap without the model query parameter, not as an _api/data request; the chained CVSS 4.0 10.0 is the researcher's score (sploit.tech, 2026-05-19), and the public exploit code ships without the working key (GitHub br0xpl/sparx_hack). No source states how widely Sparx tools are used in Swiss or EU government. Sparx's Pro Cloud Server 6.5 notes list WebEA security fixes without naming these CVEs (Sparx Systems).

entries.headline: Microsoft disrupts Fox Tempest, a signing service used for Rhysida attacks and linked to INC, Qilin and Akira affiliates
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Microsoft DCU disrupts Fox Tempest, a malware-signing service that enabled Rhysida deployments and is linked to INC, Qilin and Akira affiliates

Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit unsealed a legal case in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York against Fox Tempest, a malware-signing-as-a-service (MSaaS) operation active since May 2025. It seized the service's website, took hundreds of the virtual machines running the operation offline and blocked access to a site hosting its code (Microsoft On the Issues, 2026-05-19). Fox Tempest abused Microsoft Artifact Signing (formerly Azure Trusted Signing) to obtain Microsoft-issued code-signing certificates valid for only 72 hours, which let malware masquerade as software such as AnyDesk, Teams, PuTTY and Webex and bypass security controls. Microsoft assesses that the actor very likely used stolen identities based in the United States and Canada to pass Artifact Signing's identity validation (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-05-19).

Customers uploaded files through a web portal and, from February 2026, through pre-configured virtual machines hosted on Cloudzy infrastructure, and received signed binaries in return. They chose plans priced at $5,000, $7,500 or $9,000, with higher plans getting priority in the queue (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-05-19). Microsoft has revoked over a thousand certificates attributed to Fox Tempest (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-05-19) and reports the operators trying to move operations and customers to another code-signing service (Microsoft On the Issues, 2026-05-19).

Microsoft links Fox Tempest to Vanilla Tempest, Storm-0501, Storm-2561 and Storm-0249, which all used Fox Tempest-signed malware in active intrusions delivered through purchased advertisements, malvertising and SEO poisoning. Separately, cryptocurrency analysis ties the actor to affiliates delivering the INC, Qilin and Akira ransomware families (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-05-19). In Microsoft's case study, Vanilla Tempest bought ads that sent users searching for Microsoft Teams to fraudulent download pages serving a signed, trojanized Teams installer, which deployed the Oyster backdoor (also known as Broomstick) and in some cases Rhysida ransomware. Microsoft lists healthcare, education, government and financial services among the affected sectors, and the United States, France, India and China among the affected countries (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-05-19).

Exposure
Users who fetch AnyDesk, Teams, PuTTY or Webex installers from search results or ads rather than from the vendor, the delivery route Microsoft describes for Fox Tempest-signed malware (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-05-19).
Detection
Web proxy and DNS telemetry of installer downloads for those tools from domains that are not the vendor's, followed by endpoint telemetry of the installer establishing persistence and outbound command-and-control, the behavior Microsoft describes for the Oyster backdoor (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-05-19).

Triage: a genuine Teams, AnyDesk, PuTTY or Webex installer carries its publisher's signature. A Fox Tempest-signed copy carries a valid Microsoft-issued Artifact Signing certificate in the name of an entity that is not the product's publisher, obtained, Microsoft assesses, with stolen identities (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-05-19).

Defender takeaway
The takedown removes one signing service, not the technique, and the operators are already moving to another (Microsoft On the Issues, 2026-05-19). Trust a signed remote-access or collaboration installer only when the signer is the product's publisher.
Correction30 Sep 2026 06:54 UTCrun 2026-09-30T0639Z-auditsummarybodyclassificationtechniquesprioritytitleheadline

Microsoft assesses, rather than states, that Fox Tempest very likely used stolen identities based in the United States and Canada, and its customers paid for plans of $5,000, $7,500 or $9,000 with queue priority, not per signing run (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-05-19). INC, Qilin and Akira are tied to Fox Tempest through cryptocurrency links to affiliates delivering those ransomware families, not named as confirmed customers (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-05-19). No cited source reports European public-sector or healthcare victims of these affiliates. Earlier advice about installers spawning shells and about alerting on Key Vault certificate creation had no source. The earlier text also named the installer's file name and the seized domain; both are removed. Microsoft describes a trojanized Teams installer that deployed the Oyster backdoor (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-05-19). The court case is described by Microsoft as a legal case unsealed in the Southern District of New York (Microsoft On the Issues, 2026-05-19).

entries.headline: Any n8n user who can edit workflows could pollute prototypes or abuse the Git node; the full fix needs 1.123.43, 2.20.7 or 2.22.1
entries.html:
ROUTINECVE-2026-42231 +4updatedNATOA2

n8n CVE-2026-42231 et al.: five authenticated prototype-pollution and node flaws (CVSS 4.0 9.4) let workflow editors reach code execution or read server files

n8n fixed five flaws, all scored CVSS 4.0 9.4 and all requiring an authenticated user with permission to create or modify workflows, in two batches. On 2026-04-22 it published CVE-2026-42231, prototype pollution through the xml2js parser of XML webhook bodies (n8n, GHSA-q5f4-99jv-pgg5, 2026-04-22), and CVE-2026-42232, prototype pollution through the XML node that leads to code execution when combined with other nodes (n8n, GHSA-hqr4-h3xv-9m3r, 2026-04-22), both fixed in 1.123.32, 2.17.4 and 2.18.1. On 2026-05-13 it published CVE-2026-44789, prototype pollution through an unvalidated pagination parameter in the HTTP Request node (n8n, GHSA-c8xv-5998-g76h, 2026-05-13); CVE-2026-44790, CLI-flag injection in the Git node's Push operation that reads arbitrary files from the server (n8n, GHSA-57g9-58c2-xjg3, 2026-05-13); and CVE-2026-44791, a bypass of the CVE-2026-42232 fix in the XML node (n8n, GHSA-wrwr-h859-xh2r, 2026-05-13), all three fixed in 1.123.43, 2.20.7 and 2.22.1. The Hacker News reported the set on 2026-05-18 (The Hacker News, 2026-05-18). No source reports exploitation.

Exposure
N8n below 1.123.43, 2.20.7 or 2.22.1 where users who are not fully trusted can create or edit workflows (n8n, GHSA-c8xv-5998-g76h, 2026-05-13).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade to a release that carries both batches; until then, restrict workflow editing to trusted users and, as a short-term measure, exclude the XML, HTTP Request or Git node through NODES_EXCLUDE as the advisories describe (n8n, GHSA-57g9-58c2-xjg3, 2026-05-13) (n8n, GHSA-wrwr-h859-xh2r, 2026-05-13) (n8n, GHSA-c8xv-5998-g76h, 2026-05-13).
Correction11 Oct 2026 14:45 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryevent_dateprioritytechniquesaffected_productscvessourcesevidenceclassificationbodydeep_divedeep_dive_categoryregionssectors

n8n published the first two advisories on 2026-04-22 and the remaining three on 2026-05-13 (n8n, GHSA-q5f4-99jv-pgg5, 2026-04-22) (n8n, GHSA-c8xv-5998-g76h, 2026-05-13); a host patched only to 1.123.32, 2.17.4 or 2.18.1 is still exposed to the second batch. The advisories describe workarounds, restricting workflow editing and excluding the affected node through NODES_EXCLUDE (n8n, GHSA-57g9-58c2-xjg3, 2026-05-13). CVE-2026-44790 reads arbitrary files (n8n, GHSA-57g9-58c2-xjg3, 2026-05-13), and CVE-2026-44791 bypasses the XML node fix for CVE-2026-42232 (n8n, GHSA-wrwr-h859-xh2r, 2026-05-13). The priority moves from notable to routine: every flaw needs an authenticated user who can create or modify workflows, and no source reports exploitation.

The entry is rewritten from the five advisories with the per-advisory sources, exposure and takeaway lines, a rating and an ATT&CK mapping. The priority moves from notable to routine for authenticated-only flaws with no reported exploitation, and the deep-dive flag is cleared to match the shorter rewritten analysis.

entries.headline: MiniPlasma revived Windows Cloud Files flaw CVE-2020-17103 for a SYSTEM shell; Microsoft's June 2026 updates fix it
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2020-17103updatedNATOA1

MiniPlasma: Chaotic Eclipse PoC turns the 2020 Windows Cloud Files driver flaw CVE-2020-17103 into a SYSTEM shell on patched Windows 11; June 2026 updates fix it

Chaotic Eclipse, also known as Nightmare Eclipse, released source code and a compiled exploit for MiniPlasma on GitHub, saying that the flaw James Forshaw of Google Project Zero reported in September 2020 in the HsmOsBlockPlaceholderAccess routine of the Cloud Filter driver cldflt.sys, assigned CVE-2020-17103 and reportedly fixed in December 2020, was still present and that Google's original proof of concept worked unchanged (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-17). The exploit appears to abuse how the driver handles registry key creation through the undocumented CfAbortHydration API, which Forshaw's report said could create arbitrary registry keys in the .DEFAULT user hive without proper access checks (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-17). BleepingComputer, using a standard user account on a fully patched Windows 11 Pro system with the May 2026 updates, got a command prompt with SYSTEM privileges, and Will Dormann confirmed the exploit on the latest public Windows 11 but not on the latest Insider Preview Canary build (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-17); the researcher says success may vary because it is a race condition and that all Windows versions are likely affected (The Hacker News, 2026-05-18).

Microsoft re-released CVE-2020-17103 on 2026-06-09 to comprehensively address the flaw "recently publicly referred to as 'Mini-Plasma'" and recommends installing the June 2026 Windows updates; it rates it Important with a CVSS 3.1 base score of 7.0 and lists it as not exploited (Microsoft MSRC, CVE-2020-17103). MiniPlasma is the latest in a 2026 series from the same researcher after BlueHammer, RedSun and the UnDefend tool, all three of which were later seen exploited in attacks, and the YellowKey and GreenPlasma exploits (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-17).

Exposure
Windows systems without the June 2026 updates on which an attacker can already run code as a standard user (Microsoft MSRC, CVE-2020-17103; BleepingComputer, 2026-05-17).
Detection
In registry telemetry, creation or modification of keys under \Registry\User\Software\Policies\Microsoft\CloudFiles\BlockedApps and \Registry\User\.DEFAULT\Volatile Environment, the paths ThreatLocker advises monitoring for this exploit (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-17), especially by a standard user's process that is followed by a SYSTEM command prompt.
Defender takeaway
Install the June 2026 Windows updates, the fix Microsoft names for MiniPlasma (Microsoft MSRC, CVE-2020-17103); on a host still without them, a standard-user foothold is one public exploit away from SYSTEM (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-17).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:37 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevent_dateevidenceheadlinesectorssourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitle

Microsoft rates CVE-2020-17103 at CVSS 3.1 7.0, not 7.8, and re-released it on 2026-06-09, recommending the June 2026 Windows updates to comprehensively address the flaw now called Mini-Plasma, so it is no longer unpatched (Microsoft MSRC, CVE-2020-17103). The reproduction on fully patched Windows 11 Pro with the May 2026 updates was BleepingComputer's own test with a standard user account, and Will Dormann confirmed it separately on the latest public Windows 11 (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-17). MiniPlasma is not the third proof of concept in the series: BlueHammer, RedSun and UnDefend came first, followed by YellowKey and GreenPlasma (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-17). The monitoring the reporting gives is ThreatLocker's pair of registry paths; no source advises driver-load monitoring or says that disabling Cloud Files or OneDrive integration removes the attack surface (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-17).

entries.headline: Grafana Labs: a GitHub workflow token missed after the TanStack npm compromise let attackers take its codebase
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Grafana Labs confirms GitHub breach claimed by CoinbaseCartel: a workflow token missed after the TanStack npm compromise let attackers download its code and internal repositories

Grafana Labs said in posts on X that an unauthorized party had obtained a token granting access to its GitHub environment and downloaded its codebase, that no customer data or personal information was accessed and customer systems were unaffected, and that it would not pay the attacker's extortion demand, following FBI guidance (The Hacker News, 2026-05-17; BleepingComputer, 2026-05-18). SecurityWeek dates the confirmation to Sunday 2026-05-17, two days after the group CoinbaseCartel listed Grafana on its leak site on 2026-05-15 (SecurityWeek, 2026-05-18). In its update of 2026-05-19, Grafana said the incident originated from the TanStack npm supply-chain attack via the Mini Shai-Hulud campaign, that it detected the malicious activity on 2026-05-11 and rotated a significant number of GitHub workflow tokens, but that a missed token, from a workflow it had first deemed not impacted, gave the attackers access to its repositories (Grafana Labs, 2026-05-19); The Hacker News attributes the TanStack attack to TeamPCP (The Hacker News, 2026-05-20). The download covered public and private source code and internal repositories some teams use for operational information, including business contact names and email addresses, but not production systems or the Grafana Cloud platform; the ransom demand from an unnamed actor arrived on 2026-05-16, and Grafana has since rotated automation tokens, implemented enhanced monitoring and audited all commits since the May 11 incident (Grafana Labs, 2026-05-19).

CoinbaseCartel, active since September 2025, steals data and extorts victims without encrypting files; SecurityWeek counts 105 victims on its site, while The Hacker News, citing Halcyon and FortiGuard Labs, puts the total at 170 (SecurityWeek, 2026-05-18; The Hacker News, 2026-05-17). Security firms link the group to ShinyHunters, Scattered Spider and Lapsus$ (SecurityWeek, 2026-05-18), but ShinyHunters told BleepingComputer that CoinbaseCartel is not linked to it (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-18). Grafana's paying customers include governments, banks and infrastructure operators, and more than 7,000 organizations use the product (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-18).

Exposure
Organizations whose build pipelines took in the compromised TanStack npm packages, where any CI workflow token left unrotated afterwards stays usable, as one did at Grafana (The Hacker News, 2026-05-20). Grafana reports no impact on customer production systems or Grafana Cloud (Grafana Labs, 2026-05-19).
Detection
In source-control audit logs, repository downloads and clones made with workflow tokens, including those of workflows judged unaffected after a dependency compromise; Grafana's attackers came in through exactly such a workflow (The Hacker News, 2026-05-20).
Defender takeaway
After a dependency compromise reaches CI, rotate every workflow token, including those of workflows that look unaffected, and confirm the rotation is complete, since one missed token was enough here (The Hacker News, 2026-05-20). Grafana users have no product action to take: Grafana reports no customer impact and has audited its commits for malicious changes (The Hacker News, 2026-05-20).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:40 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationentitiesevent_dateevidenceheadlineregionssectorssourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

No source on the May 2026 breach describes a pull_request_target or Pwn-Request mechanism: Grafana says the incident originated from the TanStack npm supply-chain attack via the Mini Shai-Hulud campaign, detected on 2026-05-11, and that a GitHub workflow token missed during the rotation that followed gave the attackers access (Grafana Labs, 2026-05-19), an attack The Hacker News attributes to TeamPCP (The Hacker News, 2026-05-20). The theft was not limited to source code: the downloaded content also included internal repositories holding operational information and business contact names and email addresses, while production systems and the Grafana Cloud platform were not involved (The Hacker News, 2026-05-20). The link between CoinbaseCartel and ShinyHunters is contested, since ShinyHunters told BleepingComputer the group is not linked to it (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-18), and SecurityWeek counts 105 victims on CoinbaseCartel's site rather than about 170 (SecurityWeek, 2026-05-18). No source places Grafana in Swiss or EU public-sector monitoring estates or calls for watching unofficial Grafana plugins; Grafana says it audited all commits for malicious activity (The Hacker News, 2026-05-20).

entries.summary: Grafana Labs confirmed on 2026-05-17 that an unauthorized party used a token for its GitHub environment to download its codebase, two days after the data-extortion group CoinbaseCartel listed it on its leak site, and refused the ransom demand. Its update of 2026-05-19 traces the breach to the TanStack npm supply-chain attack attributed to TeamPCP, detected on 2026-05-11, after which a missed GitHub workflow token let the attackers in; the download also took internal repositories holding business contact names and email addresses, while customer production systems and Grafana Cloud were not affected.
entries.title: Grafana Labs confirms GitHub breach claimed by CoinbaseCartel: a workflow token missed after the TanStack npm compromise let attackers download its code and internal repositories

updates.summary: Grafana Labs traces its GitHub breach to the TanStack npm supply-chain attack attributed to TeamPCP, after which a GitHub workflow token missed during rotation let the attackers in, not to a pull_request_target Pwn-Request misconfiguration. The download was not limited to source code: it included internal repositories with business contact names and email addresses, though not production systems or Grafana Cloud. ShinyHunters denies any link to CoinbaseCartel, whose victim count is 105 by SecurityWeek's reckoning and 170 by The Hacker News's.

entries.action_label: Symantec: fast16 corrupted LS-DYNA and AUTODYN…
entries.classification_html: NATOB1
entries.headline: Symantec: fast16 corrupted LS-DYNA and AUTODYN simulations of uranium compression in nuclear detonations
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB1

Symantec and Carbon Black: the fast16 sabotage framework corrupted LS-DYNA and AUTODYN nuclear-detonation simulations; Kim Zetter argues it was contemporaneous with Stuxnet

Broadcom's Symantec and Carbon Black teams published on 2026-05-16 an analysis of fast16, the sabotage framework that SentinelOne first analyzed in April 2026 and whose oldest components date from around 2005, and confirm that its hook engine targets LS-DYNA and AUTODYN, applications used to simulate problems such as vehicle crashworthiness, material modelling and explosive simulation (Broadcom Security, 2026-05-16; The Hacker News, 2026-05-18). The framework combines a service binary that embeds a Lua 5.0 virtual machine, a boot-start filesystem filter driver that patches Intel-compiled executables on the fly as they are read from disk, and 101 byte-pattern rules in nine or ten groups for different builds of the two programs (Broadcom Security, 2026-05-16). Its hooks act only in high-explosive simulations and scale down outputs such as pressure or stress once the simulated material density passes 30 g/cm³, the threshold Broadcom says uranium reaches only under the shock compression of an implosion device, which it reads as sabotage of nuclear weapons research (Broadcom Security, 2026-05-16).

Before installing, fast16 checks for 18 endpoint-security registry keys and refuses to spread if any is present; it then registers itself as a service whose file takes the creation dates and permissions of a system binary, loads its driver as a SCSI-class filter at the next boot, and persists by hijacking a chosen application through the Image File Execution Options Debugger value (Broadcom Security, 2026-05-16). It spreads only inside its own network, enumerating domains, servers and shares and, for hosts in local address ranges, copying itself to their admin share under the logged-on user's credentials and creating a remote service (Broadcom Security, 2026-05-16). Kim Zetter, citing Symantec researchers and nuclear experts, argues that if fast16 targeted Iran in 2005 it was contemporaneous with Stuxnet rather than its predecessor, and that it fed false simulation data to engineers rather than altering weapons (Kim Zetter / ZERO DAY, 2026-05-16); Broadcom still calls it a pre-Stuxnet tool (Broadcom Security, 2026-05-16).

Exposure
Windows hosts that run Intel-compiled simulation software, specifically builds of LS-DYNA and AUTODYN from that era; the framework does not spread to hosts carrying any of the endpoint-security products it checks for (Broadcom Security, 2026-05-16).
Detection
In driver inventory telemetry, a boot-start filter driver registered under the SCSI class that is unsigned or unfamiliar; in registry telemetry, an Image File Execution Options Debugger value that launches a non-debugger binary and is deleted and re-added around each launch of the target application; in file and service telemetry, a new service binary whose timestamps match a system file; in network telemetry, one host copying an executable to the admin shares of same-subnet hosts and starting remote services (Broadcom Security, 2026-05-16).
Defender takeaway
Broadcom does not know whether a modern version of fast16 exists; operators of simulation and research-computing estates concerned about similar sabotage should inventory loaded drivers regularly, flagging unsigned or unfamiliar ones, and run tightly tuned application control (Broadcom Security, 2026-05-16). Other organizations have no decision to make.
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:42 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationevent_dateevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

SentinelOne's first public analysis of fast16 appeared in April 2026 and dated its oldest components to around 2005, about two years before Stuxnet first became active (Broadcom Security, 2026-05-16); no source places that disclosure at LABScon or reports earlier speculation that fast16 attacked centrifuges. The two framings are not settled: Kim Zetter argues that if fast16 targeted Iran in 2005 it was contemporaneous with Stuxnet rather than its predecessor (Kim Zetter / ZERO DAY, 2026-05-16), while Broadcom's analysis, published on 2026-05-16 rather than 2026-05-18, still calls it a pre-Stuxnet tool (Broadcom Security, 2026-05-16). LS-DYNA and AUTODYN are applications for simulating problems such as vehicle crashworthiness, material modelling and explosive simulation, not weapons-design codes as such, and Broadcom does not claim the hook engine is the first documented technique of its kind; the detection it supports rests on the install artifacts it documents and on inventorying unsigned or unfamiliar drivers (Broadcom Security, 2026-05-16).

It spreads only inside its own network and avoids hosts with endpoint-security products; Kim Zetter argues that, if it targeted Iran, it was contemporaneous with Stuxnet rather than a predecessor, while Broadcom still calls it pre-Stuxnet.

entries.action_label: INTERPOL Operation Ramz: 201 arrests and 53 servers…
entries.classification_html: NATOA2
entries.headline: INTERPOL Operation Ramz: 201 arrests and 53 servers seized in 13 MENA countries, among them a phishing-as-a-service site
entries.html:
ROUTINEupdatedNATOA2

INTERPOL Operation Ramz: 13 MENA countries arrest 201 suspects, seize 53 servers and dismantle a phishing-as-a-service site in Algeria

INTERPOL's Operation Ramz ran from October 2025 to 2026-02-28 across Algeria, Bahrain, Egypt, Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Oman, Palestine, Qatar, Tunisia and the UAE and focused on phishing and malware threats and on cyber scams; it led to 201 arrests, identified 382 further suspects and 3,867 victims, seized 53 servers and spread nearly 8,000 pieces of data and intelligence among the participants (INTERPOL, 2026-05-18; The Hacker News, 2026-05-18; Help Net Security, 2026-05-18). In Algeria authorities dismantled a phishing-as-a-service website, seizing a server, a computer, a mobile phone and hard drives with phishing software and scripts and taking one suspect into custody, and Moroccan authorities seized devices holding banking data and phishing software, with three people now in judicial proceedings (INTERPOL, 2026-05-18). In Qatar the operation identified compromised devices whose owners did not know they were being used to spread malicious threats, and in Oman investigators disabled a server in a private residence that held sensitive information and suffered from critical vulnerabilities, including a malware infection (INTERPOL, 2026-05-18). Jordanian police raided a fraud operation whose fake trading platform shut down once victims had deposited money and found that the 15 people running it were trafficking victims recruited from Asia with false job offers whose passports had been confiscated; two suspected organizers were arrested (INTERPOL, 2026-05-18). Group-IB, Kaspersky, the Shadowserver Foundation, Team Cymru and TrendAI supported the operation, which the EU and the Council of Europe partly funded through the CyberSouth+ project (INTERPOL, 2026-05-18).

Defender takeaway
No change for defenders outside the region: the operation targeted infrastructure and suspects in the Middle East and North Africa, and the release names no lure, kit or technique to hunt for (INTERPOL, 2026-05-18). The Jordan case documents a scam operation staffed by trafficked workers held without their passports (INTERPOL, 2026-05-18).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:41 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationevidenceheadlineregionssectorssourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitlepriority

INTERPOL says the operation focused on phishing and malware threats and on cyber scams that inflict severe cost to the region; it names no targeting of EU banking customers or payment systems, and no source forecasts follow-on advisories or links the Jordan case to Europol work (INTERPOL, 2026-05-18). In Jordan police raided a computer used for a fake trading-platform fraud and found that the 15 people running it were trafficking victims recruited from Asia whose passports had been confiscated, and two suspected organizers were arrested (INTERPOL, 2026-05-18). The server in Oman sat in a private residence and held sensitive information its owner could legitimately access, but suffered from critical vulnerabilities including a malware infection and was disabled (INTERPOL, 2026-05-18). The Algerian takedown also put one suspect in custody, and in Qatar the operation found compromised devices being used, without their owners' knowledge, to spread malicious threats (INTERPOL, 2026-05-18).

Highlights include a phishing-as-a-service website dismantled in Algeria with one arrest, phishing software and banking data seized in Morocco, compromised devices found spreading malicious threats in Qatar, and in Jordan a fake trading-platform scam run by 15 trafficking victims from Asia, whose two suspected organizers were arrested.

entries.action_label: CISA contractor's public GitHub repo exposed AWS…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: CISA contractor's public GitHub repo exposed AWS GovCloud admin keys and plaintext passwords for internal systems
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

CISA contractor's public GitHub repository exposed AWS GovCloud admin keys and plaintext passwords for internal CISA systems for up to six months

GitGuardian researcher Guillaume Valadon alerted KrebsOnSecurity on 2026-05-15 to a public GitHub repository named Private-CISA, kept by an employee of the government contractor Nightwing, that held cloud keys, tokens, plaintext passwords, logs and files describing how CISA builds, tests and deploys software (Krebs on Security, 2026-05-18). One file held administrative credentials to three AWS GovCloud servers, which Philippe Caturegli of Seralys validated as authenticating to three GovCloud accounts at a high privilege level; a CSV of browser-saved passwords listed plaintext credentials for dozens of internal CISA systems, among them LZ-DSO (Landing Zone DevSecOps), the agency's secure code development environment; and the archive also held plaintext credentials to CISA's internal Artifactory package repository (Krebs on Security, 2026-05-18). The commit logs show the administrator had disabled GitHub's default setting that blocks publishing SSH keys or other secrets, and many passwords were each platform's name followed by the current year (Krebs on Security, 2026-05-18).

The repository was created on 2025-11-13 and taken offline shortly after KrebsOnSecurity and Seralys notified CISA, but the AWS keys stayed valid for another 48 hours (Krebs on Security, 2026-05-18); Gizmodo puts the exposure at about six months, possibly much shorter depending on when each item was added (Gizmodo, 2026-05-19). Caturegli suspects the contractor used the repository to synchronize files between a work laptop and a home computer, and calls the Artifactory credentials a prime place to move laterally and backdoor software packages (Krebs on Security, 2026-05-18). CISA said it was investigating, that there was no indication any sensitive data was compromised, and that it was adding safeguards (Krebs on Security, 2026-05-18). For public bodies the case is a transferable pattern: a contractor's own repository holding an agency's privileged cloud and build-system credentials.

Exposure
Organizations whose staff or contractors can push agency material to public code repositories and can switch off the platform's secret-blocking setting, as this administrator did (Krebs on Security, 2026-05-18).
Detection
In code-hosting and secret-scanning telemetry, alerts on public repositories outside the organization's own namespace that contain its credentials, the kind of finding GitGuardian raised here; in cloud control-plane audit logs, use of long-lived access keys after the material they leaked from has been taken down, since these keys kept working for 48 hours (Krebs on Security, 2026-05-18).
Defender takeaway
When a secret leaks through a public repository, revoke the keys and passwords at once rather than relying on the takedown, and check that administrators cannot disable the code platform's secret blocking for repositories that hold agency material (Krebs on Security, 2026-05-18).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:38 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationentitiesevent_dateevidenceheadlineregionssectorssourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitlepriority

LZ-DSO, which appears to stand for Landing Zone DevSecOps, the agency's secure code development environment, was one of the dozens of internal systems whose passwords sat in the exposed CSV; the plaintext credentials to CISA's internal Artifactory package repository were a separate item in the archive (Krebs on Security, 2026-05-18). CISA did not link the exposure to staffing: it said there was no indication that any sensitive data was compromised and that it was working to add safeguards, while the loss of nearly a third of its workforce is Krebs's own context (Krebs on Security, 2026-05-18). That the repository synchronized files between a work laptop and a home computer is Caturegli's suspicion, and his point about the Artifactory credentials is a risk he describes, a prime place to move laterally and backdoor software packages, rather than an established write access (Krebs on Security, 2026-05-18). The exposure ran from the repository's creation on 2025-11-13 until it was taken offline in mid-May 2026, up to about six months (Gizmodo, 2026-05-19).
