entries.classification_html: NATOA2
entries.headline: BigBlueButton fixes predictable session tokens, an API checksum bypass and an SSRF in bbb-web (3.0.21, 3.0.23)
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-46351 +2updatedNATOA2

BigBlueButton bbb-web before 3.0.21 and 3.0.23: predictable session tokens, an API checksum bypass and an SSRF (CVE-2026-46351, CVE-2026-46353, CVE-2026-46404)

BigBlueButton, an open-source virtual classroom, published three security advisories for its bbb-web component on 2026-05-13 (ENISA EUVD-2026-44996; BigBlueButton GHSA-7959-pf2v-xc4h, 2026-05-13; BigBlueButton GHSA-43hc-5g2m-cqff, 2026-05-13; BigBlueButton GHSA-xqm3-6q7q-4v5h, 2026-05-13). Before version 3.0.21, bbb-web generated conference session tokens with insufficiently secure randomness, so a user could determine the session tokens of other users in the same session and impersonate them (CVE-2026-46351) (BigBlueButton GHSA-7959-pf2v-xc4h, 2026-05-13; ENISA EUVD-2026-44996), and supplying a presentationUploadExternalUrl parameter bypassed checksum validation, so any user could send valid requests to some endpoints without a checksum (CVE-2026-46353) (BigBlueButton GHSA-43hc-5g2m-cqff, 2026-05-13; ENISA EUVD-2026-44998). Before 3.0.23, presentation URL validation did not restrict access to site-local and link-local addresses, and the fix also pins resolved IPs when following redirects; BigBlueButton says private-address assets may be compromised if the attacker has gained additional access (CVE-2026-46404) (BigBlueButton GHSA-xqm3-6q7q-4v5h, 2026-05-13; ENISA EUVD-2026-44997). The CVSS 3.1 scores in the CVE records are 8.1 for the first two, with low privileges and no user interaction, and 6.8 for the SSRF, with high privileges and a changed scope (ENISA EUVD-2026-44996; ENISA EUVD-2026-44998; ENISA EUVD-2026-44997). Germany's BSI summarized the set as letting a remote, authenticated attacker bypass security measures and disclose confidential information (translated from German) (BSI WID-SEC-2026-1568, 2026-05-18). No source reports exploitation.

Exposure
BigBlueButton servers running bbb-web older than 3.0.21, or older than 3.0.23 for the SSRF; the token flaw needs a user inside the meeting, the checksum bypass any user of the API, and the SSRF a high-privilege user (ENISA EUVD-2026-44996; ENISA EUVD-2026-44998; ENISA EUVD-2026-44997).
Detection
In bbb-web API logs, requests carrying a presentationUploadExternalUrl parameter that reach endpoints without a valid checksum, and joins in which one participant presents another participant's session token; in egress telemetry from the BigBlueButton server, presentation fetches to site-local or link-local addresses (BigBlueButton GHSA-43hc-5g2m-cqff, 2026-05-13; BigBlueButton GHSA-7959-pf2v-xc4h, 2026-05-13; BigBlueButton GHSA-xqm3-6q7q-4v5h, 2026-05-13).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade BigBlueButton to 3.0.23 or later, which covers all three flaws; the advisories offer no workaround besides updating (BigBlueButton GHSA-xqm3-6q7q-4v5h, 2026-05-13; BigBlueButton GHSA-7959-pf2v-xc4h, 2026-05-13). Organizations without BigBlueButton have no decision to make.
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:35 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditactionsaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevent_dateevidenceheadlinepriorityregionssectorssourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

BigBlueButton published the three advisories on 2026-05-13, not 2026-05-17, and BSI's advisory followed on 2026-05-18 (BigBlueButton GHSA-7959-pf2v-xc4h, 2026-05-13; BSI WID-SEC-2026-1568, 2026-05-18). No source names the research networks, Swiss cantonal schools or German education ministries said to run BigBlueButton; BSI describes it only as an open-source web-conferencing system (BSI WID-SEC-2026-1568, 2026-05-18). The checksum bypass lets any user send valid requests to some endpoints without a checksum, rather than arbitrary authenticated API calls (BigBlueButton GHSA-43hc-5g2m-cqff, 2026-05-13), and for the SSRF, which needs a high-privilege user, BigBlueButton says only that private-address assets may be compromised if the attacker has gained additional access (BigBlueButton GHSA-xqm3-6q7q-4v5h, 2026-05-13; ENISA EUVD-2026-44997).

entries.action_label: Lower Saxony prescription auditor ARWINI: police…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Lower Saxony prescription auditor ARWINI: police confirm data theft by Kairos, which lists 2.87 TB for sale
entries.html:
ROUTINEupdatedNATOB2

ARWINI, Lower Saxony's prescription audit body: police confirm a data outflow and name the Kairos group, which lists 2.87 TB for sale

According to the Hannover police directorate, data left the system of the Arbeitsgemeinschaft Wirtschaftlichkeitsprüfung Niedersachsen (ARWINI), which processes health and billing data of statutorily insured people in Lower Saxony and audits the cost-effectiveness of prescriptions on behalf of the statutory health insurers and the Kassenärztliche Vereinigung Niedersachsen (KVN), and the police confirmed to heise online that the Kairos ransomware group is behind the attack (Heise, 2026-05-18). The attack was discovered on 2026-05-04 and all systems were shut down at once, according to the KVN as relayed by Borns IT Blog (Borns IT Blog, 2026-05-16). ARWINI said that "based on current findings, it is likely that personal and also particularly sensitive data are affected" (translated from German), potentially contact and health data and billing information of statutorily insured patients, and that the extent of the outflow was not yet established (Deutsches Ärzteblatt, 2026-05-18); it put the worst case at up to 75,000 records, while its external data protection officer told heise online it was still unclear whether and which data had left (Heise, 2026-05-18). The KVN says the records it sends each quarter are pseudonymised, with patient data anonymised but doctor and practice numbers included (Heise, 2026-05-18), and HAZ and NDR estimated more than 70,000 records (Deutsches Ärzteblatt, 2026-05-18).

Kairos has listed a 2.87 TB dataset on its leak site since 2026-05-11 and threatens to sell it, with sample files that include letters from health insurers and doctors; as of 2026-05-18 the data had not been published, and whether the attackers hold that much is unverified (Heise, 2026-05-18). The Lower Saxony data protection commissioner has received a breach notification and is examining whether it came in time, and the police are in contact with foreign authorities over Kairos, among them Spanish investigators (Heise, 2026-05-18). The case matters as a statutory health-insurance audit body in the DACH region holding health and billing data; no source states how the attackers got in.

Exposure
Health insurers, doctors and patients in Lower Saxony whose data ARWINI holds for prescription audits; the KVN says the data it supplies identify doctors and practices (Heise, 2026-05-18).
Defender takeaway
No technical decision follows, since no source names an access vector; for people possibly affected, ARWINI advises particular care with contact attempts and not opening suspicious emails or attachments (translated from German) (Deutsches Ärzteblatt, 2026-05-18).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:34 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationevidenceheadlinepriorityregionssourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

The 70,000 figure is not ARWINI's: ARWINI said personal and particularly sensitive data were likely affected and put the worst case at up to 75,000 records, while HAZ and NDR estimated more than 70,000 (Deutsches Ärzteblatt, 2026-05-18; Heise, 2026-05-18). The KVN says the patient data it sends are anonymised, with doctor and practice numbers included, so the scope of patient data remains disputed (Heise, 2026-05-18). The authorities involved are the Hannover police directorate, which confirmed the outflow and named Kairos, and the Lower Saxony data protection commissioner, which received a breach notification and is examining whether it was made in time (Heise, 2026-05-18); no source reports a notification to the BSI or classifies ARWINI under KRITIS or NIS2 rules. The discovery date of 2026-05-04 comes from the KVN as relayed by Borns IT Blog (Borns IT Blog, 2026-05-16).

ARWINI says personal and particularly sensitive data are likely affected, up to 75,000 records in the worst case, while the KVN says the patient data it supplies are anonymised; Kairos has listed a 2.87 TB dataset for sale since 2026-05-11, and no source states how the attackers got in.

entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Tycoon 2FA adds device-code phishing: victims approve token issuance to an attacker device on genuine Microsoft pages
entries.html:
HIGHupdatedNATOB2

Tycoon 2FA after the March 2026 takedown: operators add OAuth device-code phishing against Microsoft 365 alongside the credential-relay kit

eSentire's Threat Response Unit analyzed in late April 2026 a campaign by operators of the Tycoon 2FA phishing-as-a-service kit, which kept running after the March 2026 takedown led by Microsoft and Europol, that keeps the kit's in-browser tradecraft but ends in Microsoft's legitimate device-login flow instead of a credential-relay proxy (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12). The device-code variant runs beside the relay kit: eSentire still names the OfficeHome AppId as the primary marker of the credential-relay variant and treats the two AppIds as one detection set (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12), and BleepingComputer reports that the kit now supports device-code phishing (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-17).

The lure, a forwarded vendor-invoice reminder, carries a Trustifi click-tracking URL whose clean-reputation domain launders the link, and Trustifi redirects to a throwaway Cloudflare Workers subdomain that returns an AES-GCM-encrypted page decrypted in the browser (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12). The decrypted controller blanks the page for headless browsers and Burp, suppresses developer-tool shortcuts, redirects to microsoft.com when a debugger timing trap fires, checks the visitor's network owner against 230 cloud, sandbox, security-vendor, VPN and AI-crawler names, and stops rendering after a hardcoded expiry date (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12). A Microsoft-branded fake CAPTCHA then queries a Tycoon 2FA Check Domain, which serves suspected analysts a benign decoy website and real victims a Microsoft 365 voicemail lure (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12).

The voicemail page displays a user code that the operator's backend obtained from Microsoft's device-code endpoint, copies it and opens microsoft.com/devicelogin; the victim signs in at login.microsoftonline.com, approves the MFA push and consents to Microsoft Authentication Broker, and Microsoft issues access and refresh tokens to the operator's polling client, after which the kit sends the victim to their real Outlook inbox (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12). A victim already signed in sees no authentication step at all, only the consent prompt (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12). Because the Broker is a Microsoft first-party application it does not trigger unverified-publisher OAuth detections, and its token can be exchanged for Exchange, Graph and OneDrive tokens without further interaction (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12). The backend traffic still uses the CryptoJS AES-CBC layer with a hardcoded key and IV unchanged since eSentire's April 2025 analysis, which works as a kit fingerprint rather than protection, and the operators' token traffic came from Alibaba (US) hosting, which eSentire has seen across both kit variants since about 2026-04-10 in addition to the hosting providers documented before (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12).

Exposure
Microsoft Entra ID tenants that allow the OAuth device-code flow for end users; the protocol does not bind the device that requested a code to the user, so anyone who starts a device-code grant for a Microsoft first-party AppId can collect tokens from any user who consents (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12).
Detection
In Entra ID sign-in logs, successful device-code authentications (AuthenticationProtocol deviceCode, ResultType 0) from sources with no prior device-code activity, tokens issued to Microsoft Authentication Broker (AppId 29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e), and the user agents node or undici against that AppId in non-interactive sign-ins, with axios/1.x marking the credential-relay variant (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12). After revocation, repeated ResultType 50173 events with those user agents against one account show the operator still trying (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12). Revoking the session does not undo what the operator already set up: after a confirmed device-code phish eSentire revokes the refresh-token chain and reviews mailbox rules, OAuth consents and forwarding (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12).

Triage: a device-code sign-in alone can be a legitimate command-line tool or input-constrained device; eSentire's discriminators are a source with no prior device-code activity and Node.js user agents against the Broker AppId in non-interactive sign-ins, which it calls highly anomalous in production environments (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12).

Defender takeaway
Block the device-code flow with Conditional Access for all users except documented exceptions: Microsoft recommends getting as close as possible to a unilateral block (Microsoft Learn), and eSentire calls it the single control that removes this attack class for affected users (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12). eSentire adds admin consent for third-party applications, Continuous Access Evaluation and device-compliance requirements (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:30 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationentitiesevent_dateevidenceheadlineregionssectorssourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitleverification

Tycoon 2FA operators did not move away from the credential-relay kit: eSentire still names the OfficeHome AppId as the primary marker of the relay variant and treats it and the Broker AppId as one detection set, and BleepingComputer reports that the kit now supports device-code phishing (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12; BleepingComputer, 2026-05-17). The Alibaba (US) hosting seen since about 2026-04-10 is an addition to the hosting providers documented before, not a replacement (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12). The lure page shows a user code obtained by the operator's backend and tells the victim to paste it at microsoft.com/devicelogin (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-17), after which the victim sees a consent prompt reading "Are you trying to sign in to Microsoft Authentication Broker?" (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12). The detection signals eSentire publishes are successful deviceCode sign-ins from sources with no prior device-code activity, tokens issued to the Microsoft Authentication Broker AppId, node or undici user agents in non-interactive sign-ins, and ResultType 50173 after revocation (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12). eSentire says the phish does not bypass MFA but changes what MFA authorizes, and recommends blocking the device-code flow with Conditional Access as the control that removes the attack class (eSentire TRU, 2026-05-12), in line with Microsoft's advice to get as close as possible to a unilateral block (Microsoft Learn); no source says that FIDO2 sign-in defeats device-code phishing.

entries.headline: Switzerland-based THORChain lost about $10.7M when a newly joined validator broke its GG20 threshold signing
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

THORChain vault drain, about $10.7M from one vault: a newly joined validator exploited GG20 threshold signing (Switzerland-based protocol)

On 2026-05-15 an attacker drained about $10.7M from one of THORChain's five vaults, and the other four were unaffected (THORChain, 2026-05-20); THORChain's post-mortem of 2026-07-03 puts the loss at about $10M (THORChain, 2026-07-03). The Record reported one of six vaults and about $10.7M (The Record, 2026-05-15), and TRM Labs more than USD 11M across nine chains (TRM Labs, 2026-05-15). THORChain, a cross-chain liquidity protocol founded in 2018 and based in Switzerland, said initial indications were that user funds were safe and only protocol-owned funds were affected (The Record, 2026-05-15).

THORChain confirmed on the evening of 2026-05-15 that the attack exploited its GG20 threshold-signature (TSS) implementation to leak key material progressively, and that the attacker was a node operator churned into the validator set two days earlier (THORChain, 2026-05-20). Its post-mortem describes the chain: at vault setup the attacker published a Paillier key built from several small primes instead of two large ones, which passed because the library only screened out a handful of tiny factors; it then deliberately failed the MTA step of signing 864 times over two and a half days, each failure looking like routine node flakiness while leaking a fragment of other validators' key shares, until it could sign outbound transactions alone (THORChain, 2026-07-03). Two further weaknesses made the leak deterministic, a range proof whose two halves were never tied together and a blinding value drawn from far too small a range; all three sat in THORChain's fork (v0.1.6) of Binance's tss-lib, which upstream had fixed as individually minor issues in v2.0.0 (August 2023) and v3.0.0 (2024) (THORChain, 2026-07-03). THORChain says only the Paillier-modulus condition matches public research, the class documented in 2023 as BitForge and TSSHOCK (THORChain, 2026-07-03); the 2023 disclosures include Fireblocks' CVE-2023-33241 on unchecked Paillier moduli (Fireblocks, 2023-08-09) and Verichains' TSSHOCK attacks on threshold-signing proofs and their encoding (Verichains, 2023-08-10).

The solvency checker halted signing and trading on several chains within about 52 minutes, but only after the funds had left, because the attacker signed with the reconstructed key (THORChain, 2026-05-20). Chainalysis traced attacker-linked funds through Monero, Hyperliquid and Arbitrum from late April, including the ETH that bonded the malicious validator, CryptoTimes reports (CryptoTimes, 2026-05-17). TRM Labs had not attributed the theft to any actor as of 2026-05-15, while calling THORChain the bridge of choice for laundering North Korea's largest thefts (TRM Labs, 2026-05-15). Every validator has since upgraded to v3.19.1, and THORChain plans to replace GG20 with DKLS or Schnorr-based signing (THORChain, 2026-07-03).

Exposure
ECDSA threshold-signing deployments running GG20 code derived from Binance's tss-lib from before its v2.0.0 and v3.0.0 fixes, wherever a party that could be malicious joins the signing committee, which on THORChain is anyone who bonds a validator; EdDSA signing, as on Solana, is not exposed (THORChain, 2026-07-03).
Detection
Per-participant signing-protocol telemetry: THORChain names a single validator responsible for a disproportionate share of signing failures over a short period as the signal it missed, and is adding monitoring of key-sign failures per validator (THORChain, 2026-07-03). Balance-based solvency checks fire only after the funds move once the key has been rebuilt (THORChain, 2026-05-20).

Triage: failed signing rounds are routine, since validators go offline or miss timing windows; the discriminator is the aggregate, one recently admitted participant failing the same signing step far more often than its peers over days (THORChain, 2026-07-03).

Defender takeaway
For any GG20 threshold-signing deployment built on tss-lib, confirm the library carries tss-lib's v2.0.0 and v3.0.0 fixes, including verification that each party's Paillier modulus is well formed, and alert on each participant's share of signing failures (THORChain, 2026-07-03). Organisations without threshold-signing infrastructure have no decision to make.
Correction30 Sep 2026 07:16 UTCrun 2026-09-30T0639Z-auditsourcesbodyclassificationtechniquessummaryevidenceevent_dateprioritytitleheadline

The analysis above described CVE-2023-33241 as part of the TSSHOCK class. CVE-2023-33241 is Fireblocks' GG18/GG20 Paillier-key disclosure (Fireblocks, 2023-08-09), and TSSHOCK is Verichains' separate set of key-extraction attacks (Verichains, 2023-08-10). Fireblocks' flaw lies in an unchecked Paillier modulus, which it recommends detecting with a suitable zero-knowledge proof, while TSSHOCK exploits weak or insecurely implemented zero-knowledge proofs. Both let a single malicious participant extract key material (Fireblocks, 2023-08-09; Verichains, 2023-08-10).

The account of the attack above was also narrowed to its sources. The Record reports a compromised vault. The malicious validator node was the vector THORChain's first incident update confirmed, according to CryptoTimes, and the GG20 flaw was then the working theory CryptoTimes reported, supported by PeckShield, Cyvers and security teams working with THORChain rather than Chainalysis (CryptoTimes, 2026-05-17). TRM Labs calls THORChain the bridge of choice for laundering North Korea's largest thefts without naming the Lazarus Group or saying such activity dominates (TRM Labs, 2026-05-15).

Correction20 Oct 2026 08:46 UTCrun 2026-10-20T0835Z-auditbodyevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

The loss came from one of THORChain's five vaults, not six, and THORChain puts it at about $10.7M (THORChain, 2026-05-20) and in its post-mortem at about $10M (THORChain, 2026-07-03); six vaults is The Record's figure (The Record, 2026-05-15) and more than USD 11M is TRM Labs' (TRM Labs, 2026-05-15), so the six vaults and about $11M stated earlier came from those outlets, not from THORChain. The GG20 flaw was not a suspicion: THORChain confirmed on 2026-05-15 that the attack exploited its GG20 TSS implementation to leak key material progressively (THORChain, 2026-05-20), and its post-mortem of 2026-07-03 sets out the exploit chain, a malformed multi-prime Paillier key and 864 deliberately failed signing rounds combined with two further weaknesses in its tss-lib fork (THORChain, 2026-07-03).

THORChain says a validator churned in two days earlier exploited its GG20 threshold-signature implementation: a malformed multi-prime Paillier key planted at setup and 864 deliberately failed signing rounds leaked other validators' key shares until the attacker could sign alone, a chain of three weaknesses in its fork of Binance's tss-lib that upstream had fixed by 2024. updates.summary: CVE-2023-33241 is Fireblocks' own finding and TSSHOCK is Verichains' separate set of attacks, so the text names both with their own sources, describes each weakness as its source does, and drops an unsupported claim that this was a second large-scale production case. The title, headline, summary and main text give the malicious node as the vector THORChain's first incident update confirmed and the GG20 flaw as the working theory CryptoTimes reports, and no longer credit Chainalysis for it or name the Lazarus Group. The node address is removed as an indicator, the event date moves to the 2026-05-15 drain, and the priority moves from high to notable because a crypto-protocol vault drain asks no decision of Swiss public bodies within seven days. An uncited relevance paragraph is replaced by a cited takeaway, which sets CryptoTimes' view of CGGMP21 against Verichains' findings.

THORChain's own reports count one of five vaults drained for about $10.7M (later about $10M), not the six vaults and about $11M taken from The Record and TRM Labs, and confirm the GG20 threshold-signature exploit that had been described as suspected. The analysis is rewritten from THORChain's post-mortem of 2026-07-03, which describes a malformed multi-prime Paillier key and 864 deliberately failed signing rounds, with exposure, detection and triage guidance for other GG20 deployments.

entries.headline: Pwn2Own Berlin 2026 paid $1,298,250 for 47 zero-days; DEVCORE won as Exchange, ESXi and AI coding agents fell
entries.html:
ROUTINEupdatedNATOA1

Pwn2Own Berlin 2026 results: 47 zero-days and $1,298,250 awarded, DEVCORE Master of Pwn, AI coding agents and inference tools exploited

Pwn2Own Berlin 2026, ZDI's second Berlin contest after the inaugural 2025 event, ran at OffensiveCon from 14 to 16 May (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-03-12) (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-15). For 2026 ZDI split its AI category into AI Databases, Coding Agents, Local Inferences and NVIDIA (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-03-12). Targets ran fully patched in their default configurations (Zero Day Initiative, contest rules), and vendors have 90 days to patch after the zero-days are disclosed at the contest (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-15). Before it began, Hackread wrote that it had reportedly run out of space and that some researchers turned away were releasing their findings instead (Hackread, 2026-05-12).

The final totals were $1,298,250 for 47 unique zero-days; DEVCORE won Master of Pwn with 50.5 points and $505,000, ahead of STARLabs SG (25 points, $242,500) and Out Of Bounds (12.75 points, $95,750) (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-16).

Enterprise and platform targets. Orange Tsai of DEVCORE chained four logic bugs for a Microsoft Edge sandbox escape ($175,000) on Day One (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-14) and three bugs for remote code execution as SYSTEM on Microsoft Exchange ($200,000) on Day Two (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-15); neither ZDI nor BleepingComputer states whether the chain needs authentication. splitline of DEVCORE chained two bugs against Microsoft SharePoint ($100,000), and Nguyen Hoang Thach of STARLabs SG used a memory corruption bug against VMware ESXi with the cross-tenant code execution add-on ($200,000) (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-16), an entry that runs code from a guest on the hypervisor (Zero Day Initiative, contest rules). Windows 11 and Red Hat Enterprise Linux for Workstations fell to privilege escalations (improper access control, heap overflow, use-after-free, integer overflow and race-condition bugs), and NV Container Toolkit to chompie ($50,000) and to 0xDACA and Noam Trobishi with a use-after-free ($25,000) (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-14) (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-15) (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-16).

AI targets. OpenAI Codex fell to Compass Security with a single CWE-150 bug ($40,000), while a Doyensec entry used a bug previously known to the vendor and a Viettel attempt failed (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-14); Summoning Team ($20,000) (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-15) and Satoki Tsuji of Ikotas Labs, through an external control ($20,000), also exploited it (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-16). Cursor fell to Viettel ($30,000) and Compass Security ($15,000) (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-15). LM Studio fell to STARLabs SG (five bugs) and LiteLLM to k3vg3n (three bugs), both chains including SSRF and code injection and each worth $40,000 (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-14); OtterSec took LM Studio with a code injection bug ($20,000) (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-15). Out Of Bounds took Chroma with two bugs (CWE-190, CWE-362; $20,000), and NVIDIA Megatron Bridge fell three times (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-14). Every Anthropic Claude Code entry, Summoning Team's Claude Desktop entry, the Ollama entry and two LiteLLM entries hit previously known bugs or collisions (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-14) (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-15) (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-16), and an Oracle Autonomous AI Database attempt failed (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-14).

Exposure
Current releases of the products named above, whose vendors received the bugs at the contest; ZDI's result pages give no CVE ids (Zero Day Initiative, contest rules) (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-16).
Defender takeaway
No change on the results alone: no source reports these bugs used in the wild, and vendors have 90 days to patch them (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-15).
Correction21 Oct 2026 15:48 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1149Z-auditactionsaffected_productsbodyclassificationdeep_divedeep_dive_categoryevidenceheadlinekindpriorityregionssectorssourcessummarytagstechniquestitle

ZDI and BleepingComputer report the Exchange result as three chained bugs giving remote code execution as SYSTEM, and neither says the chain works without authentication (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-15) (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-15). ZDI ran no "AI Agents" category: for 2026 it split its existing AI category into AI Databases, Coding Agents, Local Inferences and NVIDIA (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-03-12), and not every AI target fell: an Oracle Autonomous AI Database attempt failed, while Chroma was a two-bug success rather than a collision (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-14). The pages report results only; they carry no patch forecast, no attack-pattern analysis of the AI targets and no hardening advice. The release of findings by researchers turned away from the contest was reported by Hackread before the contest as the researchers' own action, not ZDI's (Hackread, 2026-05-12). Vendors have 90 days to patch after the zero-days are disclosed at the contest (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-15), and the NV Container Toolkit researcher is Noam Trobishi (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-15).

entries.headline: Orange Tsai chained three Exchange bugs to SYSTEM code execution at Pwn2Own Berlin, separate from the exploited OWA flaw
entries.html:
ROUTINEupdatedNATOB2

Pwn2Own Berlin 2026: DEVCORE's Orange Tsai chains three Exchange bugs to code execution as SYSTEM, one reported to be CVE-2026-62911

On Day Two of Pwn2Own Berlin 2026, "Orange Tsai (@orange_8361) of DEVCORE Research Team chained 3 bugs to achieve Remote Code Execution as SYSTEM on Microsoft Exchange, earning $200,000 and 20 Master of Pwn points" (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-15). BleepingComputer reported the same result (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-15). The bugs were zero-days disclosed to Microsoft at the contest, which gives vendors 90 days to patch (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-15); neither source says whether the chain needs authentication. CVE-2026-42897, the exploited Outlook Web Access cross-site scripting flaw, had already been disclosed by Microsoft (Microsoft Security Response Center), so it is not one of the contest's zero-days.

Contradiction: for CVE-2026-62911, Microsoft describes an authorized attacker (CVSS 8.0) (MSRC CVE-2026-62911), while Franky's Web says the attacker does not need valid credentials (Franky's Web, 2026-08-27) and MB VRED titles its analysis a "Pre-Auth RCE" (MB VRED, 2026-08-13).

Defender takeaway
Franky's Web identifies one of the chain's bugs as CVE-2026-62911 and reports working public exploit code since late August (Franky's Web, 2026-08-27), and a public analysis of the demo makes the same link (MB VRED, 2026-08-13). Microsoft fixed CVE-2026-62911 in the August 2026 Exchange update (Exchange Server SE RTM build 15.02.2562.046, 2019 CU15 build 15.02.1748.049, 2019 CU14 build 15.02.1544.044, 2016 CU23 build 15.01.2507.072), credits Orange Tsai working with ZDI and describes an authorized attacker (CVSS 8.0) (MSRC CVE-2026-62911); on-premises Exchange below those builds is exposed, and the update is the fix.
Correction11 Oct 2026 14:37 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummarytagsregionssectorscvestechniquesaffected_productssourcesevidencesourcing_notereferencesclassificationactionsbodypriority

ZDI describes the result as remote code execution as SYSTEM on Microsoft Exchange through three chained bugs (Zero Day Initiative, 2026-05-15); neither ZDI nor BleepingComputer says the chain works without authentication, and the earlier quotation was not ZDI's wording. The chain is not CVE-2026-42897, which was a separate, exploited cross-site scripting flaw in Outlook Web Access (Microsoft Security Response Center). The priority moves from notable to routine: the contest result itself leaves nothing to apply beyond keeping Exchange current as Microsoft's fixes ship. CVE-2026-62911 was fixed in the August 2026 Exchange security update (MSRC CVE-2026-62911), and Franky's Web reports that Orange Tsai demonstrated it at Pwn2Own Berlin 2026 as part of this chain, and that working exploit code surfaced in late August (Franky's Web, 2026-08-27).

Improvement21 Oct 2026 15:50 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1149Z-auditbodyevidenceheadlinesourcessummarytitle

Microsoft's record for CVE-2026-62911 lists the August 2026 fixed builds, credits "Orange Tsai (@orange_8361) of DEVCORE Research Team working with TrendAI Zero Day Initiative" and describes "an authorized attacker", but does not mention Pwn2Own (MSRC CVE-2026-62911). The identification of CVE-2026-62911 as one of the contest chain's three bugs comes from Franky's Web (Franky's Web, 2026-08-27) and a public analysis of the demo (MB VRED, 2026-08-13); neither ZDI nor Microsoft states it. Franky's Web says the attacker does not need valid credentials, which disagrees with Microsoft's description of an authorized attacker (Franky's Web, 2026-08-27).

NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Kaspersky: Kimsuky adds Rust-based HelloDoor and httpMalice to its PebbleDash toolkit and takes over hosts through VSCode tunnels and DWAgent

Kaspersky's report covers Kimsuky (also APT43, Ruby Sleet) campaigns whose droppers it detected between August 2025 and February 2026: spear-phishing emails deliver compressed attachments disguised as documents, with lure names carrying a document extension before .jse or .pif (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-14). JSE droppers decode at least two Base64 blobs with JScript into a location such as C:\ProgramData, open the lure, then decode the payload a second time with certutil from a hidden PowerShell window and run it through regsvr32 or rundll32, while the SCR and PIF droppers decrypt theirs with XOR (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-14). HelloDoor, a Rust DLL backdoor first seen in August 2025 that Kaspersky judges early-stage, persists through an HKCU Run value that launches regsvr32 and talks to a C2 hosted through TryCloudflare, which makes the infrastructure behind it hard to trace; httpMalice (version 1.9 over HTTP or HTTPS, version 1.8 over the Dropbox API) persists as a service when elevated and through an HKCU Run value otherwise, profiles the host, captures the screen, uploads archived directories and encrypts its traffic with ChaCha20 (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-14). MemLoad runs anti-VM checks and reconnaissance, persists through scheduled tasks that run regsvr32 on its DLL every minute, and reflectively loads the RC4-encrypted httpTroy backdoor in memory for long-term access and exfiltration; the AppleSeed Spy variant collects documents, screenshots, keystrokes and the GPKI certificate directory (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-14).

For post-exploitation the group downloads the legitimate VSCode CLI, unpacks it into C:\Users\Public and runs code.exe tunnel, completing the GitHub device-code authorization with its own account so the host then talks to Microsoft-owned servers, or installs DWAgent from C:\ProgramData with a configuration linked to its own account; it also tunnels through Ngrok, and some samples are signed with certificates stolen from South Korean organizations (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-14). Targets are mainly South Korean public and private entities, and PebbleDash victims also include Brazilian defense organizations and a German defense firm (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-14).

Exposure
South Korean government bodies, AppleSeed's most frequent target, and defense, military and medical organizations, PebbleDash's focus, including defense firms abroad as in Brazil and Germany (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-14).
Detection
In process-creation telemetry, a script host running a .jse attachment that spawns a hidden PowerShell calling certutil to decode a file, followed by regsvr32 /s or rundll32 on a file in C:\ProgramData or the temp folder; in persistence artifacts, HKCU Run values or per-minute scheduled tasks named after browser checks that run regsvr32 on a DLL, and a new service whose command runs rundll32 (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-14). For the tunnel path, code.exe running a tunnel from C:\Users\Public after a GitHub device-code login, and DWAgent services installed from C:\ProgramData by a dropper (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-14).

Triage: VSCode Remote Tunnels and DWAgent are legitimate remote-access tools; in Kimsuky's use the VSCode CLI is unpacked into C:\Users\Public and started by a script dropper or installer rather than by the user, and DWAgent arrives with a preset configuration from a dropper that unpacks it into C:\ProgramData (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-14).

Defender takeaway
Where VSCode Remote Tunnels and DWAgent are not sanctioned, alert on tunnel creation and on DWAgent service installs, because both give the attacker access that bypasses detection built for malware C2 channels (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-14). Organizations in Kimsuky's target set should hunt for the dropper chain and the tunnel path described above.
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:28 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditactionsaffected_productsbodyclassificationentitiesevidenceheadlineregionssourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

httpMalice is not an HTTP-only loader but a PebbleDash-based backdoor that talks over HTTP or HTTPS in version 1.9 and through the Dropbox API in version 1.8, MemLoad is the loader that runs anti-VM checks and reconnaissance before reflectively loading httpTroy, and httpTroy is the backdoor for long-term access and data exfiltration (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-14). The report gives observations rather than detection guidance, so detection follows the dropper, persistence and tunnel artifacts it documents (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-14). HelloDoor is judged early-stage, and its TryCloudflare-hosted C2 makes its infrastructure difficult to trace; Kimsuky also tunnels through VSCode Tunneling and Ngrok (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-14). Targets are mainly South Korean, AppleSeed most often government bodies and PebbleDash the defense, military and medical sectors, and PebbleDash victims also include Brazilian defense organizations and a German defense firm over several years (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-14).

entries.headline: DHTMLX PDF Export Module before 0.7.6 executes attacker JavaScript sent to it without authentication (CVE-2026-41553)
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-41553 +2updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-41553: DHTMLX PDF Export Module executes JavaScript injected into its data parameter without authentication (CVSS 4.0 10.0), with two file-read flaws (CVE-2026-41552, CVE-2026-7182)

CERT Polska coordinated the disclosure of three vulnerabilities in DHTMLX software on 2026-05-15, reported by Łukasz Jaworski and Tomasz Holeksa of Pentest Limited (CERT Polska, 2026-05-15). In CVE-2026-41553 the PDF Export Module used by DHTMLX Gantt and Scheduler does not sanitize its data parameter, so an unauthenticated attacker can inject JavaScript that Node.js processes and executes, which can lead to server compromise; CVE-2026-41552 in the same module and CVE-2026-7182 in Diagram's export module (through the src attribute) lack HTML sanitization, so a crafted payload can include local files from the server in the generated PDF (CERT Polska, 2026-05-15). ENISA's EUVD carries CERT-PL's CVSS 4.0 scores of 10.0 for CVE-2026-41553 and 9.2 for each file-read flaw, all with a network vector, no privileges and no user interaction (ENISA EUVD-2026-30537; ENISA EUVD-2026-30538; ENISA EUVD-2026-30539). PDF Export Module version 0.7.6 fixes CVE-2026-41552 and CVE-2026-41553 and Diagram version 1.1.1 fixes CVE-2026-7182 (CERT Polska, 2026-05-15), and EUVD lists the module from 0.3.3 and Diagram from 1.0.0 as affected below those releases (ENISA EUVD-2026-30537; ENISA EUVD-2026-30539); DHTMLX's changelog for release 0.7.6 records fixed remote code execution and file read vulnerabilities (DHTMLX PDF Export Module changelog). No source reports exploitation.

Exposure
Self-hosted DHTMLX PDF Export Module services from release 0.3.3 and earlier than 0.7.6 that back Gantt or Scheduler exports, and Diagram export modules from 1.0.0 and earlier than 1.1.1, wherever an attacker can send requests to the export service (CERT Polska, 2026-05-15; ENISA EUVD-2026-30537; ENISA EUVD-2026-30539).
Detection
In process telemetry on the export host, the Node.js export service spawning shells or other child processes, and in its request logs, export requests whose data parameter carries script rather than chart data (CERT Polska, 2026-05-15). A service that ran exposed before 0.7.6 needs a compromise check after the upgrade, since anything an attacker ran or left on the host survives it.
Defender takeaway
Upgrade the PDF Export Module to version 0.7.6 or later and Diagram to 1.1.1 or later (CERT Polska, 2026-05-15). Organizations that do not self-host DHTMLX export services have no decision to make.
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:25 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditactionsaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevidenceheadlinepriorityregionssectorssourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitle

CERT Polska's advisory names the vendor, the products and the affected ranges and says nothing about where DHTMLX components are deployed, so the claim that they are widely embedded in EU e-government, healthcare scheduling and municipal planning tools has no source (CERT Polska, 2026-05-15). The disclosure covers the PDF Export Module used by DHTMLX Gantt and Scheduler and the export module of DHTMLX Diagram, not the scheduling and diagram libraries as a whole (CERT Polska, 2026-05-15). CVE-2026-41552 and CVE-2026-7182 are path-traversal flaws that let crafted HTML include local server files in the generated PDF rather than code execution, with CVSS 4.0 scores of 9.2 (ENISA EUVD-2026-30538; ENISA EUVD-2026-30539). The PDF Export Module is affected from release 0.3.3 and fixed in 0.7.6, and Diagram from 1.0.0 and fixed in 1.1.1 (ENISA EUVD-2026-30537; CERT Polska, 2026-05-15).

entries.headline: F5 BIG-IP: iControl REST flaw lets a Manager-role account run commands and escape Appliance mode (CVE-2026-41225)
entries.html:
ROUTINECVE-2026-41225updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-41225: F5 BIG-IP iControl REST lets an authenticated Manager-role account run arbitrary commands and bypass Appliance mode (May 2026 quarterly)

F5 announced on 2026-05-13 the fixes in its quarterly security notification (F5 K000160932; SecurityWeek, 2026-05-14), among them CVE-2026-41225 in BIG-IP iControl REST: an authenticated attacker with at least the Manager role can create configuration objects that allow running arbitrary commands (ENISA EUVD-2026-29986). F5 says the flaw lets a highly privileged attacker with network access to the iControl REST endpoint through the BIG-IP management port or self IP addresses escalate privileges or bypass Appliance mode restrictions, crossing a security boundary in Appliance mode deployments, and that there is no data-plane exposure (SecurityWeek, 2026-05-14). F5 scores it CVSS 4.0 8.6 (ENISA EUVD-2026-29986; SecurityWeek, 2026-05-14), and NCSC-NL lists a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.1 with a changed scope (NCSC-NL NCSC-2026-0162, 2026-05-15). Affected are BIG-IP 21.0.0 before version 21.0.0.2, 17.5.0 before version 17.5.1.6 and 17.1.0 before version 17.1.3.2, with the 16.1 branch listed as affected and, being past end of technical support, not evaluated (ENISA EUVD-2026-29986). SecurityWeek counts over 19 high-severity and 32 medium-severity fixes across BIG-IP, BIG-IQ and NGINX in the same notification, none of them exploited in the wild as of 2026-05-14 (SecurityWeek, 2026-05-14), and NCSC-NL's advisory lists 43 CVEs for BIG-IP and BIG-IQ (NCSC-NL NCSC-2026-0162, 2026-05-15).

Exposure
BIG-IP systems on the affected branches whose iControl REST endpoint is reachable through the management port or a self IP address by an account holding the Manager role or higher (ENISA EUVD-2026-29986; SecurityWeek, 2026-05-14); Appliance mode deployments lose the boundary that mode is meant to enforce (SecurityWeek, 2026-05-14).
Detection
In the BIG-IP control-plane audit log, configuration objects created through iControl REST by Manager-role accounts, especially from source addresses outside the management network or outside change windows, since creating such objects is how the flaw runs commands (ENISA EUVD-2026-29986).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade BIG-IP to version 21.0.0.2, 17.5.1.6 or 17.1.3.2 in the regular cycle, earlier where Appliance mode is the control that keeps administrators out of the shell or where iControl REST is reachable beyond the management network (SecurityWeek, 2026-05-14; ENISA EUVD-2026-29986); the 16.1 branch has no fix listed and needs a supported release (ENISA EUVD-2026-29986).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:23 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditactionsaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevent_dateevidenceheadlineprioritysectorssourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitleverification

CVE-2026-41225 is listed for BIG-IP only, in 21.0.0 before version 21.0.0.2, 17.5.0 before version 17.5.1.6 and 17.1.0 before version 17.1.3.2, with the 16.1 branch past end of technical support and not evaluated (ENISA EUVD-2026-29986); F5 published it on 2026-05-13 (SecurityWeek, 2026-05-14). The prerequisite is an authenticated account with at least the Manager role and network access to iControl REST through the management port or a self IP address, and F5 says there is no data-plane exposure (SecurityWeek, 2026-05-14); no source describes a credential-theft chain, a European public-sector deployment base or monitoring guidance. The secondary list of CVE ids grouped by flaw class did not match NCSC-NL's advisory, which gives the cleartext SSH-password exposure and the SNMP-object privilege escalation as separate flaws with their own ids (NCSC-NL NCSC-2026-0162, 2026-05-15). F5's own score is CVSS 4.0 8.6 (ENISA EUVD-2026-29986); the 9.1 comes from NCSC-NL as a CVSS 3.1 score with a changed scope (NCSC-NL NCSC-2026-0162, 2026-05-15).

F5 scores it CVSS 4.0 8.6 and calls it a control-plane issue only; fixed versions are 21.0.0.2, 17.5.1.6 and 17.1.3.2, the 16.1 branch is past end of technical support, and no exploitation was reported as of 2026-05-14.

entries.headline: Funnel Builder for WooCommerce flaw let attackers plant fake Google Tag Manager card skimmers on every checkout page
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-47100exploitedupdatedNATOB2

FunnelKit Funnel Builder for WooCommerce: unauthenticated settings write (CVE-2026-47100) exploited to plant card skimmers on checkout pages, fixed in version 3.15.0.3

Sansec reported on 2026-05-14 that it was tracking active attacks against Funnel Builder by FunnelKit, a checkout and upsell plugin used on 40,000+ WooCommerce stores, in which all versions before 3.15.0.3 let unauthenticated attackers inject arbitrary JavaScript into every checkout page (Sansec, 2026-05-14). The plugin's public checkout endpoint lets a request pick which internal method to run without checking the caller's permissions or restricting the methods, so an unauthenticated request can reach the method that writes the plugin's global settings, and whatever sits in the External Scripts setting is printed onto every Funnel Builder checkout page (Sansec, 2026-05-14). In at least one case Sansec found a payload posing as a Google Tag Manager loader beside the store's legitimate marketing tags: at page load it decodes a base64 string and loads that external script, which opens a WebSocket to the attacker's server and receives a skimmer tailored to the store that steals card numbers, CVVs, billing addresses and other personal details at checkout (Sansec, 2026-05-14). The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-47100 and rated 8.7 in CVSS 4.0 (Sansec, 2026-05-14; ENISA EUVD-2026-30936).

FunnelKit shipped version 3.15.0.3 on 2026-05-14 (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-15), released the fix within 36 hours of the first report, pushed it to older release branches through WordPress.org so many stores updated without manual action, and DNS-blocked the attacker domains it knew (Sansec, 2026-05-14). In a statement added to The Hacker News report on 2026-05-31, FunnelKit said the exploitation path had been closed and that of more than 1,300 sites it monitored in the nine days after disclosure, three showed signs of compromise before its mitigations took effect (The Hacker News, 2026-05-16).

Exposure
WooCommerce stores running Funnel Builder before version 3.15.0.3 that did not take the update; stores on 3.15.0.3 or later, including those updated automatically through WordPress.org, are not vulnerable (The Hacker News, 2026-05-16).
Detection
In the plugin's Settings > Checkout > External Scripts, entries the store did not add (Sansec, 2026-05-14); in browser-side telemetry of checkout pages, scripts loaded from unfamiliar hosts and WebSocket connections to them (Sansec, 2026-05-14). Updating does not remove a planted script, which is why FunnelKit asks customers to review that setting and remove anything unfamiliar after updating (Sansec, 2026-05-14).

Triage: Sansec calls skimmers dressed as analytics tags a recurring Magecart pattern, because reviewers skip familiar tracking code; the planted loader names Google Analytics but at page load decodes a base64 string and loads its script from another host (Sansec, 2026-05-14).

Defender takeaway
Confirm that every WooCommerce store with Funnel Builder runs version 3.15.0.3 or later and clean its External Scripts setting as FunnelKit advises (Sansec, 2026-05-14). Stores without Funnel Builder have no decision to make.
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:26 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditactionsaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevent_dateevidenceheadlineprioritysectorssourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitle

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-47100 and rated 8.7 in CVSS 4.0 (Sansec, 2026-05-14; ENISA EUVD-2026-30936). The 40,000+ figure is the number of stores using the plugin, not of exploited stores: Sansec found the fake Google Tag Manager loader in at least one case (Sansec, 2026-05-14), and FunnelKit said in a statement added to The Hacker News report on 2026-05-31 that of more than 1,300 sites it monitored in the nine days after disclosure, three showed signs of compromise before its mitigations took effect, and that the exploitation path had been closed after the fix was pushed to older branches through WordPress.org automatic updates (The Hacker News, 2026-05-16). The skimmer is tailored to each store and streamed over a WebSocket that the loader opens in the shopper's browser; no source describes WebSocket connections from the WordPress PHP process or exposure of Swiss or EU public portals, and the check FunnelKit advises is a review of the plugin's External Scripts setting (Sansec, 2026-05-14).

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-47100 (CVSS 4.0 8.7); FunnelKit pushed the fix to older branches through WordPress.org automatic updates, saw signs of compromise on 3 of more than 1,300 sites it monitored, and said the exploitation path was closed.

Sansec describes the endpoint as a public checkout endpoint without capability checks or a method allow-list, and gives no basis for a per-victim polymorphic skimmer, PHP-process WebSocket connections or exposure of Swiss and EU public portals.

entries.headline: SzafirHost before 1.2.1 can load a malicious class from a JAR that passes its signature check (CVE-2026-44088)
entries.html:
ROUTINECVE-2026-44088updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-44088: SzafirHost, KIR's qualified e-signature helper, verifies a JAR's signature and loads its classes from different parts of the file (fixed in 1.2.1)

CERT Polska coordinated the disclosure of CVE-2026-44088 in SzafirHost from Krajowa Izba Rozliczeniowa (KIR) on 2026-05-15: SzafirHost verifies the signature of a downloaded JAR file with JarInputStream, which reads from the beginning of the file, but loads classes with JarFile/URLClassLoader, which reads the ZIP Central Directory from the end (CERT Polska, 2026-05-15). An attacker who combines a genuine signed JAR with a malicious ZIP file therefore passes verification while the malicious class is loaded, which CERT Polska says can lead to remote code execution; all versions before 1.2.1 are affected and version 1.2.1 fixes the flaw (CERT Polska, 2026-05-15). ENISA's EUVD carries CERT-PL's CVSS 4.0 base score of 8.6, with a network attack vector, no privileges and active user interaction (ENISA EUVD-2026-30512). SzafirHost is the application that, with KIR's browser plugin and Java, signs documents and tax declarations with a qualified signature; accounting software prompts users to install the plugin and SzafirHost at the first signing attempt (wFirma help centre). CERT Polska does not say how a malicious JAR would reach SzafirHost, and no source reports exploitation.

Exposure
Workstations that sign with KIR Szafir qualified certificates through SzafirHost earlier than version 1.2.1 (CERT Polska, 2026-05-15; wFirma help centre).
Defender takeaway
Update SzafirHost to version 1.2.1 or later on every workstation that signs with Szafir certificates (CERT Polska, 2026-05-15). Swiss bodies are not drawn in through signature recognition: without a mutual recognition agreement between Switzerland and the EU, a foreign qualified signature is not equivalent to a qualified signature under Swiss law (BAKOM), so only organizations that sign within Poland's qualified-signature ecosystem have a decision to make.
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:21 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditactionsaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevidenceheadlineprioritysectorssourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitleverification

Switzerland does not recognise Polish qualified signatures under an eIDAS-equivalent framework: no mutual recognition agreement exists between Switzerland and the EU, and without one a foreign qualified signature is not equivalent to a qualified signature under Swiss law (BAKOM). CERT Polska states the impact as remote code execution from combining a genuine signed JAR with a malicious ZIP, in all SzafirHost versions before 1.2.1 (CERT Polska, 2026-05-15); it describes no attack on the download path, no silent signing of fraudulent documents and no list of public-sector workflows that depend on the helper. The CVSS 4.0 base score of 8.6 is CERT-PL's as the numbering authority, carried by ENISA's EUVD (ENISA EUVD-2026-30512).

threat17 May 05:00Zsingle-source · national CERTOpen finding →
Sources: CERT Polska · ENISA EUVD (EUVD-2026-30512) · wFirma · BAKOM

SzafirHost verifies a downloaded JAR's signature by reading from the start of the file but loads classes from the ZIP Central Directory at the end, so a genuine signed JAR combined with a malicious ZIP passes verification while the malicious class loads, which can lead to remote code execution; all versions before 1.2.1 are affected and 1.2.1 fixes it.

The CVSS 4.0 score of 8.6 is CERT-PL's as carried by ENISA's EUVD.

entries.headline: SentinelOne: attackers turn build servers, CI/CD runners and developer workstations into the intrusion path
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2023-42793exploitedupdatedNATOB2

SentinelOne "Living Off the Pipeline": attackers subverted TeamCity, GitLab automation, self-hosted runners and developer workstations in 2025

SentinelOne's post of 2026-05-15 describes how attackers in 2025 went after the infrastructure that builds and ships software, not only its dependencies (SentinelOne, 2026-05-15). In one case attackers exploited a vulnerable self-hosted TeamCity server (the post links JetBrains' advisory for CVE-2023-42793), created a benign-looking build configuration that a trusted build agent ran with SYSTEM privileges, deployed a backdoor into internal environments and stayed undetected for more than a year (SentinelOne, 2026-05-15). JetBrains fixed CVE-2023-42793, an unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaw, in TeamCity On-Premises 2023.05.4 (JetBrains, 2023-09-21) and warned that backdoors planted before the patch persist after it (JetBrains, 2023-10-18). In an intrusion from SentinelOne's annual threat report, a compromised GitLab service-account token was used to create projects with malicious Ansible playbooks that the organization's pipeline then executed automatically (SentinelOne, 2026-05-15).

The post's other examples target people and runners: Contagious Interview sent developers in cryptocurrency and blockchain fraudulent job offers leading to fake skill-assessment sites, where a fabricated error told them to run commands that silently installed malware with access to their SSH keys, tokens and credentials, and the Sha1-Hulud campaign registered infected systems as self-hosted GitHub runners under attacker-defined names and used workflows that ran code when someone commented in a repository discussion (SentinelOne, 2026-05-15). Malicious versions of popular build packages ran reconnaissance scripts during installation that harvested tokens and inspected environments, and phished maintainer accounts appended malicious code to legitimate package updates (SentinelOne, 2026-05-15).

Exposure
Organizations running self-hosted build servers and runners, which SentinelOne notes are often granted broad access to repositories, secrets and deployment workflows (SentinelOne, 2026-05-15); TeamCity On-Premises servers before 2023.05.4 are exposed to CVE-2023-42793 (JetBrains, 2023-09-21).
Detection
In CI/CD platform audit logs, new runner registrations and unusual runner names, new or modified pipelines created by service accounts, jobs touching unfamiliar repositories and workflows that open network tunnels; on the build runners themselves, process and credential-access telemetry for suspicious child processes, credential access attempts, reverse tunnels and persistence (SentinelOne, 2026-05-15).

Triage: compiling, downloading packages, invoking scripts and opening connections are normal build activity, so a malicious job under a valid service account on a trusted runner looks legitimate unless the account acts outside its role; SentinelOne's discriminators are who created the job, what changed, where the runner was registered and which secrets were accessed (SentinelOne, 2026-05-15).

Defender takeaway
Treat build servers and runners as high-value systems and alert on runner registrations and pipeline changes made by service accounts (SentinelOne, 2026-05-15). A TeamCity server patched to 2023.05.4 after early October 2023 still needs a compromise assessment of the server and its build agents, because JetBrains says backdoors planted earlier are likely to persist after the patch (JetBrains, 2023-10-18).
Correction21 Oct 2026 16:09 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationconfidencecvesevidenceheadlinesectorssourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

The monitoring priorities SentinelOne gives are new runner registrations and unusual runner names, new or modified pipelines created by service accounts, jobs interacting with unfamiliar repositories, workflows that establish network tunnels, and suspicious child processes, credential access attempts, reverse tunnels and persistence on build runners (SentinelOne, 2026-05-15); the post names no audit-event type, source-address criterion or specific binaries. It walks through examples rather than a three-case taxonomy, and the rogue self-hosted runners and discussion-comment workflow triggers belong to the Sha1-Hulud campaign (SentinelOne, 2026-05-15). The TeamCity case links CVE-2023-42793, an unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaw fixed in TeamCity On-Premises 2023.05.4 (JetBrains, 2023-09-21); JetBrains warns that backdoors planted before patching are likely to persist after it, so a server patched after early October 2023 needs a compromise assessment (JetBrains, 2023-10-18).

entries.headline: Unit 42: evolved Gremlin stealer hides its payload in .NET resources and hijacks live Chromium browser sessions
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Unit 42: Gremlin stealer hides its payload in XOR-encoded .NET resources and adds a crypto clipper, Discord token theft and WebSocket session hijacking

Unit 42 identified a new Gremlin stealer variant that bundles stolen browser cookies, session tokens, clipboard contents, cryptocurrency wallet data and FTP and VPN credentials into a ZIP archive named with the victim's public IP address and uploads it to an attacker-controlled site, while exfiltration through private web panels or the Telegram Bot API stays as in earlier builds (Unit 42, 2026-05-15). The variant moves its payload into the .NET resource section masked with single-byte XOR encoding, decrypts and maps each critical function into memory only when needed, and hides its strings behind a runtime decoder that reads them from an embedded encrypted resource; one sample is wrapped in a commercial packer that turns the code into custom bytecode run by a private virtual machine (Unit 42, 2026-05-15). New modules extract Discord tokens by scanning multiple paths with regex validation, watch the clipboard for wallet-address patterns and replace the victim's address with the attacker's in real time, and hijack live sessions in Chromium-based browsers over WebSocket by requesting the data directly from the running browser process, which bypasses modern cookie protections (Unit 42, 2026-05-15). The post does not describe how Gremlin is delivered.

Exposure
Endpoints with Chromium-based browsers; Gremlin targets web browsers, the clipboard and local storage for payment card details, cookies, session tokens, cryptocurrency wallet data and FTP and VPN credentials (Unit 42, 2026-05-15).
Detection
In egress telemetry, a ZIP archive named after the host's public IP address uploaded to an unfamiliar web panel, and Telegram Bot API traffic from a process that is not a messaging client; in endpoint telemetry, a process requesting session data from a running Chromium browser process, and a process that rewrites clipboard contents matching wallet-address patterns (Unit 42, 2026-05-15). Signatures on strings and exports miss current builds, because the strings and functions only appear decrypted at runtime (Unit 42, 2026-05-15).
Defender takeaway
Replace detections tuned to legacy Gremlin samples, whose function exports and internal symbols were left intact, with behavioral ones (Unit 42, 2026-05-15). On an infected host, revoke its browser sessions and rotate the Discord, FTP and VPN credentials it held, since hijacked sessions and stolen credentials stay usable after the malware is removed.
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:19 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

The analyzed variant bundles its haul into a ZIP archive named with the victim's public IP address and uploads it to an attacker-controlled site, with private web panels or the Telegram Bot API as the exfiltration methods carried over from earlier builds; Unit 42 does not describe an HTTPS POST with Telegram as a secondary channel (Unit 42, 2026-05-15). The clipper replaces any copied address matching its cryptocurrency wallet patterns, not only Bitcoin and Ethereum addresses, and saved passwords are not among the data Unit 42 lists (Unit 42, 2026-05-15). The session-hijack module works by requesting the data directly from the running Chromium-based browser process over WebSocket, and one sample is protected by a commercial packer that runs the code as custom bytecode on a private virtual machine (Unit 42, 2026-05-15).

Sources: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42

New modules steal Discord tokens, swap copied cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker's in real time and hijack live Chromium-based browser sessions over WebSocket; stolen data leaves as a ZIP uploaded to an attacker-controlled web panel, with the Telegram Bot API as an alternative channel.

entries.headline: AMD Zen 2 op-cache flaw lets local code escalate privilege, guest to host included; Ryzen needs OEM BIOS updates
entries.html:
ROUTINECVE-2025-54518updatedNATOA2

AMD-SB-7052 / CVE-2025-54518: AMD Zen 2 op-cache corruption lets local code run instructions at a higher privilege, guest to host included (CVSS 7.3); OS updates on EPYC 7002, OEM BIOS updates on Ryzen

AMD disclosed on 2026-05-12 that improper isolation of shared resources in the CPU operation cache of Zen 2-based products can cause incorrect instructions to execute at a higher privilege level; it scores CVE-2025-54518 at 7.3 on CVSS 4.0, with local access, high attack complexity and low privileges, and found it internally (AMD Product Security, 2026-05-12). Xen says code of any privilege could escalate, including userspace to kernel and guest to host, that only AMD Fam17h (Zen 2) CPUs are believed vulnerable, that all Xen versions are affected and that there is no mitigation other than its patches (Xen Project, 2026-05-12). Microsoft lists the flaw as not exploited or publicly disclosed and rates it Exploitation Unlikely, and says the latest Windows builds enable the mitigation (MSRC, CVE-2025-54518).

The fix depends on the product line: for EPYC 7002 and EPYC Embedded 7002 processors AMD's mitigation is an OS update from the OS vendor, while for Ryzen 3000, 4000, 5000, 7020 and 7030 series, Threadripper PRO 3000 WX and Ryzen Embedded V2000 AMD released Platform Initialization firmware to OEMs between October and December 2025, to be installed as an OEM BIOS update, for example ComboAM4v2 PI version 1.2.0.10 for Ryzen 3000, 4000 and 5000 desktop parts (AMD Product Security, 2026-05-12). NCSC-NL lists updates from Debian (Xen), Dell PowerEdge, Fedora, Google Cloud Platform, Lenovo and Microsoft Windows (NCSC-NL, 2026-05-15).

Exposure
Any Zen 2-based system, with the most at stake where less-trusted code shares the processor with more-privileged code, as on virtualisation hosts, since guest-to-host escalation is possible (Xen Project, 2026-05-12); the processor model tells which channel fixes it, an OS update on EPYC 7002 and a BIOS at or above AMD's listed PI version on Ryzen, Threadripper PRO and Ryzen Embedded parts (AMD Product Security, 2026-05-12).
Defender takeaway
Patch in the regular cycle, Zen 2 hypervisor and multi-tenant hosts first: AMD lists OEM BIOS updates carrying its platform-initialization versions for Ryzen-class parts (AMD Product Security, 2026-05-12), Microsoft says the mitigation for certain AMD processor models requires a Windows update (MSRC, CVE-2025-54518), and Xen hosts need the XSA-490 patch (Xen Project, 2026-05-12).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:38 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditactionsaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevent_dateevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitlepriority

The mitigation does not ship as microcode in a Windows update for every affected chip: AMD lists an OS update only for EPYC 7002 and EPYC Embedded 7002 processors, and for Ryzen 3000 to 7030 series, Threadripper PRO 3000 WX and Ryzen Embedded V2000 it recommends the Platform Initialization versions in its table, delivered as OEM BIOS updates (AMD Product Security, 2026-05-12). Microsoft says the latest Windows builds enable the mitigation, not that they carry it for all processors (MSRC, CVE-2025-54518), so a Windows build check cannot confirm a Ryzen host is protected, and a processor-ID query reports the CPU model rather than whether the mitigation is in place.

NCSC-NL lists Fedora and Lenovo among the vendors with updates (NCSC-NL, 2026-05-15).

AMD's mitigation for EPYC 7002 and EPYC Embedded 7002 is an OS update, and Microsoft says the latest Windows builds enable a mitigation for the affected AMD models without naming them, while Ryzen, Threadripper PRO and Ryzen Embedded V2000 parts need OEM BIOS updates carrying the Platform Initialization versions AMD lists. entries.headline: OpenClaw "Claw Chain": code running in the agent sandbox can expose secrets, take owner control and plant backdoors
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-44112 +3updatedNATOA2

OpenClaw "Claw Chain": four chainable sandbox, exec-allowlist and MCP loopback flaws (CVE-2026-44112, CVE-2026-44113, CVE-2026-44115, CVE-2026-44118) fixed in release 2026.4.22

Cyera disclosed four vulnerabilities in OpenClaw, an open-source platform for autonomous AI agents originally launched as Clawdbot in late 2025, on 2026-05-15 after reporting them to the maintainers in April (Cyera, 2026-05-15). OpenClaw's advisories of 2026-04-23 list the openclaw npm package up to release 2026.4.21 as affected and 2026.4.22 as fixed for all four (OpenClaw GHSA-wppj-c6mr-83jj, 2026-04-23; OpenClaw GHSA-5h3g-6xhh-rg6p, 2026-04-23; OpenClaw GHSA-x3h8-jrgh-p8jx, 2026-04-23; OpenClaw GHSA-r6xh-pqhr-v4xh, 2026-04-23). CVE-2026-44112 and CVE-2026-44113 are time-of-check/time-of-use races in the OpenShell sandbox's filesystem bridge, where a symlink swap redirects a write outside the intended mount root or makes a read return bytes from outside it (OpenClaw GHSA-wppj-c6mr-83jj, 2026-04-23; OpenClaw GHSA-5h3g-6xhh-rg6p, 2026-04-23). CVE-2026-44115 lets an allowlisted command hide shell expansion in an unquoted heredoc body, so the shell evaluates more than the approved command text shows, which Cyera says returns environment variables such as API keys and tokens (OpenClaw GHSA-x3h8-jrgh-p8jx, 2026-04-23; Cyera, 2026-05-15). CVE-2026-44118 sits on the loopback MCP path, which accepted spoofable owner-context metadata from request headers and so let a non-owner loopback client act as owner for owner-gated operations such as gateway configuration, cron scheduling and execution-environment management (OpenClaw GHSA-r6xh-pqhr-v4xh, 2026-04-23; Cyera, 2026-05-15).

Cyera's chain starts from code execution inside the OpenShell sandbox through a malicious plugin, prompt injection or compromised external input, uses the read escape and the heredoc flaw to expose credentials, secrets and files, the loopback flaw for owner-level control of the agent runtime, and the write escape to plant backdoors or change configuration; it says each step looks like normal agent behavior to traditional controls (Cyera, 2026-05-15). Cyera rates CVE-2026-44112 at CVSS 9.6 and CVE-2026-44115 at 8.8 (Cyera, 2026-05-15), VulnCheck scores them 8.4 and 8.7 in CVSS 4.0 (VulnCheck, CVE-2026-44112; VulnCheck, CVE-2026-44115), and OpenClaw's own advisory for the heredoc allowlist bypass rates it moderate (OpenClaw GHSA-x3h8-jrgh-p8jx, 2026-04-23). Cyera counts about 65,000 (Shodan) and about 180,000 (Zoomeye) publicly accessible OpenClaw instances as of May 2026 (Cyera, 2026-05-15). Neither Cyera nor the vendor advisories report exploitation.

Exposure
OpenClaw deployments running the openclaw npm package at release 2026.4.21 or earlier (OpenClaw GHSA-r6xh-pqhr-v4xh, 2026-04-23). The chain needs code execution inside the OpenShell sandbox first, so agents that install plugins or take prompts and other input from untrusted parties are in scope, and Cyera names deployments exposed to the internet without authentication or network controls in front of them as most at risk (Cyera, 2026-05-15).
Detection
In filesystem telemetry on the agent host, reads and writes by the sandbox process that resolve outside the sandbox mount root through a symlink swapped in after validation (OpenClaw GHSA-wppj-c6mr-83jj, 2026-04-23; OpenClaw GHSA-5h3g-6xhh-rg6p, 2026-04-23); in the agent's command-execution logs, approved commands carrying unquoted heredoc bodies with shell expansion (OpenClaw GHSA-x3h8-jrgh-p8jx, 2026-04-23); on the MCP loopback, owner-gated operations such as gateway or cron changes requested by a non-owner client (OpenClaw GHSA-r6xh-pqhr-v4xh, 2026-04-23; Cyera, 2026-05-15). Patching does not undo a compromise: Cyera says to assume any environment variable or credential reachable by OpenClaw processes may be compromised (Cyera, 2026-05-15), and configuration or files written outside the mount root survive the upgrade.
Defender takeaway
Upgrade every OpenClaw deployment to release 2026.4.22 or later, put internet-facing instances behind authentication or firewall controls, and rotate the API keys, tokens and bearer credentials its processes could reach (Cyera, 2026-05-15). Organizations without OpenClaw have no decision to make.
Correction21 Oct 2026 16:07 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditactionsaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevidenceheadlineprioritysourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

CVE-2026-44115 does not hide expansion tokens in environment-variable names: an allowlisted command containing an unquoted heredoc can hide shell expansion in the heredoc body, so the shell runs more than the approved text shows (OpenClaw GHSA-x3h8-jrgh-p8jx, 2026-04-23). Cyera reports about 65,000 instances on Shodan and about 180,000 on Zoomeye as two separate counts, not a combined 245,000, and its chain runs from a foothold inside the sandbox through the read escape and the heredoc flaw (credentials and files), then the loopback flaw (owner control), to the write escape (backdoors and persistence) (Cyera, 2026-05-15). The advisories list release 2026.4.21 and earlier as affected and 2026.4.22 as the fix for all four (OpenClaw GHSA-r6xh-pqhr-v4xh, 2026-04-23). The 9.6 for CVE-2026-44112 is Cyera's score; VulnCheck scores it 8.4 in CVSS 4.0 (VulnCheck, CVE-2026-44112), and OpenClaw's advisory for the heredoc bypass rates it moderate (OpenClaw GHSA-x3h8-jrgh-p8jx, 2026-04-23).

entries.summary: Cyera disclosed on 2026-05-15 four chainable flaws in the OpenClaw AI-agent platform: symlink races in the OpenShell sandbox file bridge that redirect writes (CVE-2026-44112) or reads (CVE-2026-44113) outside the mount root, shell expansion hidden in heredocs that slips past the exec allowlist (CVE-2026-44115), and a spoofable owner flag on the MCP loopback (CVE-2026-44118). From code execution inside the sandbox they let an attacker expose credentials, gain owner-level control of the agent runtime and persist; all four are fixed in openclaw release 2026.4.22.

entries.headline: Suspected Dream Market administrator "Speedstepper" arrested in Germany; US prosecutors allege he reactivated dormant wallets
entries.html:
ROUTINEupdatedNATOA2

Suspected Dream Market main administrator "Speedstepper" arrested in Germany; US indictment traces reactivated marketplace wallets and gold purchases

On 2026-05-07, in a coordinated effort by German and US law enforcement, Owe Martin Andresen, 49, was arrested in Germany on German charges, and his residence and two other locations were searched (US DEA, 2026-05-13). A US federal grand jury had indicted him on 2026-01-13 on six counts of international concealment money laundering and six counts of concealment money laundering, each carrying up to 20 years, and Germany has charged him with several counts of concealment money laundering, each punishable by up to five years (US DEA, 2026-05-13). The DOJ indictment, unsealed in the week The Record reported it, accuses him of being the main administrator of Dream Market, a darknet marketplace launched in 2013 that announced its shutdown in 2019 (The Record, 2026-05-13); the release calls him the suspected main administrator, the role whose holder used the moniker "Speedstepper" and was not identified in the earlier prosecutions (US DEA, 2026-05-13). The case is investigated by the IRS-CI Cyber Crimes Unit and the DEA Miami Counternarcotic Cyber Investigations Task Force with substantial assistance from the Bundeskriminalamt Cybercrime Unit and the Zentrale Kriminalinspektion Oldenburg; the FBI, USPIS and HSI were part of the task force that investigated the marketplace between 2016 and 2022, whose prosecutions convicted the administrators "Oxymonster" and "KITT3N" in the US and the mid-level administrator "GOWRON" in the UK (US DEA, 2026-05-13).

Prosecutors allege that in November and December 2022 Andresen moved funds from the marketplace's dormant commission wallets into new consolidated wallets, activity that could only have been initiated by someone holding Dream Market's original private keys, and that in August 2023 he used an Atlanta-based cryptocurrency service provider to buy gold bars that were shipped to his home address in Germany; in total he is alleged to have laundered over $2 million between August 2023 and April 2025 (US DEA, 2026-05-13). The US Attorney says the commissions came from selling illegal drugs, stolen personally identifiable information, counterfeit identification documents and other items (US DEA, 2026-05-13). US agencies had kept watching the marketplace's wallets after the shutdown and found them untouched until then (The Record, 2026-05-13). The searches located about $1.7 million of gold bars and over $23,000 in cash, along with information identifying bank accounts and cryptocurrency wallets holding about $1.2 million believed to be Dream Market proceeds (US DEA, 2026-05-13).

Defender takeaway
No change for enterprise defenders, since the sources describe the laundering of marketplace proceeds and no intrusion technique. For financial-crime and cryptocurrency-tracing teams the case shows that wallets left untouched for three years stayed under watch, and IRS-CI draws the lesson that "illicit actors may hide in the shadows, but their financial footprints remain" (US DEA, 2026-05-13).
Correction21 Oct 2026 16:04 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditbodyclassificationentitiesevent_dateevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytitlesectorstechniquespriority

The arrest on 2026-05-07 was a coordinated German and US effort on German charges rather than a BKA arrest: the case is investigated by the IRS-CI Cyber Crimes Unit and DEA Miami with substantial assistance from the Bundeskriminalamt Cybercrime Unit and the Zentrale Kriminalinspektion Oldenburg, while the FBI, USPIS and HSI belonged to the task force that investigated the marketplace from 2016 to 2022 (US DEA, 2026-05-13). Only the US indictment accuses Andresen of being the main administrator; the German charges are concealment money laundering (US DEA, 2026-05-13; The Record, 2026-05-13). The 2022 transfers went into new consolidated wallets, not a single wallet, and the searches located about $1.7 million of gold bars and over $23,000 in cash and identified bank accounts and wallets holding about $1.2 million, rather than seizing $1.2 million in cryptocurrency (US DEA, 2026-05-13). The marketplace commissions behind the laundering came, the US Attorney says, from selling illegal drugs, stolen personally identifiable information, counterfeit identification documents and other items (US DEA, 2026-05-13).
