entries.headline: node-ipc npm package backdoored, likely via an expired-domain maintainer takeover: three malicious versions steal developer and CI credentials on require()
entries.html:
HIGHupdatedNATOB1

node-ipc npm package backdoored, likely via an expired-domain account takeover: three malicious versions steal developer and CI credentials, flagged about three minutes after publication

On 2026-05-14, three malicious versions of the node-ipc npm package (9.1.6, 9.2.3 and 12.0.1) were published at the same time by a co-maintainer account with no prior publish history on the package (StepSecurity, 2026-05-14). The account's email domain had expired on 2025-01-10 and was re-registered on 2026-05-07, a week before the attack (The Hacker News, 2026-05-14). Socket assesses that the new domain owner could then trigger a standard npm password reset and gain publish rights without touching the maintainer's own infrastructure (Socket Security, 2026-05-14). CSO counts almost 700K weekly downloads and 424 dependent projects, while StepSecurity reports over 10 million weekly downloads (CSO Online, 2026-05-15 · StepSecurity, 2026-05-14). The 9.x releases are fabricated from the 12.x package structure, so projects on ^9, ~9.1.x, ~9.2.x, ^12 or ~12.0 ranges received a malicious build on their next install or lockfile refresh (StepSecurity, 2026-05-14). When StepSecurity published, npm's latest tag pointed to 12.0.1, so an unpinned npm install node-ipc pulled the compromised tarball (StepSecurity, 2026-05-14). As of 2026-10-21 the npm registry no longer lists 9.1.6, 9.2.3 or 12.0.1, and its latest tag points to 14.0.0 (npm registry, 2026-10-21).

The payload is an 80 KB obfuscated function appended to the CommonJS bundle node-ipc.cjs. It runs on every require('node-ipc') and uses no npm lifecycle hook, so tools that only scan preinstall and postinstall scripts miss it (StepSecurity, 2026-05-14). ESM-only consumers do not load the malicious file unless another dependency or a direct require loads node-ipc.cjs (Socket Security, 2026-05-14). The payload forks a detached child Node process that collects cloud provider credentials, SSH keys, Kubernetes tokens, GitHub CLI configuration, Terraform state, CI workflow files, .env files, shell history and macOS Keychain databases, gzips them and exfiltrates them (Socket Security, 2026-05-14 · StepSecurity, 2026-05-14). Four stacked obfuscation layers (string-array shuffling, control-flow flattening, dead-code injection and a custom reversed-nibble base-16 encoding) resist static analysis (StepSecurity, 2026-05-14). Socket found no persistence and no second-stage download, and its scanner flagged the publish within roughly three minutes (Socket Security, 2026-05-14).

Contradiction: the analyses disagree on payload details. StepSecurity and The Hacker News describe 90+ file-path patterns, an HTTPS POST channel alongside DNS TXT exfiltration, and a SHA-256 targeting gate that leaves 12.0.1 inert except on one targeted project (StepSecurity, 2026-05-14 · The Hacker News, 2026-05-14). Socket counts 113 macOS and 127 Linux patterns, says the payload uses DNS TXT queries and not HTTP, HTTPS or TLS for exfiltration, and finds the same malicious file in all three versions, with a hash gate that only changes what the module exports (Socket Security, 2026-05-14). Treat all three versions as active stealers.

Exposure
Any project whose lockfile, build cache or local npm cache holds 9.1.6, 9.2.3 or 12.0.1 and loads the package through CommonJS, directly or transitively (Socket Security, 2026-05-14).
Detection
The payload first resolves a lookalike Azure hostname through the public resolvers 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8, then sends DNS TXT queries straight to the attacker's server acting as a resolver, so the traffic never reaches corporate resolver logs (Socket Security, 2026-05-14 · StepSecurity, 2026-05-14). Look for DNS traffic from developer machines or CI runners to non-corporate resolvers and for large bursts of TXT queries: Socket estimates a 500 KiB archive produces about 29,400 of them (Socket Security, 2026-05-14). On endpoints, the payload shows as a Node process spawning a detached child Node process that runs node-ipc.cjs directly (Socket Security, 2026-05-14).
Defender takeaway
On any workstation or CI runner that loaded one of the three versions, remove it, reinstall a known clean version (9.2.1 or 12.0.0), and rotate every secret present on the host: SSH keys, npm, GitHub and GitLab tokens, cloud keys, and Kubernetes, Docker registry, Terraform and database credentials (Socket Security, 2026-05-14 · The Hacker News, 2026-05-14). Review dependencies by their entrypoints rather than only their install scripts, and prefer short-lived, scoped credentials in development and CI (Socket Security, 2026-05-14).
Correction30 Sep 2026 06:54 UTCrun 2026-09-30T0639Z-auditbodyclassificationtechniquesheadlinesummarytitle

As of 2026-09-30 no source said the malicious versions had been removed from the registry: when StepSecurity published, npm's latest tag pointed to the malicious 12.0.1 (StepSecurity, 2026-05-14). The payload fires on require() and uses no install hook, so disabling install scripts in CI does not stop it. Socket's advice is to review dependencies by their entrypoints and to rotate every secret on an affected host (Socket Security, 2026-05-14). Socket and StepSecurity disagree on the exfiltration channels, the pattern count and whether 12.0.1 is gated to one target (Socket Security, 2026-05-14 · StepSecurity, 2026-05-14), and all three versions should be treated as active. The entry previously named a domain registrar and Vue CLI and webpack tooling as dependents, which no cited source states.

Correction11 Oct 2026 14:00 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummarysourcesbody

Socket calls the expired recovery-email domain the likely vector and frames the mechanism conditionally, assuming the maintainer's npm recovery address was hosted on that domain (Socket Security, 2026-05-14); StepSecurity instead says the maintainer credentials were either freshly compromised or the account was added as a maintainer specifically for this publish (StepSecurity, 2026-05-14). How the account was taken over is therefore not established.

Improvement21 Oct 2026 08:19 UTCrun 2026-10-21T0800Z-auditsourcesbody

As of 2026-10-21 the npm registry no longer lists 9.1.6, 9.2.3 or 12.0.1, and its latest tag points to 14.0.0 (npm registry, 2026-10-21), so a fresh unpinned install no longer resolves to a malicious version; the exposure now lies with hosts, build caches and local npm caches that already hold one of the three.

entries.headline: GTIG: UNC6671 "BlackFile" vishing → AiTM → rogue-MFA → programmatic SharePoint exfiltration (1M+ files from one victim); DLS shutdown signals possible rebrand
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

GTIG: UNC6671 "BlackFile" vishing → AiTM → rogue-MFA → programmatic SharePoint exfiltration (1M+ files from one victim); DLS shutdown signals possible rebrand

Google Threat Intelligence Group published on 2026-05-15 an analysis of UNC6671, a financially motivated extortion cluster that adopted the "BlackFile" brand by February 2026 and has targeted dozens of organizations across North America, Australia and the UK (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15). Callers hired by the actor phone employees' personal mobile numbers, pose as internal IT or helpdesk staff citing a passkey migration or MFA update, and send the victim to a lookalike single sign-on portal on Tucows-registered domains, lately as organization-named subdomains with "passkey" or "enrollment" themes (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15). The operator relays the credentials and the MFA code or push approval to the real SSO provider in real time, then immediately registers a new attacker-controlled MFA device for persistence (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15). GTIG stresses that these compromises come from social engineering, not a vendor vulnerability (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15).

After access, the actor moves into connected SaaS applications (SharePoint, OneDrive, Zendesk, Salesforce), searches for strings such as "confidential" and "SSN", and exfiltrates with Python requests and PowerShell scripts through Microsoft Graph and direct HTTP GET requests against document URLs, reusing session cookies (for example FedAuth) captured during the vishing phase (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15). In one case the script downloaded more than a million files from SharePoint and OneDrive (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15). The direct-fetch method is often logged as FileAccessed rather than FileDownloaded, so it slips past SOCs that treat FileAccessed as benign (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15). In early intrusions the FileDownloaded records carried a spoofed Microsoft Office ClientAppId, which GTIG says served to bypass basic conditional access filters, while the user-agent showed python-requests or WindowsPowerShell (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15). In later intrusions the FileAccessed records named python-requests as the client application in AppAccessContext (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15). The sessions came from commercial VPN exit nodes and hosting providers (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15).

The BlackFile leak site went offline in late April 2026, came back on 2026-05-11 with a message that BlackFile "is shutting down… under this name", and was inaccessible at publication (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15). GTIG reads this as a possible transition phase rather than a permanent cessation, noting that extortion clusters commonly rebrand or disperse after shutdowns (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15). GTIG assesses UNC6671 as independent of ShinyHunters (UNC6240), although UNC6671 co-opted the ShinyHunters brand at least once (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15).

Detection
In identity-provider logs, look for new MFA factor registrations (Okta system.multifactor.factor.setup) immediately preceded by failed MFA authentications or abandoned challenges (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15). In Microsoft 365 audit logs, weigh FileAccessed as heavily as FileDownloaded when the user-agent is a scripting library or command-line tool, and flag FileAccessed bursts faster than a person can browse or whose AppAccessContext shows a headless client (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15).

Triage: an Office client identity paired with a scripting-library user-agent is the mismatch GTIG found, and GTIG reads it as scripted access rather than a person using SharePoint (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15). A session source on a commercial VPN or hosting provider that is unusual for the user adds weight (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15).

Defender takeaway
Move users who can be reached by a fake helpdesk call from SMS and push MFA to FIDO2 security keys or passkeys, which GTIG says resist this AiTM and vishing chain (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15).
Correction30 Sep 2026 06:54 UTCrun 2026-09-30T0639Z-auditbodyclassificationtechniquestitleheadlinesummarypriorityentitiessectors

GTIG describes the leak-site shutdown as a possible transition phase rather than a permanent cessation, not as a probable rebrand (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15). The detection guidance is corrected to GTIG's own: the spoofed Microsoft Office ClientAppId appeared on FileDownloaded records, later FileAccessed records named python-requests as the client, and new MFA factor registrations are suspicious when immediately preceded by failed or abandoned MFA challenges (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15). The actor reused captured session cookies such as FedAuth, and GTIG does not describe theft of application access tokens (Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-05-15).

updates.summary: GTIG's leak-site assessment is corrected from probable rebrand to a possible transition phase. The detection guidance now follows GTIG's own: the spoofed Office ClientAppId sat on FileDownloaded records, and new MFA registrations are suspicious after failed or abandoned challenges. Reuse of captured session cookies replaces an unsupported token-theft mapping, and the title and summary no longer present the one-victim figure of over a million files as a norm. An attacker-controlled domain, inline ATT&CK ids, an unsourced conditional-access recommendation, the context-only ShinyHunters link and three victim sectors GTIG does not name are removed. Priority is lowered to notable because the targeting GTIG reports is in North America, Australia and the UK, and the entry gains an ATT&CK mapping.

entries.headline: TeamPCP open-sourced its Shai-Hulud framework; Datadog maps its theft, persistence and npm-poisoning code
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Datadog analyses TeamPCP's open-sourced Shai-Hulud framework: credential and runner-memory theft, IDE and Claude Code hook persistence, OIDC npm publishing and a wipe-on-revocation daemon

On 2026-05-12 a GitHub repository appeared with what Datadog Security Labs assesses as the complete source code of the Shai-Hulud offensive framework attributed to TeamPCP; its README reads "Love - TeamPCP" and "Change keys and C2 as needed", its commits are authored as TeamPCP_OSS, and GitHub removed it shortly after publication, though not before it was forked several times (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-05-13). Datadog maps the source directly to compiled payloads seen in the wild, including those of the TanStack and UiPath compromises, and finds 19 of the 22 TeamPCP techniques described in earlier reporting implemented in it (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-05-13).

The modular TypeScript and Bun toolkit exits on systems with a Russian locale, then reads OS-specific lists of more than 100 sensitive file paths, runs gh auth token and captures the process environment, and in GitHub Actions on Linux feeds a script to sudo python3 that reads the Runner.Worker process memory for values marked secret; further providers walk the AWS credential chain including instance and container metadata, read every Kubernetes secret in every namespace and enumerate Vault (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-05-13). Data leaves AES-256-GCM encrypted over HTTPS to a campaign domain, with a fallback domain found through signed GitHub commits and, failing that, new public GitHub repositories used as dead-drops (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-05-13). Stolen GitHub tokens are used to commit VS Code folder-open tasks and Claude Code SessionStart hooks to every branch of the victim's repositories, stolen npm tokens to republish the victim's packages with a preinstall loader, and, in a release workflow it was hardcoded to target, the workflow's OIDC token to publish a poisoned package with genuine Sigstore provenance; where it attaches a stolen token it installs a LaunchAgent or systemd user service that checks the token every minute and runs rm -rf ~/ once it is revoked (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-05-13).

Exposure
CI/CD pipelines, developer workstations and cloud environments open to the documented techniques, in particular Runner.Worker memory extraction, instance and container metadata collection and IDE hook persistence; with the code public, other actors can reuse the playbook (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-05-13).
Detection
On hosts, a gh-token-monitor LaunchAgent or systemd user service, and Claude Code SessionStart hooks or VS Code folderOpen tasks that run a setup.mjs loader; in repositories, commits on any branch under a spoofed claude identity that add these hook and loader files; under stolen tokens, new public repositories with Dune-themed names; in npm, unexpected patch releases of your packages that add a preinstall script; in GitHub Actions, a disguised workflow that dumps the repository's secrets, followed by deleted workflow runs and branches (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-05-13).
Defender takeaway
Before revoking any GitHub token on a suspect host, disable the token-monitoring daemon, then rotate credentials; yank any package version that gained an unexpected preinstall script (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-05-13).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:34 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationentitiesevent_dateevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitle

The published repository's README reads "Love - TeamPCP" and "Change keys and C2 as needed", its commits are authored as TeamPCP_OSS, and GitHub removed the repository shortly after publication, though not before it was forked, so the code remains available to other actors (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-05-13). Datadog's analysis describes no pull-request exploitation, pull_request_target targeting or expression-injection capability in the code. The framework harvests credentials where it already runs, reads Runner.Worker memory, poisons repository branches and npm packages with stolen tokens, and uses a workflow's own OIDC token only inside a release workflow and for a package it was hardcoded to target, so that path was manually targeted while the token-driven spread is opportunistic (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-05-13).

The analysis also documents what defenders need for a compromise check: an exit on Russian-locale systems, a daemon that deletes the home directory when a stolen GitHub token is revoked and must be disabled before rotation, and the hook files, commits and npm releases it leaves behind (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-05-13).

Sources: Datadog Security Labs

Datadog's static analysis of 2026-05-13 finds a TypeScript and Bun toolkit that harvests more than 100 credential file paths, cloud, Kubernetes and Vault secrets and GitHub Actions runner memory, poisons repositories with VS Code and Claude Code hooks and npm packages with stolen tokens or a workflow's OIDC token, exits on Russian-locale systems, and installs a daemon that deletes the home directory when a stolen GitHub token is revoked.

Datadog's compromise checks include disabling the wipe-on-revocation daemon before rotating tokens.

entries.headline: Sophos survey: Swiss organisations reported the highest identity-breach rate of 17 countries, at 89%
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB3

Sophos State of Identity Security 2026: Swiss respondents report the highest identity-breach rate of 17 countries, at 89%

Sophos's State of Identity Security 2026, published on 2026-05-12, surveyed 5,000 IT and cybersecurity leaders across 17 countries and 14 industries: 71% reported at least one identity-related breach in the past 12 months, Switzerland reported the highest rate at 89%, followed by Mexico at 83%, and two-thirds of ransomware victims (67%) said their ransomware incident was directly tied to their most significant identity attack (Sophos, 2026-05-12). Weak management of non-human identities such as API keys and service accounts was a root cause in 41% of successful identity breaches (Sophos, 2026-05-12). Help Net Security reports that the energy, oil and gas, utilities and federal government sectors recorded the highest breach rates (Help Net Security, 2026-05-14).

Defender takeaway
No decision changes on survey figures alone; the two gaps the survey measures are checkable in one's own estate: more than half of companies reviewed unusual login attempts no more than once every three months, and only 34.3% rotated and audited non-human identities weekly or more often (Help Net Security, 2026-05-14).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:37 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationconfidenceentitiesevent_dateevidenceheadlineregionssourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitle

Sophos published the survey on 2026-05-12 (Sophos, 2026-05-12); 2026-05-14 is the date of Help Net Security's report (Help Net Security, 2026-05-14). Its ransomware finding is that two-thirds of ransomware victims (67%) said their ransomware incident was directly tied to their most significant identity attack (Sophos, 2026-05-12), and Sophos says attackers increasingly use stolen credentials as their primary mechanism for delivery (Sophos, 2026-05-12).

entries.headline: An 18-year-old NGINX rewrite-module heap overflow has a public PoC, and VulnCheck honeypots saw exploitation attempts
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-42945updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-42945, NGINX Open Source / Plus / F5 WAF products: 18-year-old heap buffer overflow in rewrite module ("NGINX Rift"), PoC public

CVE-2026-42945 (CVSS 4.0: 9.2, codename "NGINX Rift") is a heap buffer overflow present in src/http/ngx_http_script.c since NGINX 0.6.27 (2008) (depthfirst "NGINX Rift" technical writeup, 2026-05-13 · NCSC-CH Security Hub #12575, 2026-05-15). The root cause: when a rewrite directive combines an unnamed PCRE capture ($1, $2) with a replacement string containing ?, followed by another rewrite, if, or set directive in the same scope, ngx_http_script_start_args_code() sets a flag causing the write phase to URI-encode URI argument characters (expanding escapable characters such as + and & from one byte to three), while the length-calculation phase computed a shorter buffer without this escaping. The result is a deterministic out-of-bounds write into the adjacent heap allocation. F5 says the flaw may cause a heap buffer overflow in the NGINX worker process leading to a restart (ENISA EUVD, 2026-09-10). depthfirst's proof of concept achieves code execution with ASLR off, and depthfirst notes that forked workers share one heap layout, which could in theory be used to leak ASLR (depthfirst, 2026-05-13); F5's CVE description, updated on 2026-09-10, covers systems with ASLR disabled or where the attacker can bypass ASLR (ENISA EUVD, 2026-09-10). A working PoC is public at github.com/depthfirstdisclosures/nginx-rift. depthfirst's internal analysis system found the flaw on 2026-04-18; depthfirst reported it to NGINX on 2026-04-21, shared its RCE proof of concept on 2026-05-05, and F5 released the advisory on 2026-05-13 (depthfirst, 2026-05-13). NCSC-CH rated the exploitation status "UNKNOWN, Proof of Concept Available" on 2026-05-15 (NCSC-CH Security Hub #12575, 2026-05-15); VulnCheck's honeypot reports followed two days later (below). Temporary workaround: replace all unnamed captures with named captures (e.g., (?<user_id>...) → $user_id) in rewrite directives, which eliminates the vulnerable code path without requiring upgrade. Affected: NGINX Open Source 0.6.27 to 1.30.0 (nginx.org); NGINX Plus R32 to R36; Ingress Controller 3.5.0 to 3.7.2, 4.0.0 to 4.0.1 and 5.0.0 to 5.4.1; Gateway Fabric 1.3.0 to 1.6.2 and 2.0.0 to 2.5.1; Instance Manager 2.16.0 to 2.21.1; F5 WAF for NGINX 5.9.0 to 5.12.1; App Protect WAF 4.9.0 to 4.16.0 and 5.1.0 to 5.8.0; F5 DoS for NGINX 4.8.0; App Protect DoS 4.3.0 to 4.7.0 (Security Affairs, 2026-05). Fixed: NGINX Open Source 1.30.1 and 1.31.0 (nginx.org); NGINX Plus R32 P6 and R36 P4 (Security Affairs, 2026-05).

VulnCheck reported exploitation attempts against its honeypot networks; the nature of the activity and its goals are unknown (The Hacker News, 2026-05-17).

Contradiction: the NGINX project rates the flaw severity medium (nginx.org), while NCSC-CH gives a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 (NCSC-CH Security Hub #12575, 2026-05-15) and depthfirst rates it critical at 9.2 (depthfirst, 2026-05-13); the gap likely reflects the preconditions, a specific rewrite pattern and, for code execution, ASLR. NCSC-CH (NCSC-CH Security Hub #12575, 2026-05-15) and The Hacker News (The Hacker News, 2026-05-17) say code execution requires ASLR to be disabled, while F5's CVE description, as EUVD carried it on 2026-09-10, also covers attackers who can bypass ASLR (ENISA EUVD, 2026-09-10).

Exposure
A configuration with a rewrite that uses an unnamed capture and a ? in the replacement, followed by another rewrite, if or set in the same scope (depthfirst, NGINX Rift); without such a rewrite pattern with unnamed captures the flaw is not reachable (NCSC-CH Security Hub #12575, 2026-05-15).
Detection
Repeated NGINX worker crashes and automatic restarts, correlated with requests whose URI carries characters that expand when escaped (such as + and &), are the observable effect (Security Affairs, 2026-05).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade NGINX Open Source to 1.30.1, 1.31.0 or later (nginx.org) on every server whose configuration has the rewrite pattern above. Where the upgrade has to wait, replacing unnamed captures ($1, $2) with named captures in each affected rewrite directive removes the reachable path (depthfirst, NGINX Rift).
Correction11 Oct 2026 14:41 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-auditsummarycvessourcesreferencestechniquesaffected_productsclassificationbodyevent_dateactions

depthfirst reported the flaw to NGINX on 2026-04-21 and shared its code-execution proof of concept on 2026-05-05 (depthfirst, 2026-05-13); the earlier dates and the NDA had no source. VulnCheck reported exploitation attempts against its honeypots, with their purpose unknown (The Hacker News, 2026-05-17). The NGINX project rates the flaw medium (nginx.org), against the CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 NCSC-CH gives (NCSC-CH Security Hub #12575, 2026-05-15).

Correction21 Oct 2026 12:06 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1149Z-auditbodyevidenceheadlinesourcestitleactions

F5's CVE description does not limit code execution to hosts with ASLR disabled. depthfirst's proof of concept runs with ASLR off, but depthfirst notes that forked NGINX workers share one heap layout, which could in theory be used to leak ASLR (depthfirst, 2026-05-13), and F5's CVE description, updated on 2026-09-10, covers systems with ASLR disabled or where the attacker can bypass ASLR (ENISA EUVD, 2026-09-10). An enabled ASLR is therefore no reason to defer the upgrade. Where the upgrade has to wait, depthfirst's workaround is to replace unnamed captures with named captures in every affected rewrite directive (depthfirst, NGINX Rift).

entries.title: CVE-2026-42945, NGINX Open Source / Plus / F5 WAF products: 18-year-old heap buffer overflow in rewrite module ("NGINX Rift"), PoC public

updates.summary: depthfirst found the flaw on 2026-04-18, reported it on 2026-04-21 and shared its proof of concept on 2026-05-05; no source mentions an NDA or a 2026-04-28 PoC handover. The affected-version ranges for the Kubernetes and F5 products had gaps the earlier text closed over, and the NGINX project's own medium severity rating was not set against the 9.2 score. The entry gains the nginx.org advisory, Security Affairs and The Hacker News as sources, VulnCheck's honeypot exploitation attempts carried over from the duplicate entry of 2026-05-18, a contradiction line, exposure and detection lines, a rating, an ATT&CK mapping, the affected products and a link to the SAP August patch-day entry. The exploitation-status sentence now reads as NCSC-CH dated it, ahead of VulnCheck's report, and the score attributions name only what each cited page states.

Code execution was described as possible only with ASLR disabled; depthfirst notes that forked workers share one heap layout that could in theory leak ASLR, and F5's CVE description, updated on 2026-09-10, covers systems where the attacker can bypass ASLR, against NCSC-CH's narrower statement. The headline now names the public proof of concept and VulnCheck's honeypot exploitation attempts, and verbatim quotes from the GitHub advisory, depthfirst, ENISA EUVD and The Hacker News back the trigger, disclosure, ASLR and exploitation statements. A Defender takeaway now names the fixed NGINX Open Source releases and depthfirst's named-capture workaround, replacing the standing action that restated them.

entries.headline: A forged vHub peer can plant an SSH key on Cisco SD-WAN controllers without credentials; Talos ties exploitation to UAT-8616
entries.html:
CRITICALCVE-2026-20182exploitedupdatedNATOA1

CVE-2026-20182: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN peering authentication bypass (CVSS 10.0) exploited by UAT-8616; affects Controller, Manager and Validator

CVE-2026-20182 (CVSS 10.0, CWE-287) is an authentication bypass in the peering authentication of Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, Manager and, since Cisco's advisory revision of 2026-06-16, Validator, affecting all deployment types regardless of configuration (Cisco PSIRT). Rapid7 showed the mechanism on the Controller: the vdaemon DTLS control-plane service on UDP/12346 accepts a CHALLENGE_ACK claiming device type 2 (vHub) from a self-signed peer without verifying it, after which message type 14 (MSG_VMANAGE_TO_PEER) appends an attacker SSH key to /home/vmanage-admin/.ssh/authorized_keys, giving NETCONF access on TCP/830 as vmanage-admin (Rapid7, 2026-05-14). Rapid7 demonstrates the bypass with its own Metasploit module, submitted to the public Metasploit Framework repository (Rapid7, 2026-05-14). Cisco became aware of limited exploitation in May 2026 (Cisco PSIRT), and Talos attributes it to UAT-8616, a highly sophisticated actor that attempted to add SSH keys, modify NETCONF configurations and escalate to root (Cisco Talos, 2026-05-14). Talos separately tracks ten other clusters, distinct from UAT-8616, that exploit the earlier SD-WAN Manager flaws CVE-2026-20133, CVE-2026-20128 and CVE-2026-20122 with public proof-of-concept code (Cisco Talos, 2026-05-14). CISA added CVE-2026-20182 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-05-14 (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-05-14), under its existing Emergency Directive 26-03 for Cisco SD-WAN, first issued on 2026-02-25 (CISA ED 26-03).

Cisco lists no workaround; first fixed releases are 20.9.9.1, 20.12.5.4, 20.12.6.2 or 20.12.7.1, 20.15.4.4 or 20.15.5.2, 20.18.2.2 and 26.1.1.1, releases before 20.9 must migrate, and 20.10, 20.11, 20.13, 20.14 and 20.16 move to the next fixed train (Cisco PSIRT).

Exposure
Every Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, Manager and Validator below the fixed release, especially Controllers with ports exposed to the internet (Cisco PSIRT).
Detection
In /var/log/auth.log, "Accepted publickey for vmanage-admin" from an IP that is not one of the configured System IPs, and in show control connections detail or show control connections-history detail (on a Validator, show orchestrator connections detail) a peer in state up with challenge-ack 0 (Cisco PSIRT).
Defender takeaway
Run request admin-tech on every control component before upgrading to preserve evidence; on a system confirmed compromised, Cisco says the update alone will not resolve the vulnerability and TAC remediation is needed (Cisco PSIRT).
Correction11 Oct 2026 14:38 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryimmediate_actiontagsentitiestechniquesaffected_productscvessourcesevidencesourcing_notereferencesclassificationbody

CISA's Emergency Directive 26-03 was first issued on 2026-02-25; on 2026-05-14 CISA added CVE-2026-20182 to its KEV catalog under it (CISA ED 26-03) (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-05-14). The SSH-key and NETCONF path Rapid7 demonstrated is on the SD-WAN Controller (Rapid7, 2026-05-14), and Cisco has since added the Validator to the affected products (Cisco PSIRT). Talos's ten other clusters exploit the separate SD-WAN Manager flaws CVE-2026-20133, CVE-2026-20128 and CVE-2026-20122, not this one (Cisco Talos, 2026-05-14). Cisco lists no workaround and no source proposes segmentation as one. Rapid7 demonstrates the bypass with its own Metasploit module, submitted to the public Metasploit Framework repository, so a working exploit is public (Rapid7, 2026-05-14).

Builds on: A netadmin user on Cisco SD-WAN can become root through a crafted upload file; Mandiant saw…

Sources: Cisco PSIRT · Rapid7 · Cisco Talos · CISA KEV catalog · CISA ED 26-03

immediate_action.evidence_quote: In May 2026, the Cisco Product Security Incident Response Team (PSIRT) became aware of limited exploitation of this vulnerability.
immediate_action.title: Patch Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, Manager and Validator now (CVE-2026-20182, CVSS 10.0)

entries.summary: CVE-2026-20182 (CVSS 10.0) lets an unauthenticated attacker bypass peering authentication on Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, Manager and Validator and plant an SSH key for NETCONF access. Cisco saw limited exploitation in May 2026, which Talos attributes to UAT-8616; CISA added it to its KEV catalog on 2026-05-14 under Emergency Directive 26-03. There is no workaround, and a compromised system needs TAC remediation beyond the upgrade.
entries.title: CVE-2026-20182: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN peering authentication bypass (CVSS 10.0) exploited by UAT-8616; affects Controller, Manager and Validator

updates.summary: CISA did not issue Emergency Directive 26-03 on 2026-05-14: the directive dates from 2026-02-25, and on 2026-05-14 CISA added the flaw to its KEV catalog under it. The NETCONF and SSH-key path Rapid7 demonstrated is on the Controller, not the Manager; Talos names exactly ten other clusters exploiting a separate set of February flaws; the segmentation mitigation had no source; and the flaw is an authentication bypass, not code execution. The entry is rewritten with the Validator added, Cisco's indicators and pre-upgrade evidence step, the UAT-8616 attribution, verbatim evidence, a rating, an ATT&CK mapping and a link to the separate CVE-2026-20245 entry. Rapid7's Metasploit module, submitted to the public framework repository, is now named, and the flaw's status gains poc-public.

entries.headline: Composer printed GitHub Actions tokens into CI logs once GitHub's new token format arrived; fixed in 2.9.8 and 2.2.28
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-45793updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-45793, PHP Composer: GitHub Actions and GitHub App installation tokens printed in full to CI job logs when GitHub's new token format failed validation (CVSS 7.5)

Composer validates configured GitHub tokens against an allowed character set in Composer\IO\BaseIO::loadConfiguration(); GitHub's new structured format for GitHub App installation tokens contains a hyphen, fails that check, and the resulting exception prints the full token to stderr, which CI captures in the job log, while GitHub Actions' secret masker may not redact it because the message is wrapped or framed (Packagist, 2026-05-13). Any workflow that configures a GitHub App installation token, including the auto-injected GITHUB_TOKEN, into Composer's auth and then runs any Composer command hits it, and actions such as shivammathur/setup-php register GITHUB_TOKEN automatically, so no unusual configuration is needed (Packagist, 2026-05-13). The advisory's header rates CVE-2026-45793 High 7.5 while its own text calls the severity medium, and it lists Composer from 2.3.0 before 2.9.8, from 2.0.0 before 2.2.28 and from 1.0 before 1.10.28 as affected, fixed in 2.9.8, 2.2.28 and 1.10.28 (Composer, 2026-05-13). CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue did not list it as of 2026-10-21 (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-10-21).

The exposure window depends on the token: a hosted-runner GITHUB_TOKEN expires when the job ends or after six hours, and the error usually fails the job and expires it at once; on self-hosted runners it can stay valid for up to 24 hours after issuance; and tokens from actions/create-github-app-token or another GitHub App last up to an hour by default and can carry permissions broader than the workflow's own permissions: declaration (Packagist, 2026-05-13). GitHub rolled back the token change on 2026-05-13 at 14:30 UTC and planned to restart the rollout on 2026-05-18 after 14:00 UTC (Packagist, 2026-05-13).

Exposure
GitHub Actions workflows that run Composer below 2.9.8, 2.2.28 or 1.10.28 with a GITHUB_TOKEN or GitHub App installation token in Composer's auth, on repositories that received the new token format; setup-php users who did not pin the Composer version were moved to a fixed release (Packagist, 2026-05-13).
Detection
In CI job logs, the error line "Your github oauth token for github.com contains invalid characters" followed by the token itself; for each such log, check activity under that token within its validity window (Packagist, 2026-05-13).
Defender takeaway
Update Composer to 2.9.8 or 2.2.28, and where the error appears in a log, delete the log content holding the token and confirm no unexpected activity occurred under it, counting up to 24 hours for self-hosted runners and 6 hours for GitHub-hosted ones (Packagist, 2026-05-13).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:33 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesentitiesevidenceheadlinekindsourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitle

The leak was not tied to package-resolution errors: GitHub's new format for GitHub App installation tokens contains a hyphen, fails Composer's character validation when its configuration loads, and the exception prints the full token to stderr, so any workflow with such a token in Composer's auth hit it on the default path, including the auto-injected GITHUB_TOKEN (Packagist, 2026-05-13). Classic ghp_ personal access tokens are not affected by the validation bug itself, though the advisory notes the same leak applies to any future credential that fails validation (Composer, 2026-05-13). Packagist's relevant permission point is that App tokens can carry permissions broader than the workflow's own permissions: declaration, not that every GITHUB_TOKEN can write workflow files (Packagist, 2026-05-13).

The exposure was bounded: hosted-runner tokens usually expired with the failing job, self-hosted runner tokens stay valid for up to 24 hours and App tokens for up to an hour, and GitHub rolled the format change back on 2026-05-13 before planning a new rollout from 2026-05-18 (Packagist, 2026-05-13). Neither the Packagist post nor the advisory mentions Mini Shai-Hulud or exploitation; the advisory rates the flaw High 7.5, fixed in 2.9.8, 2.2.28 and 1.10.28 (Composer, 2026-05-13).

vulnerability15 May 05:00Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Packagist · Composer (GHSA-f9f8-rm49-7jv2) · CISA KEV catalog
entries.summary: Composer before 2.9.8, 2.2.28 and 1.10.28 printed the full GitHub token to stderr, and so into GitHub Actions job logs, whenever a GitHub App installation token in GitHub's new hyphenated format, including a workflow's auto-injected GITHUB_TOKEN, failed its character validation (CVE-2026-45793, High 7.5). Hosted-runner tokens usually expired with the failing job, but self-hosted runner tokens stay valid for up to 24 hours and App tokens for up to an hour; GitHub rolled back the format change on 2026-05-13 and planned to restart it on 2026-05-18.
entries.title: CVE-2026-45793, PHP Composer: GitHub Actions and GitHub App installation tokens printed in full to CI job logs when GitHub's new token format failed validation (CVSS 7.5)

updates.summary: Composer's token leak was triggered on the default path by GitHub's new hyphenated installation-token format failing Composer's validation when it loaded its configuration, not by package-resolution errors, and it concerned GITHUB_TOKEN and GitHub App installation tokens rather than personal access tokens. Hosted-runner tokens usually expired with the failing job, self-hosted runner tokens stay valid for up to 24 hours and App tokens for up to an hour, and GitHub rolled the format change back on 2026-05-13. No source links the bug to Mini Shai-Hulud, and the advisory rates it High 7.5 with fixes in 2.9.8, 2.2.28 and 1.10.28.

entries.headline: Nextcloud fixes a 2FA bypass that lets an attacker holding a user's password reach files over DAV
entries.html:
ROUTINECVE-2026-45691 +1updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-45691, Nextcloud Server and Enterprise Server: second-factor bypass on DAV endpoints by reusing a pre-2FA session cookie (CVSS 5.9)

Nextcloud's advisory for CVE-2026-45691 (Moderate, 5.9) says a session cookie created after successful password authentication but before TOTP completion could be reused as a Bearer token against DAV endpoints, granting read and write access while bypassing mandatory two-factor authentication (Nextcloud, 2026-05-13). The attacker therefore needs the user's password, which the advisory scores as low privileges with high attack complexity (Nextcloud, 2026-05-13). Server is affected from 32.0.0 and 33.0.0 and fixed in 32.0.9 and 33.0.3; Enterprise Server is affected from 29.0.0 through the 33 branch and fixed in 33.0.3, 32.0.9, version 31.0.14.5, version 30.0.17.9 and version 29.0.16.16 (Nextcloud, 2026-05-13). The same releases fix CVE-2026-45690, a second 2FA bypass by replaying a pending session token (Moderate, 5.9) (Nextcloud, 2026-05-15). The advisory lists no workaround, and CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue did not list either flaw as of 2026-10-21 (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-10-21). BSI's WID-SEC-2026-1517 covers CVE-2026-45543, CVE-2026-45544, CVE-2026-45545 and CVE-2026-45691 from the batch (BSI, 2026-05-13).

Nextcloud's other advisories of that week concern separate apps: an SQL injection in the column-type parameter of the Tables app (CVE-2026-45545, High 8.2) (Nextcloud, 2026-05-13), a missing JWT signature check in ID4me handling of the User OIDC app (CVE-2026-45156, High 8.1) (Nextcloud, 2026-05-12), and user identifiers leaked through the Calendar app's attendee suggestion endpoint (CVE-2026-45286, Moderate 4.3) (Nextcloud, 2026-05-12).

Exposure
Nextcloud Server and Enterprise Server instances below the fixed releases that rely on enforced two-factor authentication, wherever an attacker can obtain a user's password (Nextcloud, 2026-05-13).
Detection
In Nextcloud and web-server access logs, DAV requests authenticated with a Bearer token issued in a session whose two-factor step was never completed, the request pattern the bypass produces (Nextcloud, 2026-05-13).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade in the regular cycle to the fixed releases, sooner on internet-facing instances where two-factor authentication is the control that stops password reuse, since that is the protection this flaw removes (Nextcloud, 2026-05-13).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:32 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditactionsaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevidenceheadlinekindprioritysourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

The flaw is not exploitable before authentication: the reusable session cookie is created after successful password authentication, so an attacker needs the user's password (Nextcloud, 2026-05-13). Server is affected from 32.0.0 before 32.0.9 and from 33.0.0 before 33.0.3 (Nextcloud, 2026-05-13). CVE-2026-45690 is a second 2FA bypass fixed in the same releases (Moderate 5.9) (Nextcloud, 2026-05-15), not an SQL injection; the column-type SQL injection is CVE-2026-45545 in the Tables app, rated High 8.2 (Nextcloud, 2026-05-13), the User OIDC JWT signature bypass is rated High 8.1 (Nextcloud, 2026-05-12), and the Calendar attendee-suggestion leak is Moderate 4.3 (Nextcloud, 2026-05-12).

No cited source describes how widely Nextcloud is deployed in EU government or education, or states a public proof of concept or exploitation; with the password prerequisite, a Moderate score and no reported exploitation, the fix belongs in the regular patch cycle.

Server is fixed in 33.0.3 and 32.0.9 and Enterprise Server also in version 31.0.14.5, version 30.0.17.9 and version 29.0.16.16, the same releases that fix a second 2FA bypass, CVE-2026-45690.

In the same batch CVE-2026-45690 is a second 2FA bypass, the column-type SQL injection is CVE-2026-45545 (High 8.2) in the Tables app, the User OIDC JWT bypass is High 8.1 and the Calendar leak is Moderate 4.3. No source supports the claimed deployment across EU government and education, and a Moderate, password-dependent, unexploited flaw fits the regular patch cycle.

entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Belarus-aligned FrostyNeighbor hits Ukrainian government bodies with geofenced PDF lures and Cobalt Strike
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

FrostyNeighbor (Ghostwriter, UNC1151): since March 2026, geofenced PDF lures deliver a JavaScript PicassoLoader and Cobalt Strike to Ukrainian government organisations

ESET attributes new activity since March 2026 to FrostyNeighbor, also known as Ghostwriter, UNC1151, UAC-0057, TA445, PUSHCHA or Storm-0257, a long-running cyberespionage group apparently aligned with the interests of Belarus, using links in spearphishing PDFs to target governmental organisations in Ukraine (ESET, 2026-05-14). In ESET's telemetry the group's Ukrainian targeting focuses on military, defence and government, while its victimology in Poland and Lithuania is broader, spanning industry and manufacturing, healthcare and pharmaceuticals, logistics and many governmental organisations (ESET, 2026-05-14).

The lure is a blurred PDF impersonating Ukrtelecom whose download button leads to the group's delivery server; visitors outside Ukraine receive a benign PDF of the same name, while Ukrainian IP addresses receive a RAR archive holding a JavaScript first stage that shows a decoy, re-runs itself, drops a base64-embedded JavaScript PicassoLoader and builds a scheduled task from an XML template the C2 serves as a fake JPG (ESET, 2026-05-14). PicassoLoader collects the username, computer name, OS version, boot time, current time and running processes, posts them over HTTPS every 10 minutes and evaluates any response longer than 100 bytes (ESET, 2026-05-14). Operators very likely decide by hand whether the victim is of interest; if so, the C2 returns a third-stage dropper that copies rundll32.exe into %ProgramData% under another name, writes the base64-decoded Cobalt Strike beacon DLL beside it, and registers in the HKCU Run key a LNK that starts the copied rundll32 with the DLL's export (ESET, 2026-05-14).

Exposure
Governmental organisations in Ukraine are the targets of this chain; the payload is delivered only after server-side checks of the user agent and IP address and a manual operator decision, so a request from outside Ukraine sees only the benign PDF (ESET, 2026-05-14).
Detection
In process telemetry, a JavaScript file from a RAR archive that relaunches itself, followed by scheduled-task creation from a downloaded XML template; in network telemetry, a script process posting to the same HTTPS endpoint every 10 minutes; in persistence telemetry, an HKCU Run entry pointing at a LNK in %ProgramData% that starts a renamed copy of rundll32.exe loading a DLL from the same directory (ESET, 2026-05-14).

Triage: rundll32.exe is a normal Windows binary when it runs from the system directory; a copy of it under a different name in %ProgramData%, which ESET says is very likely meant to bypass detection rules, is the signal (ESET, 2026-05-14).

Defender takeaway
Because delivery is geofenced and operator-gated, a clean verdict on an Ukrtelecom-themed lure link from a sandbox outside Ukraine proves nothing; hunt on the host artefacts above instead (ESET, 2026-05-14). The Hacker News reports the same chain (The Hacker News, 2026-05-14).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:36 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationevidenceheadlinesectorssourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitleentities

The activity ESET documents since March 2026 targets governmental organisations in Ukraine (ESET, 2026-05-14); the industrial, healthcare and pharmaceutical, logistics and governmental victims in Poland and Lithuania come from ESET's introduction to the group's broader victimology, not from this campaign wave. The chain also persists: the first stage builds a scheduled task from a downloaded XML template to run PicassoLoader, and the Cobalt Strike stage copies rundll32.exe into %ProgramData% under another name and starts it from a LNK registered in the HKCU Run key (ESET, 2026-05-14), which gives defenders host artefacts to hunt where geofencing hides the network side.

threat15 May 05:00Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: ESET · The Hacker News

The JavaScript PicassoLoader it installs reports a host fingerprint every 10 minutes, and the operators very likely decide manually whether to send a dropper that runs a Cobalt Strike beacon through a renamed copy of rundll32 with Run-key persistence.

entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: China-nexus FamousSparrow re-entered an Azerbaijani energy firm three times through the same unpatched Exchange server
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2022-41040 +1exploitedupdatedNATOB2

FamousSparrow's three-wave intrusion at an Azerbaijani oil and gas company: repeated ProxyNotShell access, Deed RAT behind a two-export LogMeIn Hamachi sideload, and a blocked TernDoor attempt

Background. Bitdefender tracked an intrusion at an Azerbaijani oil and gas company from late December 2025 to late February 2026 and attributes it with moderate-to-high confidence to FamousSparrow, citing substantial overlap with the Earth Estries toolset and tradecraft; earlier public reporting placed the cluster against telecoms, government and technology targets in the United States, Asia-Pacific, the Middle East and South Africa, and this is the first public link to energy targets in the South Caucasus (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13). Bitdefender sets the targeting against Azerbaijan's larger role in European gas supply, now reaching 13 European countries, but states that this context does not establish motive (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13). The Hacker News notes that FamousSparrow is also tracked as UAT-9244 and overlaps with Earth Estries and Salt Typhoon (The Hacker News, 2026-05-13).

Initial access, three times. On 2025-12-25 the Exchange IIS worker process w3wp.exe, with MSExchangePowerShellAppPool on its command line, tried to write a web shell into a publicly accessible directory, which Bitdefender reads as ProxyNotShell exploitation; more web-shell writes followed on 12-26 and 12-29, alongside attempts to execute commands through the same process (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13). Bitdefender calls ProxyNotShell (CVE-2022-41040 and CVE-2022-41082) usable by unauthenticated attackers (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13), whereas Microsoft's advisory for CVE-2022-41082 says the attacker must be authenticated and scores both flaws with low privileges required, 8.8 and 8.0 (MSRC, CVE-2022-41040; MSRC, CVE-2022-41082). Microsoft released fixes on 2022-11-08 (MSRC, CVE-2022-41082), and CISA has listed both as known exploited since 2022-09-30 (CISA KEV catalog, 2022-09-30). After remediation removed malware from at least one system, the attackers came back to the same still-vulnerable Exchange server about a month later, and again at the end of February (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13).

Wave 1: Deed RAT behind a two-export sideload. The legitimate LogMeIn Hamachi binary LMIGuardianSvc.exe, first run from C:\TEMP, sideloaded a malicious loader and was then installed under a path chosen to mimic the legitimate Hamachi install directory, with a service named LogMeIn Hamachi starting it at boot (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13). The loader's Init export changes memory protection on StartServiceCtrlDispatcherW and patches its entry point; when the host later calls ComMain and its normal service start-up reaches that API, execution diverts into the loader, which restores the original bytes, decrypts the AES-128-CBC payload and runs shellcode that resolves APIs by hash, RC4-decrypts and LZNT1-decompresses the Deed RAT orchestrator (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13); a sandbox that runs the DLL on its own or invokes a single export sees the malware largely inactive (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13). Deed RAT's configuration names system processes such as SearchIndexer.exe and taskhost.exe as injection targets and a registry key under the Hamachi name for configuration and plugin storage, and it talks HTTPS to domains impersonating security vendors (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13). Bitdefender calls the technique an evolved DLL sideload and finds the loader closely matches one Trend Micro documented for Earth Estries, with the same exports and hook-and-restore flow (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13).

Lateral movement. From the first host the attackers opened an RDP session to a second server with a domain administrator account, launched PowerShell, and within minutes the Hamachi-based Deed RAT files appeared there; from that host atexec and smbexec-style utilities consistent with Impacket spread it to a third machine (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13).

Wave 2: TernDoor, blocked. About a month after the first wave, a renamed copy of the legitimate deskband_injector64.exe in a ProgramData subdirectory tried to sideload a malicious winmm.dll; the security product blocked execution before installation completed, and registry artefacts showed an attempt to create a kernel-driver service (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13). From recovered memory pages Bitdefender identifies a Mofu loader chain and assesses the partially recovered payload as TernDoor (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13).

Wave 3. At the end of February the attackers deployed Deed RAT again through the same chain with a modified configuration, the components moved to C:\Recovery and new injection targets (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13).

Exposure
On-premises Exchange servers without Microsoft's 2022-11-08 ProxyNotShell fixes (MSRC, CVE-2022-41082); Bitdefender warns that attackers will keep exploiting unpatched servers until they are patched or taken offline (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13). HealthChecker's -VulnerabilityReport switch collects the vulnerability state of every Exchange server in an environment (Microsoft CSS-Exchange, 2025-10-29).
Detection
In process and file telemetry on Exchange, w3wp.exe writing .aspx files to publicly accessible directories under MSExchangePowerShellAppPool; in memory and EDR telemetry, changes to the first bytes of commonly hooked APIs such as StartServiceCtrlDispatcherW by unsigned code; in service-creation events, a kernel-driver service (Type 1) whose image path is under ProgramData, Temp or another user-writable directory; in authentication logs, RDP from internal hosts with domain administrator credentials outside maintenance windows, followed by PowerShell and executable downloads; and Impacket atexec or smbexec use (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13). The Wave 1 chain also leaves a LogMeIn Hamachi service and LMIGuardianSvc.exe on hosts with no sanctioned Hamachi install (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13).

Triage: legitimate Exchange maintenance rarely writes web-accessible script files through the IIS worker process, and legitimate applications rarely patch system API entry points, which signed system components or documented security tools do when they must (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13).

Defender takeaway
After removing malware from an Exchange-originated intrusion, the decision that ends it is patching the entry point and rotating every domain administrator credential used during the intrusion, since Bitdefender's lesson from this intrusion is that actors re-exploit the same access path until the vulnerability is patched and compromised credentials are rotated; where Exchange cannot be patched at once, segment it so a compromise does not grant domain-wide access (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:26 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesentitiesevidenceheadlineregionssourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitlepriority

Bitdefender presents Azerbaijan's expanded gas exports to 13 European countries as context that does not establish motive, and attributes the intrusion with moderate-to-high confidence to FamousSparrow as likely affiliated with the Chinese APT ecosystem (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13); no source states a motive of Chinese state actors. Prior reporting placed the cluster against telecoms, government and technology targets, and Bitdefender cites toolset and tradecraft overlap with Earth Estries rather than shared infrastructure (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13). The sideload is what Bitdefender calls an evolved technique: its loader closely matches a Deed RAT loader Trend Micro documented for Earth Estries, and no source calls the Hamachi host new for the cluster or the binary signed (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13).

The second wave's TernDoor installation was blocked by the security product before it completed, and TernDoor is Bitdefender's assessment from recovered memory pages (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13). The re-entries came through the same still-vulnerable Exchange server, and Bitdefender's lesson is patching plus rotation of compromised credentials; no surviving web shell or scheduled task is reported, no source describes cumulative updates rolling back fixes, and the persisted loader sat in a path mimicking the legitimate Hamachi install directory, so a hunt that trusts that path misses it (Bitdefender, 2026-05-13). Microsoft's advisory says ProxyNotShell requires an authenticated attacker (MSRC, CVE-2022-41082), while Bitdefender describes it as unauthenticated.

entries.summary: Bitdefender documented an intrusion at an Azerbaijani oil and gas company from late December 2025 to late February 2026 that it attributes with moderate-to-high confidence to the China-nexus FamousSparrow cluster. The attackers came back three times through the same vulnerable on-premises Exchange server (ProxyNotShell), ran Deed RAT through a LogMeIn Hamachi binary whose malicious loader splits its trigger across two exports and a hooked StartServiceCtrlDispatcherW call, attempted TernDoor in a second wave that security software blocked, and moved laterally with a domain administrator account over RDP and Impacket-style tools.

entries.headline: Leaked chats of The Gentlemen ransomware group show its edge-device access, NTLM relay and EDR-kill toolkit
entries.html:
HIGHupdatedNATOB2

The Gentlemen RaaS: leaked internal chats show Fortinet and Cisco edge access, NTLM relay, ADCS abuse and EDR-kill tooling, mapped by Check Point Research

On 2026-05-04 the administrator of The Gentlemen ransomware-as-a-service programme acknowledged on underground forums that the group's internal backend database, Rocket, had leaked; a seller offered the data for 10,000 USD, and Check Point Research obtained a 44.4 MB partial copy of the internal chats while the seller's screenshot showed about 16.22 GB in total (Check Point Research, 2026-05-13). DynaRisk's analyst counted 8,200 lines of internal chat text with timestamps largely matching Moscow working hours (BankInfoSecurity, 2026-05-11).

The chats describe initial access usually through exposed edge devices, with a focus on Fortinet FortiGate and Cisco, by brute-forcing web and VPN panels, exploiting known vulnerabilities and buying access; the group tracks CVE-2024-55591 in the FortiOS management interface without the chats showing exploitation steps, evaluates a proof of concept for CVE-2025-32433 in Erlang SSH, and scans domains for NTLM relay paths including CVE-2025-33073 to feed relay tooling (Check Point Research, 2026-05-13). After access the operators seek domain administrator rights through Active Directory discovery, certificate-services abuse (enumerating ADCS misconfigurations ESC1 to ESC17) and local privilege escalation, dump LSASS and browser sessions, tamper with EDR using tools that block or delay security processes at start-up and bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver techniques, keep access through Cloudflare tunnels and the ZeroPulse and Velociraptor remote-access frameworks, and exfiltrate from NAS, backup and virtualisation systems; the administrator also announced locker upgrades that unhook NTDLL and patch ETW (Check Point Research, 2026-05-13). DynaRisk adds that the group regularly discussed ways to disable endpoint security tools, modify Group Policy Objects and gain domain admin privileges, and targeted NAS, Exchange, storage and backup systems to prevent recovery (BankInfoSecurity, 2026-05-11).

Check Point counts about 332 victims published on the leak site in the first five months of 2026 and 412 in total, and links 29 campaigns to 8 affiliate contact IDs, including the administrator's, who also carries out infections himself; a separate, earlier Check Point investigation of one affiliate's intrusion found a SystemBC command-and-control server holding more than 1,570 victims (Check Point Research, 2026-05-13).

Exposure
Internet-facing Fortinet FortiGate and Cisco VPN and management interfaces, Active Directory domains where NTLM relay is possible, and certificate services with misconfigured templates are the paths the chats describe (Check Point Research, 2026-05-13).
Detection
In endpoint telemetry, processes that stop EDR services from starting and user processes that patch ETW or unhook NTDLL; in directory telemetry, enumeration of ADCS templates and NTLM relay scanning; in network and host inventory, remote-access agents and Cloudflare tunnel clients IT did not deploy (Check Point Research, 2026-05-13); in change logs, Group Policy modifications after a domain-admin compromise, and discovery sweeps of hypervisors, NAS and backup servers before encryption (BankInfoSecurity, 2026-05-11).
Defender takeaway
During an active Gentlemen incident, capture the memory of the running ransomware process (an EDR memory capture, a process dump or a full RAM image) before killing it or rebooting: the free decryptor Bedrock Safeguard released in April 2026 recovers per-file keys only from such an image, is best-effort and has no master key (Bedrock Safeguard, 2026-04-21), and the group shipped a same-day patch after its release (BankInfoSecurity, 2026-05-11).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:30 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationentitiesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

The decryptor Bedrock Safeguard released in April 2026 does not let victims recover without payment in general: it extracts per-file keys from a memory image of the ransomware process captured while it was running, is best-effort and may be partial, and without such an image cannot recover files, because there is no master key (Bedrock Safeguard, 2026-04-21); the group issued a same-day patch (BankInfoSecurity, 2026-05-11). The 1,570 figure is the victim count on one affiliate's SystemBC command-and-control server from an earlier Check Point investigation, and Check Point draws no under-reporting conclusion from it (Check Point Research, 2026-05-13).

The chats describe initial access usually, not almost exclusively, through edge devices, by brute force, known vulnerabilities and bought access; CVE-2024-55591 is one of the CVEs the group tracks for potential use without the chats showing exploitation, no CWMP or TR-069 vector appears, ETW patching and NTDLL unhooking are locker upgrades rather than functions of the EDR-blocking tools, and the certificate-services enumeration runs through NetExec rather than certutil (Check Point Research, 2026-05-13). The 8,200 chat lines are DynaRisk's count (BankInfoSecurity, 2026-05-11), and Check Point lists ZeroPulse as a remote-access framework the group uses without describing its internals (Check Point Research, 2026-05-13).

The chats show access through Fortinet and Cisco edge devices by brute force, known vulnerabilities and bought access, NTLM relay and certificate-services abuse, tools that block EDR at start-up, ZeroPulse and Velociraptor for remote access and Cloudflare tunnels for persistence; Check Point counts about 332 leak-site victims in the first five months of 2026. A free decryptor released in April recovers files only from a memory image of the ransomware process captured while it was running.

updates.summary: The free Gentlemen decryptor released in April 2026 recovers files only from a memory image of the ransomware process captured while it ran, has no master key and predates the leak, so trying decryption before negotiating does not help most victims; capturing the running locker's memory does. The 1,570 figure is victims of one affiliate's SystemBC server from an earlier Check Point investigation, not hidden ransomware victims, and the group tracks CVE-2024-55591 among other CVEs without the chats showing exploitation. Initial access usually runs through Fortinet and Cisco edge devices by brute force, known vulnerabilities and bought access, the ETW and NTDLL tampering belongs to the locker, and the 8,200 chat lines are DynaRisk's count.

entries.headline: Ivanti's May 2026 batch fixes an authenticated Xtraction file-read and HTML-write flaw (CVSS 9.6), no exploitation known
entries.html:
ROUTINECVE-2026-8043 +2updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-8043, Ivanti Xtraction: authenticated file read and HTML write (CVSS 9.6), patched with an Endpoint Manager SQL injection to RCE and a Virtual Traffic Manager admin command injection in Ivanti's May 2026 batch

Ivanti's May 2026 security update of 2026-05-12 discloses vulnerabilities in Secure Access Client, Xtraction, Virtual Traffic Manager and Endpoint Manager (EPM), and Ivanti says it has no evidence of any of them being exploited in the wild (Ivanti, 2026-05-12); SecurityWeek counts seven flaws across the four advisories (SecurityWeek, 2026-05-13). The most severe, CVE-2026-8043, is external control of a file name in Xtraction before version 2026.2 that lets a remote authenticated attacker read sensitive files and write arbitrary HTML files to a web directory, leading to information disclosure and possible client-side attacks; Ivanti scores it 9.6, with low privileges required and a changed scope (ENISA EUVD, 2026-05-12).

The batch also fixes CVE-2026-8111, an SQL injection in the EPM web console before 2024 SU6 that lets a remote authenticated attacker achieve remote code execution, scored 8.8 (ENISA EUVD, 2026-05-12), and CVE-2026-8051, an OS command injection in Virtual Traffic Manager before 22.9r4 that lets a remote authenticated attacker with admin privileges achieve remote code execution, scored 7.2 (ENISA EUVD, 2026-05-12). CERT-FR lists the affected versions as EPM before 2024 SU6, Secure Access Client before 22.8R6, Virtual Traffic Manager before 22.9r4 and Xtraction before 2026.2 (CERT-FR, 2026-05-13).

Exposure
Any Xtraction installation before version 2026.2 is attackable by a user with a low-privilege account (ENISA EUVD, 2026-05-12); the EPM web console before 2024 SU6 by any authenticated user (ENISA EUVD, 2026-05-12); Virtual Traffic Manager before 22.9r4 only by holders of admin credentials (ENISA EUVD, 2026-05-12).
Detection
No exploitation or exploit detail is published; on Xtraction servers, file-integrity telemetry on the web directory surfaces HTML files that no release or administrator placed there, the artifact the write primitive leaves (ENISA EUVD, 2026-05-12).
Defender takeaway
Patch in the regular cycle, Xtraction first by severity: Xtraction 2026.2, EPM 2024 SU6, Virtual Traffic Manager 22.9r4 and Secure Access Client 22.8R6 (CERT-FR, 2026-05-13); Ivanti says it has no evidence of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild (Ivanti, 2026-05-12).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:20 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditactionsaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevent_dateevidenceheadlineprioritysourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitle

CVE-2026-8043 lets a remote authenticated attacker read sensitive files and write arbitrary HTML files to a web directory, leading to information disclosure and possible client-side attacks (ENISA EUVD, 2026-05-12); it is not a remote code execution flaw, and no source describes a route from the HTML write to a web shell. Endpoint Manager is affected before 2024 SU6 and fixed in 2024 SU6 (ENISA EUVD, 2026-05-12; CERT-FR, 2026-05-13). Ivanti says it has no evidence of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild (Ivanti, 2026-05-12).

With no evidence of exploitation in the wild (Ivanti, 2026-05-12), the batch is a regular-cycle patch. The batch also covered Secure Access Client, fixed in 22.8R6 (CERT-FR, 2026-05-13).

entries.headline: Dutch inspectorate finds the hacked cervical-screening lab ran no NEN 7510 audit or periodic risk assessment
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOA2

Dutch IGJ: Clinical Diagnostics labs failed NEN 7510 at the time of the July 2025 Nova breach, which reached data of about 941,000 people through an account without MFA in unmonitored legacy systems

The Dutch Health and Youth Care Inspectorate (IGJ) concluded on 2026-05-13 that the business units Clinical Diagnostics LCPL BV and NMDL BV in Rijswijk "did not meet the standard either at the time of the hack or during an inspection visit in December 2025" (translated from Dutch): among other gaps, no independent audit of information security had been carried out and processing risks had not been mapped periodically, so the company could not determine which data-security measures it needed (IGJ, 2026-05-13). The Wabvpz requires organisations working with patient data to meet NEN 7510, and IGJ says working to the norm could have reduced the likelihood of an incident like this and limited its consequences (IGJ, 2026-05-13).

Computable reports from the inspection that the company could not establish how the attackers gained access to the compromised user account, which had a 16-character password but no active multi-factor authentication, and that the legacy environments the attackers entered had dropped out of the security operations centre's monitoring through human error, because the SOC wrongly believed them inactive, so anomalous patterns in the logs went unnoticed (Computable, 2026-05-13). Data of about 941,000 people, mostly cervical-cancer screening participants, was viewed or stolen, and Computable reports that the company paid a ransom (Computable, 2026-05-13). The ransomware-as-a-service group Nova had threatened in July 2025 to leak the data, and the screening agency said the lab could not confirm that 941,000 was the full extent (GovInfoSecurity, 2025-09-03).

IGJ asked the company to demonstrate NEN 7510 compliance at short notice; under the Wabvpz it cannot impose punitive measures, while the Dutch data protection authority (AP), which is investigating under the GDPR, can, and the company says an external audit came out positive and certification is expected soon (IGJ, 2026-05-13). IGJ is using the case to call on healthcare providers to work demonstrably to NEN 7510, with a certificate or an independent assessment, and to check actively that the labs and other third parties they use comply (Computable, 2026-05-13).

Exposure
Healthcare providers in the Netherlands that process patient data are bound by NEN 7510 under the Wabvpz (IGJ, 2026-05-13), and IGJ's supervision will now look at whether they verify their labs and other suppliers (Computable, 2026-05-13).
Detection
What hid this intrusion was monitoring coverage, not missing signatures: legacy environments that were still reachable had been dropped from SOC collection as inactive, and the account used had no second factor, so the checks that would have caught it are a reconciliation of SOC log sources against systems still reachable and a review of authentication logs for accounts without multi-factor authentication (Computable, 2026-05-13).
Defender takeaway
For any organisation whose sensitive data is processed by a laboratory or other service provider, ask for an independent assessment of that provider's information security, as IGJ now expects of Dutch healthcare providers, and confirm that legacy environments holding the data are either decommissioned or inside monitoring scope (Computable, 2026-05-13).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:23 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationentitiesevidenceheadlineprioritysourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitle

IGJ asked Clinical Diagnostics to demonstrate NEN 7510 compliance at short notice rather than demanding certification, and the company reports a positive external audit with certification expected soon (IGJ, 2026-05-13). IGJ's release speaks of a data hack and an inspection visit in December 2025; it says working to the norm could have reduced the likelihood of such an incident and limited its consequences, not that the breach scale was their proximate result, and it states no relationship to ISO/IEC 27001 (IGJ, 2026-05-13). The call on all healthcare providers to prove NEN 7510 compliance, including at the labs they use, is reported by Computable from the inspection (Computable, 2026-05-13). Ransomware by Nova and the figure of 941,000 come from press reporting, and the screening agency said the lab could not confirm that this was the full extent (GovInfoSecurity, 2025-09-03).

No cited source compares NEN 7510 with Switzerland's electronic patient record rules or describes the security of Swiss providers. Computable's account of the inspection adds the access vector, a compromised account without multi-factor authentication in legacy environments that had dropped out of SOC monitoring (Computable, 2026-05-13).

Sources: IGJ · Computable · GovInfoSecurity

According to Computable, attackers used a compromised account without multi-factor authentication in legacy environments that had dropped out of SOC monitoring, and data of about 941,000 people, mostly cervical-cancer screening participants, was viewed or stolen.
