entries.headline: A Pwn Request, cache poisoning and runner-memory OIDC theft let attackers publish 84 malicious TanStack npm versions
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-45321exploitedupdatedNATOA1

Mini Shai-Hulud hits TanStack: a pull_request_target Pwn Request, Actions cache poisoning and OIDC token theft from runner memory published 84 malicious @tanstack versions with valid provenance

On 2026-05-11 between 19:20 and 19:26 UTC an attacker published 84 malicious versions across 42 @tanstack/* npm packages by chaining a pull_request_target "Pwn Request", GitHub Actions cache poisoning across the fork and base-repository trust boundary, and extraction of an OIDC token from the runner's memory; no npm token was stolen and the publish workflow itself was not modified (TanStack, 2026-05-11). StepSecurity, which detected the publishes, and Wiz attribute the wave to TeamPCP's Mini Shai-Hulud worm, which hit UiPath, Mistral AI and other npm packages the same day, though Wiz found a payload bug that leaves the malware non-functional in the @uipath and @mistralai packages (StepSecurity, 2026-05-11; Wiz, 2026-05-12). The worm's first wave had compromised four official SAP npm packages on 2026-04-29 through malicious preinstall scripts (The Register, 2026-04-30). The TanStack compromise is CVE-2026-45321, scored 9.6 (TanStack advisory, 2026-05-11), which CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-05-27 with known ransomware campaign use (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-05-27).

The chain, from TanStack's timeline (TanStack, 2026-05-11):

  1. Staging. On 2026-05-10 the attacker forked TanStack/router into a repository renamed to evade fork-list searches and committed a roughly 30,000-line bundled JavaScript payload under the history package, with a fabricated author identity and a commit message that suppressed CI on push; the post-mortem names two attacker GitHub accounts.
  2. Pwn Request. On 2026-05-11 at about 10:49 a pull request titled as a work-in-progress build simplification triggered the bundle-size and labeler workflows, both on pull_request_target, which needs no first-time-contributor approval. At 11:11 the benchmark job checked out the PR's merge ref and ran pnpm install and the bundle-size build, executing the payload.
  3. Cache poisoning. The payload wrote into the pnpm store under the key the release workflow computes, and the cache action's post-job save stored the 1.1 GB poisoned store in the base repository's cache scope; the job's read-only permissions: did not stop it, because cache writes use a runner-internal token. At 11:31 the attacker force-pushed the PR back to the main branch head, leaving a zero-file change, and closed it.
  4. Detonation. At 19:15 a re-run of the release workflow, and at 19:16 a fresh run triggered by a legitimate merge, restored the poisoned store. Attacker binaries run during the build located the Runner.Worker process, read its memory through /proc/<pid>/maps and /proc/<pid>/mem, took the OIDC token the runner mints in memory for a job with id-token: write, and posted the packages directly to the npm registry, using the same memory-dump script as the tj-actions/changed-files compromise of March 2025. Tests failed, so the workflow's own Publish Packages step was skipped.

The packages carry valid SLSA provenance tied to TanStack's release workflow; provenance proves which pipeline built a package, not that the pipeline behaved, so a compromised build step yields a validly attested malicious package (StepSecurity, 2026-05-11).

The payload. Installing an affected version resolves an optional dependency on a github: URL naming the TanStack repository, which GitHub serves from an orphan commit in the fork network; npm installs that commit's dependencies, including the Bun runtime, and runs its prepare lifecycle script, which executes a 2.3 MB obfuscated JavaScript file shipped at the tarball root and then exits with an error so npm silently discards the optional install (TanStack advisory, 2026-05-11). Behind three obfuscation layers, it queries the AWS instance metadata service with the IMDSv2 flow and the ECS credential endpoint, reads the local Vault agent, reads files from more than 100 hardcoded paths, and in CI pipes a memory-reading script to sudo python3 to pull every value the runner marks as secret (StepSecurity, 2026-05-11); NCSC-CH groups the paths as cloud credentials, SSH, Git, developer and AI tools, crypto wallets, VPN configurations, messaging apps, shell history and Kubernetes (NCSC-CH, 2026-05-12). It exfiltrates encrypted data through the Session messenger's file-upload network and through GitHub commits on branches named to look like Dependabot's, spreads by finding npm tokens that bypass two-factor checks, enumerating the maintainer's other packages and, in CI, exchanging the OIDC token for per-package publish tokens, and writes workflows disguised as CodeQL analysis that serialise all repository secrets (StepSecurity, 2026-05-11). Persistence is a Claude Code SessionStart hook, a VS Code folder-open task, and a LaunchAgent on macOS or systemd user service on Linux that checks the GitHub API every 60 seconds and deletes the user's home directory once the stolen token is revoked (NCSC-CH, 2026-05-12).

Exposure
Any developer machine or CI runner that ran npm install, pnpm install or yarn install against an affected version on 2026-05-11 (TanStack advisory, 2026-05-11). For maintainers, the same chain is open wherever a pull_request_target workflow checks out and builds fork code in a cache scope that a release job with id-token: write later restores (TanStack, 2026-05-11).
Detection
In package manifests and tarballs, an optional dependency on a github: URL pinned to a commit and a large JavaScript file at the package root that the files list does not declare; in runner process telemetry, the Bun runtime installed during npm install and python3 processes reading /proc/*/mem; in registry and repository history, two versions of one package published minutes apart and unexpected commits on Dependabot-style branches (StepSecurity, 2026-05-11). TanStack names publishes that do not come from the workflow's defined publish step as the signal to watch for (TanStack, 2026-05-11). On hosts, added Claude Code hooks, VS Code folder-open tasks and a token-monitoring LaunchAgent or systemd user service (NCSC-CH, 2026-05-12).
Defender takeaway
On any host that installed an affected version, isolate and image the machine before revoking any token, because revocation triggers the wipe (StepSecurity, 2026-05-11), then rotate the AWS, GCP, Kubernetes, Vault, GitHub, npm and SSH credentials reachable from it (TanStack, 2026-05-11). For repositories, never check out or build an untrusted pull request under pull_request_target (GitHub Security Lab, 2021-08-03); where a fork-reachable job needs a cache, use the separate restore action, which has no save step (actions/cache README); and treat npm audit signatures as proof of which pipeline built a package, not that it was clean (npm Docs; StepSecurity, 2026-05-11).
Correction21 Oct 2026 16:08 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevent_dateevidenceheadlinesectorssourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitle

Mini Shai-Hulud's first wave hit four official SAP npm packages on 2026-04-29 with malicious preinstall scripts (The Register, 2026-04-30). In the TanStack compromise no reconnaissance step is reported; the pull request added a bundled payload file that the pull_request_target benchmark job executed when it checked out and built the PR's merge ref, rather than slipping in lockfile, dependency or .github changes, and the release job never reached its publish step: tests failed, Publish Packages was skipped, and the malware published directly with the OIDC token it read from runner memory (TanStack, 2026-05-11). No npm token was needed for that publish, but the payload itself steals credentials and spreads with them (StepSecurity, 2026-05-11).

The SLSA provenance on the malicious packages is genuine, an attestation of a compromised pipeline rather than a forgery, and no source ties it to EU procurement (StepSecurity, 2026-05-11). The payload runs from the prepare script of an optional git dependency, not from postinstall (TanStack advisory, 2026-05-11), and its memory scraper runs as sudo python3, so a filter for non-root readers of /proc/<pid>/mem misses it (StepSecurity, 2026-05-11). The compromise is CVE-2026-45321, scored 9.6 (TanStack advisory, 2026-05-11) and listed by CISA as known exploited on 2026-05-27 (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-05-27). The cache action has no save: false input; restore-only caching is the separate restore action (actions/cache README), npm verifies attestations with npm audit signatures (npm Docs), and GitHub Security Lab warns that combining the pull_request_target trigger with an explicit checkout of an untrusted pull request may lead to repository compromise (GitHub Security Lab, 2021-08-03).

threat13 May 05:00Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: StepSecurity · TanStack · TanStack (GitHub Security Advisory) · Wiz · NCSC-CH Security Hub · The Register · CISA KEV catalog · GitHub Security Lab · GitHub (actions/cache README) · npm Docs
entries.summary: On 2026-05-11 between 19:20 and 19:26 UTC an attacker published 84 malicious versions of 42 @tanstack/* npm packages through TanStack's own release workflow by chaining a pull_request_target Pwn Request, GitHub Actions cache poisoning and extraction of the workflow's OIDC token from runner memory; no npm token was stolen (TanStack). The install-time payload steals cloud, GitHub, npm and SSH credentials, spreads to its victims' other packages and plants a service that wipes the home directory when the stolen token is revoked (StepSecurity, NCSC-CH). The compromise is CVE-2026-45321 (CVSS 9.6), in CISA's KEV catalog since 2026-05-27.
entries.title: Mini Shai-Hulud hits TanStack: a pull_request_target Pwn Request, Actions cache poisoning and OIDC token theft from runner memory published 84 malicious @tanstack versions with valid provenance

updates.summary: Mini Shai-Hulud first hit official SAP npm packages on 2026-04-29, and in the TanStack compromise of 2026-05-11 the fork pull request added a payload file that the pull_request_target benchmark job built; the release job's own publish step was skipped while the malware published directly with the OIDC token it read from runner memory. The provenance on the malicious packages is genuine rather than forged, the payload runs from a prepare script of an optional git dependency and its memory scraper runs under sudo. The compromise is CVE-2026-45321, scored 9.6 and in CISA's KEV catalog since 2026-05-27, and the restore-only cache action and npm audit signatures replace a cache option and a command that do not exist.

entries.headline: A PAN-OS Captive Portal overflow gives unauthenticated attackers root on exposed firewalls; Unit 42 saw tunnelling and AD enumeration afterwards
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-0300exploitedupdatedNATOA1

CVE-2026-0300: PAN-OS User-ID Authentication Portal unauthenticated root RCE, exploited by a likely state-sponsored cluster; fixed builds for every supported branch

CVE-2026-0300 is a buffer overflow in the User-ID Authentication Portal (Captive Portal) service of PAN-OS that lets an unauthenticated attacker execute code with root privileges on PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls by sending crafted packets; Prisma Access, Cloud NGFW and Panorama are not affected (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT). Palo Alto scores it CVSS 4.0 9.3 where the portal is reachable from untrusted networks and 8.7 where it is restricted to trusted internal addresses, and reports limited exploitation against portals exposed to untrusted addresses or the internet (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT). CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-05-06 (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-05-06). Fixed builds are listed for every supported branch: 12.1.4-h5 and 12.1.7; 11.2.4-h17, 11.2.7-h13, 11.2.10-h6 and 11.2.12; 11.1.4-h33, 11.1.6-h32, 11.1.7-h6, 11.1.10-h25, 11.1.13-h5 and 11.1.15; 10.2.7-h34, 10.2.10-h36, 10.2.13-h21, 10.2.16-h7 and 10.2.18-h6; older unsupported versions must move to a supported fixed version, and the advisory's table still marks 12.1.7 with an ETA of 05/28 (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT).

Unit 42 attributes the exploitation to CL-STA-1132, a cluster of likely state-sponsored activity: unsuccessful exploitation attempts began on 2026-04-09, and a week later the attackers achieved code execution and injected shellcode (Unit 42, 2026-05-07). They then cleared crash kernel messages and nginx crash entries and records, deployed the tunnelling tools EarthWorm and ReverseSocks5, enumerated Active Directory with the firewall's service-account credentials, and deleted ptrace injection evidence; on 2026-04-29 a SAML flood against the compromised device promoted a second device to active, inheriting the same internet-facing traffic, and that device was then targeted too (Unit 42, 2026-05-07).

Exposure
A PA-Series or VM-Series firewall below the fixed build for its branch on which both of Palo Alto Networks' conditions hold: the User-ID Authentication Portal is configured (Device > User Identification > Authentication Portal Settings), and an interface management profile with Response Pages enabled is attached to an L3 interface in a zone where untrusted or internet traffic can enter; restricting the portal to trusted zones and disabling Response Pages in the Interface Management Profile of every L3 interface where untrusted traffic can enter, or disabling the portal, removes the exposure (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT). Threat ID 510019 (Applications and Threats content 9097-10022) blocks the attack for Threat Prevention subscribers and needs PAN-OS 11.1 or later (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT).
Detection
On the firewall, gaps in crash and kernel logs, deleted nginx crash records, outbound tunnelling connections from the firewall, and Active Directory queries made with the firewall's service account are the behaviours Unit 42 describes; a second device promoted to active after a burst of SAML traffic is a further signal (Unit 42, 2026-05-07). Patching does not remove a foothold, so a device that was exposed before its fixed build needs a compromise check.
Update13 May 2026 05:00 UTCrun 2026-05-13-c148b9a5actionscvesevidencetagsbody

Palo Alto Networks released the first wave of fixed PAN-OS builds on 2026-05-13, covering the 12.1, 11.2, 11.1 and 10.2 branches; the advisory still lists 12.1.7 with an ETA of 2026-05-28 (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT). Prisma Access, Cloud NGFW and Panorama remain unaffected, and Threat ID 510019 remains the interim control for unpatched devices on PAN-OS 11.1 or later (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT). CISA lists the flaw in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-05-06).

Correction11 Oct 2026 14:34 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryevent_datetechniquesaffected_productscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteclassificationactionsbody

Fixed builds are now listed for every supported PAN-OS branch, so the interim mitigation is no longer the only option (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT). Unit 42's date of 2026-04-09 marks the first unsuccessful exploitation attempts; the attackers achieved code execution a week later, and Unit 42 attributes the activity to a single likely state-sponsored cluster, CL-STA-1132, with exploitation described as limited (Unit 42, 2026-05-07). Threat ID 510019 requires PAN-OS 11.1 or later (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT).

vulnerability12 May 05:00Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Palo Alto Networks PSIRT · Unit 42 · CISA KEV catalog

Unit 42 ties the limited exploitation since April to one likely state-sponsored cluster, CL-STA-1132; CISA lists it as exploited, and fixed builds now exist for every supported branch.
entries.title: CVE-2026-0300: PAN-OS User-ID Authentication Portal unauthenticated root RCE, exploited by a likely state-sponsored cluster; fixed builds for every supported branch

updates.summary: UPDATE (originally covered 2026-05-12): Palo Alto Networks released the first wave of patched PAN-OS builds on 2026-05-13 for the actively-exploited Captive Portal pre-auth RCE, covering PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1, 11.2 and 12.1 (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, last updated 2026-05-07; patch table confirmed 2026-05-13).

The title, summary and main analysis still said no fixed build had shipped; fixed builds exist for every supported branch. Unit 42's 2026-04-09 date is the first unsuccessful attempt, with code execution a week later, and Unit 42 describes one cluster and limited exploitation, not several clusters. The entry is rewritten to the current state with the two-condition exposure test, the 9.3 and 8.7 CVSS 4.0 scores, Unit 42's post-exploitation behaviours as detection guidance, a per-branch action, verbatim evidence, a rating, an ATT&CK mapping and the affected product; the KEV-deadline framing and workflow language are removed. The Detection and main-analysis sentences on the April SAML flood now use Unit 42's own description, a second device promoted to active, and the Exposure line states the advisory's two-condition test.

entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: ShinyHunters claims 275 million records from Canvas; Instructure struck an agreement with the gang after a second intrusion defaced school portals
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Instructure Canvas breach: ShinyHunters exploits a Free-for-Teacher flaw twice, defaces about 330 login portals, and Instructure reaches an agreement with the actor

Instructure detected unauthorized activity on 2026-04-29 (The Register, 2026-05-12) and disclosed a security incident on Friday, 2026-05-01 (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-03). It said the information involved covers names, email addresses, student ID numbers and messages among users of affected institutions, with no evidence that passwords, dates of birth, government identifiers or financial information were involved (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-03). ShinyHunters claimed the attack, first for "nearly 9,000 schools" and 275 million individuals (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-03), later for about 3.65 TB holding about 275 million records from about 8,800 schools (The Register, 2026-05-12). Instructure says the criminals exploited a vulnerability in its Free-for-Teacher learning system; on 2026-05-07 ShinyHunters used the same vulnerability to deface about 330 Canvas school login portals, and Instructure took Canvas into maintenance mode to contain the activity (The Register, 2026-05-12). Seven Dutch universities disconnected Canvas (NL Times, 2026-05-09), and VU Amsterdam notified the Dutch data protection authority (Techzine EU, 2026-05-08).

After ShinyHunters set a final deadline of end of day 2026-05-12 (The Register, 2026-05-12) for those affected to negotiate before the data was leaked (Infosecurity Magazine, 2026-05-11), Instructure said on 2026-05-11 that it had reached an agreement with the actor, received "digital confirmation of data destruction (shred logs)" and an assurance that no Instructure customers would be extorted as a result of the incident (Inside Higher Ed, 2026-05-11). The chairman of the US House Homeland Security Committee asked Instructure for a briefing on both intrusions (The Record, 2026-05-12). Instructure retained CrowdStrike for forensic analysis and incident response (The Register, 2026-05-12).

Defender takeaway
The agreement does not make the data safe: treat the names, email addresses, student IDs and messages of Canvas users as exposed when planning breach notifications and phishing awareness, whatever the vendor's destruction confirmation says.
Update09 May 2026 05:00 UTCrun 2026-05-09-migratedregionssectorssourcestagsbody

Instructure later attributed the intrusion to a vulnerability in its Free-for-Teacher learning system, and ShinyHunters set a pay-or-leak deadline for 2026-05-12 (The Register, 2026-05-12).

Update10 May 2026 05:00 UTCrun 2026-05-10-001entitiesprioritysourcesbody

ShinyHunters left a message on Canvas on the evening of Thursday 2026-05-07 after breaking in again (DutchNews.nl, 2026-05-08). Seven Dutch universities, VU Amsterdam, the University of Amsterdam, Erasmus University Rotterdam, Tilburg University, Eindhoven University of Technology, Maastricht University and the University of Twente, disconnected Canvas (NL Times, 2026-05-09), and VU Amsterdam reported the incident to the Dutch data protection authority (Techzine EU, 2026-05-08). After the first incident Instructure had deployed patches, increased monitoring and rotated application keys (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-03).

Update12 May 2026 05:00 UTCrun 2026-05-12-cd1ab844sectorssourcestagsbody

On 2026-05-11 Instructure said it had reached a deal with the actor and received "digital confirmation of data destruction (shred logs)", without disclosing the deal's monetary value (Inside Higher Ed, 2026-05-11). Instructure also confirmed the second intrusion of 2026-05-07, in which about 330 school login portals were defaced through the same Free-for-Teacher vulnerability (The Register, 2026-05-12). ShinyHunters had set a final deadline of end of day 2026-05-12 for individual institutions to contact it, and Instructure's statement says no customers will be extorted as a result of the incident (The Register, 2026-05-12); (Inside Higher Ed, 2026-05-11). CrowdStrike is assisting with the forensic analysis (The Register, 2026-05-12).

Update13 May 2026 05:00 UTCrun 2026-05-13-c148b9a5regionssourcesbody

Late on 2026-05-11, US House Homeland Security Committee Chairman Andrew Garbarino wrote to Instructure CEO Steve Daly requesting a briefing by 2026-05-21 on both Canvas intrusions, the volume of data accessed, containment measures and coordination with federal law enforcement and CISA (The Record, 2026-05-12); (The Register, 2026-05-12). The same evening Instructure announced its agreement with ShinyHunters (The Record, 2026-05-12). ShinyHunters' claim covers about 275 million records from about 8,800 schools (The Register, 2026-05-12).

Correction11 Oct 2026 14:19 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryevent_dateprioritytechniquessourcesverificationsourcing_noteclassificationbodyregions

ShinyHunters claims about 275 million records from about 8,800 schools; about 330 is the number of school login portals it defaced on 2026-05-07 (The Register, 2026-05-12). No source supports the earlier figures of 330 institutions in six countries or 16 million records, and the 44 Dutch institutions are names on ShinyHunters' own victim list as BNR reviewed it, not confirmed victims (NL Times, 2026-05-05); seven Dutch universities disconnected Canvas (NL Times, 2026-05-09). Instructure attributes both intrusions to a vulnerability in its Free-for-Teacher system, not to a compromised LTI integration account, and the actor is ShinyHunters; the earlier references to WorldLeaks, a EUR 3.2 million demand, a 3 GB sample and German or Dutch regulator inquiries had no source. Instructure announced its agreement with the actor on 2026-05-11 and said no customers would be extorted as a result (Inside Higher Ed, 2026-05-11).

entries.summary: ShinyHunters stole names, email addresses, student IDs and messages from Instructure's Canvas through a vulnerability in its Free-for-Teacher system, claiming about 275 million records from about 8,800 schools, then defaced about 330 school login portals through the same flaw on 2026-05-07. Seven Dutch universities disconnected Canvas. Instructure announced an agreement with the actor on 2026-05-11, and a US House committee requested a briefing.
entries.title: Instructure Canvas breach: ShinyHunters exploits a Free-for-Teacher flaw twice, defaces about 330 login portals, and Instructure reaches an agreement with the actor

updates.summary: UPDATE (originally covered 2026-05-08):

**Canvas/Instructure UPDATE; ShinyHunters claims a second intrusion despite the May 8 patch and "continued active access". Seven Dutch universities (VU Amsterdam, UvA, Erasmus, Tilburg, TU/e, Maastricht, Twente) executed emergency Canvas disconnects on/before 2026-05-09; Dutch DPA notified by VU Amsterdam.** Original 2026-05-12 extortion deadline now two days away; Instructure rotated application keys and required customer API client re-authorisation.

**Instructure paid ShinyHunters; double Canvas intrusion confirmed; per-institution leak deadline is today (2026-05-12).** Ransom acknowledged and "shred logs" received for the platform-wide dataset; a second intrusion on 2026-05-07 defaced ~330 institution portals via the same Free-for-Teacher flaw, and ShinyHunters has now set a fresh per-institution payment deadline (The Register, 2026-05-12). European universities reliant on Canvas should treat the platform-wide settlement as legally unverifiable destruction.

UPDATE (originally covered 2026-05-12): Late on 2026-05-11, US House Homeland Security Committee Chairman Andrew Garbarino sent a formal letter to Instructure CEO Steve Daly ahead of the 2026-05-12 ShinyHunters extortion deadline, demanding a briefing by 2026-05-21 on the circumstances of both Canvas intrusions …

Most of the headline figures had no source: 330 was the number of defaced login portals, not institutions; six countries, 16 million records, 44 Dutch institutions confirmed as victims and German or Dutch regulator inquiries appear nowhere (the 44 are names on the actor's own list); the actor is ShinyHunters, not WorldLeaks, and no EUR 3.2 million demand, 3 GB sample or LTI service-account vector was reported. The entry is rewritten from its sources, the earlier sections are corrected in place (dates of the second notice and the agreement, Instructure's statement that the agreement covers all customers, unsupported UK university statements and speculation removed), the dead SURF source is dropped, and the entry gains its rating and ATT&CK mapping. Priority moves from high to notable. NL Times is added as the source for the seven Dutch universities that disconnected Canvas. The agreement sentence is cited to Inside Higher Ed alone, the Dutch disconnections to NL Times, and the Free-for-Teacher attribution in the 2026-05-09 section is marked as a later statement.

entries.headline: NCSC-UK: finding vulnerabilities with AI improves nothing without a process to fix what it finds
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOA2

NCSC-UK: 10 questions to ask when using AI models to find vulnerabilities

NCSC-UK published on 2026-05-11 ten questions to answer before using an AI model to find vulnerabilities, written by its Head of Vulnerability Management Group (NCSC-UK, 2026-05-11). It warns that just finding vulnerabilities "does nothing to improve your security" and "could even make your security worse", and asks whether a process exists to receive, prioritise and fix what AI finds without overwhelming teams (NCSC-UK, 2026-05-11). Its risk questions cover information leakage, securing the infrastructure used, sandboxing the system so it can only talk to the LLM and the code base, whether to give it production access, the permissions given to the LLM, spending all the money, time and people on finding rather than fixing, terms and data-retention policies, and legality (NCSC-UK, 2026-05-11). It ties prioritisation to exploitability: of more than 40,000 CVEs assigned in 2025, CISA's catalogue tracked about 400 new ones as exploited, around 40 of them zero-days when first exploited (NCSC-UK, 2026-05-11).

Defender takeaway
Before pointing an AI model at code or infrastructure, make sure the vulnerability-management process can absorb what it finds, sandbox the system to the model and the code base, decide deliberately on production access and the permissions it gets, and start with the external attack surface, verifying results with both AI and humans (NCSC-UK, 2026-05-11).
Correction21 Oct 2026 16:09 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationevidenceheadlinesourcessummarytechniquestitle

The ten questions contain no item on false-positive overhead for defenders; the nearest is resourcing: "How can I avoid spending all my money/time/people finding vulnerabilities, and have nothing left to fix them?" (NCSC-UK, 2026-05-11). NCSC-UK's warning is that just finding vulnerabilities does nothing to improve security and could even make it worse (NCSC-UK, 2026-05-11); it does not say AI-accelerated discovery leaves an organisation worse off or criticise buying AI tools, and its data and permissions questions ask about information leakage, production access and what permissions the LLM is given, without mentioning secrets or a compromised agent.

research13 May 05:00Zsingle-source · national CERTOpen finding →
Sources: NCSC-UK

The questions cover the process for fixing what AI finds, prioritising exploitable flaws, information leakage, sandboxing, production access, the permissions given to the model, data retention and legality.

entries.action_label: New TrickMo variant hides its C2 in The Open…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: New TrickMo variant hides its C2 in The Open Network and turns infected phones into network pivots
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

TrickMo C: Android banking trojan moves its C2 onto The Open Network and turns infected phones into SOCKS5 and SSH network pivots

ThreatFabric identified a new TrickMo variant between January and February 2026 that is progressively replacing its predecessor in campaigns against banking and wallet customers in France, Italy and Austria (ThreatFabric, 2026-05-11). The on-device feature set is largely unchanged: once the user grants the accessibility-service permission the bot coerces, the operator gets overlay credential phishing, keylogging, screen recording and streaming, remote control, and SMS and notification interception that silently suppresses one-time-password messages, while the offensive code arrives as a module fetched from operator infrastructure at runtime (ThreatFabric, 2026-05-11). Campaign tags point to TikTok-themed apps delivered over Facebook (ThreatFabric, 2026-05-11); the droppers pose as adult-friendly versions of TikTok and the malware as Google Play Services (The Hacker News, 2026-05-12).

Command and control now runs over The Open Network: an embedded native TON proxy starts on a loopback port, the bot's HTTP client sends every request through it to .adnl hostnames resolved inside the TON overlay, and the few clearnet names it still needs are resolved over public DNS-over-HTTPS (ThreatFabric, 2026-05-11). New operator commands run curl, DNS lookups, ping, multi-port TCP-connect probes and traceroute from the device's network position, open SSH local-forward and remote-forward tunnels, the latter reaching into the corporate or home LAN the phone is on, and start an authenticated SOCKS5 proxy whose traffic appears to come from the victim's IP and so defeats IP-based fraud checks (ThreatFabric, 2026-05-11). The Pine hooking framework and a full set of NFC permissions are bundled but unused, which ThreatFabric reads as preparation for features delivered at runtime later (ThreatFabric, 2026-05-11).

Exposure
Android users of banking, fintech, wallet and authenticator apps in France, Italy and Austria, by the campaign tags; any corporate or home network an infected phone joins is reachable to the operator through the remote-forward tunnel (ThreatFabric, 2026-05-11).
Detection
Network-edge traffic analysis sees only encrypted TON traffic that cannot be told apart from other TON applications, and takedowns of the C2 lose effect (ThreatFabric, 2026-05-11), so the signals sit on the device and around it: in mobile-device inventories, an app presenting itself as Google Play Services that holds the accessibility-service permission (The Hacker News, 2026-05-12), and in internal network telemetry, TCP-connect sweeps, DNS lookups and traceroutes originating from a phone's address (ThreatFabric, 2026-05-11).
Defender takeaway
ThreatFabric judges domain takedowns largely ineffective against this variant and network blocking less effective (ThreatFabric, 2026-05-11), so the control point is the device: on managed Android devices, restrict app installs from outside the official store and accessibility-service grants, and handle an infected phone that has joined a corporate network as a foothold in that network as well as a fraud case. Security Affairs reports the same findings (Security Affairs, 2026-05-12).
Improvement21 Oct 2026 20:19 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

ThreatFabric's point about the TON transport is that traffic analysis at the network edge sees only encrypted TON traffic, indistinguishable from any other TON application's, and that domain takedowns lose effect because the endpoints live inside the overlay (ThreatFabric, 2026-05-11); it does not say TON shares standard internet routes, and no source describes "unusual entitlements" as a signal. The Pine hooking framework and the NFC permissions are bundled but not exercised, which ThreatFabric reads as capability reserved for features delivered at runtime later, possibly NFC-targeted, not as contactless-payment interception in development (ThreatFabric, 2026-05-11). The droppers are TikTok look-alikes delivered through Facebook campaigns (ThreatFabric, 2026-05-11; The Hacker News, 2026-05-12); no source says ads. The observable activity is on the device: accessibility-service grants to an app posing as Google Play Services, and network probes originating from a phone inside the LAN (ThreatFabric, 2026-05-11).

research13 May 05:00Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: ThreatFabric · The Hacker News · Security Affairs
entries.summary: ThreatFabric reported on 2026-05-11 a redesigned TrickMo Android banking trojan, tracked since January to February 2026 in campaigns against banking and wallet users in France, Italy and Austria, that routes its command-and-control traffic through an embedded TON proxy to .adnl endpoints, which blunts domain takedowns and network blocking. New operator commands run network reconnaissance from the phone and open SSH tunnels and an authenticated SOCKS5 proxy, giving attackers reach into the network the device is on and an exit node on the victim's IP.
entries.title: TrickMo C: Android banking trojan moves its C2 onto The Open Network and turns infected phones into SOCKS5 and SSH network pivots

updates.summary: ThreatFabric's point about TrickMo's TON transport is that edge traffic analysis cannot tell its encrypted C2 from other TON applications and that domain takedowns lose effect, not that TON shares standard internet routes. The bundled Pine framework and NFC permissions are unused and read as reserved for future runtime-delivered features rather than as contactless-payment interception in development, and the droppers are TikTok look-alikes delivered through Facebook campaigns, not ads.

entries.action_label: Microsoft's MDASH agent harness found 16 Windows…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Microsoft's MDASH agent harness found 16 Windows networking CVEs, including four Critical remote code execution flaws
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Microsoft MDASH: multi-model agentic scanning harness credited with 16 Windows networking and authentication CVEs, four of them Critical remote code execution flaws

Microsoft's Autonomous Code Security team disclosed MDASH on 2026-05-12, a harness that orchestrates more than 100 specialised agents across an ensemble of frontier and distilled models in a prepare, scan, validate, dedupe and prove pipeline: debater agents argue each finding's reachability and exploitability, and the prove stage constructs and executes triggering inputs where the bug class admits it, to prove the vulnerability exists (Microsoft, 2026-05-12). Microsoft lists 16 CVEs its engineering teams found with MDASH across the Windows network stack and adjacent services, 10 kernel-mode and 6 user-mode, most of them reachable from a network position with no credentials (Microsoft, 2026-05-12).

Four are Critical remote code execution flaws: CVE-2026-33827, a race-driven use-after-free in tcpip.sys; CVE-2026-33824, a double-free in the IKEEXT service, which runs as LocalSystem, triggered by two UDP packets; CVE-2026-41089, an unauthenticated CLDAP filter stack overflow in netlogon.dll; and CVE-2026-41096, a heap out-of-bounds flaw in dnsapi.dll triggered by a crafted UDP DNS response (Microsoft, 2026-05-12). Microsoft released the first two on 2026-04-14, scored 8.1 with high attack complexity and 9.8, both rated Exploitation Less Likely (MSRC, CVE-2026-33827; MSRC, CVE-2026-33824), and the other two on 2026-05-12, both scored 9.8, the Netlogon flaw rated Exploitation Less Likely and the DNS client flaw Exploitation Unlikely (MSRC, CVE-2026-41089; MSRC, CVE-2026-41096). The MDASH write-up describes the tcpip.sys trigger as crafted IPv4 packets carrying the Strict Source and Record Route option (Microsoft, 2026-05-12), while the advisory's FAQ describes a crafted IPv6 packet sent to a node where IPsec is enabled (MSRC, CVE-2026-33827).

Microsoft's benchmark figures are its own: all 21 vulnerabilities planted in a private test driver found with zero false positives, recall of 96% on 28 historical MSRC cases in clfs.sys and 100% on 7 in tcpip.sys, which it describes as retrospective recall on internal code with a finite case count, and an 88.45% success rate on CyberGym's 1,507 vulnerability reproduction tasks drawn from 188 OSS-Fuzz projects (Microsoft, 2026-05-12). The harness is used by Microsoft security engineering teams and tested by a small set of customers in a limited private preview (Microsoft, 2026-05-12; The Register, 2026-05-13).

Exposure
CVE-2026-33824 is reachable without credentials over UDP/500 on any host configured as an IKEv2 responder (RRAS VPN, DirectAccess, Always-On VPN infrastructure, or any machine with an inbound connection security rule); a host with the IKEEXT service but no responder policy is not vulnerable, and where a responder policy exists the service starts on the first inbound IKE packet (Microsoft, 2026-05-12). CVE-2026-41089 is attacked with a crafted network request to a Windows server acting as a domain controller (MSRC, CVE-2026-41089).
Detection
In network telemetry on UDP/500, the IKEv2 trigger Microsoft describes: an IKE_SA_INIT carrying Microsoft's "IPsec Security Realm Id" vendor-ID payload followed by a single IKEv2 fragment that reassembles immediately (Microsoft, 2026-05-12).
Defender takeaway
Confirm the April 2026 updates on IKEv2 responders and the May 2026 updates on domain controllers and other Windows hosts, prioritising the systems that expose these services, since Microsoft scores all four as exploitable over the network with no privileges required (MSRC, CVE-2026-33827; MSRC, CVE-2026-33824; MSRC, CVE-2026-41089; MSRC, CVE-2026-41096). MDASH's prove stage confirms that a bug exists by triggering it; for exploitability, Microsoft's advisory ratings are the reference (Microsoft, 2026-05-12). Where IKEv2 hosts cannot be patched at once, Microsoft's interim step is to block inbound UDP 500 and 4500 on systems that do not use IKE, or allow them only from known peer addresses, which reduces the attack surface but does not replace the update (MSRC, CVE-2026-33824).
Correction21 Oct 2026 16:01 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationevent_dateevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

Microsoft describes MDASH's prove stage as constructing and executing triggering inputs where the bug class admits it, to prove that a vulnerability exists (Microsoft, 2026-05-12); it does not say every finding was proven exploitable, and its advisories rate CVE-2026-33827, CVE-2026-33824 and CVE-2026-41089 Exploitation Less Likely and CVE-2026-41096 Exploitation Unlikely (MSRC, CVE-2026-33827; MSRC, CVE-2026-33824; MSRC, CVE-2026-41089; MSRC, CVE-2026-41096). CVE-2026-33827 and CVE-2026-33824 were patched in April 2026, not in the May update, and six of the 16 bugs are user-mode while the cohort also covers http.sys and telnet.exe, so they are not all network-stack kernel flaws (Microsoft, 2026-05-12).

Microsoft did not call the 16 CVEs a first production run, and gives no June date: the harness is already being tested by a small set of customers in a limited private preview (Microsoft, 2026-05-12). The benchmark figures come from Microsoft's blog rather than The Register, and the tcpip.sys recall covers 7 historical MSRC cases (Microsoft, 2026-05-12). No cited source describes DirectAccess or Always-On VPN deployment in Swiss or EU government estates; the IKEv2 flaw is reachable only on hosts configured as IKEv2 responders (Microsoft, 2026-05-12).

entries.headline: Centreon fixes SQL injection in eight Infra Monitoring components and command injection in MBI (CERTFR-2026-AVI-0572)
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOA2

CERTFR-2026-AVI-0572: Centreon April 2026 bulletin, SQL injection in eight components, command injection in MBI and XSS in MAP

Centreon published its April 2026 monthly security bulletin for Centreon Infra Monitoring on 2026-05-12: SQL injection through string concatenation across legacy PHP files in Anomaly Detection, Auto Discovery, AWIE, BAM, DSM, License Manager, MAP and Open Tickets (CVSS 8.8 each), command injection through a dos2unix exec call in MBI (CVSS 8.8) and an XSS in MAP through altered SVG images (CVSS 6.8), each listed with no reference identifier (Centreon, 2026-05-12). CERT-FR relayed it as CERTFR-2026-AVI-0572 with remote code execution, SQL injection and XSS as the risks, and lists no CVE identifiers (CERT-FR, 2026-05-12). The first fixed releases are Anomaly Detection 24.10.10 and 25.10.5, Auto Discovery 24.10.13 and 25.10.5, AWIE 24.10.6 and 25.10.6, BAM 24.10.14 and 25.10.5, DSM 24.10.6 and 25.10.3, License Manager 24.10.9 and 25.10.4, MAP 24.10.17 and 25.10.5, MBI 24.04.15, 24.10.17 and 25.10.5, and Open Tickets 24.10.11 and 25.10.6 (CERT-FR, 2026-05-12). Neither source states whether exploitation needs authentication or reports exploitation as of 2026-05-12 (Centreon, 2026-05-12; CERT-FR, 2026-05-12).

Exposure
Centreon installations running any of the nine listed components below the fixed release of their branch (CERT-FR, 2026-05-12); the components are installed and updated on the Central Server (Centreon, 2026-05-12).
Defender takeaway
Update the affected components on the Central Server to the fixed release of their branch, and back up any customised Open Tickets provider configuration before updating, as Centreon advises (Centreon, 2026-05-12).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:48 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationentitiesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

Centreon's bulletin lists every fix with no reference identifier and CERT-FR's advisory has no CVE section, so no CVE identifiers exist for this release (Centreon, 2026-05-12; CERT-FR, 2026-05-12). The flaws are SQL injection through string concatenation in legacy PHP files of eight components, command injection through a dos2unix exec call in MBI and an XSS through altered SVG images in MAP, each with its own fixed release per branch (CERT-FR, 2026-05-12). The Fortinet, Exim, Microsoft and SAP vulnerabilities patched the same week are separate advisories, not part of this Centreon release, and neither Centreon advisory describes Centreon's deployment in public-sector networks or the monitored-host credentials it holds (CERT-FR, 2026-05-12).

entries.headline: SPIP 4.4.14 fixes two RCE flaws, one reachable from the public area on certain nginx setups (CERTFR-2026-AVI-0564)
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOA2

CERTFR-2026-AVI-0564: SPIP before 4.4.14, two remote code execution flaws in the private area and, on certain nginx configurations, the public area

SPIP's maintenance team released SPIP 4.4.14 on 2026-05-12 to fix two security flaws, a remote code execution (RCE) flaw in the private area and an RCE flaw in the public area that is limited to the use of certain nginx configurations, reported by Louka Jacques-Chevallier (Laluka), Baptiste Rolando, Arthur Deloffre (Vozec), jvoisin and Cezame (SPIP, 2026-05-12). The bulletin states that "these flaws are not covered by the security screen" (translated from French), so SPIP's built-in screen gives no interim protection; it gives no technical detail beyond the nginx condition, and the release's change list also includes better sanitisation of HTTP_HOST and a fix to REMOTE_USER handling under nginx (SPIP, 2026-05-12). CERT-FR's CERTFR-2026-AVI-0564 lists SPIP versions before 4.4.14 as affected with remote arbitrary code execution as the risk, refers to the SPIP bulletin for the fix and names no CVE identifiers (CERT-FR, 2026-05-12).

Exposure
SPIP sites on any version before 4.4.14 (CERT-FR, 2026-05-12); the public-area flaw is reachable only on sites served with certain nginx configurations, which the bulletin does not specify (SPIP, 2026-05-12).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade SPIP to 4.4.14, directly or through spip_loader version 8.0.5; the security screen is not a mitigation for these two flaws (SPIP, 2026-05-12).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:47 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationentitiesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

SPIP's bulletin describes the public-area flaw only as limited to certain nginx configurations and names no exploit pattern, so there are no template or gadget signatures in access logs and no specific reverse-proxy location rule to audit for (SPIP, 2026-05-12). Its statement that "these flaws are not covered by the security screen" (translated from French) means the screen does not block them and the upgrade to 4.4.14 is the only fix; the bulletin counts two flaws (SPIP, 2026-05-12), and neither it nor CERT-FR gives figures on SPIP's use by ministries, universities or Swiss cantons (CERT-FR, 2026-05-12).

entries.headline: SAP patches unauthenticated code execution in Commerce Cloud and authenticated SQL injection in S/4HANA search
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-34263 +1updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-34263 and CVE-2026-34260: SAP Commerce Cloud unauthenticated code injection and S/4HANA Enterprise Search SQL injection (May 2026 Patch Day)

SAP released its May 2026 security notes on 2026-05-12, among them Note 3733064 for CVE-2026-34263 in SAP Commerce Cloud (HY_COM 2205, COM_CLOUD 2211 and 2211-JDK21) and Note 3724838 for CVE-2026-34260 in SAP S/4HANA's Enterprise Search for ABAP (SAP_BASIS 751 to 758 and 816), both rated Critical at CVSS 9.6 (SAP, May 2026); Onapsis counts seventeen new and updated notes, three of them HotNews (Onapsis, 2026-05-12). CVE-2026-34263 stems from improper Spring Security configuration that lets an unauthenticated user perform malicious input injection resulting in arbitrary server-side code execution (EUVD-2026-29372); Onapsis traces it to an overly permissive security configuration with improper rule ordering that allows malicious configuration upload and code injection (Onapsis, 2026-05-12), and SAP's vector requires user interaction (SAP, May 2026). CVE-2026-34260 lets an authenticated attacker inject SQL through user-controlled input that the application concatenates into its queries (EUVD-2026-29371); the affected code only allows reading data, so confidentiality and availability are affected but integrity is not (Onapsis, 2026-05-12). The cycle's third HotNews note, 3747787 of 2026-04-30, covers the variant of the Shai-Hulud worm that injected malicious code into SAP Cloud Application Programming npm packages available for two to four hours on 2026-04-29 (Onapsis, 2026-05-12). SAP makes no mention of exploitation in the wild (SecurityWeek, 2026-05-12).

Exposure
SAP Commerce Cloud HY_COM 2205, COM_CLOUD 2211 and 2211-JDK21 for CVE-2026-34263, and S/4HANA systems with Enterprise Search for ABAP on SAP_BASIS 751 to 758 or 816 for CVE-2026-34260 (SAP, May 2026); NCSC-CH notes that CVE-2026-34263 needs only network access to the vulnerable services, while CVE-2026-34260 needs basic authenticated access (NCSC-CH, 2026-05-12).
Defender takeaway
Apply SAP Notes 3733064 and 3724838 in the regular patch cycle, Commerce Cloud first because its flaw needs no authentication (SAP, May 2026); teams whose developers fetched SAP Cloud Application Programming npm packages on 2026-04-29 check them against HotNews Note 3747787 (Onapsis, 2026-05-12).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:50 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditactionsaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevidenceheadlineprioritysourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

CVE-2026-34260 needs authentication: it is an SQL injection through user-controlled input in S/4HANA's Enterprise Search for ABAP (EUVD-2026-29371), and because the affected code only reads data its integrity impact is none, so the reach is database reads and availability rather than full read and write (Onapsis, 2026-05-12). CVE-2026-34263 in Commerce Cloud needs no authentication but SAP's vector requires user interaction (SAP, May 2026), and its root cause is improper Spring Security configuration (EUVD-2026-29372). HotNews Note 3747787 for the SAP Cloud Application Programming npm compromise was released on 2026-04-30 (Onapsis, 2026-05-12), and none of the cited sources links either product to Swiss federal programmes or says how often Commerce Cloud deployments face the internet.

entries.headline: Exim 4.99.3 fixes an unauthenticated use-after-free in BDAT handling on GnuTLS builds (CVE-2026-45185)
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-45185updatedNATOA1

CVE-2026-45185 "Dead.Letter": Exim use-after-free in BDAT/CHUNKING on GnuTLS builds, fixed in 4.99.3

The Exim maintainers published EXIM-Security-2026-05-01.1 (CVE-2026-45185, Critical, CVSS 9.8) on 2026-05-12 after a report from Federico Kirschbaum of XBOW on 2026-05-01: when a client sends a TLS close_notify alert before a BDAT body transfer is complete and follows it with a final byte in cleartext on the same TCP connection, Exim writes into a buffer already freed during the TLS teardown and corrupts the heap, and an attacker only needs to establish a TLS connection and use the CHUNKING (BDAT) extension (Exim advisory, 2026-05-12). Exim 4.97 up to and including 4.99.2 built with USE_GNUTLS=yes are affected, OpenSSL builds are not, and 4.99.3 fixes the flaw by resetting the input-processing stack when a TLS close notification arrives during a BDAT transfer; there is no known mitigation other than upgrading (Exim advisory, 2026-05-12). XBOW's write-up places the freed memory in Exim's TLS transfer buffer, into which the still-active BDAT receive wrapper's call to ungetc() writes a single newline, and notes that GnuTLS is the default TLS library on many Debian-based distributions, including Ubuntu (XBOW, 2026-05-12). During the disclosure window an LLM guided step by step by XBOW Native produced working exploits against non-PIE builds, first without ASLR and then with ASLR, the latter running its payload through Exim's ${run} expansion, which forks bash; against the default PIE build no full exploit was reported: the researcher's side got as far as leaking a stack address, while the LLM never got as far as a leak (XBOW, 2026-05-12).

Exposure
Exim 4.97 to 4.99.x built with GnuTLS that advertise STARTTLS and CHUNKING (oss-security, 2026-05-12); XBOW worked from Exim 4.97 as it ships in default Debian-based installations, including Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (XBOW, 2026-05-12).
Detection
Process lineage on mail servers: the Exim daemon forking a shell that opens an outbound TCP connection, the path XBOW's ASLR chain used to run its payload and return data outside the SMTP session (XBOW, 2026-05-12).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade GnuTLS-built Exim to 4.99.3; the maintainers know no other mitigation (Exim advisory, 2026-05-12). OpenSSL builds need no action.
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:55 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

The LLM-built exploits covered non-PIE builds only, first without ASLR and then with ASLR; against the default PIE build the researcher's side got as far as leaking a stack address and the LLM never reached a leak, so no full exploit was reported (XBOW, 2026-05-12). The Exim maintainers state there is no known mitigation other than upgrading, so suppressing the CHUNKING advertisement is not a vendor-endorsed workaround, and their advisory, not XBOW's post, sets the CVSS 9.8 and the affected range of 4.97 up to and including 4.99.2 on builds using GnuTLS, fixed in 4.99.3 (Exim advisory, 2026-05-12). Exposure further requires STARTTLS and CHUNKING to be advertised (oss-security, 2026-05-12).

vulnerability13 May 05:00Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: XBOW · oss-security (Exim maintainers) · The Hacker News · Exim security advisory EXIM-Security-2026-05-01.1
entries.summary: Exim 4.99.3, released on 2026-05-12, fixes CVE-2026-45185 (CVSS 9.8), a remotely reachable use-after-free in the GnuTLS backend: a client that sends a TLS close_notify before a BDAT body is complete and then one cleartext byte makes Exim write into its freed TLS transfer buffer, corrupting the heap. It affects Exim 4.97 to 4.99.2 built with GnuTLS that advertise STARTTLS and CHUNKING; GnuTLS is the default TLS library on many Debian-based distributions including Ubuntu, and the only mitigation is the upgrade.

entries.headline: Fortinet fixes unauthenticated code execution in the FortiAuthenticator API and the FortiSandbox web UI
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-44277 +1updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-44277 and CVE-2026-26083: unauthenticated code execution in the Fortinet FortiAuthenticator API and the FortiSandbox web UI

CVE-2026-44277 is an improper access control flaw (CWE-284) on FortiAuthenticator's API endpoints that may let an unauthenticated attacker execute unauthorized code or commands through crafted requests; it affects FortiAuthenticator 6.5.0 to 6.5.6, 6.6.0 to 6.6.8, 8.0.0 and 8.0.2, is fixed in 6.5.7, 6.6.9 and 8.0.3, does not affect FortiAuthenticator Cloud, and can be worked around by disabling API access on exposed interfaces under Network, Interfaces, Access Rights (Fortinet FG-IR-26-128). CVE-2026-26083 is a missing authorization flaw (CWE-862) in the web UI of FortiSandbox, FortiSandbox Cloud and FortiSandbox PaaS with the same effect through HTTP requests; FortiSandbox is fixed in 4.4.9 and 5.0.2, FortiSandbox Cloud 5.0 in 5.0.6 and FortiSandbox PaaS 4.4 and 5.0 in 4.4.9 and 5.0.2, while FortiSandbox Cloud 23 and 24 and PaaS 21.3 to 23.4 must migrate to a fixed release (Fortinet FG-IR-26-136). Fortinet discovered both internally, rates each Critical with a CVSSv3 base score of 9.8 and a temporal score of 9.1, and marked neither as known exploited when it published on 2026-05-12 (Fortinet FG-IR-26-128; Fortinet FG-IR-26-136). ENISA's EUVD records carry the 9.1 figure and also list FortiAuthenticator 6.4.0 to 6.4.10 and FortiSandbox 4.2.1 to 4.2.8 as affected (EUVD-2026-29729; EUVD-2026-29550), branches for which Fortinet's advisories, as read on 2026-10-21, name no fixed release (Fortinet FG-IR-26-128; Fortinet FG-IR-26-136).

Exposure
FortiAuthenticator and FortiSandbox appliances, and FortiSandbox Cloud and PaaS instances, on the affected releases whose API or web UI an attacker can reach over the network (NCSC-CH, 2026-05-13); FortiAuthenticator Cloud is not affected (Fortinet FG-IR-26-128).
Detection
Management-interface access logs on the appliances: requests to the FortiAuthenticator API or the FortiSandbox web UI from sources outside the administrators' networks, since both flaws are reached through unauthenticated requests to those interfaces (Fortinet FG-IR-26-128; Fortinet FG-IR-26-136).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade FortiAuthenticator to 6.5.7, 6.6.9 or 8.0.3 and FortiSandbox to 4.4.9 or 5.0.2 (Cloud 5.0.6), and migrate FortiSandbox Cloud 23 and 24 and PaaS 21.3 to 23.4 to a fixed release; until FortiAuthenticator is upgraded, disable API access on its exposed interfaces (Fortinet FG-IR-26-128; Fortinet FG-IR-26-136).
Improvement21 Oct 2026 20:53 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitleevent_date

Fortinet rates both flaws at a CVSSv3 base score of 9.8 with a temporal score of 9.1 (Fortinet FG-IR-26-128; Fortinet FG-IR-26-136), and 9.1 is the figure ENISA's EUVD records carry (EUVD-2026-29729). The EUVD records also list FortiAuthenticator 6.4.0 to 6.4.10 and FortiSandbox 4.2.1 to 4.2.8 as affected (EUVD-2026-29550), branches for which Fortinet names no fixed release, and FortiSandbox Cloud 23 and 24 and PaaS 21.3 to 23.4 must migrate to a fixed release (Fortinet FG-IR-26-136). The mitigation Fortinet gives until FortiAuthenticator is upgraded is to disable API access on exposed interfaces under Network, Interfaces, Access Rights (Fortinet FG-IR-26-128).

entries.headline: BWH Hotels says attackers had access to a guest-reservation web application from October 2025 until April 2026
entries.html:
ROUTINEupdatedNATOB2

BWH Hotels (Best Western, WorldHotels, Sure Hotels): attackers had access to a guest-reservation web application for about six months

BWH Hotels, which operates more than 4,000 hotels including WorldHotels, Best Western Hotels & Resorts and Sure Hotels, told affected guests that it discovered the intrusion on 2026-04-22 and that the attackers had had access since 2025-10-14 to a web application holding guest names, email addresses, phone numbers and reservation details; payment and other financial information was not stored there, and how many guests are affected is unclear (SecurityWeek, 2026-05-12). The Register says the affected data goes back to 2025-10-14 and also includes home addresses, reservation numbers, dates of stay and special requests, that BWH took the application offline and revoked the unauthorised access, and that BWH has notified the appropriate regulatory agencies (The Register, 2026-05-11). No source states how the attackers got in, and no known cybercrime group has claimed the attack (SecurityWeek, 2026-05-12).

Defender takeaway
With no access vector disclosed there is no detection or patching decision; guests should expect scams and phishing that reuse their reservation details, the misuse BWH itself is concerned about (SecurityWeek, 2026-05-12).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:46 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditbodyclassificationconfidenceentitiesevidenceheadlineprioritysourcessourcing_notesummarytitleverificationtechniques

BWH Hotels owns the WorldHotels, Best Western Hotels & Resorts and Sure Hotels brands, and the exposed fields are names, email addresses, telephone numbers, home addresses and reservation details, with no payment or bank details involved (The Register, 2026-05-11). SecurityWeek, quoting the guest emails, says the attackers had access from 2025-10-14 until the intrusion was discovered on 2026-04-22, while The Register says the affected data goes back to 2025-10-14; neither source discloses how the attackers got in or how many guests are affected (SecurityWeek, 2026-05-12), and BWH says only that it notified the appropriate regulatory agencies (The Register, 2026-05-11).

entries.action_label: Foxconn confirms a cyberattack on North American…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Foxconn confirms a cyberattack on North American factories; Nitrogen claims 8 TB of Apple, Nvidia and other project data
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Foxconn confirms a cyberattack on some North American factories after Nitrogen claims theft of 8 TB of customer project data

Foxconn said some of its factories in North America suffered a cyberattack, that its cybersecurity team activated its response mechanism to keep production and delivery going and that the affected factories were resuming normal production; a spokesperson declined to say how many factories were hit (The Record, 2026-05-12), and Foxconn declined to confirm that any customer's information was taken (The Register, 2026-05-12). The Nitrogen ransomware gang took credit on Monday 2026-05-11 (The Record, 2026-05-12), claiming 8 TB of data comprising more than 11 million files, with confidential instructions, internal project documentation and technical drawings related to projects at Intel, Apple, Google, Dell and Nvidia, among others (The Register, 2026-05-12). Workers at the Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin campus reported a network collapse from Friday 2026-05-01, according to The Cybersec Guru as quoted by 9to5Mac, and AppleInsider reports that a Houston, Texas facility also appears to have been affected (9to5Mac, 2026-05-12). Nitrogen's ransomware is believed to have been created with a builder based on the defunct Conti ransomware, and Barracuda describes the group as first observed in 2023 (The Record, 2026-05-12); Coveware found that a coding mistake in Nitrogen's ESXi encryptor overwrites four bytes of the public key, so files are encrypted with a corrupted key that nobody, the attackers included, can decrypt (Coveware, 2026-02-02).

Exposure
Foxconn's customers, whose project documentation Nitrogen claims to hold, although Foxconn has not confirmed that any customer data was taken (The Register, 2026-05-12).
Defender takeaway
After a Nitrogen encryption of ESXi hosts, analyse the encrypted files against the specific encryptor sample before relying on a decryptor, since the encryptor Coveware examined leaves files without viable backups unrecoverable (Coveware, 2026-02-02); no access vector is public, so the incident changes no patching or detection decision.
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:56 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationconfidenceevidenceheadlineprioritysourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitleentities

Foxconn's statement confirms that some of its North American factories suffered a cyberattack and are resuming normal production; it does not name sites, a start time or how long production stopped, and Foxconn declined to say how many factories were hit or to confirm that customer data was taken (The Record, 2026-05-12; The Register, 2026-05-12). Wisconsin, Ohio, Texas, Virginia, Indiana and several sites in Mexico are where Foxconn has factories, and Foxconn declined to say how many were impacted (The Record, 2026-05-12); the Mount Pleasant outage from 2026-05-01 comes from workers quoted by The Cybersec Guru, and Houston from AppleInsider (9to5Mac, 2026-05-12). Coveware's finding concerns Nitrogen's ESXi encryptor, whose bug leaves files unrecoverable even for the attackers, and its advice is to analyse encrypted files against the specific malware sample before assuming they can or cannot be recovered (Coveware, 2026-02-02).

Workers at the Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin plant reported a network outage from 2026-05-01, and Coveware has documented a bug in Nitrogen's ESXi encryptor that leaves files unrecoverable even by the attackers.

entries.action_label: GTIG finds a criminal zero-day exploit it believes…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: GTIG finds a criminal zero-day exploit it believes was built with AI; its discovery may have prevented mass exploitation
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

GTIG AI Threat Tracker (May 2026): an AI-developed zero-day 2FA bypass prepared for mass exploitation, AI decoy code in Russia-nexus malware and PROMPTSPY's Gemini agent

Google Threat Intelligence Group's AI Threat Tracker of 2026-05-11, drawn from Mandiant incident response engagements, Gemini and GTIG's own research, follows its February 2026 report on AI-related threat activity (GTIG, 2026-05-11).

An AI-developed zero-day prepared for mass exploitation

GTIG observed prominent cybercrime actors partnering to plan a mass vulnerability-exploitation operation around a zero-day exploit, implemented in a Python script, that bypasses two-factor authentication on a popular open-source, web-based system administration tool; GTIG worked with the vendor to disclose the flaw and disrupt the activity, and says its counter-discovery may have prevented the exploit's use (GTIG, 2026-05-11). The bypass requires valid user credentials and stems from a high-level semantic logic flaw, a trust assumption the developer hardcoded, rather than from memory corruption or input sanitisation (GTIG, 2026-05-11). GTIG does not believe Gemini was used but has high confidence that an AI model supported the discovery and weaponisation, citing abundant educational docstrings, a hallucinated CVSS score and a textbook Pythonic structure with detailed help menus and a clean _C ANSI colour class (GTIG, 2026-05-11). Google did not name the tool (The Hacker News, 2026-05-11). Contradiction: The Hacker News calls this the first time AI was put to use in the wild for exploit generation (The Hacker News, 2026-05-11), whereas GTIG says the planned mass exploitation may have been prevented (GTIG, 2026-05-11).

State actors using AI for vulnerability research and infrastructure

UNC2814 prompted Gemini with expert security personas to support vulnerability research into embedded targets including TP-Link firmware and Odette File Transfer Protocol (OFTP) implementations, and APT45 sent thousands of repetitive prompts that recursively analyse different CVEs and validate proof-of-concept exploits (GTIG, 2026-05-11). APT27 used Gemini to develop a fleet-management application likely meant for an operational relay box network, with the hop count hardcoded to three and mobile Wi-Fi and router devices among the supported types (GTIG, 2026-05-11). Actors also prompt models for the organisational hierarchies and third-party relationships of large enterprises to tailor phishing lures, one tried to identify the exact computer model a high-value target used, and a suspected PRC-nexus actor ran the agentic tools Hexstrike and Strix against a Japanese technology firm and an East Asian cybersecurity platform (GTIG, 2026-05-11).

Malware with AI-generated decoys and an AI-driven Android backdoor

Russia-nexus activity against Ukrainian organisations delivers CANFAIL and LONGSTREAM, which use LLM-generated decoy code to obfuscate their malicious functionality: CANFAIL's source carries LLM comments labelling unused filler blocks, and LONGSTREAM queries the system's daylight-saving status 32 times to pad the script with benign-looking activity (GTIG, 2026-05-11). PROMPTFLUX and HONESTCUE, which call the Gemini API to generate or obfuscate code, featured in GTIG's earlier reports (GTIG, 2026-05-11). The Android backdoor PROMPTSPY, first identified by ESET, runs an agent module that serialises the visible user interface through the Accessibility API, sends it to the gemini-2.5-flash-lite model in an HTTP POST and turns the JSON reply into simulated taps and swipes; it can replay captured PINs or lock patterns, lays an invisible overlay over the uninstall button and can rotate its Gemini API keys and VNC relay through its C2 (GTIG, 2026-05-11).

Pooled LLM access and attacks on AI components

UNC6201 tried a public script that registers and immediately cancels premium LLM accounts, and UNC5673, a PRC-nexus cluster with notable overlaps with TEMP.Hex that has targeted government sectors mainly in South and Southeast Asia, uses Claude-Relay-Service and CLI-Proxy-API to pool Gemini, Claude and OpenAI accounts (GTIG, 2026-05-11). TeamPCP (UNC6780) gained initial access through compromised PyPI packages and malicious pull requests to GitHub repositories including those of Trivy, Checkmarx, LiteLLM and BerriAI, embedded the SANDCLOCK credential stealer to extract AWS keys and GitHub tokens from build environments and monetised them with ransomware and data-theft extortion groups; GTIG adds that the LiteLLM compromise could expose considerable AI API secrets (GTIG, 2026-05-11).

Exposure
The zero-day needs valid user credentials on an administration tool GTIG does not name (GTIG, 2026-05-11); build environments that pulled the TeamPCP-compromised Trivy, Checkmarx, LiteLLM or BerriAI components held the AWS keys and GitHub tokens SANDCLOCK went after (GTIG, 2026-05-11).
Detection
For exploit scripts under triage, GTIG's markers of LLM authorship are dense educational docstrings, a hallucinated CVSS score and a textbook structure with help menus and ANSI colour classes; on Android, PROMPTSPY's trace is an app posting accessibility-derived UI dumps to the Gemini API over HTTP (GTIG, 2026-05-11).
Defender takeaway
The unnamed zero-day gives no patch or hunt to act on; the decision falls on build pipelines that consumed the compromised Trivy, Checkmarx, LiteLLM or BerriAI components, which treat the AWS keys and GitHub tokens those environments held as stolen, and, where LiteLLM ran, the AI API secrets GTIG says its compromise could expose (GTIG, 2026-05-11).
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:41 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationentitiesevidenceheadlineprioritysourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

GTIG reports the first zero-day exploit it believes was developed with AI, prepared by criminals for a planned mass-exploitation event that its counter-discovery may have prevented, not an exploit confirmed in use in the wild; the 2FA bypass also requires valid user credentials (GTIG, 2026-05-11). CANFAIL and LONGSTREAM do not call an LLM at runtime: they carry LLM-generated decoy code to obfuscate their functionality, and the report's example of malware driven by an LLM at runtime is the Android backdoor PROMPTSPY (GTIG, 2026-05-11). UNC5673 overlaps with TEMP.Hex rather than being it, and uses relay tooling to pool LLM accounts; the report does not describe stolen LLM API keys as a primary objective or a criminal market for them, and its only point on AI API secrets is that the LiteLLM compromise could expose them (GTIG, 2026-05-11). TeamPCP entered through compromised PyPI packages and malicious pull requests to GitHub repositories, and embedded SANDCLOCK to take AWS keys and GitHub tokens from build environments (GTIG, 2026-05-11).

Sources: Google Threat Intelligence Group · The Hacker News · Help Net Security · SecurityWeek · The Register
entries.summary: Google Threat Intelligence Group's AI Threat Tracker of 2026-05-11 reports the first zero-day exploit it believes was developed with AI: a Python 2FA bypass for a popular open-source web-based system administration tool that needs valid credentials, which criminals planned to use in mass exploitation before GTIG's coordinated disclosure may have prevented it. The report also documents LLM-generated decoy code in the Russia-nexus CANFAIL and LONGSTREAM malware, the Android backdoor PROMPTSPY driving devices through Gemini, PRC and DPRK actors using Gemini for vulnerability research, pooled LLM access, and TeamPCP's supply-chain compromises of AI components.
entries.title: GTIG AI Threat Tracker (May 2026): an AI-developed zero-day 2FA bypass prepared for mass exploitation, AI decoy code in Russia-nexus malware and PROMPTSPY's Gemini agent

updates.summary: GTIG reports a zero-day exploit it believes was developed with AI that criminals planned to use in mass exploitation and that its disclosure may have prevented, not one confirmed in use in the wild; it needs valid credentials. CANFAIL and LONGSTREAM embed LLM-generated decoy code as obfuscation rather than calling an LLM at runtime, PROMPTSPY is the report's AI-driven malware, and UNC5673 pools LLM accounts; the report ties neither stolen LLM keys nor SANDCLOCK to a criminal market for AI access, and TeamPCP's entry points were compromised PyPI packages and malicious pull requests.

entries.action_label: A rogue Checkmarx Jenkins AST plugin build that…
entries.classification_html: NATOA2
entries.headline: A rogue Checkmarx Jenkins AST plugin build that hunts credentials was live for about 31 hours; TeamPCP claimed it
entries.html:
HIGHupdatedNATOA2

Checkmarx Jenkins AST plugin backdoored: rogue build 2026.5.09 swept build hosts for credentials on 2026-05-09/10, the third wave of malicious Checkmarx artifacts since March (TeamPCP claimed)

On Saturday 2026-05-09 a rogue build, version 2026.5.09, of the Checkmarx Jenkins AST plugin was uploaded to repo.jenkins-ci.org outside the plugin's release pipeline; it broke the plugin's version scheme and had no git tag or GitHub release (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-11). Checkmarx says an external service account modified the plugin and published it to the Jenkins Marketplace, that the malicious window ran from 2026-05-09 01:25 UTC to 2026-05-10 08:47 UTC, and that the attacker used access obtained in the March incident, which began with credentials taken in the Trivy supply-chain attack on 2026-03-19 (Checkmarx, updated 2026-07-06). It is the third wave of malicious Checkmarx artifacts after GitHub Actions and Open VSX extensions on 2026-03-23 and a KICS Docker image, VS Code and DevAssist extensions and a GitHub Action on 2026-04-22 (Checkmarx, updated 2026-07-06). The payload determines the operating system (Windows, Linux or macOS), then walks a list of file paths for common applications on that system looking for credentials, with crypto wallets, VPNs, AWS and GitHub among the targets; Checkmarx had found no references to Jenkins in it, and Mandiant found no threat-actor access to the Checkmarx One SaaS environment (Checkmarx, updated 2026-07-06).

TeamPCP claimed the compromise (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-11), and researcher Adnan Khan and SOCRadar report that the group gained access to the plugin's GitHub repository and renamed it "Checkmarx-Fully-Hacked-by-TeamPCP-and-Their-Customers-Should-Cancel-Now", with the description "Checkmarx fails to rotate secrets again. with love – TeamPCP" (The Hacker News, 2026-05-11). Google Threat Intelligence Group tracks TeamPCP as UNC6780 and says that in the late-March compromises (Trivy, Checkmarx, LiteLLM, BerriAI) the group embedded the SANDCLOCK credential stealer to extract cloud secrets such as AWS keys and GitHub tokens from build environments (GTIG, 2026-05-11).

Exposure
Any Jenkins instance that installed or updated the Checkmarx AST plugin to build 2026.5.09 during the malicious window (SOCRadar, 2026-05-11); Checkmarx names 2.0.13-829.vc72453fa_1c16 of 2025-12-17 or earlier and the clean replacements 2.0.13-848.v76e89de8a_053 and 2.0.13-847.v08c0072b_2fd5 as safe (Checkmarx, updated 2026-07-06).
Detection
In Jenkins plugin inventories and update history, the checkmarx-ast-scanner plugin at version 2026.5.09; on hosts that ran it, file-access telemetry showing the build process reading the credential files of wallets, VPN clients, AWS and GitHub, which is what the payload's path sweep produces (Checkmarx, updated 2026-07-06). Checkmarx also advises restricting CI runner egress to an allowlist and monitoring outbound connections for unexpected domains (Checkmarx, updated 2026-07-06).
Defender takeaway
Where a pipeline ran build 2026.5.09, rotate all credentials that pipeline had access to, as Checkmarx recommends (Checkmarx, updated 2026-07-06), and investigate for lateral movement or persistence (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-11). Checkmarx's standing advice holds beyond this build: pin to specific SHAs rather than mutable tags and treat CI runner credentials as short-lived and tightly scoped (Checkmarx, updated 2026-07-06).
Correction21 Oct 2026 15:57 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesentitiesevent_dateevidenceheadlinekindregionssourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitle

No CVE covers the rogue plugin build: CVE-2026-33634 is the Trivy flaw in which a threat actor used compromised credentials on 2026-03-19 to publish a malicious Trivy release and move the trivy-action tags to credential-stealing code (GitHub Advisory Database, 2026-03-21), the attack Checkmarx names as the source of the attacker's access (Checkmarx, updated 2026-07-06). No source names SANDCLOCK as the Jenkins payload; GTIG uses the name for the stealer of the late-March compromises and describes it extracting cloud secrets such as AWS keys and GitHub tokens, not LLM API keys (GTIG, 2026-05-11). Checkmarx lists crypto wallets, VPNs, AWS and GitHub among the applications the payload targets, and Mandiant found no threat-actor access to the Checkmarx One SaaS environment (Checkmarx, updated 2026-07-06).

The earlier waves were GitHub Actions and Open VSX extensions in March and the KICS Docker image with updated extensions and a GitHub Action in April (Checkmarx, updated 2026-07-06). PCPJack is a separate cloud worm whose first act is to evict TeamPCP tooling (SentinelLABS, 2026-05-07), and no cited source links it to the plugin. The defacement renamed the plugin's GitHub repository, not the build (The Hacker News, 2026-05-11), and exposure did not depend on auto-update: any instance that pulled build 2026.5.09 during the window installed the compromised plugin (SOCRadar, 2026-05-11).

Sources: The Hacker News · Checkmarx · BleepingComputer · SOCRadar · Google Threat Intelligence Group · GitHub Advisory Database (Aqua Security Trivy) · SentinelLABS
entries.summary: A modified build 2026.5.09 of the Checkmarx Jenkins AST plugin, published to the Jenkins Marketplace outside the plugin's release pipeline, was live from 2026-05-09 01:25 to 2026-05-10 08:47 UTC; its payload walks an OS-specific list of file paths looking for credentials of crypto wallets, VPNs, AWS and GitHub (Checkmarx). Checkmarx says the attacker reused access obtained in the March 2026 Trivy compromise, and TeamPCP claimed the attack, the third wave of malicious Checkmarx artifacts since late March. Checkmarx recommends rotating every credential a pipeline that ran the build could reach.
