entries.headline: A German court found a phishing victim not grossly negligent after a bank-branded letter, a cloned portal and a call led her to enrol the attackers' device
entries.html:
ROUTINEupdatedNATOB2

Berlin court orders Apobank to refund EUR 218,000 lost to a letter, QR-code and phone scam that enrolled the attackers' own device

Landgericht Berlin II ruled on 2026-04-22 (38 O 293/25) that Apobank may not refuse to refund about EUR 218,000 on grounds of gross negligence: a bank-branded letter asked the customer to register a new security procedure, its QR code led to a cloned banking portal, a caller posing as the bank guided her through the process, and photographing a QR code let the attackers enrol their own device; the judgment is not yet final and the customer bears only the EUR 50 statutory share (Borncity, 2026-05-09). Beyond the holding, the chamber remarked that the login and the attackers' new-device registration came from entirely different IP addresses and providers and that the bank did not block this discrepancy automatically (heise online, 2026-05-08).

Contradiction: Borncity has a QR code in the letter leading to the manipulated page (Borncity, 2026-05-09), while heise reports that the customer was asked to set up two-factor authentication during her usual login through her browser's favourites bar (heise online, 2026-05-08).

Defender takeaway
The attack's decisive step was a device enrolment authorised by the victim, so the control point is the enrolment itself: a new authenticator registered from a network or provider different from the session that requested it deserves a hold and an out-of-band confirmation (heise online, 2026-05-08).
Correction11 Oct 2026 14:33 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-auditkindtitleheadlinesummaryevent_dateprioritytagsregionssectorstechniquessourcesclassificationbody

The court's holding is that the customer was not grossly negligent, so the bank must refund the loss (Borncity, 2026-05-09); its comments on the IP and provider mismatch were remarks beyond the decision, which the claimant's lawyer called technically still amateurish (heise online, 2026-05-08). No cited source mentions PSD2 or a duty to trigger strong customer authentication, and the judgment is described as not yet final rather than under appeal.

entries.summary: Landgericht Berlin II ruled on 2026-04-22 (38 O 293/25, not yet final) that Apobank must refund about EUR 218,000 because its customer was not grossly negligent: a bank-branded letter with a QR code led to a cloned banking portal, a caller posing as the bank guided her, and photographing a QR code enrolled the attackers' own device.
entries.title: Berlin court orders Apobank to refund EUR 218,000 lost to a letter, QR-code and phone scam that enrolled the attackers' own device

updates.summary: The court did not impose a PSD2 duty to run IP analytics or trigger strong authentication; it held the customer not grossly negligent and remarked, beyond the holding, that the bank could have blocked the device registration given the IP and provider mismatch. No appeal is reported, only that the judgment is not yet final; the Swiss and public-sector generalisation and the law-enforcement tag had no basis, and the unreadable law-firm source is replaced by Borncity. The QR-code device-enrolment step is added, with a rating, an ATT&CK mapping and priority routine. A contradiction line records that heise has the customer reaching the fake prompt through her usual login rather than a QR code.

entries.headline: Kaspersky details an xrdp pre-auth stack overflow fixed since January; exploitation of canary-protected builds needs a separate leak
entries.html:
ROUTINECVE-2025-68670updatedNATOA2

CVE-2025-68670: xrdp pre-authentication stack overflow (CVSS 9.1), fixed in 0.10.5 in January; canary-protected builds need a second flaw to exploit

The xrdp project published advisory GHSA-rwvg-gp87-gh6f on 2026-01-27: xrdp before 0.10.5 contains an unauthenticated stack-based buffer overflow in the processing of user domain information during the connection sequence, rated critical with CVSS 3.1 9.1, which could let a remote attacker execute arbitrary code (xrdp, 2026-01-27). The impact is lessened where xrdp was built with stack canary protection, because a second vulnerability would then be needed to leak the canary value (xrdp, 2026-01-27). Kaspersky researchers, who reported the flaw on 2025-12-05, published their technical analysis on 2026-05-08: the vulnerable function copies a domain name of up to 512 bytes into a 256-byte stack buffer, the maintainers fixed it in 0.10.5 and backported the patch to 0.9.27 and 0.10.4.1, and Kaspersky's proof of concept stops at the canary check (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-08). No source reports exploitation.

Exposure
Xrdp servers before 0.10.5 other than the 0.9.27 and 0.10.4.1 backport releases (Kaspersky Securelist). Running xrdp -v shows the compiler flags; -fstack-protector, -fstack-protector-strong or -fhardened indicate canary protection, which the project says not to rely on in production (xrdp, 2026-01-27).
Defender takeaway
A patch-cycle upgrade rather than an emergency: pre-authentication reach makes it worth closing on any xrdp host reachable from untrusted networks, but canary-protected builds need an additional leak primitive (xrdp, 2026-01-27).
Correction11 Oct 2026 14:22 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryevent_dateprioritycvestechniquessourcesclassificationactionsbodyverification

The xrdp project disclosed and fixed this flaw on 2026-01-27 and scores it CVSS 9.1; builds with stack canary protection need a second vulnerability to leak the canary before the overflow can be exploited (xrdp, 2026-01-27). Kaspersky's article of 2026-05-08 is the reporting researchers' technical analysis, not the first disclosure (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-08). The table of other CVEs that closed the earlier text belonged to unrelated findings and carried values their own sources contradict.

Sources: xrdp project · Kaspersky Securelist

Kaspersky published its technical analysis on 2026-05-08. Builds compiled with stack canary protection need a second vulnerability to leak the canary; no exploitation is reported.
entries.title: CVE-2025-68670: xrdp pre-authentication stack overflow (CVSS 9.1), fixed in 0.10.5 in January; canary-protected builds need a second flaw to exploit

updates.summary: The flaw was not newly disclosed on 2026-05-08: the xrdp project published its advisory and fix on 2026-01-27, and Kaspersky's article of 2026-05-08 is the researchers' later technical analysis. The entry omitted the project's CVSS 9.1 and the precondition that canary-protected builds need a second vulnerability, asserted a deployment breadth no source gives, and ended with a table of seven unrelated CVEs carrying wrong values; the table, the generic VPN action and the unsourced deployment claim are removed. The project advisory becomes the primary source, with a rating, an ATT&CK mapping and priority routine.

entries.headline: Unauthenticated directory traversal in Spring Cloud Config Server; open-source fixes only for the 4.3 and 5.0 branches
entries.html:
ROUTINECVE-2026-40982updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-40982: Spring Cloud Config Server unauthenticated directory traversal (CVSS 9.1); open-source fixes only for 4.3.x and 5.0.x

Spring published CVE-2026-40982 on 2026-05-06: a request with a specially crafted URL can lead to a directory traversal in the spring-cloud-config-server module, which serves text and binary files to applications (Spring, 2026-05-06). The flaw affects 5.0.0 to 5.0.2, 4.3.0 to 4.3.2, 4.2.0 to 4.2.6, 4.1.0 to 4.1.9 and 3.1.13 and earlier; open-source fixes are 5.0.3 and 4.3.3, while 4.2.7, 4.1.10 and 3.1.14 are available through enterprise support only, and Spring lists no other mitigation (Spring, 2026-05-06). HeroDevs gives the CVSS 3.1 score as 9.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N), unauthenticated and low-complexity (HeroDevs, 2026-05-08). HeroDevs first says an attacker can read or write arbitrary files the server process can access, then that the Config Server's resource endpoints are read-only, so the direct impact is information disclosure of secrets, credentials or any other file the server process can read, although the vector scores integrity High (HeroDevs, 2026-05-08). CERT-FR relayed the advisory together with the companion flaws CVE-2026-40981, CVE-2026-41002 and CVE-2026-41004 (CERT-FR, 2026-05-07). No source reports exploitation.

Exposure
Config Server instances on the affected versions that untrusted clients can reach; in typical Spring Cloud deployments the Config Server centralizes secrets for an entire fleet of microservices, which is what the disclosure exposes (HeroDevs, 2026-05-08).
Defender takeaway
A patch-cycle item for most estates, because, in analyst judgement, Config Server usually serves internal clients only; any instance that was reachable from outside its trust zone should be patched first and the secrets it serves rotated.
Correction11 Oct 2026 14:24 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryevent_dateprioritytagsregionscvesaffected_productstechniquessourcesclassificationactionsbody

CVE-2026-40982 scores CVSS 9.1, not 9.8 (HeroDevs, 2026-05-08), and Spring describes a directory traversal, not code execution (Spring, 2026-05-06). Open-source fixes exist only for the 5.0 and 4.3 branches; the 4.2, 4.1 and 3.1 fixes are available through enterprise support only (Spring, 2026-05-06).

Improvement21 Oct 2026 12:08 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1149Z-auditbodyheadline

HeroDevs states that the Config Server's resource endpoints are read-only, so the direct impact of the traversal is information disclosure: secrets, credentials or any other file the server process can read, which in typical deployments includes the secrets the Config Server centralizes for a fleet of microservices (HeroDevs, 2026-05-08). The same post also says an attacker can read or write arbitrary files, and the CVSS vector it gives scores integrity High (HeroDevs, 2026-05-08); Spring's advisory describes only a directory traversal (Spring, 2026-05-06).

entries.headline: LiteLLM SQL injection: attackers targeted stored credentials 36 hours after disclosure; patching does not undo exposure
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-42208exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-42208: LiteLLM Proxy pre-authentication SQL injection in API-key verification, first exploitation attempt 36 hours after the advisory, CISA KEV-listed (CVSS 4.0 9.3)

LiteLLM's advisory GHSA-r75f-5x8p-qvmc, published on 2026-04-20, describes a SQL injection in the proxy's API-key verification: the caller-supplied value was not passed to the database as a separate parameter, and the flaw is fixed in 1.83.7 (LiteLLM, 2026-04-20). Bishop Fox confirmed that versions 1.81.16 through 1.83.6 are exploitable without credentials from any LLM API route, through the Authorization: Bearer value reaching PrismaClient.get_data(); the response is always the same HTTP 401, so exploitation runs over a time-based blind channel using PostgreSQL's pg_sleep() (Bishop Fox, 2026-05-06). On a stock Docker Compose deployment with the Postgres sidecar, the application database user is a superuser, which raises the impact beyond reading metadata (Bishop Fox, 2026-05-06). Virtual keys are stored as SHA-256 hashes, but the provider credentials are stored for use (Bishop Fox, 2026-05-06) (Sysdig, 2026-04-27).

Sysdig observed the first exploitation attempt 36 hours and seven minutes after the advisory reached the global database, with queries against LiteLLM_VerificationToken (virtual keys, including the master key), litellm_credentials (stored upstream provider credentials) and litellm_config (Sysdig, 2026-04-27). Sysdig saw no follow-through: no authenticated calls with exfiltrated keys, no virtual-key minting through /key/generate and no reuse of provider credentials, so its finding is the speed and precision of the enumeration rather than a confirmed compromise; it still advises treating any internet-facing instance on a vulnerable version as compromised (Sysdig, 2026-04-27). CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-05-08 (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-05-08). The published workaround, general_settings.disable_error_logs: true, closes only one of the two code paths that reach the vulnerable query (Bishop Fox, 2026-05-06).

Exposure
LiteLLM Proxy 1.81.16 through 1.83.6 with the default PostgreSQL backend, reachable by untrusted clients (Bishop Fox, 2026-05-06).
Detection
In proxy access logs, HTTP 401 responses to LLM API routes that take several seconds instead of under 100 milliseconds, from bearer values that are not sk- virtual keys, and proxy log errors stating that a virtual key was expected to start with sk- (Bishop Fox, 2026-05-06). LiteLLM provides a helper to review PostgreSQL query history for the injection (LiteLLM, 2026-04-29).
Defender takeaway
Upgrading stops new extraction but not the use of keys already taken: any instance exposed during the window needs its stored provider credentials rotated (Sysdig, 2026-04-27).
Correction11 Oct 2026 14:25 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryevent_datetagscvesaffected_productstechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_noteclassificationactionsbody

Sysdig, not Bishop Fox or LiteLLM, reported the attackers' queries against LiteLLM_VerificationToken, litellm_credentials and litellm_config, and the first attempt came 36 hours and seven minutes after the advisory (Sysdig, 2026-04-27); no source gives 26 hours. The flaw is a SQL injection in the key lookup (LiteLLM, 2026-04-20), and Bishop Fox's analysis is dated 2026-05-06 (Bishop Fox, 2026-05-06).

Improvement21 Oct 2026 12:09 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1149Z-audittitlesummarybodyevidenceheadline

Sysdig's observation was an exploitation attempt without follow-through: it saw no authenticated calls with exfiltrated keys, no virtual-key minting through /key/generate and no reuse of provider credentials, and calls its finding "the speed and precision of the schema-enumeration attempt, not a confirmed compromise" (Sysdig, 2026-04-27). Sysdig still advises treating any internet-facing instance on a vulnerable version as compromised and rotating every virtual key, master key and provider credential it stores (Sysdig, 2026-04-27).

vulnerability09 May 05:00Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: LiteLLM (BerriAI) · Sysdig · Bishop Fox · LiteLLM · CISA KEV catalog

Sysdig saw the first exploitation attempt 36 hours after the advisory, with queries against the tables holding virtual keys, stored provider credentials and proxy configuration, but no follow-on use of extracted keys; CISA added it to its KEV catalog on 2026-05-08.
entries.title: CVE-2026-42208: LiteLLM Proxy pre-authentication SQL injection in API-key verification, first exploitation attempt 36 hours after the advisory, CISA KEV-listed (CVSS 4.0 9.3)

updates.summary: Bishop Fox's analysis is dated 2026-05-06, not 2026-04-30, and the three targeted tables come from Sysdig's exploitation observation, which was uncited. Exploitation began about 36 hours after the advisory, not 26; the flaw is a SQL injection, not an authentication bypass; and the evidence record quoted the entry itself. The entry is rewritten with the LiteLLM advisory as primary source, Sysdig's observation, the affected range and the partial workaround, labelled exposure and detection guidance, a rotation action, a rating and an ATT&CK mapping.

Sysdig's 36-hour observation is now described as Sysdig describes it, an exploitation attempt with no follow-on use of extracted keys and no confirmed compromise; Sysdig's advice to treat exposed instances as compromised and rotate their keys stands.

entries.headline: Have I Been Pwned loads about 197,000 Zara customer emails after ShinyHunters leaked data it says came from Anodot tokens against BigQuery
entries.html:
ROUTINEupdatedNATOB3

Zara customer emails exposed through a former Inditex technology provider; ShinyHunters claims Anodot token abuse and leaks the data

Inditex says databases hosted by a former technology provider, holding information about business relationships with customers in different markets, were accessed, and that customers' names, phone numbers, addresses, credentials and payment information were not; it has notified the relevant authorities but has not named the provider or attributed the breach (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-08). Have I Been Pwned found about 197,000 unique email addresses with product SKUs, order IDs and the market each support ticket originated in (Have I Been Pwned). ShinyHunters claims it stole the data with Anodot authentication tokens used against BigQuery and leaked a 140 GB archive (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-08); Have I Been Pwned describes the group's publication as a terabyte allegedly including 95 million support-ticket records (Have I Been Pwned).

Defender takeaway
The claimed path is a third-party analytics platform's token reaching a cloud data warehouse, so the control is the scope and lifetime of tokens granted to analytics providers, including former ones, whose access should be revoked when the relationship ends (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-08).
Correction11 Oct 2026 14:33 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryprioritytagsregionstechniquessourcesverificationclassificationbody

Inditex confirms only that a former technology provider's databases were accessed (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-08); the analytics-platform route is ShinyHunters' claim about Anodot tokens (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-08). The email, order and support-ticket fields come from Have I Been Pwned's analysis, and the records concern customers in different markets, and no source limits them to the EU (Have I Been Pwned) (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-08). The size of the leak differs between sources, 140 GB (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-08) against about a terabyte (Have I Been Pwned).

entries.action_label: Trojanised, validly signed DAEMON Tools installers…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Trojanised, validly signed DAEMON Tools installers ran a profiler on thousands of machines and a backdoor on about a dozen machines
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

DAEMON Tools Lite supply-chain compromise: signed installers deliver a profiler worldwide, with a backdoor and QUIC RAT reserved for a dozen targets in Russia, Belarus and Thailand

Kaspersky found that DAEMON Tools installers distributed from the product's legitimate website and signed with the developer's certificates had been trojanised from 2026-04-08: in versions 12.5.0.2421 to 12.5.0.2434 the helper binaries DTHelper.exe, DiscSoftBusServiceLite.exe and DTShellHlp.exe, signed by AVB Disc Soft, were compromised, and version 12.6.0.2445 no longer contains the malicious behaviour (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-05). At startup the trojanised binaries activate a backdoor that sends GET requests to a domain typosquatting the vendor's download site; when the server replies with a shell command, it runs through cmd.exe, which in the observed cases ran PowerShell to download an executable into C:\Windows\Temp and execute it, the first payload being a .NET information collector (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-05). Kaspersky saw several thousand infection attempts in more than 100 countries, 10% of the affected systems belonging to organizations, and most received only the information collector (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-05). A minimalistic backdoor reached about a dozen machines of government, scientific, manufacturing and retail organizations in Russia, Belarus and Thailand, and was used to deploy QUIC RAT against one organization, an educational institution in Russia; QUIC RAT supports HTTP, UDP, TCP, WSS, QUIC, DNS and HTTP/3 for command and control and can inject payloads into notepad.exe and conhost.exe (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-05). Chinese strings in the collector may imply a Chinese-speaking actor, but Kaspersky does not attribute the compromise, and whether the intent is espionage or big-game hunting is unclear (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-05). The developer says only the free Lite edition was affected (The Record, 2026-05-06).

Exposure
Endpoints that installed or updated DAEMON Tools Lite to a version from 12.5.0.2421 to 12.5.0.2434 from 2026-04-08 onward (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-05).
Detection
In DNS and proxy telemetry, a DAEMON Tools binary beaconing at startup to a lookalike of the vendor's download domain is the earliest signal; in process telemetry, the same binary spawning cmd.exe and then PowerShell that downloads a file into C:\Windows\Temp and executes it follows when the server issues a command (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-05). Injection into notepad.exe or conhost.exe shortly after such a chain points to QUIC RAT (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-05).
Defender takeaway
A validly signed installer from the vendor's own site was the delivery vehicle, so code-signing trust did not help; inventory DAEMON Tools Lite installations, upgrade or remove them, and hunt the helper-to-PowerShell chain on any host that ran an affected version (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-05).
Correction11 Oct 2026 14:29 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryevent_dateprioritytagsregionssectorsaffected_productstechniquessourcesclassificationbody

Kaspersky reports no EU government victim: EU countries are among the more than 100 countries with infection attempts, which mostly delivered an information collector, while the backdoor reached about a dozen machines in Russia, Belarus and Thailand and QUIC RAT a single educational institution in Russia (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-05). Its QUIC RAT description is limited to the C2 protocols and injection into notepad.exe and conhost.exe; the keylogging, SOCKS proxy and tunnelling capabilities given earlier had no source. Kaspersky does not attribute the compromise and calls its intent unclear.

Sources: Kaspersky Securelist · Kaspersky blog · Help Net Security · The Record

Kaspersky saw several thousand infection attempts in more than 100 countries, mostly delivering an information collector; a backdoor reached about a dozen machines at government, scientific, manufacturing and retail organizations in Russia, Belarus and Thailand, and QUIC RAT one Russian educational institution. Version 12.6.0.2445 no longer includes the malicious behaviour Kaspersky describes.

updates.summary: The headline victimology was wrong: no EU government victim is reported; EU countries appear only among infection attempts, the backdoor reached about a dozen machines in Russia, Belarus and Thailand, and QUIC RAT one educational institution in Russia. Kaspersky does not describe keylogging, SOCKS proxying or tunnelling for QUIC RAT, does not attribute the attack, and calls the intent unclear; the Linux masquerade and asymmetric-cryptography mappings had no source. The Securelist report becomes the primary source, the espionage and China-nexus tags are removed, and the entry gains a rating and a supported ATT&CK mapping. Priority moves from high to notable. The startup behaviour and the Detection line now lead with the backdoor's beacon to a typosquatted vendor domain, which precedes any cmd.exe execution.

entries.action_label: Kaspersky: attackers use leaked AWS IAM keys to…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Kaspersky: attackers use leaked AWS IAM keys to send phishing and fabricated-thread BEC through legitimate Amazon SES accounts
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Phishing and BEC through hijacked Amazon SES accounts: leaked IAM keys let attackers send mail that passes SPF, DKIM and DMARC

Kaspersky reports that phishing sent through Amazon Simple Email Service (SES) rose in January 2026 and stayed steady through the first quarter (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-04). Attackers mostly reach SES through leaked AWS IAM access keys that developers leave in public GitHub repositories, ENV files, Docker images, configuration backups or publicly accessible S3 buckets; bots built on the open-source secret scanner TruffleHog find the keys, and the attackers then check each key's permissions and sending limits (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-04). Because the mail is sent from legitimate infrastructure, it passes SPF, DKIM and DMARC, almost always carries .amazonses.com in its Message-ID header, and comes from sender IPs that reputation blocklists cannot block without blocking all SES mail (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-04).

A common early-2026 lure was a fake electronic-signature notification whose link led to a sign-in form hosted on amazonaws.com (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-04). In a business-email-compromise case Kaspersky investigated, an email posing as an employee went to the company's finance department with a fabricated thread about an outstanding invoice and PDF attachments holding only payment details and supporting documentation, with no malicious link or QR code (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-04). BleepingComputer reported the research the same day (BleepingComputer, 2026-05-04).

Exposure
Any AWS account whose IAM access keys have leaked into a public repository, container image, backup or bucket can be turned into a phishing sender; an organization is exposed both as the owner of such keys and as a recipient of SES-sent mail (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-04).
Detection
In mail-gateway telemetry, SES-sent messages almost always carry .amazonses.com in the Message-ID header; a message from an unfamiliar SES sender whose link resolves to a sign-in form on amazonaws.com, or an invoice thread to finance with PDFs holding only payment details and supporting documentation, is the pattern Kaspersky describes (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-04). On the AWS side, in analyst judgement, SES sending activity by an IAM key that has no history of sending mail is the signal for a hijacked key.
Defender takeaway
Authentication results do not separate this mail from legitimate SES mail, so payment-change and invoice requests need out-of-band verification regardless of a passing DMARC result. For your own AWS accounts, Kaspersky advises least-privilege IAM keys, roles instead of long-lived keys, MFA, IP restrictions and automated key rotation with regular audits (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-04).
Correction11 Oct 2026 14:15 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryevent_dateregionstechniquessourcesverificationclassificationbody

Kaspersky's report names no sector, country or manufacturing victim; its business-email-compromise case is a single fabricated invoice thread sent to a company's finance department (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-04). The earlier text said Kaspersky observed finance departments at European manufacturing firms being targeted, which no source supports, and cited a Securelist address that does not exist. In most cases attackers use leaked IAM access keys.

The mail passes SPF, DKIM and DMARC and comes from sender IPs reputation blocklists will not block; lures include fake e-signature notices leading to sign-in forms on amazonaws.com and a fabricated invoice thread sent to a finance department.

entries.headline: Kaspersky: exploit kits added new Office, Windows and Linux exploits in Q1 2026, while old Equation Editor and archive-handling flaws still dominate detections
entries.html:
ROUTINEupdatedNATOB2

Kaspersky Q1 2026 vulnerability landscape: veteran Office and archiver flaws still lead detections, and a new Protected View and MSHTML chain appeared in attacks

Kaspersky's report on the Q1 2026 vulnerability landscape finds that exploit kits expanded again with new exploits for Microsoft Office, Windows and Linux, while veteran vulnerabilities, led by the Equation Editor flaws CVE-2018-0802 and CVE-2017-11882 and archiver flaws including CVE-2023-38831 and CVE-2025-8088, still account for the largest share of detections (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-07). Among the newcomers, the Protected View bypasses CVE-2026-21509 and CVE-2026-21514 and the MSHTML flaw CVE-2026-21513 were used together in a single chain against Windows systems, and Metasploit returned to the top of the C2 frameworks Kaspersky tracks (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-07).

Defender takeaway
The detections are dominated by old Office and archive-handling flaws, so unpatched legacy Office and archiver installations remain the exposure to close first (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-07).
Correction11 Oct 2026 14:20 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryevent_dateprioritytagstechniquessourcesclassificationbody

Kaspersky's Q1 2026 report does not mention PDF readers, V8 browser exploitation, ransomware operators buying zero-days or Excel macros delivered through cloud storage; its finding on shares is that veteran vulnerabilities account for the largest share of detections, and the Protected View and MSHTML chain is one notable newcomer, not the most exploited class (Kaspersky Securelist, 2026-05-07). The earlier text cited a Securelist address that does not exist.

entries.action_label: Dragos: poor IT/OT segmentation in 81% of…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Dragos: poor IT/OT segmentation in 81% of assessments, and compromised VPN or jump-host credentials involved in 73% of its all-time incident cases
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Dragos OT Cybersecurity Year in Review (2025 data): 81% of assessments found poor IT/OT segmentation and 73% of all-time IR cases involved compromised VPN or jump-host credentials

Dragos released its ninth annual OT Cybersecurity Year in Review, covering 2025, on 2026-02-17. Its field findings: "81 percent of assessments identified poor IT/OT segmentation. 73 percent of all-time IR cases involved compromised VPN or jumphost credentials", only 46% of assessments found adequate OT network monitoring, 56% of penetration tests abused living-off-the-land tools without triggering alerts, and 30% of incident cases began with operational issues the asset owner could not explain (Dragos, 2026-02-17). Dragos tracked 119 ransomware groups affecting 3,300 industrial organisations in 2025, up from 80 groups in 2024, and says many incidents are mislabelled as IT incidents when Windows servers hosting SCADA software or engineering workstations are compromised, and that ransomware groups target VMware ESXi hypervisors hosting OT applications (Dragos, 2026-02-17). A 2026-05-07 follow-up adds that 49% of Dragos Services reports carried elevated remote-access findings and 53% identified internet-facing systems (Dragos, 2026-05-07).

Exposure
OT networks reachable from enterprise IT, and remote access into OT through VPN or jump hosts protected by reusable credentials.
Detection
Interactive logins into OT jump hosts or engineering workstations from new source addresses or outside maintenance windows, and any traffic crossing the IT/OT boundary that no documented conduit explains.
Defender takeaway
The two findings point at the same fix, so put phishing-resistant MFA and session brokering on every VPN and jump-host path into OT, and treat an unexplained process anomaly as a trigger for a security investigation, since Dragos found 82% of organisations lack that criterion (Dragos, 2026-02-17).
Correction30 Sep 2026 07:14 UTCrun 2026-09-30T0639Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryevent_datetechniquessourcesevidenceclassificationbody

The earlier text said 81% of incident-response engagements found no meaningful segmentation and quoted a 62% remote-access entry vector, a 34% process-level figure, NIS2 inventory gaps and IEC 62443 guidance. Dragos's figure is "81 percent of assessments identified poor IT/OT segmentation" (Dragos, 2026-02-17), and the other figures appear on no Dragos page, so they are removed. Dragos's credential figure is that compromised VPN or jump-host credentials were involved in 73% of all-time incident cases, not that they caused them or were stolen (Dragos, 2026-02-17).

Sources: Dragos, Inc.

entries.headline: GLPI patches stored XSS and missing-authorization flaws in 10.0.25 and 11.0.7; no exploitation reported
entries.html:
ROUTINECVE-2026-32312 +6updatedNATOA2

GLPI 10.0.25 and 11.0.7 fix seven CVEs: three stored XSS flaws and missing-authorization bugs that let users delete files and items

GLPI released versions 11.0.7 and 10.0.25 on 2026-04-29 as security releases (GLPI, 2026-04-29) (GLPI, 2026-04-29). The CVE-assigned fixes are three stored cross-site scripting flaws rated High, in the knowledge base (CVE-2026-5385, listed in both branches' release notes), in ITIL costs (CVE-2026-40108, 11.x) and in asset locks (CVE-2026-42321, 10.x); arbitrary file deletion by a technician (CVE-2026-42317, High) and arbitrary item deletion via planning (CVE-2026-42318, High); arbitrary file access (CVE-2026-42320, Medium); and an unauthorized export of form structure (CVE-2026-32312, Medium, 11.x) (GLPI, 2026-04-29) (GLPI, 2026-04-29). The knowledge-base flaw's own advisory gives only 11.0.0 and later as affected, patched in 11.0.7 (GLPI, GHSA-2fg5-jg72-h338), and the asset-lock flaw affects 10.0.4 and later on the 10.x branch (GLPI, GHSA-hwjc-8228-55x4). GLPI's per-CVE advisories score the seven flaws from 5.1 to 8.4 under CVSS 4.0 (GLPI, GHSA-cg63-qchq-q626) (GLPI, GHSA-2fg5-jg72-h338) (GLPI, GHSA-w7mr-3vwm-2j22) (GLPI, GHSA-hwjc-8228-55x4) (GLPI, GHSA-rhmv-j773-4gvh) (GLPI, GHSA-jf72-cvjh-px5w) (GLPI, GHSA-58j6-94cf-gcx5). CERT-FR relayed the releases in CERTFR-2026-AVI-0551 on 2026-05-07, covering GLPI before 10.0.25 and before 11.0.7 (CERT-FR, 2026-05-07). No source reports exploitation.

Exposure
GLPI installations before 10.0.25 on the 10.x branch or before 11.0.7 on the 11.x branch (GLPI, 2026-04-29) (GLPI, 2026-04-29).
Defender takeaway
A standard patch-cycle upgrade; the stored XSS flaws matter most where the technician or administrator accounts that can write knowledge-base, cost or asset content are shared or weakly protected, because technicians and administrators later view that content.
Correction11 Oct 2026 14:17 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryevent_dateprioritycvestechniquessourcesverificationclassificationbody

GLPI's release notes classify the seven CVEs as stored cross-site scripting (CVE-2026-5385, CVE-2026-40108, CVE-2026-42321), arbitrary file and item deletion (CVE-2026-42317, CVE-2026-42318), arbitrary file access (CVE-2026-42320) and an unauthorized export of form structure (CVE-2026-32312) (GLPI, 2026-04-29) (GLPI, 2026-04-29). The earlier text called CVE-2026-32312 an SSRF, listed four of the CVEs as stored or reflected XSS, and described CVE-2026-5385 as a policy bypass and CVE-2026-40108 as a data-integrity flaw. CERT-FR published its advisory on 2026-05-07 (CERT-FR, 2026-05-07); 2026-04-29 is the date of GLPI's releases. GLPI's per-CVE advisories do carry CVSS 4.0 scores, from 5.1 to 8.4 (GLPI, GHSA-cg63-qchq-q626) (GLPI, GHSA-2fg5-jg72-h338), and the stored XSS risk sits with the privileged accounts that can write the affected content.

Improvement21 Oct 2026 12:07 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1149Z-auditcvesbody

The release notes for both 10.0.25 and 11.0.7 list the knowledge-base stored XSS, CVE-2026-5385 (GLPI, 2026-04-29) (GLPI, 2026-04-29), but its advisory gives only 11.0.0 and later as affected, patched in 11.0.7 (GLPI, GHSA-2fg5-jg72-h338); upgrading both branches covers either reading. The asset-lock stored XSS, CVE-2026-42321, affects 10.0.4 and later on the 10.x branch (GLPI, GHSA-hwjc-8228-55x4).

entries.classification_html: NATOA1
entries.headline: Opening a folder with a crafted shortcut sends the user's NTLM hash to an attacker. Exploited, and re-fixed in July 2026
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-32202exploitedupdatedNATOA1

CVE-2026-32202 in Windows Shell: an incomplete fix for an APT28-exploited LNK flaw leaks NTLM hashes when a folder is opened, exploited and re-released in July (CVSS 4.3)

Microsoft describes CVE-2026-32202 as a "protection mechanism failure in Windows Shell" that "allows an unauthorized attacker to perform spoofing over a network", scored CVSS 4.3 and fixed on 2026-04-14; its record now shows exploitation detected (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2026-04-14). The flaw is what remained of Microsoft's February fix for CVE-2026-21510, which APT28 exploited together with CVE-2026-21513 through crafted LNK files: the February patch stopped code execution and the SmartScreen bypass, but Windows Explorer still opens an SMB connection to the attacker's server when it renders the folder that holds the shortcut, a connection "sending the victim's Net-NTLMv2 hash to the attacker, which can later be used for NTLM relay attacks and offline cracking" (Help Net Security, 2026-04-29). CISA added CVE-2026-32202 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-04-28 (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-04-28). No cited source says who exploits this CVE; the APT28 link belongs to its predecessors (Help Net Security, 2026-04-29).

Exposure
Supported Windows 10, 11 and Windows Server builds without the July 2026 update, on networks that allow outbound SMB to the internet. Microsoft's record, revised on 2026-07-28, says the CVE "has been re-released to comprehensively address the vulnerability" and recommends installing the July 2026 updates (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2026-04-14).
Detection
Outbound SMB (TCP/445) or NTLM authentication from workstations to external addresses, especially right after a user browses a downloaded folder or archive containing .lnk files.
Defender takeaway
The low score understates it, because the leak needs no click on the shortcut. Install the July 2026 updates, not only the April ones, and block outbound SMB at the perimeter, which also cuts the relay path for the next variant.
Correction30 Sep 2026 07:14 UTCrun 2026-09-30T0639Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryevent_datetagstechniquesaffected_productssourcesevidenceverificationsourcing_noteclassificationbody

The earlier text said APT28 had weaponised CVE-2026-32202 against EU government ministries. APT28's exploitation concerns the predecessor flaws CVE-2026-21510 and CVE-2026-21513, and CVE-2026-32202 is what their February fix left open (Help Net Security, 2026-04-29). No source names who exploits this CVE, so the attribution is removed. The April 2026 update is also not the whole fix: Microsoft re-released the CVE on 2026-07-28 "to comprehensively address the vulnerability" and recommends the July 2026 updates (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2026-04-14).

entries.action_label: CERT-FR: keep autonomous AI assistants off…
entries.classification_html: NATOA2
entries.headline: CERT-FR: keep autonomous AI assistants off workstations; use them only in isolated sandboxes holding no sensitive data
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOA2

CERTFR-2026-ACT-016: CERT-FR says autonomous AI assistants such as OpenClaw must not be deployed on workstations until proven secure

CERT-FR's advisory CERTFR-2026-ACT-016, published on 2026-04-13, addresses autonomous personal assistants such as OpenClaw, Claude Cowork and open-source equivalents, whose adoption has grown strongly since early 2026. Unlike chat assistants, they execute commands, control the browser, read and write files, manage calendars and send mail, triggered by a text message through applications such as Slack, WhatsApp or Discord (CERT-FR, 2026-04-13). Plugins can be loaded dynamically and, depending on the integration model, run as trusted code with the application's privileges, which widens the software supply chain; prompt injection is an intrinsic weakness of the underlying language models, and an agent that orchestrates operating-system-level tools raises the risk of unauthorized command execution and data exfiltration through prompt injection or hijacked messages (CERT-FR, 2026-04-13). The advisory's risk list has five items: compromise of the user's workstation through a vulnerability in these tools, most of them still in beta; leakage of sensitive data by the agents to uncontrolled external resources; excessive access rights over all of the user's office applications (mail, calendar, file manager, business and HR applications); sharing of login credentials with the agents and their potential leakage; and loss of control over the agents' actions on the workstation, including destructive actions that damage the integrity or availability of business applications or data (CERT-FR, 2026-04-13).

CERT-FR's position is that such assistants must not be deployed on workstations and their use should be prohibited until the product is stabilised and proven from a security standpoint; they must in no case be deployed in production, only in isolated test sandboxes holding no sensitive data, and the same applies to mobile deployments (CERT-FR, 2026-04-13). Where they are used, the main lever is configuration hardening: limit the tools and actions available to the strict minimum, require human validation for any system command or action with side effects, run the agent in a sandbox, and allowlist the channels and interlocutors that may trigger it, for example only on an explicit mention of the agent (CERT-FR, 2026-04-13).

Exposure
Any workstation or phone where users have installed an autonomous assistant with access to mail, calendar, files or business applications, typically as unvalidated Shadow IT (CERT-FR, 2026-04-13).
Defender takeaway
Treat autonomous desktop AI assistants as unapproved software on production workstations: block installations not validated by IT and security, and allow them only in isolated sandboxes without production data, secrets or personal data (CERT-FR, 2026-04-13).
Correction11 Oct 2026 14:16 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryevent_dateentitiestechniquessourcesclassificationbody

CERT-FR's advisory concerns autonomous personal assistants on workstations, not agentic orchestration platforms, and does not mention the Model Context Protocol; its supply-chain concern is plugins that load dynamically and run as trusted code (CERT-FR, 2026-04-13). Its recommendations are to keep these assistants off workstations and out of production, confine them to isolated sandboxes, restrict their tools, require human validation for system commands and allowlist the channels that may trigger them. The earlier text attributed guardrails, tool-call allowlisting and a rule to treat all agent output as untrusted to CERT-FR, and named products the advisory does not mention.

Improvement21 Oct 2026 12:06 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1149Z-auditsummarybodyheadline

CERT-FR's advisory lists five risks: compromise of the user's workstation through a vulnerability in these tools, most of them still in beta; leakage of sensitive data by the agents to uncontrolled external resources; excessive access rights over the user's office applications; sharing of login credentials with the agents and their potential leakage; and loss of control over the agents' actions, including destructive ones (CERT-FR, 2026-04-13).

Its risk list covers workstation compromise through flaws in these mostly beta tools, data leakage to uncontrolled external resources, excessive access to office applications, leakage of login secrets shared with the agents, and destructive actions beyond the user's control.

entries.action_label: Eurail sent breach letters to 308,777 travellers on…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Eurail sent breach letters to 308,777 travellers on 2026-03-27, three months after attackers copied its customer files
entries.html:
ROUTINEupdatedNATOB2

Eurail breach: 308,777 travellers notified three months after a December 2025 data theft exposed names and passport numbers, and DiscoverEU participants' IBANs and health data may also be involved

Eurail, the Netherlands-based seller of Interrail and Eurail passes and supplier of the EU's DiscoverEU programme, says an unauthorized actor transferred files from its network on 2025-12-26 and sent letters on 2026-03-27 to 308,777 people whose names and passport numbers were exposed (BleepingComputer, 2026-04-09), and the European Commission told DiscoverEU participants that passport or ID copies, IBANs and health data may also be involved (European Commission, 2026-01-13). Eurail's February disclosure said the attackers reached the travellers' data after breaching its customer database (BleepingComputer, 2026-04-09).

Defender takeaway
There is no access vector or actor to hunt, and Eurail, which warned in February that a sample of the stolen data had been published on Telegram, advises affected customers to watch for phishing and scams and to change their Rail Planner app password wherever it is reused (BleepingComputer, 2026-04-09).
Correction30 Sep 2026 07:13 UTCrun 2026-09-30T0639Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryevent_dateprioritysourcesverificationclassificationbodytechniques

The earlier text said Eurail began sending notifications in late April 2026 and that the Dutch data protection authority and the EDPS had opened reviews of the delay. entries.headline: Die Linke took parts of its IT infrastructure offline after a suspected Qilin attack; Qilin listed it without samples
entries.html:
ROUTINEupdatedNATOB2

Qilin claims a ransomware attack on the German party Die Linke; the party has not confirmed data theft

Die Linke detected a cyberattack on its IT network on Thursday, 26 March 2026, took parts of its IT infrastructure offline as a precaution and filed a criminal complaint. In a statement the next day it said it had indications of a ransomware attack by the Qilin group and that its member database was not affected (Die Linke, 2026-03-27). Heise reported that it had not yet been definitively clarified which internal data had been compromised (Heise Online, 2026-03-27). Qilin added the party to its leak site on 2026-04-01 without publishing data samples (BleepingComputer, 2026-04-03). Contradiction: BleepingComputer's headline says the party confirmed the data theft, while its own text says the party stopped short of confirming a data breach (BleepingComputer, 2026-04-03). The party says the attackers aim to publish sensitive internal data and personal information of headquarters staff, and that it cannot assess whether or to what extent this will succeed or has already happened (Die Linke, 2026-03-27).

The sources give no access vector, so the transferable ground is the target class: German political parties have been targeted by cyberattacks before (The Record, 2026-04-06), and Die Linke describes ransomware attacks as often part of hybrid warfare and this one as aimed at weakening democratic structures (Die Linke, 2026-03-27).

Correction30 Sep 2026 07:12 UTCrun 2026-09-30T0639Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryevent_dateprioritytechniquessourcesevidenceverificationclassificationbodysourcing_noteconfidence

The earlier text said the party confirmed in April 2026 that its data was encrypted and exfiltrated, that Qilin claimed 1.5 TB, and that the state data protection authority was notified. Die Linke disclosed the attack on 2026-03-27 (Heise Online, 2026-03-27), Qilin listed it on 2026-04-01 without samples (BleepingComputer, 2026-04-03), Heise reported that which internal data was compromised had not yet been definitively clarified (Heise Online, 2026-03-27), and the party says it cannot assess whether the attackers' aim of publishing internal data will succeed or has already occurred (Die Linke, 2026-03-27). The 1.5 TB and notification claims appear in no reachable source and are removed.

entries.classification_html: NATOB3
entries.headline: An intrusion posing as Chaos ransomware stole data without encrypting it, and Rapid7 ties it to Iran's MuddyWater through a code-signing certificate and C2
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB3

Rapid7 links a Chaos-branded extortion intrusion to MuddyWater with moderate confidence: Teams screen-sharing harvested credentials and MFA, and no files were encrypted

Rapid7 investigated an early-2026 intrusion that presented as an attack by the Chaos ransomware-as-a-service operation and assesses, "with moderate confidence", that it is linked to MuddyWater (Seedworm), the Iranian state-sponsored group, on the strength of a code-signing certificate and command-and-control infrastructure (Rapid7, 2026-05-06). The actor opened external one-on-one Microsoft Teams chats, moved victims into screen-sharing sessions, had them type credentials into locally created text files and change their MFA configuration to include attacker-controlled devices, then established persistence with the remote management tools DWAgent and AnyDesk (Rapid7, 2026-05-06). It authenticated to internal systems, including a domain controller, with several compromised accounts and deployed a downloader for the Darkcomp backdoor that Rapid7 says is firmly attributed to MuddyWater (Rapid7, 2026-05-06). The actor exfiltrated data and demanded ransom under the Chaos brand by email, but forwent file encryption in favour of data theft and long-term persistence (Rapid7, 2026-05-06). Rapid7 reads the false flag as deniability for espionage and prepositioning, particularly in the US; Chaos itself had claimed 36 victims by late March 2026 (Rapid7, 2026-05-06). The Hacker News reported the research the same day (The Hacker News, 2026-05-06).

Detection
In collaboration-platform audit telemetry, an external-tenant Teams one-on-one chat that moves to screen sharing, followed by a new MFA device registration for the same user, is the chain Rapid7 describes (Rapid7, 2026-05-06). On endpoints, DWAgent or AnyDesk installed outside change control and credential text files created during a support session are the follow-on signals (Rapid7, 2026-05-06).

Triage: legitimate external Teams support sessions exist; the discriminator is an MFA method added during or right after a chat with an external tenant, a step a genuine support session has no reason to include.

Defender takeaway
An extortion demand with no encryption is not proof of a criminal actor. Restrict external Teams chat and screen sharing to approved tenants, and require out-of-band verification before any MFA change requested in a chat.
Correction11 Oct 2026 14:21 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryevent_datetagsregionsentitiestechniquessourcesverificationsourcing_noteconfidenceclassificationbody

Rapid7, not Deep Instinct, reported this intrusion, and it links it to MuddyWater only "with moderate confidence" (Rapid7, 2026-05-06). The actor encrypted nothing: it used the Chaos brand to demand ransom by email after stealing data. Rapid7 describes no government or defence victim in this intrusion and describes the prepositioning as "particularly in the US". The Teams chats with screen sharing were the main intrusion path, not a parallel vector, and Rapid7 describes no certificate theft or forging; the code-signing certificate is attribution evidence.

Sources: Rapid7 · The Hacker News
entries.summary: Rapid7 assesses with moderate confidence that an early-2026 intrusion presented as a Chaos ransomware attack was MuddyWater activity, based on a code-signing certificate and C2 infrastructure. The actor used external Microsoft Teams chats and screen sharing to have victims type credentials into local text files and add attacker-controlled MFA devices, persisted with DWAgent and AnyDesk, moved over RDP to a domain controller, exfiltrated data and demanded ransom by email without encrypting any files.
entries.title: Rapid7 links a Chaos-branded extortion intrusion to MuddyWater with moderate confidence: Teams screen-sharing harvested credentials and MFA, and no files were encrypted

updates.summary: The cited Deep Instinct source does not exist; the research is Rapid7's report of 2026-05-06. The actor did not deploy encrypting Chaos payloads but used the Chaos brand for extortion without encrypting files, Rapid7 links it to MuddyWater only with moderate confidence, and Rapid7 describes no government or defence victim in this intrusion. The prose ATT&CK ids were wrong (Spearphishing Voice, certificate theft, encryption); the entry is rewritten from Rapid7 with the Teams screen-sharing, MFA and remote-tool chain, a corrected mapping (adding the curl payload downloads as ingress tool transfer), labelled guidance, a rating and medium confidence.

Verification & coverage notes

Window: gap 24.0 h from 2026-10-23T0256Z-intel, window 26 h, developing-story window 72 h. The container clock agreed with the network date (skew 0 s) and the first fetch of origin/main was current.
